Like a conversation where everyone reflexively glances at the person at the head of the table, whether or not they’re relevant.

_extra.analogy: Like a conversation where everyone reflexively glances at the person at the head of the table, whether or not they’re relevant.
_extra.deeper: Attention weights must sum to one, so when a token has nothing important to focus on, the model learns to offload that leftover attention somewhere harmless — usually the first token. Understanding this fixed a real bug: naively dropping early tokens in long conversations wrecked models until people realized those tokens were load-bearing sinks. It’s a small quirk with outsized practical impact.
_extra.lens_pm: An obscure detail that quietly governs whether long, streaming chats stay coherent.
_extra.lens_eng: The tendency of softmax attention to allocate residual mass to initial tokens, aiding long-context stability.

title: Audio Generation
definition: Automatically creating sound or audio content from scratch or from a description.
examples: Text prompt: "Dog barking at distance" -> generated audio of a dog bark. Or: "Electronic lo-fi hip-hop beat" - the model produces the music.
A composer writing a melody - the model generates the notes and tones.

_extra.analogy: A composer writing a melody - the model generates the notes and tones.
_extra.deeper: Raw waveform generation (difficult, high-dimensional) vs. spectrogram generation (compact, then vocoded back). Autoregressive (SampleRNN, WaveNet) vs. non-autoregressive (FastSpeech, diffusion). Text-to-speech, music generation, and sound effect synthesis use different architectures. Transformer-based models and diffusion models show promise. Challenge: long-range coherence, realistic timbre, and diversity.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables text-to-speech, generative music, game sound design, accessibility, content creation.
_extra.lens_eng: Architectures: Diffusion models (Riffusion, MusicGen), autoregressive transformers. Datasets: AudioSet, FSD50K. Metrics: mel-cepstral distortion (MCD), log-magnitude RMSE.

title: Autoencoder
definition: A network that learns to squeeze data down and rebuild it, keeping only what matters.
examples: A denoising autoencoder can take a grainy scan, compress it, and reconstruct a clean version.
Like zipping a file and unzipping it — if the copy still looks right, the middle captured the essence.

_extra.analogy: Like zipping a file and unzipping it — if the copy still looks right, the middle captured the essence.
_extra.deeper: An encoder shrinks the input into a small “bottleneck” representation, and a decoder tries to reconstruct the original from it. Because the bottleneck is smaller than the input, the network is forced to keep the important structure and drop the noise. It’s used for compression, denoising, and learning useful representations — the ancestor of the VAE.
_extra.lens_pm: A simple building block for compression, cleanup, and feature learning.
_extra.lens_eng: An encoder–decoder trained to minimize reconstruction error through a low-dimensional bottleneck.

title: AutoGen
definition: Microsoft's framework for building multi-agent conversations where agents play roles and negotiate solutions.
examples: Create a 'user proxy' agent, a 'coder' agent, and a 'planner' agent. They chat with each other over token limits until they converge on a plan, code, and tests.
A Slack channel where bots argue and agree their way to a solution—structured debate automation.

_extra.analogy: A Slack channel where bots argue and agree their way to a solution—structured debate automation.
_extra.deeper: AutoGen treats multi-agent as a conversational protocol. Agents are Python objects with state; they send messages to each other, have conversation history, and can interrupt or agree. It's more stateful than CrewAI. Useful for back-and-forth reasoning but tokenization can explode if agents are verbose.
_extra.lens_pm: Good for workflows that need negotiation, debate, or internal validation before action.
_extra.lens_eng: Conversation-first design; built-in state management and tool registry; Python native.

title: AutoGPT
definition: An early autonomous agent framework that chains together GPT calls, memory, and tool use to pursue a goal over multiple steps.
examples: 'Find me the cheapest flights from NYC to Tokyo this week.' AutoGPT spins up: searches flights, compares prices, queries hotels, summarizes the options, asks clarifying questions.
A to-do list that runs itself—you give it an objective, it breaks it into tasks, executes them, checks progress, and keeps going.

_extra.analogy: A to-do list that runs itself—you give it an objective, it breaks it into tasks, executes them, checks progress, and keeps going.
_extra.deeper: AutoGPT was viral because it showed agents before agents were productized. It's a relatively simple loop: goal → break into subtasks → execute → reflect → loop. No sophisticated planning, just greedy step-by-step execution and memory management. It opened minds but isn't where production agents live today.
_extra.lens_pm: Demonstrated that agents could be useful; inspired the entire agentic-coding category.
_extra.lens_eng: Loop-based design with basic memory and reflection; tokenization-heavy and prone to context drift.

title: Automated Grading
definition: Using code or models to score outputs automatically instead of hiring humans to rate each one.
examples: You run 10,000 predictions through a BLEU grader in seconds. With humans, it would take weeks.
Like a school using a computer to grade multiple-choice tests instead of hiring teachers.

_extra.analogy: Like a school using a computer to grade multiple-choice tests instead of hiring teachers.
_extra.deeper: Automated grading is necessary at scale but has limits. Rule-based graders work for narrow tasks (exact match, length); learned graders (LLM judges) work for subjective tasks but introduce bias. Best practice: automate at scale, validate on a sample with humans.
_extra.lens_pm: Automated grading enables rapid iteration. Use it for fast feedback loops, validate with humans periodically.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement efficient graders; cache results; monitor for drift between automated and human judgments.

title: Automatic prompt engineering
definition: Using algorithms (often other LLMs) to automatically generate and refine prompts, replacing manual trial-and-error.
examples: APE: give it a task and a small eval set, it generates 100 candidate prompts, scores them, and returns the best.
A machine that writes recipes, tests them, and iterates — faster than a human chef.

_extra.analogy: A machine that writes recipes, tests them, and iterates — faster than a human chef.
_extra.deeper: Common approaches: (1) LLM generates candidate prompts; (2) Evaluate on test set; (3) Mutate top prompts and repeat. Challenges: eval set quality (small sets are noisy), cost (evaluating many prompts is expensive), and transferability (best prompt for one model/task may not work for another).
_extra.lens_pm: Faster iteration, less manual effort, sometimes better prompts.
_extra.lens_eng: Use libraries like DSPy or custom scripts. Set up robust eval metrics. Validate on held-out data.

title: Autonomous Agent
definition: An AI system that takes a goal and runs the whole way to done without a human in the loop for each step.
examples: You say “file my expenses for the trip,” and it reads the receipts, categorizes them, fills the form, and submits — no clicks from you.
A contractor you hand a key and a punch list — they let themselves in, do the work, and call you when it’s finished.

_extra.analogy: A contractor you hand a key and a punch list — they let themselves in, do the work, and call you when it’s finished.
_extra.deeper: It’s the same loop — think, act, observe, repeat — just with the human approvals removed. Autonomy is a dial, not a switch: more autonomy means more speed and less oversight, so the failure modes get bigger too. The honest catch is that a wrong turn early can compound into a very confident, very wrong result before anyone notices.
_extra.lens_pm: Higher autonomy trades human effort for risk — decide per task how much you’re willing to let it run alone.
_extra.lens_eng: The control loop iterates without blocking on human approval between actions, bounded only by stop conditions and guardrails.

title: Autonomy
definition: How much an agent is trusted to act on its own before it has to stop and ask a human.
examples: A coding agent with low autonomy shows each edit for approval; with high autonomy it edits, tests, and commits before you ever look.
The difference between an intern who checks every email with you and a deputy you let sign things while you’re away.

_extra.analogy: The difference between an intern who checks every email with you and a deputy you let sign things while you’re away.
_extra.deeper: Autonomy is a spectrum, not a switch — from suggest-only, to act-with-approval, to fully self-directed. More autonomy means more done unattended and more that can go wrong unattended. The practical craft is matching the level to the stakes: high for reversible, low-cost actions; a human gate for anything expensive or irreversible.
_extra.lens_pm: The core trust dial — set it by how bad an unsupervised mistake would be.
_extra.lens_eng: The degree to which the agent loop runs without human confirmation between actions.

title: Autonomy risk
definition: The danger from a model that can act on its own over long horizons — acquire resources, copy itself, resist being stopped.
examples: Evaluators test whether an agent can autonomously set up cloud accounts, make money, and replicate itself across machines without human steps.
The difference between a power tool that needs your hand on it and one that keeps running after you let go, out of reach.

_extra.analogy: The difference between a power tool that needs your hand on it and one that keeps running after you let go, out of reach.
_extra.deeper: This is the capability side of the classic AI-safety worry: an agent competent enough to pursue goals over time may resist shutdown or acquire resources (see instrumental convergence). Evals probe self-replication, long-horizon planning, and evading oversight. Containment and kill-switch measures are the operational responses.
_extra.lens_pm: The risk that turns a helpful assistant into a system that is hard to switch off.
_extra.lens_eng: Test long-horizon autonomous task completion, resource acquisition, and self-replication under sandboxed conditions.

title: Autoregressive
definition: Writing one token at a time, each new word chosen from all the words so far — including the ones it just wrote.
examples: When a model streams its answer word by word on screen, you’re literally watching autoregression happen.
Predictive text that keeps going: it guesses the next word, commits, then guesses again from the fuller sentence.

_extra.analogy: Predictive text that keeps going: it guesses the next word, commits, then guesses again from the fuller sentence.
_extra.deeper: Each step feeds the model everything generated up to now and asks for the next token. That token gets appended and the loop repeats. It’s why generation is sequential and can’t fully parallelize, and why an early wrong turn can snowball.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s why responses stream in and why latency scales with output length.
_extra.lens_eng: Factorizing p(sequence) as a product of next-token conditionals, decoding left to right.

title: Autoscaling
definition: Automatically spinning up more instances when traffic spikes and tearing them down when it drops.
examples: Your inference service normally runs 2 replicas; at 9am traffic jumps and the system automatically brings 5 more online; by noon it scales back to 2.
A restaurant that hires temp workers when the lunch rush hits and sends them home at 2pm.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant that hires temp workers when the lunch rush hits and sends them home at 2pm.
_extra.deeper: Autoscaling uses metrics like CPU, memory, or request queue depth to decide when to add or remove instances. Scaling *up* takes time (cold start overhead); scaling *down* means losing capacity mid-spike if you're not careful. Metrics lag behind actual load, so good autoscaling tuning matters.
_extra.lens_pm: Autoscaling lets you handle spikes without overpaying for idle capacity.
_extra.lens_eng: Set scaling thresholds carefully — too aggressive and you'll waste money on temporary instances; too conservative and you'll serve slow responses during spikes.

title: Avatar Generation
definition: Creating a digital character or persona - either from text description or by personalizing a template.
examples: "A professional woman, brown hair, glasses, smiling" - generates a realistic avatar. Or: input a photo -> generates anime-style version of that person.
Character design: an artist sketches a character; the model generates a 3D or 2D avatar automatically.

_extra.analogy: Character design: an artist sketches a character; the model generates a 3D or 2D avatar automatically.
_extra.deeper: 2D (image, video) vs. 3D (mesh, point cloud). Text-to-avatar: generate image/model from prompt. Photo-to-avatar: style transfer or 3D reconstruction. Challenges: identity preservation, realism, animation (can the avatar move naturally?). Methods: GANs, diffusion models, NeRF for 3D. Real-time avatars (gaming) vs. high-quality offline (cinema).
_extra.lens_pm: Powers gaming, metaverse, virtual events, and personalized digital representations.
_extra.lens_eng: 2D: text-to-image + style transfer. 3D: text-to-3D (NeRF, diffusion) or photogrammetry. Models: DreamFusion.

title: AWQ
definition: A newer quantization method that quantizes less aggressively on activations that matter most, beating GPTQ on speed.
examples: AWQ-quantized models run faster than GPTQ at the same quantization bit-width because the runtime is more efficient.
Like GPTQ's smarter cousin — spends effort protecting the parts that do the most work.

_extra.analogy: Like GPTQ's smarter cousin — spends effort protecting the parts that do the most work.
_extra.deeper: AWQ observes that some activations contribute more to the output than others (high variance). It protects those by scaling them up before quantization, then scales back down. It's also designed to be faster to run (not just faster to quantize). AWQ trades off against GPTQ: sometimes GPTQ is more accurate, sometimes AWQ is faster.
_extra.lens_pm: AWQ is gaining adoption for inference optimization — speeds up inference compared to GPTQ.
_extra.lens_eng: AWQ runtimes are optimized for speed; check if your inference engine supports it.

title: BabyAGI
definition: A simplified, educational agent that creates tasks, prioritizes them, and executes them in a loop.
examples: Tell BabyAGI to 'learn about machine learning.' It creates tasks like 'Read neural network paper,' 'Run linear regression code,' 'Build MNIST classifier,' and works through them.
A student who writes a study plan, does the first task, sees the result, updates the plan, moves to the next—very methodical.

_extra.analogy: A student who writes a study plan, does the first task, sees the result, updates the plan, moves to the next—very methodical.
_extra.deeper: BabyAGI is intentionally minimal—it's a few hundred lines of Python. It loops: read task list, execute top task with GPT, get result, feed result back into task-list generation. It shows the core agent idea without real-world bells (error recovery, long-context memory). Great teaching tool; not a production framework.
_extra.lens_pm: Lowered the bar for experimenting with agentic loops; spawned the agent framework ecosystem.
_extra.lens_eng: Tiny implementation (~100 lines); uses only basic function-calling and list management.

title: Backdoor attack
definition: Secretly training a model to behave normally until it sees a hidden trigger, then misbehave on command.
examples: A model classifies images correctly until a tiny yellow sticker appears in the corner, which the attacker trained as a switch to force a wrong label.
A vending machine that works fine for everyone, but dispenses free product to whoever taps a secret knock.

_extra.analogy: A vending machine that works fine for everyone, but dispenses free product to whoever taps a secret knock.
_extra.deeper: The attacker poisons a slice of training data so the model links a rare trigger pattern to an attacker-chosen output, while accuracy on clean inputs stays high enough to pass review. That normal-looking behavior is what makes backdoors hard to catch. It usually rides in through poisoned data or a tampered pretrained checkpoint.
_extra.lens_pm: A model can pass all your evals and still carry a hidden switch, which is why model provenance matters.
_extra.lens_eng: Trigger-conditioned poisoning creates a spurious feature-to-target link; detect via activation clustering, trigger reconstruction, or fine-tuning on clean data.

title: Backpropagation
definition: The algorithm that figures out how much each weight contributed to the error, so it can be corrected.
examples: After a wrong prediction, backprop pushes the error signal backward layer by layer, giving each weight its share of the blame.
Like tracing a factory defect back through the assembly line to see which station caused it, and by how much.

_extra.analogy: Like tracing a factory defect back through the assembly line to see which station caused it, and by how much.
_extra.deeper: Backpropagation applies the chain rule from calculus to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight efficiently, in a single backward pass through the network. It’s what makes training deep networks tractable — without it, computing all those derivatives would be hopeless. Paired with an optimizer, it’s the mechanism that turns “the model was wrong” into concrete weight updates.
_extra.lens_pm: The math that makes learning possible at all; you rarely touch it, but every trained model depends on it.
_extra.lens_eng: Chain-rule computation of loss gradients w.r.t. all params in one backward pass; feeds the optimizer.

title: Bag of words
definition: Represent text as an unordered collection of word counts, ignoring grammar and word order — simple, fast, and surprisingly effective.
examples: Classify emails as spam or not: extract every word, count occurrences, feed counts to a classifier. "Free money winner you" looks spammy by frequency alone.
Like describing a book by listing every word that appears and how often, forgetting sentences and structure.

_extra.analogy: Like describing a book by listing every word that appears and how often, forgetting sentences and structure.
_extra.deeper: Bag of words discards all word order: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" are identical. This is a huge limitation, but the tradeoff is simplicity and speed. You vectorize text as a histogram of word frequencies or binary presence. With simple methods like Naive Bayes or logistic regression, it works decently for classification tasks. Neural networks and embeddings replaced it because they capture word order and semantics, but BoW remains useful as a baseline and for very large-scale classification where speed matters.
_extra.lens_pm: A durable baseline that's fast and interpretable; useful when neural models overkill.
_extra.lens_eng: A text vectorization method where documents become vectors of word counts, losing order and syntax.

title: Base model
definition: The raw, pretrained model before anyone taught it to follow instructions or be polite — powerful but unruly.
examples: Hand a base model “Q: capital of France? A:” and it may just keep inventing more Q&As.
A brilliant improviser who hasn’t learned to answer the actual question you asked.

_extra.analogy: A brilliant improviser who hasn’t learned to answer the actual question you asked.
_extra.deeper: A base model only knows how to continue text, because that’s all it was trained to do. The chat model you actually use is a base model plus alignment steps (instruction tuning, preference training) that teach it to treat your message as a request to fulfill rather than a passage to extend.
_extra.lens_pm: Usually not what you want directly — the instruction-tuned version is the usable product.
_extra.lens_eng: Pretrained-only checkpoint (next-token objective), pre-alignment; completes rather than instructs.

title: batch API
definition: An API endpoint where you upload a file of requests, pay a discount for processing in batch (not real-time), and get results back when they're ready.
examples: You have 10,000 customer reviews to classify. Upload a JSON lines file to the batch API at 50% cost, queue it, retrieve results in an hour.
Bulk mail—drop off 1000 letters at the post office, get a discount, pick them up tomorrow.

_extra.analogy: Bulk mail—drop off 1000 letters at the post office, get a discount, pick them up tomorrow.
_extra.deeper: Batch APIs trade latency for cost. You don't get results immediately, but you pay 50% less per token. Good for non-urgent work (nightly processing, backfill, evaluation runs). Implementation: upload JSONL → get batch ID → poll status → download results.
_extra.lens_pm: Cuts costs for large-scale offline inference; enables affordable batch analytics.
_extra.lens_eng: Async processing; bulk JSONL uploads; usually 50% discount.

title: Batch inference
definition: Processing multiple requests together in one forward pass instead of one at a time, which is much faster per request.
examples: Instead of running the model 100 times on 100 individual prompts, you group them into batches of 32 and run 4 batches — same total compute but much faster wall-clock time.
Sending 10 letters in one mail batch instead of 10 separate trips to the post office.

_extra.analogy: Sending 10 letters in one mail batch instead of 10 separate trips to the post office.
_extra.deeper: Batching amortizes the overhead of a forward pass (loading model to GPU, cache management) across multiple requests. Batch size is limited by memory. Small batches waste compute potential; large batches need more memory. Good inference systems balance request throughput with latency via continuous batching (requests arrive and leave asynchronously).
_extra.lens_pm: Batching is the #1 lever for throughput — more requests per second with the same hardware.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement continuous batching so requests don't block; use dynamic batch sizes.

title: Batching
definition: Waiting for multiple requests to arrive, then processing them together instead of one at a time.
examples: Your inference server holds requests for 100ms. During that time, 32 requests arrive. You process all 32 together.
A bus waiting for 30 passengers before leaving, instead of driving immediately with one person.

_extra.analogy: A bus waiting for 30 passengers before leaving, instead of driving immediately with one person.
_extra.deeper: Batching amortizes overhead and uses hardware efficiently. But it increases latency for requests that arrive early in the batch window — they wait for later requests. This is the classic throughput-vs-latency tradeoff. You tune the batch window and max batch size for your workload.
_extra.lens_pm: Batching makes your hardware work for you. Smaller batches = more serving cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement queue-based batching. Tune max batch size and timeout. Monitor for queue buildup under load.

title: Batch normalization
definition: Normalization computed across a batch of examples — huge for vision, awkward for language.
examples: ResNets and image models lean on batch norm; transformers mostly skipped it for layer norm.
Curving a test using the whole class’s scores that day: great when the class is big and stable, shaky when it’s tiny.

_extra.analogy: Curving a test using the whole class’s scores that day: great when the class is big and stable, shaky when it’s tiny.
_extra.deeper: BatchNorm normalizes each feature using statistics across the current batch. It accelerated deep vision training dramatically, but its batch-dependence causes trouble with small batches, variable sequence lengths, and inference-time mismatch. Language models largely moved on.
_extra.lens_pm: Mostly a vision-era tool; if you’re in language land you’ll rarely touch it.
_extra.lens_eng: Normalizes over the batch dimension per feature; batch-dependent, dominant in CNNs, rare in transformers.

title: Batch size
definition: How many examples the model looks at before making one weight update.
examples: A batch size of 256 means the model averages the error over 256 examples, then takes one optimization step.
Like how many quiz answers you grade before adjusting your teaching — a few gives quick but jumpy feedback, many gives a steadier read.

_extra.analogy: Like how many quiz answers you grade before adjusting your teaching — a few gives quick but jumpy feedback, many gives a steadier read.
_extra.deeper: Batch size trades gradient quality against speed and memory: larger batches give smoother, more reliable gradient estimates and use hardware efficiently, but need more memory and can generalize slightly worse. Smaller batches are noisier but sometimes find better minima. It interacts tightly with the learning rate — change one and you often must retune the other.
_extra.lens_pm: A core cost-and-quality knob; it’s bounded by your GPU memory and coupled to the learning rate.
_extra.lens_eng: Examples per gradient update; larger = smoother gradients + more memory, coupled to learning rate; extendable via accumulation.

title: Beam search
definition: A decoding trick that keeps several candidate sentences alive at once and picks the best-scoring whole path.
examples: An older translation system runs beam width 5, exploring five partial translations in parallel before settling on the most probable finished one.
Like planning a road trip by keeping your top few routes open at each junction instead of committing to the first turn that looks good.

_extra.analogy: Like planning a road trip by keeping your top few routes open at each junction instead of committing to the first turn that looks good.
_extra.deeper: Greedy decoding commits to the single best token each step and can paint itself into a corner; beam search hedges by tracking the k highest-scoring sequences and expanding all of them. It shines in translation and captioning, but for open-ended chat it tends to produce bland, repetitive text, which is why sampling methods largely replaced it.
_extra.lens_pm: Great when there’s one “right” output like a translation; wrong when you want lively, varied prose.
_extra.lens_eng: Maintains k partial hypotheses ranked by cumulative log-prob, expanding and pruning to k each step until end tokens fire.

title: Benchmark
definition: A standard test that lets you compare how well different models solve the same problem.
examples: MMLU is a benchmark of multiple-choice questions spanning history, math, science. Every model's score on MMLU is directly comparable.
Like a race track where every runner covers the same distance under the same conditions.

_extra.analogy: Like a race track where every runner covers the same distance under the same conditions.
_extra.deeper: Benchmarks democratize progress by making it measurable and reproducible. They're invaluable for tracking improvement, but they have downsides: models can overfit to them (especially if trained on leaked data), they might not correlate with real-world performance, and they can bake in existing biases. Good benchmarks are diverse, hard to game, and regularly retired as models solve them.
_extra.lens_pm: Use benchmarks to track progress and communicate it clearly, but don't mistake benchmark scores for product quality.
_extra.lens_eng: Evaluate on multiple benchmarks and always include held-out, human-annotated test sets.

title: BERT
definition: An encoder that reads a whole sentence in both directions at once to understand it — great at reading, not built for writing.
examples: For years, Google Search used BERT to better grasp what a query actually meant.
Like a proofreader who scans the entire sentence before judging any one word, rather than reading strictly left to right.

_extra.analogy: Like a proofreader who scans the entire sentence before judging any one word, rather than reading strictly left to right.
_extra.deeper: BERT is encoder-only: it looks at all the words at once (bidirectional) and is trained by masking random words and predicting them. That makes it excellent at classification, search, and understanding tasks, but it can’t naturally generate long text the way a decoder-based model does. Generative LLMs eventually stole the spotlight, but BERT-style encoders still quietly power a lot of search and retrieval.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap, fast option when you need to understand or classify text, not write it.
_extra.lens_eng: An encoder-only transformer pretrained with masked-language-modeling and next-sentence objectives.

title: Best-of-n
definition: Generate several answers and return only the one a scorer likes best — better output for more compute.
examples: For a tricky query, the system samples five completions, ranks them with a reward model, and shows the top-ranked reply.
Asking three people to draft the same email and sending only the strongest one.

_extra.analogy: Asking three people to draft the same email and sending only the strongest one.
_extra.deeper: Best-of-n trades inference compute for quality: sample n candidates, score them with a reward or verifier, output the winner. It reliably lifts quality but with diminishing returns and n-times the cost. It is closely tied to rejection sampling — same generate-and-filter idea — and its scores can be distilled back into the model so you get the benefit without paying at serve time.
_extra.lens_pm: A dial to buy better answers with more compute, useful when quality matters more than latency.
_extra.lens_eng: Sample n outputs, rank with a scorer, return the argmax; quality rises sublinearly with n.

title: BF16
definition: A 16-bit floating-point format (from Google Brain) that keeps the same range as float32 but with less precision.
examples: Float32 can represent 0.0000001 to 1000000000. BF16 can too, but with fewer distinct values in between.
A wide-angle lens that captures a larger field of view but at lower pixel density.

_extra.analogy: A wide-angle lens that captures a larger field of view but at lower pixel density.
_extra.deeper: BF16 is better than FP16 for training stability because it keeps float32's range. This matters for transformer training where gradients span many orders of magnitude. It's becoming standard in recent models (PaLM, Gemini). The downside: less hardware support than FP16 (though Nvidia newer GPUs support it).
_extra.lens_pm: Emerging standard. Expect more models to use it.
_extra.lens_eng: Use BF16 for training if your hardware supports it. Performance is similar to FP16 with better stability.

title: Bi-Encoder
definition: A model that embeds query and document separately, so you can precompute and search millions fast.
examples: A bi-encoder embeds every document once ahead of time; at query time you embed just the question and do a fast vector search.
Two people writing independent summaries, then comparing notes — quick, but they never actually read together.

_extra.analogy: Two people writing independent summaries, then comparing notes — quick, but they never actually read together.
_extra.deeper: A bi-encoder maps query and document to vectors independently, which is exactly what lets you embed the whole corpus in advance and retrieve with fast similarity search. The cost of that independence is missing fine-grained interactions between query and document, so it is less precise than a cross-encoder. The standard pattern pairs them: bi-encoder for fast recall, cross-encoder to rerank.
_extra.lens_pm: The workhorse that makes large-scale semantic search fast; usually backed by a reranker for precision.
_extra.lens_eng: Independent query/doc encoders enabling precomputed ANN; loses cross-attention precision, hence the rerank pairing.

title: Bias
definition: When a model's outputs systematically favor or disfavor certain groups — usually because its training data did.
examples: A hiring model trained mostly on male resumes starts ranking women lower — not because it was told to, but because the data leaned that way.
A mirror that doesn't reflect everyone equally — it shows some people clearly and distorts others.

_extra.analogy: A mirror that doesn't reflect everyone equally — it shows some people clearly and distorts others.
_extra.deeper: Bias enters at every stage: data collection (who's represented), labeling (whose judgments), model design (what's optimized), and deployment (who's affected). It's not just a technical bug — it reflects and can amplify real-world inequities.
_extra.lens_pm: Systematic unfairness in AI output — a legal, ethical, and reputational risk that needs active monitoring.
_extra.lens_eng: Systematic skew from data/labeling/optimization; mitigate via diverse data, audits, disaggregated eval.

title: Bias term
definition: A constant a neuron adds no matter what, so it isn’t forced to pass through zero.
examples: Without a bias, a neuron given all-zero input must output zero; the bias lets it say something else.
The base fare on a taxi meter — you pay it before the distance charge even starts.

_extra.analogy: The base fare on a taxi meter — you pay it before the distance charge even starts.
_extra.deeper: In y = Wx + b, the bias is b: a learnable offset that shifts the activation up or down independent of the input. Small thing, but it gives each neuron freedom to set its own baseline. Note: “bias” here is unrelated to fairness or social bias — same word, different sense.
_extra.lens_pm: Pure mechanism; matters to you mainly as a reminder that model “bias” has two totally different meanings.
_extra.lens_eng: The additive constant b in an affine layer, one learnable scalar per output unit.

title: Bidirectional Model
definition: A model that reads each word using context from both its left and its right at the same time.
examples: To fill in “the ___ barked,” a bidirectional model uses “barked” on the right to guess “dog.”
Like understanding a pun only after you’ve read the whole sentence, not word by word as it arrives.

_extra.analogy: Like understanding a pun only after you’ve read the whole sentence, not word by word as it arrives.
_extra.deeper: Because it sees the full sentence at once, it can use future words to interpret earlier ones, which is great for understanding but incompatible with left-to-right generation. That’s why bidirectional models like BERT dominate comprehension tasks while generative chatbots use one-directional (causal) attention. The direction of attention is the whole difference.
_extra.lens_pm: Superb for understanding tasks; structurally unable to generate text on its own.
_extra.lens_eng: A model with unmasked attention, conditioning each position on the full sequence.

title: Biorisk
definition: The danger that a model meaningfully helps someone create a biological weapon.
examples: Red-teamers test whether a model gives non-experts actionable uplift toward synthesizing a dangerous pathogen, and safety training is tuned to refuse it.
Worrying less about the library having a chemistry book and more about it having a personal tutor who walks you through every step.

_extra.analogy: Worrying less about the library having a chemistry book and more about it having a personal tutor who walks you through every step.
_extra.deeper: The concern is "uplift" — not whether facts exist online, but whether the model lowers the skill barrier by planning, troubleshooting, and connecting steps. It is among the most tightly guarded categories, with dedicated classifiers, refusals, and expert-run evals. Measuring it responsibly is itself sensitive work.
_extra.lens_pm: One of the highest-severity risks, often subject to explicit safety commitments and external testing.
_extra.lens_eng: Evaluate end-to-end task uplift for non-experts, not fact recall; guard with layered refusals and dedicated classifiers.

title: Blackboard
definition: A shared space where multiple agents post partial results and read each other’s work.
examples: Three research agents each write their notes to a common blackboard, and a fourth agent reads the whole board to write the final summary.
A whiteboard in a war room — everyone scribbles findings on it and glances up to see what others added.

_extra.analogy: A whiteboard in a war room — everyone scribbles findings on it and glances up to see what others added.
_extra.deeper: The blackboard is an old AI idea reborn for agents: instead of agents messaging each other directly, they all read and write one common store. It decouples them — an agent doesn’t need to know who will use its output, just where to put it. The risk is contention and staleness: agents acting on half-finished notes, or overwriting each other, unless you’re careful about how the board is structured.
_extra.lens_pm: A blackboard lets agents collaborate without tight wiring, but shared scratch space needs structure to stay useful.
_extra.lens_eng: A shared read/write store agents post intermediate results to, decoupling producers from consumers.

title: BLEU
definition: A metric that measures how much generated text overlaps with reference text—once the standard for machine translation, now mostly legacy.
examples: Model generates: 'The cat sat on the mat.' Reference: 'The cat sat on the mat.' BLEU scores high due to n-gram overlap.
Like checking if a student's essay quotes match the required source material.

_extra.analogy: Like checking if a student's essay quotes match the required source material.
_extra.deeper: BLEU counts matching n-grams (sequences of n words) between generated and reference text. It's fast and language-agnostic, but it doesn't understand meaning. A paraphrase with different words gets low BLEU even if it's better. Research has largely moved to ROUGE and semantic metrics because BLEU doesn't correlate well with human judgment.
_extra.lens_pm: BLEU is outdated for modern NLG tasks. Don't ship decisions based on BLEU scores.
_extra.lens_eng: Use ROUGE, semantic similarity, or human eval instead.

title: Blue-Green Deployment
definition: Keep two identical production environments—blue (current) and green (next)—flip traffic only after green is healthy.
examples: Both blue and green clusters run in parallel; traffic flows to blue; green is tested and validated; flip the load balancer to green; decommission blue.
Having a stunt double ready; if the double is fine, the star walks off stage and the double takes over.

_extra.analogy: Having a stunt double ready; if the double is fine, the star walks off stage and the double takes over.
_extra.deeper: Zero-downtime deployment with instant rollback. Requires double the infrastructure cost temporarily. Good for large, monolithic systems. Can pair with canary for even lower risk. Requires health checks and smoke tests to validate green before flip.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables high-confidence, zero-downtime deployments at cost of doubled temporary infrastructure.
_extra.lens_eng: DNS or load balancer points to blue or green; deployment automation validates green, then flips the selector; blue remains on standby for instant rollback.

title: BM25
definition: A classic keyword-ranking formula that scores documents by how well their words match the query.
examples: Searching “quarterly revenue Anthropic,” BM25 ranks highest the docs that use those exact, uncommon words most.
A smart word-counter — rewards documents that use your rare search terms often, but doesn’t double-count common filler.

_extra.analogy: A smart word-counter — rewards documents that use your rare search terms often, but doesn’t double-count common filler.
_extra.deeper: BM25 is decades old and still a workhorse: it scores on term frequency (how often a query word appears) balanced against how rare that word is overall and how long the document is. It’s fast, needs no training, and is unbeatable at matching exact terms — names, codes, jargon — which is precisely where embeddings struggle. That durability is why nearly every hybrid search still has BM25 doing the keyword half.
_extra.lens_pm: The old keyword approach still beats fancy embeddings on exact terms — don’t retire it, combine with it.
_extra.lens_eng: A sparse ranking function scoring on term frequency, inverse document frequency, and length normalization.

title: Browser Agent
definition: An agent that navigates the web for you — opening pages, clicking, filling forms, reading results.
examples: “Find the cheapest direct flight next Friday and start the booking” — the agent opens a travel site, searches, compares, and fills the passenger form.
An intern you send off to “go find this online and book it,” who comes back with the confirmation.

_extra.analogy: An intern you send off to “go find this online and book it,” who comes back with the confirmation.
_extra.deeper: Browser agents work over the page — sometimes via the DOM, sometimes via screenshots — issuing navigate, click, and type actions in a loop. They stumble on the modern web’s defenses: logins, captchas, pop-ups, and layouts that change under them. And because they act on live sites, prompt-injection from a malicious page is a genuine risk, so what they’re allowed to do should be fenced.
_extra.lens_pm: The dream of “just do this task on the web,” bounded by how hostile the real web is.
_extra.lens_eng: An agent that controls a browser via DOM or vision, emitting navigation and interaction actions against live pages.

title: Byte-Level Model
definition: A model that treats text as a raw stream of bytes, so nothing is ever “out of vocabulary.”
examples: A byte-level model can process a garbled log file full of odd characters without special handling.
Like a scanner that reads any document as pixels — it never trips over a font or symbol it hasn’t seen.

_extra.analogy: Like a scanner that reads any document as pixels — it never trips over a font or symbol it hasn’t seen.
_extra.deeper: Every piece of text is ultimately bytes, so a byte-level model has a tiny fixed alphabet and can represent literally anything — code, emoji, any language. The price is much longer sequences, since a word becomes many bytes, which strains attention and speed. Architectural tricks that group bytes internally are how researchers try to keep it affordable.
_extra.lens_pm: Maximum robustness to weird input, paid for in sequence length and compute.
_extra.lens_eng: A model with a byte vocabulary, trading a fixed small alphabet for longer sequences.

title: Byte-pair encoding
definition: The recipe most tokenizers use to build a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most common pairs of symbols.
examples: Training a tokenizer, BPE starts from raw bytes and merges frequent pairs until “ing” and “tion” become single tokens.
Like inventing shorthand: you notice “th” appears constantly, so you give it one squiggle, then merge more from there.

_extra.analogy: Like inventing shorthand: you notice “th” appears constantly, so you give it one squiggle, then merge more from there.
_extra.deeper: Starting from individual characters or bytes, BPE counts adjacent pairs, merges the most frequent into a new symbol, and repeats thousands of times. The result is a vocabulary where common strings are one token and rare ones split into subwords — a data-driven balance of vocabulary size against sequence length.
_extra.lens_pm: The unglamorous step that decides your token economics before a model ever runs.
_extra.lens_eng: Greedy merge algorithm over a corpus that iteratively fuses the highest-frequency adjacent symbol pair into the vocab.

title: Caching
definition: Storing computed results so you don't have to recompute them when the same request comes in again.
examples: If 10 users all ask the same question, the first call generates the answer; the next 9 see the cached result instantly.
Writing down yesterday's math homework so you don't have to solve it again today.

_extra.analogy: Writing down yesterday's math homework so you don't have to solve it again today.
_extra.deeper: Caching happens at multiple levels: KV caching during a single forward pass (storing attention keys and values), prompt caching (reusing embeddings of long context), and application-level caching (storing full responses). Cache misses waste compute; cache hits save both latency and money.
_extra.lens_pm: Caching is the fastest, cheapest way to speed up responses — if you can predict repeated patterns.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement cache-key semantics carefully — wrong keys cause stale responses; too many cache layers and debugging becomes hell.

title: Calculator Tool
definition: A simple tool that does exact math for the model, which is otherwise shaky at arithmetic.
examples: To compute a 17.5% tip on $84.60, the agent calls the calculator rather than guessing, and returns the exact figure.
Handing a brilliant essayist a pocket calculator — great with words, best not trusted to multiply in their head.

_extra.analogy: Handing a brilliant essayist a pocket calculator — great with words, best not trusted to multiply in their head.
_extra.deeper: Language models predict likely text, and “likely” often isn’t “correct” for numbers, so they fumble multi-digit arithmetic in ways that look confident. A calculator tool offloads the math to code that’s actually right. It’s the canonical example of why tool use exists at all: don’t make the model do what a two-line function does perfectly.
_extra.lens_pm: The clearest illustration of tools covering a model’s known weak spots.
_extra.lens_eng: A tool that evaluates arithmetic or symbolic expressions exactly, offloading computation the model does unreliably.

title: Calibration
definition: When a model's confidence matches its actual accuracy—it says 90% confident on things it's right about 90% of the time.
examples: The model predicts a label and assigns 95% confidence. If you look at all predictions with 95% confidence, 95% are correct.
Like a weather forecast that says 80% rain and it actually rains 80% of the days it predicts that.

_extra.analogy: Like a weather forecast that says 80% rain and it actually rains 80% of the days it predicts that.
_extra.deeper: Uncalibrated models are dangerous because you trust them more than you should. Neural nets are often overconfident. You can improve calibration by temperature scaling (adjusting softmax temperature after training) or post-hoc calibration on a holdout set. Perfect calibration is impossible if you don't have labeled examples for every prediction.
_extra.lens_pm: Check model calibration before shipping—an overconfident model that's wrong will erode trust.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure calibration with calibration plots; apply temperature scaling if miscalibrated.

title: Canary
definition: A unique marker planted in data so you can later tell if it leaked or got memorized.
examples: A benchmark embeds a rare string in its questions; if a model can recite it, you know the benchmark contaminated its training data.
A dyed banknote in the till — if it shows up somewhere it shouldn’t, you know exactly where it came from.

_extra.analogy: A dyed banknote in the till — if it shows up somewhere it shouldn’t, you know exactly where it came from.
_extra.deeper: Canaries are unique, unlikely-to-occur tokens dropped into documents, datasets, or benchmarks. Finding one where it should not be proves leakage — training-data contamination, a data exfiltration path, or unauthorized copying. Named for the canary in a coal mine: a cheap early-warning signal.
_extra.lens_pm: A near-free tripwire that tells you when your test set has quietly leaked into a model.
_extra.lens_eng: Embed unique tokens to detect memorization, benchmark contamination, or exfiltration; presence downstream is proof of leak.

title: Canary Deployment
definition: Rolling out a new model to a small fraction of traffic first, then gradually increasing if metrics look good.
examples: Route 5% of requests to the new model v1.1, monitor latency and accuracy, then increment to 50% if all looks well.
Coal miners brought canaries into mines to detect poisonous gas early; new model is your canary.

_extra.analogy: Coal miners brought canaries into mines to detect poisonous gas early; new model is your canary.
_extra.deeper: Mitigates blast radius of buggy or degraded models. Requires ability to split traffic, capture metrics, and rollback automatically. Drift detection rules trigger automated rollback. Can run multiple versions in parallel to compare. Good for high-stakes production systems.
_extra.lens_pm: Dramatically reduces risk of model updates while maintaining continuous improvement velocity.
_extra.lens_eng: Traffic router (Envoy, istio, or application code) weights requests; observability pipeline monitors canary metrics vs baseline; automated rollback if error rate or latency exceeds threshold.

title: Canary evaluation
definition: Rolling out a change to a small fraction of real users and monitoring for problems before going to 100%.
examples: You deploy a new model to 5% of search traffic. If latency stays good and click-through rate doesn't drop, roll to 10%. If anything breaks, rollback immediately.
A canary in a coal mine — send in a small probe first to check for danger.

_extra.analogy: A canary in a coal mine — send in a small probe first to check for danger.
_extra.deeper: Canary deployments reduce risk but require automated monitoring and quick rollback. You need alarms for latency, errors, and engagement metrics. The cost of rollback must be lower than the cost of breaking all users. And you need enough traffic in the canary to detect real problems (5% might miss low-frequency bugs).
_extra.lens_pm: Standard practice for high-stakes changes. Non-negotiable for production services.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement traffic splitting, automated metric collection, and rollback triggers. Monitor continuously.

title: Capability Discovery
definition: How an agent finds out at runtime what tools and abilities are available to it.
examples: On connecting to an MCP server, the agent asks “what can you do?” and gets back a live list of tools it can call.
Walking into a new workshop and reading the labels on the drawers before you start a job.

_extra.analogy: Walking into a new workshop and reading the labels on the drawers before you start a job.
_extra.deeper: Instead of hard-coding a fixed tool list, discovery lets an agent query its environment and adapt to whatever’s connected. This is a big part of why protocols like MCP took off — plug in a new server and the agent just sees the new tools. The catch is that more discoverable tools means more choices to get wrong, so discovery usually pairs with filtering to keep the active set manageable.
_extra.lens_pm: Discovery is what lets one agent work across many tools without a code change for each — it’s the extensibility story.
_extra.lens_eng: The agent queries connected servers or a registry at runtime to enumerate available tools and their schemas.

title: Capability evaluation
definition: Testing whether a model can perform a specific skill (math, code, reasoning) at all, regardless of perfect execution.
examples: Does the model know how to do chain-of-thought reasoning on math problems? You ask a few hard math questions and see if it attempts reasoning steps.
A driver's test where you just check whether someone can parallel park, not how perfectly.

_extra.analogy: A driver's test where you just check whether someone can parallel park, not how perfectly.
_extra.deeper: Capability eval answers "can this model do the thing?" Benchmark eval answers "how well?" Capabilities emerge unpredictably as models scale, so capability eval is how researchers discover new abilities. The catch: a model might have the capability but fail due to prompting, temperature settings, or just bad luck on the sample.
_extra.lens_pm: Tells you what to expect from a model before detailed benchmarking.
_extra.lens_eng: Write tests for each capability. Use simple examples first. Track emergence curves as models scale.

title: Capacity
definition: How much a model can potentially learn — roughly, how complex a pattern it can represent.
examples: A tiny model can’t capture the nuance of legal text — too little capacity — while a huge one memorizes the training set instead of generalizing.
Like the size of a suitcase: a bigger one holds more, but an oversized bag half-empty just gets messy and heavy.

_extra.analogy: Like the size of a suitcase: a bigger one holds more, but an oversized bag half-empty just gets messy and heavy.
_extra.deeper: Capacity grows with parameters, depth, and width, and it sets the ceiling on complexity a model can fit. Too little and you underfit; too much for your data and you overfit or waste compute. The art is matching capacity to the amount and richness of data, which is exactly what scaling laws try to quantify.
_extra.lens_pm: Bigger isn’t automatically better — capacity has to be matched to the data and the task.
_extra.lens_eng: Informal measure of a model’s expressive range, scaling with parameter count, depth, and width.

title: Capacity Factor
definition: A dial that sets how many tokens each expert is allowed to handle before it starts dropping the overflow.
examples: An engineer raises the capacity factor from 1.0 to 1.25 after noticing tokens were being dropped when too many routed to one expert at once.
A restaurant setting covers per table — go over and the extra guests wait outside or get turned away.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant setting covers per table — go over and the extra guests wait outside or get turned away.
_extra.deeper: Experts run in fixed-size buffers for hardware efficiency, so each has a hard cap: capacity = factor × (tokens ÷ experts). A factor above 1 leaves slack for uneven routing; tokens beyond the cap get dropped or passed through untouched. Higher factor means fewer drops but more wasted compute on half-empty buffers.
_extra.lens_pm: A quiet quality-versus-cost knob most people never see but that shapes both.
_extra.lens_eng: The multiplier on the per-expert token buffer size in a MoE layer; overflow tokens are dropped past the cap.

title: Cascade
definition: A chain of fallbacks — try model A, if it fails try B, if that fails try C.
examples: Route to vLLM (fast), fall back to TensorRT (slower), fall back to ONNX Runtime (slowest).
Calling your boss, then their boss, then the CEO if each person is unavailable.

_extra.analogy: Calling your boss, then their boss, then the CEO if each person is unavailable.
_extra.deeper: Cascading adds redundancy and flexibility. You get graceful degradation — the system is still responsive even if preferred options fail. The tradeoff: increased complexity, higher costs (you pay for unused backups), and potential cascading failures if not designed carefully.
_extra.lens_pm: Cascades provide safety but are expensive — use when reliability matters more than cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement cascades with clear failure policies; avoid cascades that degrade UX (slow fallback = bad UX).

title: Catastrophic forgetting
definition: When training a model on something new makes it abruptly lose skills it already had.
examples: You fine-tune a model heavily on legal text and suddenly it’s worse at basic math it used to handle easily.
Like cramming for a new language so hard that last year’s subject leaks out of your head entirely.

_extra.analogy: Like cramming for a new language so hard that last year’s subject leaks out of your head entirely.
_extra.deeper: Neural networks store knowledge in shared weights, so updating them for a new task can overwrite the patterns that supported old ones. It’s a central obstacle to sequential learning and aggressive fine-tuning. Mitigations include mixing old data back in, freezing parts of the network, using PEFT so the base stays intact, or regularizing weights to resist large changes.
_extra.lens_pm: Why fine-tuning can quietly degrade a model elsewhere — always test the skills you didn’t train on.
_extra.lens_eng: Overwriting of prior representations during new-task training; countered by rehearsal, freezing, PEFT, or regularization.

title: Causal Attention
definition: Attention where every token can see the past and present but never the future.
examples: In GPT-style generation, causal attention ensures token five is predicted from tokens one through four only.
Writing a story where you can reread earlier pages but the next ones haven’t been written yet.

_extra.analogy: Writing a story where you can reread earlier pages but the next ones haven’t been written yet.
_extra.deeper: Causal attention applies a triangular mask so position i attends only to positions ≤ i. This enforces the autoregressive assumption — predict the next token from prior context — and lets training on a full sequence teach every next-token prediction at once. It’s the reason decoder-only language models can be trained efficiently and generate coherently.
_extra.lens_pm: The rule that makes left-to-right text generation consistent between training and real use.
_extra.lens_eng: Triangular masking restricting each position to attend only to itself and earlier positions.

title: Causal Language Model
definition: A model that can only look leftward — predicting each word from the words before it, never after.
examples: Every generative chatbot is a causal LM: it produces text one token at a time, each based only on what came before.
Like writing a story with a card covering everything you haven’t written yet — you decide the next word from what’s already on the page.

_extra.analogy: Like writing a story with a card covering everything you haven’t written yet — you decide the next word from what’s already on the page.
_extra.deeper: “Causal” means the attention is masked so a token can attend to earlier positions but not future ones, which is exactly what lets the model generate text left to right. It’s the standard setup for GPT-style models. The constraint is also its power: by never peeking ahead, it can be trained on plain text and then generate coherently.
_extra.lens_pm: The default shape of any model that writes, chats, or completes text.
_extra.lens_eng: A model with causal (left-to-right) attention masking, trained on next-token prediction.

title: Cerebras
definition: AI chip company building the Wafer Scale Engine (WSE); massive wafer-sized chips for training and inference.
examples: Cerebras WSE is bigger than traditional GPUs; claims faster training.
The ambitious alternative; betting on a different chip design philosophy.

_extra.analogy: The ambitious alternative; betting on a different chip design philosophy.
_extra.deeper: Cerebras builds full-wafer chips (no chiplets) to reduce latency and increase compute density. High-risk bet; used by enterprises for large-scale training.
_extra.lens_pm: Differentiation through silicon; hard to execute.
_extra.lens_eng: Cerebras is a real alternative to NVIDIA for large-scale training; ecosystem smaller.

title: Chain of Tools
definition: Using several tools in sequence, where each one’s output feeds the next.
examples: The agent searches for a company, feeds the result into a scraper, then pipes that into a summarizer — three tools, one flow.
An assembly line — one station’s finished part becomes the raw material for the next.

_extra.analogy: An assembly line — one station’s finished part becomes the raw material for the next.
_extra.deeper: Chaining lets an agent solve problems no single tool can, by composing them: search then read then compute, each step consuming the last result. The reliability question is the whole chain, not each link — an early error propagates and compounds, so a good search feeding a bad extractor still yields garbage. Longer chains are more capable and more fragile at once.
_extra.lens_pm: Composing tools unlocks bigger tasks, but every added link is another place to break.
_extra.lens_eng: Sequential tool invocations where each output becomes the next call’s input, forming a data pipeline.

title: Chain of thought
definition: Letting the model reason out loud in steps before answering — it gets more right when it shows its work.
examples: Nudging “let’s work through this step by step” measurably boosts hard math and logic problems.
Doing long division on paper instead of trying to hold it all in your head.

_extra.analogy: Doing long division on paper instead of trying to hold it all in your head.
_extra.deeper: Newer reasoning models do this internally, spending extra compute to think before replying. The visible scratchpad became a hidden one — same idea, just more of it, and often no longer shown to you.
_extra.lens_pm: Letting the model reason step by step — better accuracy on hard tasks, now built into reasoning models.
_extra.lens_eng: Intermediate reasoning tokens before the answer; boosts multi-step tasks, often internalized in reasoning models.

title: Chart understanding
definition: Extracting data and insight from visual plots — bar charts, line graphs, pie charts — so a model can answer questions about trends and values.
examples: A financial AI model looks at a revenue chart in a PDF report, identifies the trend line, and tells an analyst that Q3 dipped 15% compared to Q2.
Reading a chart is like someone describing a pattern verbally: "sales went up last quarter" is richer than just the numbers.

_extra.analogy: Reading a chart is like someone describing a pattern verbally: "sales went up last quarter" is richer than just the numbers.
_extra.deeper: This is harder than it seems. Axes need interpretation (time scale, value scale), legend colors matter, and the model must infer relationships between visual elements. Some approaches use OCR on axis labels plus structural reasoning. Others train multimodal models end-to-end on chart-question-answer pairs.
_extra.lens_pm: Turns static images into queryable data — users ask questions of charts without manual transcription.
_extra.lens_eng: Combines vision (detecting axes, bars, lines) with NLP (interpreting labels). Output can be structured data or natural language answers.

title: Chatbot
definition: A system that conducts a text (or voice) conversation with users, remembering context across turns.
examples: ChatGPT: you ask questions, it answers, you follow up, it understands the prior context.
A friend you can text anytime; they remember what you've said and respond thoughtfully.

_extra.analogy: A friend you can text anytime; they remember what you've said and respond thoughtfully.
_extra.deeper: Modern chatbots are language models with conversation history in the context window. Earlier systems used intent classification + template responses. Today's best-in-class use instruction-tuned LLMs. Key challenges: managing context length, handling off-topic or adversarial input, maintaining personality, and staying relevant over long conversations.
_extra.lens_pm: First point of contact for customer support, onboarding, and engagement.
_extra.lens_eng: Keep a message buffer (system + user/assistant turns). Feed full history to the model each turn. Manage token limits.

title: ChatGPT
definition: OpenAI's conversational AI product, launched November 2022; first LLM to reach mainstream adoption.
examples: Launched publicly free (limited GPT-3.5-turbo), reached 1 million users in a week, 100 million in two months.
The moment LLMs became real to the world; a chatbot that felt genuinely smart.

_extra.analogy: The moment LLMs became real to the world; a chatbot that felt genuinely smart.
_extra.deeper: ChatGPT is GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 fine-tuned on conversation data with RLHF. The chat interface (with history) makes it feel more personal than an API. Plus subscription ($20/mo) includes GPT-4 and plugins.
_extra.lens_pm: The product that validated LLM demand; set expectations for performance and price.
_extra.lens_eng: RLHF applied to conversation is powerful; users prefer ChatGPT's tone over raw GPT.

title: Chat template
definition: The fixed format of special markers that tells a model who said what — system, user, assistant — in a conversation.
examples: Behind a chat interface, your message gets wrapped with role markers like a user tag before the model ever sees it.
A screenplay's formatting: character names and stage directions so everyone knows whose line is whose.

_extra.analogy: A screenplay's formatting: character names and stage directions so everyone knows whose line is whose.
_extra.deeper: Models do not inherently know turn boundaries; a chat template encodes them with special tokens marking system, user, and assistant roles. The model is trained with this exact format, so using a mismatched template at inference degrades quality or breaks behavior. It is a small, rigid contract that carries a lot of weight — get the template wrong and even a great model acts confused.
_extra.lens_pm: An invisible formatting layer whose correctness quietly determines whether a model behaves right.
_extra.lens_eng: The role-delimiting token format a model was trained on; must match exactly at inference.

title: Checkpoint
definition: A saved snapshot of a model’s parameters at a moment in training, so you can stop, resume, or ship it.
examples: If a training run crashes at hour 300, you reload the last checkpoint instead of starting over.
A save point in a video game — freeze progress now, come back to exactly here later.

_extra.analogy: A save point in a video game — freeze progress now, come back to exactly here later.
_extra.deeper: A checkpoint is the full set of weights written to disk mid- or post-training. It lets you resume interrupted runs, compare versions, roll back a bad update, or deploy a specific state. “The model you use” is really one chosen checkpoint.
_extra.lens_pm: Every deployed model is a specific checkpoint — pin the version so behavior doesn’t shift under you.
_extra.lens_eng: Serialized parameter (and optimizer) state at a training step, used for resumption and deployment.

title: Checkpoint Averaging
definition: Average several saved snapshots from a single training run into one steadier final model.
examples: Rather than shipping the last step, a team averages the final five checkpoints and gets a small, free quality gain.
Blending a few photos of a moving subject to cancel the blur and get one sharp shot.

_extra.analogy: Blending a few photos of a moving subject to cancel the blur and get one sharp shot.
_extra.deeper: Late in training the weights oscillate around a good region rather than settling exactly. Averaging several nearby checkpoints lands you in a flatter, more robust center of that region, which usually generalizes a touch better than any single snapshot. It’s a standard, near-zero-cost finishing move.
_extra.lens_pm: A no-downside trick to slightly improve the final model from runs you already completed.
_extra.lens_eng: Averaging parameters of consecutive checkpoints from one run to reduce oscillation-driven variance.

title: Checkpointing
definition: Save memory during training by throwing away intermediate results and recomputing them later, trading extra compute for a smaller footprint.
examples: A model that would not fit on a single GPU suddenly trains fine once activation checkpointing is turned on, at the cost of a slightly slower step.
Not keeping every rough draft on your desk — you rewrite a page when you need it instead of storing all of them.

_extra.analogy: Not keeping every rough draft on your desk — you rewrite a page when you need it instead of storing all of them.
_extra.deeper: A normal backward pass needs the activations from the forward pass held in memory. Checkpointing keeps only a few of them and recomputes the rest on demand during backprop. You pay for it with a second partial forward pass, but peak memory drops sharply — often the difference between a run that fits and one that OOMs.
_extra.lens_pm: One of the levers that lets a bigger model train on the hardware you already have.
_extra.lens_eng: Discard intermediate activations and recompute them in the backward pass to cut peak memory at the cost of ~30% more compute.

title: Chinchilla scaling
definition: The finding that for a given compute budget, models should be smaller and trained on far more data than people assumed.
examples: Chinchilla matched a much larger model using fewer parameters but roughly four times the training tokens, at the same compute.
Realizing a smaller pot on the stove longer cooks better than a giant pot rushed — more time with the heat beats sheer size.

_extra.analogy: Realizing a smaller pot on the stove longer cooks better than a giant pot rushed — more time with the heat beats sheer size.
_extra.deeper: DeepMind's 2022 study showed the compute-optimal ratio is roughly 20 training tokens per parameter — meaning earlier giant models were under-trained. It shifted the field toward smaller, data-hungrier models, which also happen to be cheaper to run. In practice teams now often train well past the Chinchilla point because inference savings justify over-training a smaller model.
_extra.lens_pm: It quietly rewrote sizing decisions industry-wide and made strong small models the norm.
_extra.lens_eng: Empirical result: ~20 tokens/param is compute-optimal; smaller models on more data beat larger under-trained ones.

title: Chroma
definition: Lightweight, open-source vector database optimized for embedding storage and retrieval; easy to embed in Python applications.
examples: Add `chroma.Client()` to your Python app, store embeddings, run similarity search without external infrastructure.
SQLite for embeddings; minimal, embeddable, no server needed.

_extra.analogy: SQLite for embeddings; minimal, embeddable, no server needed.
_extra.deeper: Chroma is embedded (in-process) by default; also offers a server mode. Simpler API than Weaviate; trades flexibility for ease of use.
_extra.lens_pm: Great for prototyping and small projects; easy onboarding.
_extra.lens_eng: Embedded mode means no network latency; good for dev/testing; production can scale to server mode.

title: Chunk Boundaries
definition: Where you cut a document into pieces — and how a bad cut can slice an idea in half.
examples: A naive splitter cuts a document every 500 characters and splits "do not exceed" onto one chunk and "the dosage" onto the next, so neither retrieves the warning intact.
Tearing a recipe across the middle of the ingredient list — each half is useless without the other.

_extra.analogy: Tearing a recipe across the middle of the ingredient list — each half is useless without the other.
_extra.deeper: Chunking has to happen for retrieval, but where you cut matters enormously. Fixed-size splits are simple but ignore meaning, stranding half a thought on either side of a boundary. Smarter approaches cut on natural seams — paragraphs, headings, sentences — so each chunk is a coherent unit. Get boundaries wrong and even perfect retrieval returns fragments the model can’t use.
_extra.lens_pm: An unglamorous knob that quietly decides whether retrieved snippets are usable or garbled.
_extra.lens_eng: Prefer semantic/structural split points (headings, sentences) over fixed-length cuts to keep chunks self-contained.

title: Chunk Size
definition: How big each piece of a document is when you split it for retrieval — a surprisingly high-stakes knob.
examples: A team switches from 1000-token chunks to 300-token ones and suddenly answers get sharper because passages are more focused.
Cutting a sandwich: too big to fit the box, too small and the filling falls out.

_extra.analogy: Cutting a sandwich: too big to fit the box, too small and the filling falls out.
_extra.deeper: Chunk size trades context for precision. Large chunks keep surrounding meaning but dilute the embedding and waste tokens; small chunks are precise but can strand a fact from the sentence that explains it. There is no universal best — it depends on content and query style — so it is one of the first things worth tuning, often with a bit of overlap between chunks.
_extra.lens_pm: One of the cheapest levers on answer quality; worth experimenting with early.
_extra.lens_eng: Token/char span per chunk; governs embedding specificity vs. context retention, usually tuned with overlap.

title: Chunking
definition: Slicing long documents into bite-size passages so retrieval can fetch just the relevant piece, not the whole file.
examples: A 40-page manual gets split into ~300-word chunks, each embedded and searchable on its own.
Cutting a book into index cards so you can pull the one paragraph you need.

_extra.analogy: Cutting a book into index cards so you can pull the one paragraph you need.
_extra.deeper: Chunk too big and retrieval drags in irrelevant text that dilutes the answer; too small and you sever the context a passage needs to make sense. A little overlap between chunks keeps ideas from being cut mid-thought. It’s unglamorous, but chunking quality quietly decides RAG quality.
_extra.lens_pm: A boring knob with outsized impact on answer quality — worth tuning early.
_extra.lens_eng: Segmenting docs into overlapping passages sized for the embedding model and context budget.

title: Citation
definition: Asking a model to reference specific sources or quote passages from documents when making claims.
examples: "According to *Document A, page 3*: 'The policy took effect January 1.'" vs. just "The policy took effect January 1."
Like academic footnotes: every claim points back to where it came from.

_extra.analogy: Like academic footnotes: every claim points back to where it came from.
_extra.deeper: Citations reduce hallucination when grounding is available (e.g., with RAG). The model outputs text and source spans. This is harder than it sounds: the model must track which input came from where, and synthesized or paraphrased text breaks naive citation. Some approaches use token-level attention or explicit prompting to force citation.
_extra.lens_pm: Builds trust. Users see where facts come from. Regulatory requirement in some industries.
_extra.lens_eng: Prompt with structured input marking source boundaries. Parse output to extract quotes + source refs. Validate that quotes actually appear in the source.

title: Citation Grounding
definition: Making the model point to the exact source for each claim, so answers are checkable.
examples: A research assistant answers "revenue grew 12%" with a clickable link to the sentence in the 10-K that says so.
A term paper with footnotes — you can flip to the reference and confirm the writer didn’t make it up.

_extra.analogy: A term paper with footnotes — you can flip to the reference and confirm the writer didn’t make it up.
_extra.deeper: Citation grounding ties each generated statement back to a retrieved passage, usually by having the model reference chunk IDs it was given. It boosts trust and makes hallucinations catchable, since a claim with no supporting source is a red flag. The hard part is faithfulness — models can cite a source that doesn’t actually support the claim, so citations reduce but do not eliminate the need to verify.
_extra.lens_pm: The feature that turns "trust me" into "check for yourself"; a big driver of user trust in RAG.
_extra.lens_eng: Claim-to-chunk linking via referenced IDs; improves verifiability but citation faithfulness itself must be checked.

title: Classification Head
definition: A small output layer that maps the model’s understanding to a choice among fixed categories.
examples: A spam filter puts a classification head on a text encoder to output “spam” or “not spam.”
Like the final judge at a science fair who takes all the deliberation and stamps one ribbon: first, second, or third.

_extra.analogy: Like the final judge at a science fair who takes all the deliberation and stamps one ribbon: first, second, or third.
_extra.deeper: It takes a pooled representation of the input and projects it to one score per class, with the highest score winning. You can bolt it onto a frozen or fine-tuned backbone to specialize a general model for a specific labeling task. It’s the standard way to turn an understanding model into a decision-maker.
_extra.lens_pm: The cheap add-on that turns a language model into a categorizer.
_extra.lens_eng: A projection from a pooled representation to per-class logits for a fixed label set.

title: Classifier-Free Guidance
definition: A technique to steer diffusion models toward a condition (like text) without training a separate classifier - by blending conditional and unconditional predictions.
examples: During training, sometimes drop the text prompt (unconditional). At generation, predict both paths - with and without text - then interpolate. This nudges the model toward the text without an external model.
Instead of hiring a critic to rank your sketches, you sketch two versions (one from imagination, one from description) and blend them.

_extra.analogy: Instead of hiring a critic to rank your sketches, you sketch two versions (one from imagination, one from description) and blend them.
_extra.deeper: Classic guidance requires a separate trained classifier (expensive, adds latency). CFG trains with random prompt dropout, so the model learns unconditional generation. At inference, compute both: unconditional pred and conditional pred, then blend: final = uncond + scale x (cond - uncond). Introduced in GLIDE; now standard in Stable Diffusion and others. No extra model, simple, effective. Scale controls influence; high scale can over-flatten diversity.
_extra.lens_pm: Cheaper than training a classifier; enables real-time control without external dependencies.
_extra.lens_eng: Requires training with conditional dropout. At inference, two forward passes. Typical scale: 7-15.

title: Claude
definition: Anthropic's line of language models, including Claude 1, 3.5 Sonnet, and Opus; built with alignment and safety as first-class concerns.
examples: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (2024) matches GPT-4 on many benchmarks while showing fewer false refusals and better instruction-following.
The safety-first alternative to GPT; makes different trade-offs.

_extra.analogy: The safety-first alternative to GPT; makes different trade-offs.
_extra.deeper: Claude uses constitutional AI instead of just RLHF; models are trained to be helpful but also to point out problems in requests. Accessible via API and web chat. Opus is the largest/most capable; Sonnet is the balanced choice; Haiku is fast.
_extra.lens_pm: Differentiation: alignment is a feature, not a liability. Attracts safety-conscious enterprises.
_extra.lens_eng: Constitutional AI leads to fewer false refusals and more nuanced behavior. Long context (200k tokens) is a practical advantage.

title: CLIP
definition: OpenAIs model that learns to match image and text embeddings, enabling zero-shot classification and semantic image search without any training.
examples: CLIP can classify images into 1000 categories without seeing a single example—just from the class names like "Labrador" or "Poodle."
Learning that "dog photo" and "text: dog" are similar without ever being told "class 0 is dog."

_extra.analogy: Learning that "dog photo" and "text: dog" are similar without ever being told "class 0 is dog."
_extra.deeper: Trained on 400M image-text pairs from web using contrastive loss: pull matching pairs close, push mismatched pairs apart. Image and text encoders output embeddings in shared space.
