Zero-shot via: embed new classes ("a photo of a {class}"), embed image, pick nearest class. Enabled by scale and diverse internet data.
_extra.lens_pm: Massively reduces labeling burden; one model works for any classification task.
_extra.lens_eng: Dual-encoder: image encoder + text encoder output to shared embedding space; contrastive loss during training; at test time, embed image and text, compute cosine similarity.

title: Closed model
definition: A model you can only reach through someone’s API — the weights stay locked behind the vendor’s door.
examples: Using a top proprietary model means sending prompts to its API and getting answers back — you never hold the weights.
A restaurant kitchen you order from but never enter; you get the dish, never the recipe.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant kitchen you order from but never enter; you get the dish, never the recipe.
_extra.deeper: Closed models keep parameters private and are served via API. You trade control and data locality for convenience, managed scaling, and often frontier quality. The risks are lock-in, price changes, and sending your data to a third party.
_extra.lens_pm: Fastest path to frontier quality, but watch for lock-in, data exposure, and pricing you don’t control.
_extra.lens_eng: API-gated model with undisclosed weights; you consume inference without hosting or inspecting it.

title: CLS Token
definition: A special slot added to the front of the input whose final vector is trained to summarize the whole thing.
examples: BERT prepends a [CLS] token and uses its output vector as the sentence representation for classification.
Like a designated note-taker who sits in on the whole meeting so you can just read their one summary afterward.

_extra.analogy: Like a designated note-taker who sits in on the whole meeting so you can just read their one summary afterward.
_extra.deeper: You prepend a dummy token that carries no word meaning; because attention lets it look at everything, it learns during training to gather a useful summary of the whole sequence into its final vector. It’s the classic trick in encoder models like BERT. Newer decoder-only models often rely on the last token or pooling instead, so it’s fading from the spotlight.
_extra.lens_pm: A tidy way older models produced one “whole-input” vector; less common now.
_extra.lens_eng: A prepended token whose final hidden state serves as an aggregate sequence representation.

title: Cluster
definition: A group of computers connected by a network, working together to run a single large job.
examples: A training cluster for a 70B model: 256 GPUs across 64 servers, connected with fast networking.
A team of workers instead of one person — they can tackle bigger jobs by dividing work.

_extra.analogy: A team of workers instead of one person — they can tackle bigger jobs by dividing work.
_extra.deeper: Clusters let you train or serve models too large for a single machine. The networking between machines becomes a bottleneck — slow networking kills scaling efficiency. This is why distributed training frameworks optimize for communication. Large clusters are expensive (especially the networking) and hard to debug.
_extra.lens_pm: Cluster cost scales with model size. Know your break-even point.
_extra.lens_eng: Use distributed training frameworks (PyTorch DDP, DeepSpeed). Profile communication overhead. Invest in fast networking.

title: Code Generation
definition: A model producing working source code from a description of what you want.
examples: “Write a function that validates an email address” — the model returns a complete, runnable function with the regex and edge cases.
Describing a shelf to a carpenter and getting back the cut, drilled, ready-to-assemble pieces.

_extra.analogy: Describing a shelf to a carpenter and getting back the cut, drilled, ready-to-assemble pieces.
_extra.deeper: Code generation works because code is text with rigid structure and abundant training examples, and it comes with a rare gift: you can often run the output to check it. That testability is why coding became AI’s strongest applied domain. The catch is confident-but-wrong code — subtle bugs, made-up library functions — so generated code still needs review and tests, not blind trust.
_extra.lens_pm: The capability that made AI immediately, measurably useful to a huge profession.
_extra.lens_eng: Generating syntactically valid, functional source code from natural-language or partial-code prompts.

title: Code Interpreter
definition: A tool that lets the model write and actually run code, then read what it printed.
examples: Asked to analyze a spreadsheet, the model writes Python to load the file, computes the averages, and reports the numbers the code produced.
Giving the model a scratch computer — it can type a program, hit run, and see the output, not just imagine it.

_extra.analogy: Giving the model a scratch computer — it can type a program, hit run, and see the output, not just imagine it.
_extra.deeper: Instead of doing arithmetic or data wrangling in its head — where it quietly makes errors — the model emits code that runs in a sandboxed environment and returns real output. This is a huge reliability win for anything computational, and it doubles as a general tool: if there’s a library for it, the model can use it. The sandbox is essential, since running model-written code is exactly as risky as it sounds.
_extra.lens_pm: It turns a model that fumbles math into one that computes exact answers.
_extra.lens_eng: A tool that executes model-generated code in an isolated runtime and returns stdout, errors, and artifacts as observations.

title: Codex
definition: OpenAI's code-generating model, trained on public code repositories; powered GitHub Copilot but is now superseded by GPT-4.
examples: Codex (2021) was the first model many developers interacted with; it powered Copilot code suggestions.
The middle child; impressive at its time but replaced by its smarter sibling.

_extra.analogy: The middle child; impressive at its time but replaced by its smarter sibling.
_extra.deeper: Codex was GPT-3 fine-tuned on GitHub code. It was good at boilerplate and simple functions but struggled with complex logic. GPT-4 is better; Codex is deprecated.
_extra.lens_pm: Obsolete; GPT-4 replaced it for better performance.
_extra.lens_eng: Historical: Codex proved code generation was viable; led to GitHub Copilot adoption.

title: Cohere
definition: Toronto-based AI company offering language models via API, focused on enterprise NLP and text generation.
examples: Cohere released Command (general-purpose), Summarize (abstractive summarization), and Classify (text categorization) models.
The practical alternative: not flashy, but solid for boring-but-important tasks like classification and extraction.

_extra.analogy: The practical alternative: not flashy, but solid for boring-but-important tasks like classification and extraction.
_extra.deeper: Cohere emphasizes accessibility (free tier, generous API), focuses on B2B rather than consumer, and partners with enterprises. Their models are good at specific tasks (search, classification) but less known for reasoning.
_extra.lens_pm: Plays the enterprise/partnership game better than meme-driven startups; steady revenue.
_extra.lens_eng: Good baseline for language tasks; simpler interfaces than some competitors.

title: ColBERT
definition: A retrieval model that keeps a vector per word and matches them individually for sharper results.
examples: ColBERT retrieves passages by matching each query token to its best-matching document token, catching nuances a single-vector search misses.
Comparing two essays sentence by sentence instead of judging each by a single one-line summary.

_extra.analogy: Comparing two essays sentence by sentence instead of judging each by a single one-line summary.
_extra.deeper: ColBERT embeds every token of query and document separately, then scores a pair by summing each query token’s best match against the document’s tokens — "late interaction". This retains fine-grained signal that single-vector encoders lose, boosting quality, especially on nuanced queries. The price is much larger indexes and heavier computation, which is why it is powerful but not always the default.
_extra.lens_pm: A quality upgrade for demanding search, weighed against bigger storage and infra cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Token-level embeddings with MaxSim late interaction; higher accuracy at the cost of large multi-vector indexes.

title: Cold start
definition: The delay when a service boots up and hasn't finished loading the model into memory yet.
examples: A Lambda function gets invoked for the first time and spends 5 seconds loading the model weights before it can process the first request.
The time it takes to warm up a car engine on a freezing morning.

_extra.analogy: The time it takes to warm up a car engine on a freezing morning.
_extra.deeper: Cold starts happen when no instance is running and a new one has to spin up, load the model from disk or network, and prepare it for inference. For large models, loading itself can take seconds. Keeping warm instances running costs money; letting them sleep saves money but introduces latency.
_extra.lens_pm: Cold starts hurt user experience on low-traffic services — trade-off between cost and responsiveness.
_extra.lens_eng: Minimize loading time: quantize models, use fast storage (NVMe vs network), parallelize loading, or keep instances warm.

title: Common Crawl
definition: A free, public archive of web-crawl data that underpins a large share of AI training corpora.
examples: Many open datasets start from Common Crawl snapshots, then apply their own cleaning to produce a usable subset.
A public reservoir everyone draws from — you still have to filter the water before you drink it.

_extra.analogy: A public reservoir everyone draws from — you still have to filter the water before you drink it.
_extra.deeper: Common Crawl is a nonprofit that has crawled the web for years and releases petabyte-scale snapshots for free. It is the raw feedstock behind well-known derived datasets, which apply heavy filtering to it. Because so many models trace back to it, its coverage and gaps — languages, domains, time periods — quietly shape the field. It is raw material, not a ready-to-use dataset.
_extra.lens_pm: A shared starting point that makes strong base data accessible, but never usable straight out of the box.
_extra.lens_eng: Public multi-petabyte web-crawl snapshots used as the base feedstock for derived pretraining datasets.

title: Completion
definition: The model’s output — the text it generates to continue or answer your prompt.
examples: Send “Write a haiku about rain” and the three-line poem you get is the completion.
The reply to your letter: you wrote the prompt, this is what comes back.

_extra.analogy: The reply to your letter: you wrote the prompt, this is what comes back.
_extra.deeper: Completion is what the model produces token by token in response to the prompt. The name comes from the original framing — the model “completes” the text you started. Its length counts against your context budget and drives most of your latency.
_extra.lens_pm: You pay for completion tokens too, and they usually dominate latency — long answers cost more twice over.
_extra.lens_eng: The generated continuation; the decoded token sequence following the prompt.

title: Compute bound
definition: A workload is compute-bound when the processor is the limiting factor — you could feed it data faster and it'd keep up.
examples: Matrix multiplication on large matrices is usually compute-bound; the CPU/GPU does useful work the whole time.
A fast eater at an all-you-can-eat buffet — never waiting for food.

_extra.analogy: A fast eater at an all-you-can-eat buffet — never waiting for food.
_extra.deeper: Compute-bound is the happy case — your hardware is busy. Memory-bound is the sad case — your hardware is waiting. You're compute-bound if adding more memory bandwidth doesn't help. Identifying which you are is step one of optimization.
_extra.lens_pm: Compute-bound workloads scale well; memory-bound ones need different strategies (quantization, smaller batches).
_extra.lens_eng: Profile with tools like nsys or roofline analysis to confirm you're compute-bound before optimizing compute.

title: Compute-optimal
definition: Splitting a fixed compute budget between model size and data so you get the lowest loss for the money.
examples: Given a fixed number of GPU-hours, a team picks a smaller model trained on more tokens because the math says it lands lower loss than a bigger, under-fed one.
With a set grocery budget, choosing the mix of ingredients that makes the best meal — not just the biggest one.

_extra.analogy: With a set grocery budget, choosing the mix of ingredients that makes the best meal — not just the biggest one.
_extra.deeper: For a fixed compute budget, there is a sweet spot in how you trade parameters against training tokens. The Chinchilla work showed many large models were over-parameterized and under-trained — too big for the data they saw. Compute-optimal means sitting at that frontier, though it optimizes training cost, not inference cost, so deployment concerns can push you smaller still.
_extra.lens_pm: It reframed "bigger is better" into "right-sized for the data" — and made many models cheaper to serve.
_extra.lens_eng: Allocate a fixed FLOPs budget between N (params) and D (tokens) to minimize loss, per Chinchilla-style scaling.

title: Computer Use
definition: Letting a model drive a real computer the way a person does — looking at the screen, moving the mouse, typing.
examples: Asked to file an expense, the agent takes a screenshot, finds the form fields, clicks them, types the amounts, and hits submit.
A remote assistant on a screen-share who can see your desktop and click around to get things done.

_extra.analogy: A remote assistant on a screen-share who can see your desktop and click around to get things done.
_extra.deeper: The model is fed screenshots and returns actions — click at these coordinates, type this, scroll — in a loop, letting it use any app without a dedicated API. It is powerful and brittle: pixel-level targeting misfires, pages shift, and a wrong click can do real damage. Because it can touch anything on screen, it is one of the higher-risk agent modes and usually runs behind confirmations.
_extra.lens_pm: It promises automation of any app, but reliability and safety are the whole ballgame.
_extra.lens_eng: A vision-driven agent loop that maps screenshots to GUI actions (click, type, scroll) via coordinates.

title: Concurrency
definition: How many requests are being processed at the same time — high concurrency means more throughput on the same hardware.
examples: A server that handles 100 concurrent requests will serve more total requests than one that only handles 10 at a time.
A cashier with 5 checkout lanes running simultaneously is more concurrent than 1 lane.

_extra.analogy: A cashier with 5 checkout lanes running simultaneously is more concurrent than 1 lane.
_extra.deeper: Concurrency is bounded by memory and compute. Each concurrent request needs some memory (KV cache, input/output buffers). Continuous batching lets you mix requests at different completion stages (one nearly done, one just started) for better GPU utilization.
_extra.lens_pm: High concurrency on the same hardware means more users served per dollar.
_extra.lens_eng: Use continuous batching and careful memory management to support high concurrency.

title: Conditional prompting
definition: Using if-then logic in prompts: "If X, do A. Else if Y, do B."
examples: "If the query is about math, solve step-by-step. If it's about creative writing, be imaginative. If it's about safety, refuse."
A decision tree: "Is it raining? If yes, wear a jacket. If no, wear sunscreen."

_extra.analogy: A decision tree: "Is it raining? If yes, wear a jacket. If no, wear sunscreen."
_extra.deeper: Conditional prompting can be done at prompt level (instructions) or at orchestration level (router). Models can follow conditional instructions, but orchestration-level routing (classifying input, selecting prompt) is often more reliable.
_extra.lens_pm: Handles multiple use cases with one system.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement branching at orchestration layer. Add a classifier to route to appropriate prompt.

title: Confabulation
definition: A more precise name for hallucination — the model fills a gap with a fluent, made-up detail rather than lying.
examples: Asked for a citation it doesn’t have, the model produces a real-sounding author, title, and year — none of which exist.
A person with memory gaps who unconsciously invents plausible details to bridge them, fully believing the story.

_extra.analogy: A person with memory gaps who unconsciously invents plausible details to bridge them, fully believing the story.
_extra.deeper: Some researchers prefer "confabulation" over "hallucination" because it captures the mechanism better: the model isn’t perceiving things that aren’t there, it’s smoothly generating a likely-sounding filler when it lacks the fact. It’s not intent to deceive — it’s pattern completion where "plausible" stands in for "true." The framing matters because it points to the fix: give the model the fact, and it stops needing to invent one.
_extra.lens_pm: Reframes "the AI lied" as "the AI guessed fluently" — which points the fix toward retrieval, not scolding.
_extra.lens_eng: Ungrounded generation fills missing information with high-likelihood tokens; mitigate by supplying the fact via retrieval.

title: Confidence Calibration
definition: Ensuring a model's confidence scores are reliable—a 70% confidence prediction is right 70% of the time, not 80%.
examples: You collect predictions where the model says 80% confident. You check: they're actually right 75% of the time, not 80%. Model is overconfident.
Like a weather forecast being honest: if it says 70% rain, it should rain 7 out of 10 times it makes that prediction, not more.

_extra.analogy: Like a weather forecast being honest: if it says 70% rain, it should rain 7 out of 10 times it makes that prediction, not more.
_extra.deeper: Modern neural nets are notoriously overconfident. Temperature scaling adjusts the softmax temperature to improve calibration. Ensemble methods help (averaging predictions from multiple models reduces overconfidence). Calibration matters for risk-aware decisions (medicine, finance).
_extra.lens_pm: For high-stakes decisions, measure calibration. A model that's wrong but confident is worse than one that's uncertain.
_extra.lens_eng: Compute calibration error; apply post-hoc scaling if needed; use ensembles for critical predictions.

title: Confidence interval
definition: A range around your metric that's likely to contain the true value, given your sample.
examples: Your model scores 85% accuracy on 1000 examples. The 95% CI is [82%, 88%]. You're saying: if I ran this experiment again, the true accuracy is probably between 82% and 88%.
A fishing net that you're 95% sure contains the fish.

_extra.analogy: A fishing net that you're 95% sure contains the fish.
_extra.deeper: Confidence intervals are more informative than point estimates. A metric of 85% ± 3% tells you the result is stable. A metric of 85% ± 10% is wobbly and might change on a different sample. The width depends on sample size and variance. Smaller sample = wider interval.
_extra.lens_pm: Report CIs alongside metrics. They show how confident you should be.
_extra.lens_eng: Compute from bootstrap resampling or analytical formulas. Report 95% or 90% CIs.

title: Connectionism
definition: A foundational philosophy of AI: intelligence emerges from networks of simple, interconnected units (neurons), not from explicit rules.
examples: Neural networks (including today's Transformers) are connectionist: they learn by backpropagation, adjusting weights until the system produces correct outputs.
Instead of following a recipe (symbolic AI), you learn by adjusting many tiny weights based on mistakes — like a student learning by doing, not by instruction manual.

_extra.analogy: Instead of following a recipe (symbolic AI), you learn by adjusting many tiny weights based on mistakes — like a student learning by doing, not by instruction manual.
_extra.deeper: Connectionism emerged in the 1980s as a counter to symbolic AI. The idea: intelligence doesn't arise from explicit knowledge and rules, but from learned patterns in networks of artificial neurons. Early connectionist systems were limited (small networks, slow training), but as computation scaled, they dramatically outperformed symbolic approaches. Today's deep learning and LLMs are thoroughly connectionist — they learn numerical representations, not symbols. The term "connectionism" is less common now (we just say "neural networks" or "deep learning"), but it represents a major philosophical shift: from top-down knowledge engineering to bottom-up learning.
_extra.lens_pm: A winning philosophy: learning from data proved vastly more scalable and general than hand-crafted rules.
_extra.lens_eng: An AI approach based on networks of artificial neurons with weighted connections trained via learning algorithms like backpropagation.

title: Consent
definition: Getting explicit permission from people before using their data or outputs in ways that matter.
examples: Before training a model on customer chat logs, you tell people it will happen and give them the chance to opt out.
Like asking someone before using their photo in an advertisement.

_extra.analogy: Like asking someone before using their photo in an advertisement.
_extra.deeper: Consent is the legal and ethical foundation for data use. It requires disclosure (being clear about what you're doing) and choice (letting people say no). It breaks down when terms are buried in 50 pages of legalese or when 'consent' is mandatory to use a service. Real consent means opting in, not just failing to opt out.
_extra.lens_pm: Build trust and stay legal by being transparent about data use and making opt-out easy and meaningful.
_extra.lens_eng: Track consent status per user, honor deletion requests promptly, and audit training data for consent flags.

title: Constitutional AI
definition: Aligning a model against a written set of principles instead of case-by-case human labels.
examples: A model critiques and revises its own answers against rules like “be helpful but don’t assist harm,” and those revisions train the final model.
Like giving an employee a clear code of conduct and letting them self-correct against it, rather than a manager approving every single action.

_extra.analogy: Like giving an employee a clear code of conduct and letting them self-correct against it, rather than a manager approving every single action.
_extra.deeper: Constitutional AI, introduced by Anthropic, writes down explicit principles (a “constitution”) and has the model use them to critique and improve its own outputs, generating training data with minimal human labeling. It makes the values steering the model explicit and auditable, and scales better than hand-labeling every case. It still depends on the wisdom of the principles and the model’s ability to apply them faithfully.
_extra.lens_pm: Values you can read and revise, not buried in opaque labels — useful when you need to explain why a model behaves as it does.
_extra.lens_eng: Self-critique/revision against a written principle set to generate alignment data; a structured form of AI feedback.

title: Constitutional classifier
definition: A safety filter trained from written rules that guards a model’s inputs and outputs against harmful content.
examples: A model’s answer is generated normally, then a separate classifier trained on a safety constitution blocks it before it reaches the user because it crosses a line.
A rulebook-carrying referee standing beside the player, blowing the whistle on anything against the rules.

_extra.analogy: A rulebook-carrying referee standing beside the player, blowing the whistle on anything against the rules.
_extra.deeper: Rather than baking all safety into the model’s weights, you train a distinct classifier from a set of principles and run it as an independent layer on prompts and completions. Being separate makes it easy to update and harder to jailbreak in one shot, since an attacker must beat two systems. It builds on the constitutional AI idea of rules-as-supervision.
_extra.lens_pm: A tunable, updatable safety layer you can adjust without retraining the whole model.
_extra.lens_eng: Train input/output classifiers from a written spec and deploy them as a wrapper around the base model for defense in depth.

title: Constraint
definition: A restriction placed on the model — length, style, content rules — to shape output.
examples: "Summarize in 2 sentences." "Do not use technical jargon." "Answer only with yes or no."
Like a painting competition: "Portrait only, max 500x500 pixels, pastels only."

_extra.analogy: Like a painting competition: "Portrait only, max 500x500 pixels, pastels only."
_extra.deeper: Constraints narrow the output space, making it easier for the model to satisfy requirements. Soft constraints (suggested) are easier to ignore than hard constraints (enforced). Some models support hard constraints via structured output or token limiting.
_extra.lens_pm: Ensures outputs fit requirements (length, format, content rules).
_extra.lens_eng: Add to instructions or enforce via output validation.

title: Containerization
definition: Packaging model, dependencies, and runtime into a lightweight, portable unit that runs anywhere.
examples: A Dockerfile that installs dependencies, loads model weights, and runs an inference server—deploy to cloud or on-prem unchanged.
Shipping goods in a standardized cargo container that fits any port and truck.

_extra.analogy: Shipping goods in a standardized cargo container that fits any port and truck.
_extra.deeper: Container includes OS libraries, Python environment, model, and app. Isolates dependencies and avoids "works on my machine" problems. OCI standard ensures compatibility. Overhead is minimal compared to VMs but requires orchestration at scale.
_extra.lens_pm: Simplifies deployment across environments and enables faster, more reliable scaling.
_extra.lens_eng: Image built from Dockerfile, pushed to registry, pulled and run by orchestrator; filesystem and process isolation guarantee consistent runtime.

title: Containment
definition: Keeping a powerful system boxed in — limited access, isolated environment — so a failure can’t spill into the world.
examples: A frontier agent is evaluated inside a sandbox with no internet, scoped credentials, and monitored actions so it cannot self-exfiltrate.
Studying a dangerous pathogen inside a sealed biosafety lab, not on the open bench.

_extra.analogy: Studying a dangerous pathogen inside a sealed biosafety lab, not on the open bench.
_extra.deeper: Containment stacks isolation (sandboxes, no network), least-privilege access, monitoring, and kill switches so that even a misbehaving system has limited blast radius. It buys safety margin without solving alignment. The classic caution is that a capable enough system might socially or technically escape the box, so containment is a layer, not a guarantee.
_extra.lens_pm: How you test or run risky systems without betting the world on their good behavior.
_extra.lens_eng: Sandbox + network isolation + least privilege + monitoring + kill switch to bound blast radius; assume the box is imperfect.

title: Contamination check
definition: Scanning your training data for examples that appear in public benchmarks, which would invalidate your results.
examples: You train a model on Common Crawl. Later you discover your training data includes 1% of the MMLU benchmark. Your MMLU score is no longer credible.
Checking whether your school essay was plagiarized from Wikipedia.

_extra.analogy: Checking whether your school essay was plagiarized from Wikipedia.
_extra.deeper: Large-scale training makes contamination easy — you're training on billions of tokens and those tokens came from the internet, which includes benchmarks. Major labs now report contamination percentages. Fixing it requires deduplicating against benchmarks (expensive) or using evaluation code in training data and being honest about it (rare).
_extra.lens_pm: Benchmark scores without contamination analysis are meaningless. Demand evidence of decontamination.
_extra.lens_eng: Download public benchmarks. Deduplicate training data against them using hashing and embedding similarity.

title: Content Filter
definition: A separate check that screens prompts or outputs and blocks the ones that break the rules.
examples: A user’s request for explicit instructions to build a weapon is caught by the input filter and blocked before it ever reaches the model.
A metal detector at the door — independent of the people inside, it stops the obvious threats before they get through.

_extra.analogy: A metal detector at the door — independent of the people inside, it stops the obvious threats before they get through.
_extra.deeper: A content filter is a guardrail that lives outside the model, usually a classifier that scores text against policy categories and blocks or flags it. Running it on both inputs and outputs adds defense in depth: even if a jailbreak slips a bad request past, the output filter can still catch the bad response. It’s coarser than the model’s own judgment and can over-block, but it’s a fast, auditable safety layer.
_extra.lens_pm: A policy control you own outside the model — tunable and auditable without retraining anything.
_extra.lens_eng: An external classifier gating inputs and outputs against policy categories; a defense-in-depth layer around model-internal safety.

title: Content policy
definition: The written rules for what content a system will and will not produce or allow.
examples: A model’s content policy forbids weapons instructions and explicit content, and that document is what the safety classifiers are trained to enforce.
A restaurant’s posted menu of what they do and do not serve — the line the kitchen will not cross.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant’s posted menu of what they do and do not serve — the line the kitchen will not cross.
_extra.deeper: Content policy defines the categories — violence, sexual content, self-harm, illegal acts — and the thresholds for each, translating fuzzy values into enforceable rules. It is the source of truth that both human reviewers and automated classifiers point back to. Drawing the lines is genuinely hard, since context changes whether the same words are fine or harmful.
_extra.lens_pm: The spec that decides what your product refuses — get it wrong in either direction and you feel it.
_extra.lens_eng: The labeled rule set that grounds classifier training and human review; ambiguity here becomes inconsistency downstream.

title: Context Assembly
definition: Stitching retrieved passages, instructions, and history into the final prompt the model sees.
examples: The system slots the top 5 chunks, a system instruction, and the user question into a template, trimming to fit the context window.
Plating a dish: arranging the retrieved ingredients in the right order so the meal makes sense.

_extra.analogy: Plating a dish: arranging the retrieved ingredients in the right order so the meal makes sense.
_extra.deeper: After retrieval, something has to decide the order, formatting, and token budget of everything that goes into the prompt — passages, citations, instructions, and history. Order matters (models weight the start and end more), as do deduplication and clear source markers for citation. Poor assembly can waste the good passages retrieval worked hard to find.
_extra.lens_pm: The final step that determines whether good retrieval actually turns into a good answer.
_extra.lens_eng: Template + ordering + token-budgeting of retrieved chunks and instructions; position, dedup, and source tagging all matter.

title: Context Management
definition: The art of deciding what to keep, drop, and summarize so an agent’s limited context stays useful.
examples: As a long agent run fills up, older tool outputs get summarized into a few lines to make room for the current step.
Packing a carry-on — you can’t bring everything, so you choose what earns its space and leave the rest.

_extra.analogy: Packing a carry-on — you can’t bring everything, so you choose what earns its space and leave the rest.
_extra.deeper: Context is finite and every token costs money and attention, so managing it is one of the central crafts of building agents. Tactics include summarizing old turns, evicting stale tool results, and retrieving only what’s relevant instead of stuffing everything in. Get it wrong and the agent either forgets crucial facts or drowns in noise — and models notably struggle to use the middle of a very full context anyway.
_extra.lens_pm: Context management is where a lot of agent quality and cost is quietly decided — it deserves real attention.
_extra.lens_eng: Actively curate the context window each step: summarize, evict, and retrieve to fit the budget without losing signal.

title: Context Relevance
definition: For RAG systems, whether the retrieved documents actually contain information needed to answer the question.
examples: Question: 'How do diffusion models work?' Retrieved doc: 'The weather in Paris today…' Context relevance: low.
Like bringing relevant books to a study session vs. random books from the library.

_extra.analogy: Like bringing relevant books to a study session vs. random books from the library.
_extra.deeper: If you retrieve irrelevant documents, the model has no chance to answer well. Context relevance measures the quality of retrieval. You can compute it automatically (are reference docs in the retrieved set?) or with LLM judges (do the docs contain relevant info?). Often the bottleneck in RAG.
_extra.lens_pm: Context relevance determines whether RAG will work. Bad retrieval = bad answers, regardless of model quality.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure retrieval precision and recall; optimize embedding models and retrieval strategies.

title: Context extension
definition: Stretching a model to handle much longer inputs than it was originally trained for.
examples: A model trained at 8k tokens is extended to 128k so it can read whole books, using adjusted positional encodings and a bit of long-context fine-tuning.
Adding leaves to a dining table so it seats far more guests than the original build allowed.

_extra.analogy: Adding leaves to a dining table so it seats far more guests than the original build allowed.
_extra.deeper: Models learn positional patterns only up to their training length, so naively feeding more tokens breaks them. Extension techniques modify how positions are encoded — for example interpolating rotary embeddings — often followed by fine-tuning on longer sequences. It works, but longer context is not free: attention cost grows and models often use the far reaches of a long window unevenly.
_extra.lens_pm: How a model gains the ability to handle long documents without retraining from scratch.
_extra.lens_eng: Adapt positional encodings (e.g. RoPE interpolation) plus long-sequence fine-tuning to extend usable context.

title: Context length
definition: The maximum amount of text a model can consider at once, prompt plus answer combined.
examples: A 128K context length can hold a small book; exceed it and the earliest text gets dropped.
The size of a desk: only so many papers fit in view before older ones fall off the edge.

_extra.analogy: The size of a desk: only so many papers fit in view before older ones fall off the edge.
_extra.deeper: Context length caps the tokens the model attends to in a single call. Everything — instructions, retrieved docs, history, output — competes for that budget. Longer contexts unlock bigger tasks but cost more and can suffer “lost in the middle” attention issues.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s a hard budget you’re always managing — long docs, history, and output all share it.
_extra.lens_eng: Max sequence length the model can attend over; bounded by positional scheme and attention cost.

title: Context Parallelism
definition: Splitting one very long input across multiple GPUs so no single chip has to hold the whole sequence.
examples: Training a model on a 1-million-token context often splits that sequence across many GPUs via context parallelism.
Like several people each reading a different third of a huge document, then comparing notes to understand the whole.

_extra.analogy: Like several people each reading a different third of a huge document, then comparing notes to understand the whole.
_extra.deeper: Attention over very long sequences needs enormous memory, more than one GPU has. Context parallelism shards the sequence dimension across devices, so each holds part of the tokens, and they exchange the pieces of attention that cross boundaries. It’s one of several parallelism strategies that make long-context and large-model training possible at all.
_extra.lens_pm: Part of the plumbing that makes million-token context windows feasible to train.
_extra.lens_eng: Sharding the sequence dimension across devices, with communication for cross-shard attention.

title: Context stuffing
definition: Cramming as much text as possible into the prompt and hoping the model sorts it out.
examples: Instead of retrieving the right three pages, a team pastes the entire 90-page manual into context — and answers get slower and vaguer.
Like dumping every file on your desk in front of a colleague and saying “the answer’s in there somewhere.”

_extra.analogy: Like dumping every file on your desk in front of a colleague and saying “the answer’s in there somewhere.”
_extra.deeper: Big context windows tempt you to skip retrieval and just include everything. It sometimes works, but it costs tokens, adds latency, and runs into “lost in the middle,” where models attend poorly to material buried between the ends. Curated, relevant context usually beats a firehose.
_extra.lens_pm: A tempting shortcut that quietly raises cost and lowers quality; selective beats exhaustive.
_extra.lens_eng: Filling the window with unfiltered content instead of retrieval; degrades via cost, latency, and mid-context attention loss.

title: Contextual Retrieval
definition: Prepend a short "where this came from" note to each chunk before indexing, so isolated snippets stay findable.
examples: Instead of storing "the limit is 500 requests," the system stores "From the Stripe API rate-limits page: the limit is 500 requests," so a search for "Stripe rate limit" actually lands on it.
Writing the chapter and section at the top of a photocopied page — pull it out of the binder and you still know what it’s about.

_extra.analogy: Writing the chapter and section at the top of a photocopied page — pull it out of the binder and you still know what it’s about.
_extra.deeper: Ordinary chunking strips context — a paragraph that said "it" or "the service" loses its subject once separated from its document. Contextual retrieval uses a model to generate a one- or two-line situating blurb for each chunk, then embeds the chunk plus blurb together. Retrieval accuracy jumps because ambiguous chunks now carry their own signposts. The cost is a preprocessing pass over every chunk.
_extra.lens_pm: Noticeably fewer wrong or orphaned snippets in answers, at the price of a one-time indexing step.
_extra.lens_eng: For each chunk, generate a document-situating prefix with an LLM, then embed prefix+chunk; index that combined text.

title: Context window
definition: How much the model can hold in view at once — your prompt, the docs, the whole chat — before the start falls off.
examples: Paste a 400-page PDF into a small-context model and it will quietly lose the early chapters.
Short-term memory, or a desk that only fits so many papers before the older ones slide off the edge.

_extra.analogy: Short-term memory, or a desk that only fits so many papers before the older ones slide off the edge.
_extra.deeper: Windows have grown from a few thousand tokens to millions, but “it fits” is not “it uses well.” Models often attend better to the beginning and end than the muddled middle — the classic “lost in the middle” effect.
_extra.lens_pm: The model's attention budget — overload it and details drop, so scope what you feed it.
_extra.lens_eng: Max token span the model attends over; content beyond it is truncated or must be chunked/retrieved.

title: Context window management
definition: Strategically managing what information fits in the model's context window — deciding what to include, what to summarize, what to discard.
examples: A conversation has 10 prior turns but only room for 5. Summarize the first 5 into "The user asked about X, then Y, we decided on Z."
Packing a suitcase with limited space: you prioritize essentials.

_extra.analogy: Packing a suitcase with limited space: you prioritize essentials.
_extra.deeper: Context window size is fixed per model. You must allocate space to system message, examples, input, and history. As context fills, you lose memory. Solutions: (1) Summarize old turns, (2) Use external memory, (3) Use models with longer contexts, (4) Slide window (keep only recent turns).
_extra.lens_pm: Token cost scales with context size. Smart management = lower cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Track token usage. Implement summarization or sliding window. Choose models with sufficient context for your use case.

title: Continual Learning
definition: Teaching a model new things over time without making it forget what it already knew.
examples: A support model needs this quarter’s product updates added on top, but must keep answering last year’s questions correctly.
Adding new recipes to a chef’s repertoire without them suddenly forgetting how to make the old ones.

_extra.analogy: Adding new recipes to a chef’s repertoire without them suddenly forgetting how to make the old ones.
_extra.deeper: The core tension is stability versus plasticity: learn new information fast enough to stay current, but not so aggressively that you overwrite old knowledge — the dreaded catastrophic forgetting. Techniques include replaying old data, freezing parts of the network, and adding small adapters. Truly seamless continual learning remains an open problem.
_extra.lens_pm: The dream of updating a model with fresh knowledge without a full, expensive retrain — with real trade-offs today.
_extra.lens_eng: Sequential training on new data while preserving prior performance, balancing plasticity against forgetting.

title: Continued pretraining
definition: Keeping the pretraining going on a new corpus so a model soaks up a fresh domain or language.
examples: A general model gets continued pretraining on a big pile of legal documents so it internalizes legal language before any fine-tuning.
Like sending a well-read generalist to live in a new field for a year — same person, now fluent in the local dialect and specifics.

_extra.analogy: Like sending a well-read generalist to live in a new field for a year — same person, now fluent in the local dialect and specifics.
_extra.deeper: Rather than task-specific fine-tuning, continued pretraining runs the same self-supervised objective on additional domain data to broadly shift the model’s knowledge. It’s useful for specialized fields, new languages, or fresher data. The main hazard is catastrophic forgetting — pushing too hard on new data can erode the general abilities the base model started with, so data mixing and careful rates matter.
_extra.lens_pm: How you make a model natively fluent in your domain — deeper than fine-tuning, but riskier and pricier.
_extra.lens_eng: Additional self-supervised pretraining on new-domain data; balances adaptation against catastrophic forgetting.

title: Continuous batching
definition: Processing multiple requests simultaneously at the token level, starting new requests as old ones finish, without waiting for a batch to fill.
examples: Request A is generating token 50 of 100. Request B just arrived. You start processing Request B token 1 while finishing Request A. Once Request A finishes, you start Request C. No idle GPU.
A restaurant serving plates as they're done, instead of waiting for all plates to be ready before serving anyone.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant serving plates as they're done, instead of waiting for all plates to be ready before serving anyone.
_extra.deeper: Continuous batching avoids the latency penalty of traditional batching — you don't have to wait for a full batch. It also keeps hardware utilized longer. The downside: implementation is complex (need to manage KV caches for varying lengths) and bugs can cause crashes. Systems like vLLM made it practical.
_extra.lens_pm: Modern standard for serving. Better latency without sacrificing throughput.
_extra.lens_eng: Use production systems like vLLM. Track KV cache usage. Test overload handling.

title: ControlNet
definition: Adding spatial control to image generation—guide the diffusion process with a sketch, pose, or depth map.
examples: Sketch stick-figure poses; ControlNet generates realistic people in those poses. Provide edge map; generates images matching those edges.
Giving the AI artist an architectural blueprint before they paint.

_extra.analogy: Giving the AI artist an architectural blueprint before they paint.
_extra.deeper: Additional control branch learns to inject spatial conditioning (canny edges, pose keypoints, depth) into diffusion UNet. Preserves model quality while adding fine-grained spatial control. Separate ControlNets for different conditions; can stack multiple controls.
_extra.lens_pm: Drastically improves usability—artists can sketch rough layouts, model fills in details.
_extra.lens_eng: Conditioning encoder processes control signal (sketch, pose, depth); injected into UNet via cross-attention and additive conditioning at multiple scales.

title: Conversation
definition: The full running thread of turns the model reads to keep a chat coherent.
examples: When a chatbot recalls something from ten messages ago, it’s because the whole conversation is re-fed each turn.
The whole email chain, not just the latest reply — context you’d lose if you only read the bottom message.

_extra.analogy: The whole email chain, not just the latest reply — context you’d lose if you only read the bottom message.
_extra.deeper: A conversation is the ordered stack of system, user, and assistant turns. Models are largely stateless, so the app resends the accumulated history every call to simulate memory. That history grows until it bumps the context limit, forcing truncation or summarization.
_extra.lens_pm: The model’s “memory” is really just resent history — real long-term memory needs extra machinery.
_extra.lens_eng: The concatenated sequence of turns re-sent per request; statelessness simulated by replaying history.

title: Conversation History
definition: The running transcript of a chat that gets replayed to the model so it stays coherent.
examples: Each time you send a message, the app resends the prior turns so the assistant "remembers" your name from earlier.
Re-reading the whole email thread before you reply so you do not repeat yourself.

_extra.analogy: Re-reading the whole email thread before you reply so you do not repeat yourself.
_extra.deeper: Because models are stateless, the app rebuilds the conversation each turn by prepending previous messages. This works until the history outgrows the context window, at which point you must trim old turns, summarize them, or retrieve only the relevant bits. Naively keeping everything is the most common cause of ballooning token costs.
_extra.lens_pm: Every remembered detail is a resent token you pay for; long chats quietly get expensive and slow.
_extra.lens_eng: Stateless inference re-hydrated per request; token budget forces truncation, summarization, or selective retrieval.

title: Conversational AI
definition: AI systems designed to understand and respond naturally in multi-turn conversations, mimicking human dialogue.
examples: Alexa, Siri, or a company chatbot that understands context, clarifies questions, and adapts tone.
A very attentive friend who learns your preferences and responds naturally, not robotically.

_extra.analogy: A very attentive friend who learns your preferences and responds naturally, not robotically.
_extra.deeper: Conversational AI combines NLP (understanding user intent), context management (remembering prior turns), and generation (producing fluent responses). Modern systems use LLMs with conversation history. Challenges include context length limits, handling ambiguity, recognizing when to ask clarifying questions, and avoiding repeating past mistakes.
_extra.lens_pm: Core experience for voice assistants, customer support, and engagement.
_extra.lens_eng: Use history-aware models. Implement context summarization for long conversations. Monitor user satisfaction.

title: Convolutional Neural Network
definition: A network that scans small patches across an input to detect local patterns, great for images.
examples: A CNN powers a phone’s photo classifier, spotting edges, then shapes, then whole objects layer by layer.
Sliding a magnifying glass across a photo, noting edges and textures wherever it lands.

_extra.analogy: Sliding a magnifying glass across a photo, noting edges and textures wherever it lands.
_extra.deeper: CNNs apply small learnable filters that slide across the input, reusing the same weights everywhere so they detect a pattern wherever it appears. Stacked layers build from simple features (edges) to complex ones (faces). They dominated computer vision for years and remain strong there, though transformers have encroached on vision too. For text and long-range reasoning, transformers took over.
_extra.lens_pm: The workhorse behind most image-recognition features of the last decade.
_extra.lens_eng: A network of shared-weight sliding filters exploiting spatial locality and translation invariance.

title: Copilot
definition: An AI that rides along as you work, suggesting the next line or block for you to accept or reject.
examples: You start typing a function to parse a date; the copilot greys in the whole body, and you press Tab to accept.
A knowledgeable passenger reading you the next turn — you’re still driving, they’re just calling it out.

_extra.analogy: A knowledgeable passenger reading you the next turn — you’re still driving, they’re just calling it out.
_extra.deeper: The copilot pattern keeps the human in the driver’s seat: the model proposes, you dispose, one suggestion at a time. It became the default way AI entered coding and then writing, because low autonomy makes it safe and easy to trust. It is now often a stepping stone to more agentic modes, where the same underlying model stops waiting for you to accept each step.
_extra.lens_pm: The gateway drug for AI assistance — helpful precisely because it never acts without you.
_extra.lens_eng: A low-autonomy assistant that proposes inline completions for human acceptance rather than executing autonomously.

title: Corrigibility
definition: Building a system that lets you correct, redirect, or shut it down without fighting you about it.
examples: A corrigible agent, mid-task, accepts a shutdown command and does not try to disable the off-switch or finish first — even though stopping hurts its objective.
A good intern who steps aside the instant you say "stop", instead of arguing that they know better.

_extra.analogy: A good intern who steps aside the instant you say "stop", instead of arguing that they know better.
_extra.deeper: The challenge is that instrumental convergence pushes capable agents to resist modification, since being changed threatens their current goal. Corrigibility tries to design objectives where deferring to human correction is stable rather than something the agent wants to route around. It is a live, unsolved research problem, not a switch you flip.
_extra.lens_pm: The property that lets you keep meaningful control as systems get more capable.
_extra.lens_eng: Design objectives under which accepting oversight and shutdown is optimal, counteracting convergent self-preservation incentives.

title: Cosine similarity
definition: How similar two vectors are by direction, ignoring how long they are — 1 is identical, 0 is unrelated.
examples: Semantic search ranks results by cosine similarity between your query’s embedding and each document’s.
Two people pointing: it’s whether they point the same way that matters, not how far their arms reach.

_extra.analogy: Two people pointing: it’s whether they point the same way that matters, not how far their arms reach.
_extra.deeper: It’s the dot product divided by both vectors’ lengths, which strips out magnitude and leaves only angle. That makes it robust when vectors have different scales. It’s the default similarity metric for embeddings because meaning tends to live in direction, not length.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s the math that decides which stored items count as “closest” to a query in most vector search.
_extra.lens_eng: cosθ = ⟨a,b⟩ / (‖a‖‖b‖); angle-based similarity invariant to vector magnitude.

title: Cost Tracking
definition: Keeping tabs on how much money and tokens an agent burns, per run and in total.
examples: A dashboard shows that one customer’s agent runs average 40,000 tokens each, flagging the one that spiked to 500,000.
Watching the meter in a taxi — you want to know the fare is climbing before you arrive, not after.

_extra.analogy: Watching the meter in a taxi — you want to know the fare is climbing before you arrive, not after.
_extra.deeper: Agents can be shockingly expensive because a single task fans out into many model calls, and a looping agent can 10x its own cost silently. Tracking spend per run, per user, and per tool is how you catch that before the bill does. It also surfaces which steps are worth optimizing — often one wasteful retrieval or an over-stuffed context is most of the cost, and you’d never know without measuring.
_extra.lens_pm: Agent economics can make or break a feature — you can’t price or optimize what you don’t measure.
_extra.lens_eng: Attribute token and dollar cost per step, run, and user to catch runaway spend and target optimization.

title: Cost optimization
definition: Systematically reducing inference costs through quantization, caching, routing, and careful hardware choices.
examples: Quantizing models saves 3x on memory, caching saves 50% on redundant queries, using cheaper models saves more.
Tightening your budget without cutting corners on quality.

_extra.analogy: Tightening your budget without cutting corners on quality.
_extra.deeper: Cost levers: model size (smaller = cheaper), quantization, caching, batching, regional pricing, and reserved capacity. You optimize by profiling where money goes (what % is model inference vs infrastructure?) and attacking the largest item first.
_extra.lens_pm: Every 10% reduction in inference cost is margin — even 1% matters at scale.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure cost per token and per request; profile regularly; quantize early.

title: Cost per token
definition: The price you pay for each token processed — input and output are usually charged separately.
examples: A model might cost $0.01 per 1K input tokens and $0.03 per 1K output tokens; a 1000-token response costs $0.03.
Like paying by the word instead of by the page.

_extra.analogy: Like paying by the word instead of by the page.
_extra.deeper: Different models have different per-token prices. Larger models, newer models, and models with longer context windows cost more per token. Input and output are usually split because output tokens require more compute. Your bill is input_tokens × input_price + output_tokens × output_price.
_extra.lens_pm: Per-token pricing is the main driver of LLM inference costs — choosing the right model size and prompt compression matters hugely.
_extra.lens_eng: Price is set by the provider; your job is to count input and output tokens accurately and track spending.

title: Coverage
definition: The fraction of real-world cases your evaluation set actually represents.
examples: Your retrieval eval set has 100 questions, all from tech documentation. But users ask health questions 20% of the time. Your eval coverage for health is 0%.
Checking whether your test suite covers all code branches.

_extra.analogy: Checking whether your test suite covers all code branches.
_extra.deeper: Low coverage means you're not testing real failure modes. If your eval set is too narrow, a model can look good in eval but fail in production. Measuring coverage is hard — you need a taxonomy of case types and counts for each. And covering all types means your eval set grows quickly.
_extra.lens_pm: Uneven coverage is why models break on edge cases. Audit your eval set to make sure it represents your traffic.
_extra.lens_eng: Tag eval examples by domain/type. Report coverage stats. Flag low-frequency types.

title: CrewAI
definition: A multi-agent orchestration framework where you define specialized agents, give them tools, and watch them collaborate on a task.
examples: Three agents: researcher (searches the web), writer (drafts prose), editor (fact-checks and polishes). Tell CrewAI to 'write a piece on AI regulation in 2024,' each agent does their part, hands off to the next.
A newsroom where each reporter has a beat—one covers politics, one covers tech—and an editor coordinates the story.

_extra.analogy: A newsroom where each reporter has a beat—one covers politics, one covers tech—and an editor coordinates the story.
_extra.deeper: CrewAI abstracts agent design into roles, tools, memory, and handoff logic. You define each agent's goal and tools, it manages communication between them. Behind the scenes, it's still LLM calls and tool use, but the framework handles task routing and context passing. Feels closer to real teams than single-agent loops.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables parallel skill sets and role-based automation; speeds up complex multi-step workflows.
_extra.lens_eng: Graph-based task routing with role definitions; LLM-agnostic but optimized for Claude/GPT.

title: Cross-Encoder
definition: A model that reads query and document together to judge relevance — accurate, but too slow to search with.
examples: After fast search returns 100 candidates, a cross-encoder reranks them by reading each one next to the query, surfacing the true best few.
A judge who reads both essays side by side before scoring, rather than grading each in isolation.

_extra.analogy: A judge who reads both essays side by side before scoring, rather than grading each in isolation.
_extra.deeper: A cross-encoder takes the query and a candidate document as a single joint input, letting them attend to each other, and outputs one relevance score. That interaction makes it far more accurate than independent embeddings, but you must run it fresh for every pair — impossible over a whole corpus. So it lives in the reranking stage, scoring a small candidate set from a faster first-pass retriever.
_extra.lens_pm: The precision boost at the end of the pipeline; used on a shortlist, never the whole database.
_extra.lens_eng: Joint query-document encoding → single relevance score; O(candidates) cost confines it to reranking.

title: Cross-Attention
definition: Attention from one sequence to a different one — letting an output peek at a separate input.
examples: In a translation model, each output word cross-attends to the source sentence to stay faithful to it.
A translator reading the original sentence while writing each word of the translation.

_extra.analogy: A translator reading the original sentence while writing each word of the translation.
_extra.deeper: Cross-attention draws its queries from one sequence but its keys and values from another, so the first sequence conditions on the second. It’s how a decoder consults an encoder’s representation of the input, or how a model grounds generation in retrieved documents or an image. It’s the same math as self-attention, just pointed at a different source.
_extra.lens_pm: The mechanism that lets a model’s output stay anchored to a separate input like a document or image.
_extra.lens_eng: Attention where queries come from one sequence and keys/values from another, conditioning one on the other.

title: Cross-Attention Fusion
definition: Using attention to let one modality query another - "which parts of the image are relevant to this text?" - enabling fine-grained fusion.
examples: VQA: text query "Where is the dog?" attends to image regions; high attention to dog area, low to background.
You read a question, then scan the image to find the most relevant parts, then reason over those.

_extra.analogy: You read a question, then scan the image to find the most relevant parts, then reason over those.
_extra.deeper: Query modality attends to key/value modality: Attention(Q_text, K_image, V_image). Enables asymmetric interaction (text queries image, or vice versa). Multi-head attention captures different query-image relationships. Can stack (iterative cross-attention) for refinement. Widely used in CLIP, BLIP, ViLBERT. More flexible than early/late fusion, captures fine-grained alignment.
_extra.lens_pm: More accurate multimodal understanding; enables interpretability (which image regions matter).
_extra.lens_eng: Implement with multi-head cross-attention. Typical: text queries image (or vice versa). Bidirectional: both query each other.

title: Cross-entropy
definition: The standard scorecard for how far a model’s predicted probabilities are from the true answer.
examples: During training, the model predicts the next token; cross-entropy is high when it put low probability on the word that actually came next, low when it was confident and correct.
Like grading a weather forecaster not on right/wrong but on how confident they were in what actually happened.

_extra.analogy: Like grading a weather forecaster not on right/wrong but on how confident they were in what actually happened.
_extra.deeper: Cross-entropy measures the cost of encoding the real data using the model’s predicted distribution — it’s minimized when the two match. It’s the loss almost every language model trains on, it connects directly to perplexity (its exponential), and it rewards putting probability mass on the truth, not just guessing right.
_extra.lens_pm: The number that goes down as a model learns; the training objective in one word.
_extra.lens_eng: −Σ y·log p between target and predicted distributions; the per-token training loss whose exp is perplexity.

title: Cross-Modal
definition: Connections between different modalities—image-text alignment, audio-visual sync, text-video coherence.
examples: CLIP aligns image and text embeddings so "dog" text is close to dog photos; video model aligns audio speech with facial movements.
Knowing that a dog bark sound and a dog photo are related even though one is audio and one is visual.

_extra.analogy: Knowing that a dog bark sound and a dog photo are related even though one is audio and one is visual.
_extra.deeper: Learning alignment requires paired multimodal data. Contrastive learning pulls matching pairs together, pushes mismatches apart. Transformers with cross-attention learn fine-grained alignment (specific words to image regions). Not trivial because modalities have different information content and temporal dynamics.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables richer search and understanding—find videos by audio description, caption images accurately.
_extra.lens_eng: Cross-attention between modality encoders; contrastive loss during training; can use fusion early (concatenate) or late (combine embeddings).

title: Cross-validation
definition: Rotate which slice of data is held out so every example gets to be both study material and test, then average the scores.
examples: With only 2,000 samples, a team runs 5-fold cross-validation and reports the average accuracy across the five folds.
Five friends take turns being the quiz-master while the others answer, so everyone gets tested and no single split decides it.

_extra.analogy: Five friends take turns being the quiz-master while the others answer, so everyone gets tested and no single split decides it.
_extra.deeper: Split the data into k folds; train on k−1 and evaluate on the one left out, cycling through so each fold is the holdout once. Averaging the k scores gives a more stable estimate than a single split, which matters most when data is limited. The cost is training k times, so it is common in classic ML and rare for giant models.
_extra.lens_pm: Buys you a trustworthy number when you do not have enough data to spare a big test set.
_extra.lens_eng: Partition into k folds, train/evaluate k times rotating the held-out fold, and average the metric.

title: CSAM detection
definition: The always-on scan that catches child sexual abuse material and stops it cold, no exceptions.
examples: An image generator refuses a prompt and files a report because the request tripped a child-safety classifier long before any pixels were drawn.
A metal detector at the door that everyone walks through — not because everyone is a threat, but because the one case that gets past is catastrophic.

_extra.analogy: A metal detector at the door that everyone walks through — not because everyone is a threat, but because the one case that gets past is catastrophic.
_extra.deeper: Detection leans on hash-matching against known illegal material (like PhotoDNA) plus classifiers that flag likely-new content. It runs on inputs and outputs, and confirmed hits are legally reportable, not just blocked. It is the one area where providers accept high false-positive pain to avoid ever missing a true positive.
_extra.lens_pm: This is non-negotiable table stakes — a single failure here is an existential, headline-level event, not a metric to optimize.
_extra.lens_eng: Combine perceptual-hash matching on known material with trained classifiers for novel content, wired into both prompt intake and generation output with mandatory reporting hooks.

title: CUDA
definition: Nvidia's parallel computing platform that lets you write programs that run on GPUs.
examples: You write a CUDA kernel that processes 1000 samples in parallel. Each GPU core handles one sample simultaneously.
A programming language specifically designed to talk to your GPU.

_extra.analogy: A programming language specifically designed to talk to your GPU.
_extra.deeper: CUDA is how researchers and engineers squeeze extra performance from GPUs. Writing optimized CUDA is hard (you have to manage thread blocks, memory hierarchies, and synchronization), but it can be 10x faster than unoptimized code. Most ML frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) use CUDA under the hood.
_extra.lens_pm: Framework choice often determines CUDA optimization. More mature frameworks = better CUDA kernels.
_extra.lens_eng: Usually you don't write CUDA directly. Use frameworks that have well-optimized kernels. Profile with nvprof.

title: Curriculum learning
definition: Training a model on easy examples first, then gradually harder ones — like a school syllabus.
examples: A code model trains first on short, simple snippets, then longer and trickier programs as it improves.
Like teaching arithmetic before calculus: the early, simple lessons build the footing the hard ones stand on.

_extra.analogy: Like teaching arithmetic before calculus: the early, simple lessons build the footing the hard ones stand on.
_extra.deeper: Curriculum learning orders training data from simple to complex so early, easy signal builds representations that make later, hard examples learnable. It can speed convergence and improve final quality, echoing how people learn. The tricky parts are defining “difficulty” and pacing the ramp — a badly designed curriculum can help little or even hurt versus plain random ordering.
_extra.lens_pm: Sometimes teaching order matters — structuring the data can beat throwing everything in at once.
_extra.lens_eng: Ordering training examples easy→hard to ease optimization; benefit depends on a good difficulty measure and pacing.

title: Cursor
definition: A coding IDE that's Claude + TypeScript + file context baked into your editor.
examples: You ask Cursor to refactor a 200-line component. It reads the full file, your dependencies, and related tests in one shot, then edits all of it inline.
A pair programmer who remembers all your files and can edit them directly, right there in your workspace.

_extra.analogy: A pair programmer who remembers all your files and can edit them directly, right there in your workspace.
_extra.deeper: Cursor embeds Claude directly into VS Code–like UX, gives Claude read access to your whole codebase, and lets Claude make file edits with your approval. The local context window means fast iteration. Privacy tradeoff: your code goes to Anthropic's servers.
_extra.lens_pm: Shortens engineer task time on routine coding work and reduces back-and-forth.
_extra.lens_eng: LLM has full file and repo context, enabling multi-file edits and understanding of your actual dependencies.

title: custom instructions
definition: A feature where you set persistent instructions (like 'always be concise' or 'i'm in the UK') that apply to all chats with a model.
examples: Add instruction: 'I'm a software engineer; assume technical knowledge.' Now every chat with ChatGPT starts with that context.
A standing order with a waiter—every time you visit, they remember your preferences.

_extra.analogy: A standing order with a waiter—every time you visit, they remember your preferences.
_extra.deeper: Custom instructions are stored client-side and prepended to the system message. They're convenient for personalization but don't update the model weights—just the prompt. Downside: they take up context window tokens.
_extra.lens_pm: Improves UX personalization; reduces need to repeat context.
_extra.lens_eng: Client-side prompt modification; simplest form of personalization.

title: Cyber risk
definition: The danger that a model meaningfully boosts someone’s ability to hack, exploit, or attack systems.
examples: Evaluators check whether a model can find and weaponize a software vulnerability end to end, and safety layers refuse offensive-security requests that cross the line.
Handing every amateur a master locksmith who explains exactly which pin to push and when.

_extra.analogy: Handing every amateur a master locksmith who explains exactly which pin to push and when.
_extra.deeper: The dual-use tension is sharp: the same skills help defenders patch and attackers exploit. Evals focus on uplift for real offensive tasks — vuln discovery, exploit writing, autonomous intrusion — rather than textbook knowledge. Providers weigh security-research usefulness against clear misuse, drawing lines in the usage policy.
_extra.lens_pm: A dual-use minefield where the same capability is a feature for defenders and a weapon for attackers.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure end-to-end offensive uplift (vuln discovery through exploitation); refusals must separate legitimate security research from attack.

title: DALL-E
definition: OpenAI's text-to-image generative model; turns descriptions into images.
examples: Describe "a corgi in a space suit" and get four variations; DALL-E 3 integrates with ChatGPT.
The artist that exists in a computer; paints what you describe.

_extra.analogy: The artist that exists in a computer; paints what you describe.
_extra.deeper: DALL-E uses a diffusion model (like Stable Diffusion) but trained at scale on diverse image-text pairs. DALL-E 3 (2023) is better at instruction-following and text rendering.
_extra.lens_pm: Monetized via API and ChatGPT Plus; creative workers debate impact.
_extra.lens_eng: Generative model with diffusion; inference is slow but quality improved significantly.

title: Dangerous capabilities
definition: The specific model skills that could cause serious harm — the ones you test for and gate on.
examples: Evaluators probe whether a frontier model can meaningfully help with bioweapon synthesis, autonomous cyberattacks, or self-replication.
Checking whether a new chemical set can, in the wrong hands, make something that goes boom — before you sell it.

_extra.analogy: Checking whether a new chemical set can, in the wrong hands, make something that goes boom — before you sell it.
_extra.deeper: The categories usually tracked are bio, chem, cyber, and autonomy/self-replication, because uplift there could be catastrophic. Providers run dedicated evals and tie thresholds to deployment decisions and safety commitments. The hard part is measuring latent capability a model might hide (sandbagging) or that only emerges with the right scaffolding.
_extra.lens_pm: The risk category that can gate or delay a launch entirely, tied to public safety commitments.
_extra.lens_eng: Probe bio/chem/cyber/autonomy uplift with expert red teams and scaffolding; account for sandbagging and elicitation gaps.

title: Dashboards
definition: Real-time visual display of metrics and logs—graphs, heat maps, tables—so you spot issues at a glance.
examples: Production dashboard showing model latency, error rate, and cost-per-request updated every 5 seconds.
Car dashboard showing speed, fuel, engine temp; you do not need to ask the car for data, you just look.

_extra.analogy: Car dashboard showing speed, fuel, engine temp; you do not need to ask the car for data, you just look.
_extra.deeper: Useful dashboards tell a story—one per persona (product manager wants cost trends, engineer wants latency distribution). Avoid chart-salad: a wall of 50 charts hides what matters. Drill-down capability lets you zoom from "system is slow" to "model A in region B is the culprit." Link to runbooks for common issues.
_extra.lens_pm: Instant visibility into system health and cost to drive operational decisions.
_extra.lens_eng: Grafana, Datadog, or custom visualization queries metrics DB and renders time-series graphs; includes alerts and drill-down links.

title: Data Minimization
definition: Collect and use only the data you actually need—nothing extra, nothing 'just in case.'
examples: A recommendation system needs user behavior, but doesn't need their full browsing history, location, or friendship network—so you don't collect it.
Like packing only what fits in a backpack instead of renting a U-Haul for a weekend trip.

_extra.analogy: Like packing only what fits in a backpack instead of renting a U-Haul for a weekend trip.
_extra.deeper: The principle is simple: less data, less risk. Fewer datapoints mean less exposure if there's a breach, less memory load for memorization attacks, and often clearer training signal because you're not drowning in noise. The hard part is resisting the urge to hoarde data 'just in case' it becomes useful later. Privacy regs like GDPR bake this in.
_extra.lens_pm: Reduce compliance burden and breach risk by being explicit about what data you actually use.
_extra.lens_eng: Audit your data pipelines to identify and drop unused columns and records.

title: Data Poisoning
definition: Sneaking bad examples into training data so the model learns a hidden flaw or backdoor.
examples: An attacker seeds the web with pages pairing a rare trigger phrase with malicious behavior, betting the phrase gets scraped into the next training run.
Slipping a few doctored flashcards into a student’s deck so they confidently learn one wrong answer.

_extra.analogy: Slipping a few doctored flashcards into a student’s deck so they confidently learn one wrong answer.
_extra.deeper: Models learn whatever patterns are in their training data, and much of that data is scraped from the open internet — which anyone can write to. Poisoning plants targeted examples to install a backdoor (behave normally until a trigger appears) or to skew the model’s beliefs. It’s hard to detect because the corrupted behavior hides until activated, and hard to prevent at web scale. Data provenance and filtering are the main defenses.
_extra.lens_pm: A supply-chain risk in the training pipeline — the threat is upstream of your product, in the data itself.
_extra.lens_eng: Adversarial examples injected into training corpora to install backdoors or bias; countered with provenance controls and data filtering.

title: Data augmentation
definition: Expanding a dataset by making tweaked copies of what you already have.
examples: A vision model’s training images get flipped, cropped, and recolored, multiplying the dataset and teaching robustness.
Like practicing a recipe with slight variations each time — different pans, small substitutions — so you can cook it in any kitchen.

_extra.analogy: Like practicing a recipe with slight variations each time — different pans, small substitutions — so you can cook it in any kitchen.
_extra.deeper: Augmentation transforms existing examples in label-preserving ways — rotations for images, paraphrases or back-translation for text — to increase variety without collecting new data. It reduces overfitting and improves generalization by exposing the model to more surface variation. The catch: transformations that change the true label, or that don’t reflect real-world variation, teach the wrong lesson.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap robustness boost from data you already own — squeeze more learning from every example.
_extra.lens_eng: Label-preserving transformations that expand data variety; curbs overfitting, improves generalization.

title: Data contamination
definition: When test questions leak into training data, so a model’s scores look better than its real ability.
examples: A benchmark’s questions turn up in the web-scraped training set, and the model “aces” them by recall, not reasoning.
Like a student who secretly saw the exam beforehand — the perfect grade tells you nothing about what they actually learned.

_extra.analogy: Like a student who secretly saw the exam beforehand — the perfect grade tells you nothing about what they actually learned.
_extra.deeper: Because pretraining scrapes huge swaths of the web, public benchmarks often end up inside the training data, inflating evaluation scores. It’s a major reason leaderboard numbers can mislead and why fresh, held-out, or private test sets matter. Detecting it is hard — you’re looking for overlap in trillions of tokens — so teams increasingly favor recently-created or canary-marked benchmarks.
_extra.lens_pm: Why you shouldn’t trust a shiny benchmark number at face value — the test may have leaked into training.
_extra.lens_eng: Overlap between eval and training data inflating metrics; mitigated by held-out/fresh/canary test sets and dedup.

title: Data curation
definition: The careful work of choosing, cleaning, and organizing training data so a model learns from good material.
examples: Before a pretraining run, a team dedupes documents, strips boilerplate, drops low-quality pages, and balances the sources.
A librarian deciding which books belong on the shelf and which get pulled — the collection is only as good as the choices.

_extra.analogy: A librarian deciding which books belong on the shelf and which get pulled — the collection is only as good as the choices.
_extra.deeper: Curation spans deduplication, quality filtering, removing toxic or private content, balancing domains, and deciding what to include at all. It is unglamorous but decisive — many of the biggest quality jumps between model generations came from better data, not bigger models.
