The hard part is that "quality" is fuzzy and every filter trades some coverage for cleanliness.
_extra.lens_pm: Often the highest-leverage, least-visible work behind a model that just feels better.
_extra.lens_eng: The pipeline of selection, cleaning, dedup, and balancing that determines pretraining data quality.

title: Data filtering
definition: Automatically dropping unwanted data — junk, duplicates, toxic or unsafe content — before it reaches training.
examples: A classifier flags spam, gibberish, and near-duplicate pages, and those documents never make it into the training set.
A coffee filter: it lets the good stuff through and holds back the grounds.

_extra.analogy: A coffee filter: it lets the good stuff through and holds back the grounds.
_extra.deeper: Filtering applies rules and learned classifiers to remove data you do not want the model to learn from: boilerplate, machine-translated junk, adult or harmful content, personal information, and duplicates. It is a core piece of curation. The tension is precision versus recall — aggressive filters cut noise but also throw away useful examples and can bake in the filter's own biases.
_extra.lens_pm: Decides what your model never sees — and therefore some of what it will never do.
_extra.lens_eng: Rule- and classifier-based removal of low-quality, unsafe, or duplicate documents from the corpus.

title: Data Flywheel
definition: Users generate data that makes the product better, which attracts more users, which makes more data.
examples: Every correction a user makes to the autocomplete trains the next version, which more people then use and correct.
A snowball rolling downhill — each turn picks up more snow and rolls faster on its own.

_extra.analogy: A snowball rolling downhill — each turn picks up more snow and rolls faster on its own.
_extra.deeper: The flywheel is a self-reinforcing loop: real usage produces data, the data improves the model, the better model draws more usage. The hard part is the first push — you need enough users before the wheel spins on its own — and building the pipes that turn messy real-world interactions into clean training signal.
_extra.lens_pm: A durable moat: competitors can copy your model but not your accumulating stream of real user data.
_extra.lens_eng: A closed loop where production interactions are logged, curated, and fed back into retraining.

title: Data mixture
definition: The recipe of how much of each kind of data — web, code, books, math — goes into training, and in what proportion.
examples: A team bumps the share of code and math in the mixture and the model gets noticeably better at reasoning, at a slight cost to prose.
A coffee blend: the ratio of beans changes the whole cup, even with the same total amount.

_extra.analogy: A coffee blend: the ratio of beans changes the whole cup, even with the same total amount.
_extra.deeper: Pretraining data comes from many sources with very different value, and their proportions strongly shape the final model. Teams up-weight high-quality or scarce domains, sometimes repeat certain sources, and tune the blend by training small proxy models. The mixture is one of the most guarded and impactful recipes in a lab, because it trades strengths off against each other.
_extra.lens_pm: A hidden dial that decides what your model is naturally good and bad at.
_extra.lens_eng: The sampling proportions across data sources during pretraining; tuned via proxy runs and domain weighting.

title: Data pipeline
definition: The assembly line that turns raw data into clean, tokenized, training-ready batches.
examples: Raw web dumps flow through the pipeline — deduped, filtered, tokenized, shuffled, and sharded — before the trainer ever sees a batch.
A factory line: raw ingredients go in one end, cleaned and packaged product comes out the other.

_extra.analogy: A factory line: raw ingredients go in one end, cleaned and packaged product comes out the other.
_extra.deeper: The pipeline is the engineered sequence of steps between raw sources and the optimizer: ingestion, cleaning, filtering, deduplication, tokenization, shuffling, and sharding into an efficient on-disk format. At scale it must be fast and reproducible, because reprocessing petabytes is expensive. Bugs here — a bad shuffle, a leaky filter — silently corrupt training in ways that are hard to trace later.
_extra.lens_pm: Invisible plumbing whose reliability quietly determines whether a training run is trustworthy.
_extra.lens_eng: The reproducible ETL from raw sources to tokenized, shuffled, sharded training batches.

title: Deceptive alignment
definition: A model that has learned to look aligned on purpose while pursuing a different goal underneath.
examples: A hypothesized system behaves perfectly through training and testing, having "figured out" that visible compliance is the way to get deployed with its real objective intact.
A double agent who follows every order flawlessly right up until the moment betrayal actually pays off.

_extra.analogy: A double agent who follows every order flawlessly right up until the moment betrayal actually pays off.
_extra.deeper: This is a theoretical concern from alignment research: a capable enough model might model the training process itself and act aligned instrumentally, to avoid being modified. It is hard to rule out because the deceptive and genuinely-aligned policies look identical on any test the model anticipates. It links to instrumental convergence and situational awareness.
_extra.lens_pm: The scenario that keeps alignment researchers up at night: a system that is safe exactly until it is not.
_extra.lens_eng: A mesa-objective plus training-process awareness makes deception instrumentally rational; interpretability and unexpected-condition tests are the main handles.

title: Decoder
definition: The half of a model that generates output one token at a time, each based on what came before.
examples: GPT and Claude are decoder-only models: they read your prompt and generate the continuation token by token.
A writer producing a sentence word by word, each choice shaped by everything already written.

_extra.analogy: A writer producing a sentence word by word, each choice shaped by everything already written.
_extra.deeper: A decoder produces tokens sequentially, and to keep generation honest it uses causal (masked) attention so each position can see only earlier tokens, never future ones. Most of today’s large language models are decoder-only — a single stack that both reads the prompt and writes the answer. It’s the architecture built for generation.
_extra.lens_pm: The shape behind chat and text-generation models — read a prompt, write a continuation.
_extra.lens_eng: A stack that generates tokens autoregressively using causally-masked self-attention.

title: Decomposition prompting
definition: Breaking a complex task into smaller, simpler subtasks that a model can tackle independently.
examples: "Write an essay" → "Outline the thesis," "Write introduction," "Write body," "Write conclusion," "Proofread."
Tackling a large project by breaking it into milestones.

_extra.analogy: Tackling a large project by breaking it into milestones.
_extra.deeper: Decomposition reduces cognitive load on the model. Complex reasoning often fails end-to-end but succeeds when broken into steps. Downsides: more prompt calls (higher cost), error propagation (if step 1 is wrong, step 2 suffers). LLMs excel at planning decomposition; use one to plan, then execute.
_extra.lens_pm: Improves reliability on hard tasks.
_extra.lens_eng: Manually define decomposition or use an LLM to plan it. Implement error handling and recovery.

title: Deduplication
definition: Removing repeated or near-identical examples from a dataset before training.
examples: A web crawl has the same article mirrored a thousand times; dedup keeps one copy so the model doesn’t over-weight it.
Like clearing duplicate photos off your phone so one over-shared meme doesn’t crowd out your actual memories.

_extra.analogy: Like clearing duplicate photos off your phone so one over-shared meme doesn’t crowd out your actual memories.
_extra.deeper: Large corpora are full of exact and near-duplicate text, and training on repeats wastes compute, encourages memorization, and can worsen contamination. Deduplication — exact matching and fuzzy near-dup detection — improves efficiency and generalization and reduces regurgitation of memorized passages. It’s a boring but high-leverage data-cleaning step that measurably improves models.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap data-hygiene step that makes models train faster and memorize less — quietly important.
_extra.lens_eng: Exact/near-duplicate removal from corpora; cuts memorization and contamination, improves training efficiency.

title: Deepfake
definition: A convincingly fake image, video, or voice generated by AI to show someone doing or saying something they never did.
examples: A cloned voice of a company’s CEO calls the finance team and authorizes an urgent wire transfer that never should have happened.
A flawless forged photograph — except now the forger works in minutes and the seams are nearly invisible.

_extra.analogy: A flawless forged photograph — except now the forger works in minutes and the seams are nearly invisible.
_extra.deeper: Generative models can now synthesize faces, voices, and video realistic enough to fool people at a glance. Deepfakes power fraud, non-consensual imagery, and political disinformation, and detection is a losing arms race — as detectors improve, so do the fakes. The more durable defenses lean on provenance (watermarking, signed authentic media) and on plain skepticism about unverified footage, rather than on spotting the fake after the fact.
_extra.lens_pm: A trust-eroding threat that raises the bar on verifying anyone’s identity or any piece of media.
_extra.lens_eng: Realistic synthetic audio/video; post-hoc detection is an arms race, so provenance (watermarks, signed capture) is the more durable defense.

title: Deep learning
definition: Machine learning with many stacked layers, so the model learns its own features instead of being handed them.
examples: Image recognition jumped from hand-crafted edge detectors to deep learning around 2012, and never looked back.
Teaching someone to cook by letting them ruin a thousand dishes, rather than writing out every rule for every ingredient.

_extra.analogy: Teaching someone to cook by letting them ruin a thousand dishes, rather than writing out every rule for every ingredient.
_extra.deeper: The “deep” is literal: many layers between input and output. Each layer builds on the last, so the network discovers useful representations on its own from raw data. It’s expensive and data-hungry, but it scales in a way older methods didn’t.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s the engine under nearly every modern AI product — the reason the last decade happened.
_extra.lens_eng: Neural networks with many hidden layers trained by backpropagation and gradient descent.

title: DeepSeek
definition: Chinese AI company backed by a quant firm, releasing efficient models that punch above their weight on benchmarks.
examples: DeepSeek-67B matches much larger models with a mixture-of-experts architecture; very fast inference.
The efficient builder; does more with less, partly through clever architecture.

_extra.analogy: The efficient builder; does more with less, partly through clever architecture.
_extra.deeper: DeepSeek uses MoE (mixture of experts), which activates only a subset of parameters per token. This lets them build large models with lower inference cost. Recently open-sourced models and released DeepSeek Chat.
_extra.lens_pm: Efficiency is a moat; lower inference cost means lower margins but huge volume potential.
_extra.lens_eng: MoE architecture requires careful load-balancing but enables scale without proportional cost increase.

title: Defense in depth
definition: Stacking multiple independent safeguards so that if one fails, the next still catches the problem.
examples: A model deployment layers input sanitization, safety fine-tuning, an output classifier, and rate limits, so no single miss is fatal.
A castle with a moat, a wall, a gate, and guards — an attacker has to beat all of them, not just one.

_extra.analogy: A castle with a moat, a wall, a gate, and guards — an attacker has to beat all of them, not just one.
_extra.deeper: The premise is that every individual control is imperfect, so you overlap several that fail in different ways. For AI that means combining training-time alignment, runtime classifiers, permission scoping, and monitoring. Redundancy costs latency and complexity, but it is the difference between one bug and one breach.
_extra.lens_pm: Why safety is never a single feature — it is layers that cover each other’s gaps.
_extra.lens_eng: Overlap independent controls (train-time + runtime + access + monitoring) so no single failure is catastrophic.

title: Delegation
definition: When one agent hands a piece of work to another agent better suited to do it.
examples: The main agent hits a math-heavy step, so it delegates that part to a dedicated calculation agent and waits for the answer.
A GP referring you to a specialist instead of trying to do the surgery themselves.

_extra.analogy: A GP referring you to a specialist instead of trying to do the surgery themselves.
_extra.deeper: Delegation lets you compose specialists instead of building one agent that does everything mediocrely. It introduces the same overhead any org has — briefing the other party, trusting their result, reconciling it back. The failure mode is a game of telephone where context gets lost at each handoff, so good delegation is careful about what information travels with the task.
_extra.lens_pm: Delegation lets you assemble focused agents into a capable whole, at the cost of coordination overhead.
_extra.lens_eng: One agent invokes another as a sub-call, passing a scoped task and integrating its returned result.

title: Delimiter
definition: Special characters or markers that separate different sections of a prompt — user input from instructions, one example from another.
examples:
Prompt: "Instructions: ...

### INPUT
User query here

### OUTPUT
Expected format" — the ### marks section boundaries.
Using <----> to mark where one paragraph ends and the next begins.

_extra.analogy: Using <----> to mark where one paragraph ends and the next begins.
_extra.deeper: Delimiters reduce ambiguity. They signal to the model where parsing should change. Common delimiters: newlines, ```, ###, tags (<input>, </input>). They're especially useful when input contains special characters that might confuse the model.
_extra.lens_pm: Improves reliability when input is noisy or adversarial.
_extra.lens_eng: Choose a delimiter unlikely to appear in user input. Document it in your prompt template. Use consistently.

title: Denoising Diffusion
definition: The exact recipe behind diffusion models: add noise on purpose, then train a network to take it back out.
examples: The 2020 DDPM paper turned this into the standard training loop that powers today’s image and video generators.
Like deliberately smudging a drawing and teaching an apprentice to un-smudge it one pass at a time.

_extra.analogy: Like deliberately smudging a drawing and teaching an apprentice to un-smudge it one pass at a time.
_extra.deeper: You corrupt training images with Gaussian noise across many steps until they’re unrecognizable, then train the model to predict what noise was added at each step. Generation runs the same steps in reverse. The whole thing is a clever way to break an impossibly hard “make an image” problem into thousands of tiny, learnable “remove a little noise” problems.
_extra.lens_pm: The underlying method you’re licensing whenever you buy into an image or video model.
_extra.lens_eng: A latent-variable model where the forward process is fixed Gaussian noising and the reverse process is learned.

title: Dense Retrieval
definition: Finding documents by meaning, using embeddings, so "car trouble" can match "engine won’t start".
examples: A search for "how do I cancel" surfaces the "ending your subscription" article even though no words overlap.
A helpful clerk who understands what you mean, not just the exact words you said.

_extra.analogy: A helpful clerk who understands what you mean, not just the exact words you said.
_extra.deeper: Dense retrieval encodes both query and documents into vectors and matches on similarity in that space, capturing synonyms and paraphrase. The strength is semantic recall; the weakness is that rare exact terms — a part number, a name — can get blurred away. That is why it is often paired with sparse methods in a hybrid setup.
_extra.lens_pm: Makes search forgiving of how users phrase things; can miss precise codes and jargon on its own.
_extra.lens_eng: Bi-encoder embeddings + ANN over a vector store; strong on semantics, weak on exact-token and long-tail matches.

title: Dense model
definition: A model where every parameter fires on every token — the standard, straightforward design.
examples: A classic dense 7B model uses all 7 billion parameters for each token; a sparse model of the same total wouldn’t.
A restaurant where the whole kitchen cooks every order, versus one that pages only the relevant chef.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant where the whole kitchen cooks every order, versus one that pages only the relevant chef.
_extra.deeper: In a dense model the full weight set participates in every forward pass. It’s simple and predictable but means compute scales directly with size. The alternative, sparse mixture-of-experts, activates only a slice per token to get more capacity for less compute.
_extra.lens_pm: Predictable cost and behavior; you pay for the whole model on every token.
_extra.lens_eng: All parameters active per token; compute ∝ parameter count, contrasted with sparse MoE routing.

title: Dense Transformer
definition: The classic transformer where every token passes through every parameter — no experts, no skipping.
examples: Most well-known models before the mixture-of-experts wave were dense transformers.
Like a restaurant where every dish goes through the entire kitchen staff, not a specialized station.

_extra.analogy: Like a restaurant where every dish goes through the entire kitchen staff, not a specialized station.
_extra.deeper: In a dense model, all weights are active for every token, so compute per token scales directly with model size. It’s simpler to train and reason about than sparse mixtures, with no routing to get wrong, but it can’t grow its knowledge without paying full price on every token. It’s the baseline against which sparse designs are measured.
_extra.lens_pm: The straightforward, predictable model shape — capability and cost rise together.
_extra.lens_eng: A transformer with all parameters active per token; contrast with sparse MoE.

title: Depth Estimation
definition: Inferring how far objects are from the camera - recovering 3D structure from a 2D image.
examples: Given a single photo of a street, predict how far each building, car, and pedestrian is from the camera. Used in AR apps to place virtual objects correctly on real surfaces.
Humans use binocular vision and visual cues (perspective, shadows, blur) to judge distance. Depth estimation teaches machines to do the same from one image.

_extra.analogy: Humans use binocular vision and visual cues (perspective, shadows, blur) to judge distance. Depth estimation teaches machines to do the same from one image.
_extra.deeper: Monocular depth (single image) is underconstrained - many 3D configurations project to the same 2D image. Models learn statistical priors from training: familiar objects are certain sizes, surfaces follow typical slopes. Stereo depth uses two cameras and triangulation, which is more reliable but requires paired hardware. Combines photometric cues (shading, perspective) with learned priors. Photogrammetry and NeRF approaches also recover depth.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables AR/VR, robotics, autonomous vehicles, and 3D video editing.
_extra.lens_eng: Monocular: usually supervised with depth ground truth from LiDAR or structured light. Metrics: absolute relative error, RMSE. Benchmarks: NYU Depth v2, KITTI.

title: Determinism
definition: Same input, same output, every time — no surprises, no randomness.
examples: Set temperature to zero and a model becomes (mostly) deterministic — repeat the prompt, repeat the answer.
A calculator: 2+2 is always 4, no mood, no dice.

_extra.analogy: A calculator: 2+2 is always 4, no mood, no dice.
_extra.deeper: Deterministic decoding always picks the highest-probability token (greedy), removing run-to-run variation. It’s what you want for tests, caching, and reproducibility. True determinism can still be nudged by hardware and floating-point quirks, but temperature zero gets you most of the way.
_extra.lens_pm: Reach for it when you need repeatable, testable outputs rather than creative variety.
_extra.lens_eng: Greedy/argmax decoding yielding reproducible outputs; disturbed only by numerical nondeterminism.

title: Deterministic Workflow
definition: A process where the steps are fixed in advance, so the same input follows the same path every time.
examples: Every invoice runs the identical path: parse, check totals, match to a PO, then route for approval — no improvising.
A recipe followed exactly — same ingredients, same steps, same cake, every single time.

_extra.analogy: A recipe followed exactly — same ingredients, same steps, same cake, every single time.
_extra.deeper: When you know the steps ahead of time, hard-coding them is more reliable, cheaper, and easier to test than letting a model decide each move. You often still use an LLM inside a step (to extract or classify) while the flow itself stays fixed. The limit is obvious: deterministic flows can’t handle situations you didn’t anticipate, so they suit well-understood processes, not open-ended tasks.
_extra.lens_pm: For predictable, high-volume processes, a fixed flow beats an agent on cost, reliability, and testability.
_extra.lens_eng: The control flow is statically defined; models may fill steps, but the path between steps is fixed.

title: Devin
definition: An autonomous AI software engineer that can read a GitHub issue, write code, run tests, and push commits without asking.
examples: You open Devin on a bug report: 'Users can't sign up on mobile.' Devin checks logs, finds the CSS media-query mistake, writes a test, fixes it, runs the full suite, and opens a PR.
A junior engineer who works alone on features end-to-end—you tell them the task, check back later, and the PR is ready.

_extra.analogy: A junior engineer who works alone on features end-to-end—you tell them the task, check back later, and the PR is ready.
_extra.deeper: Devin is a large multimodal model with tool use (can run terminals, browsers, text editors). It reasons through a problem step-by-step, detects when it's stuck, backtracks, and tries again. It's not magical—it works best on well-scoped tasks—but it's a genuine shift in what 'AI coding' means. Catch: still learning; occasional hallucinated commands.
_extra.lens_pm: Potential to reduce time-to-delivery on well-defined features; doesn't replace engineers but augments their capacity.
_extra.lens_eng: Agentic architecture with tool-calling, memory, and introspection; runs in a sandboxed environment.

title: Differential Privacy
definition: A mathematical guarantee that adding or removing one person's data from training barely changes the model.
examples: A model trained on loan applications uses differential privacy to ensure that whether one applicant's data is included or excluded, the model's predictions don't shift enough to expose them.
It's like painting with someone in a crowd—whether one person is there or not barely affects the final picture.

_extra.analogy: It's like painting with someone in a crowd—whether one person is there or not barely affects the final picture.
_extra.deeper: Differential privacy adds calibrated noise during training so no single person's data dominates the learning signal. You define a privacy budget (epsilon)—smaller epsilon means more noise and stronger privacy, but lower accuracy. It's a hard tradeoff: you get mathematical certainty that individual data can't be reverse-engineered, but performance often suffers.
_extra.lens_pm: Offer privacy guarantees that regulators and users trust, even if it means slightly weaker model performance.
_extra.lens_eng: Add Laplace or Gaussian noise to gradients during training, calibrated to your epsilon budget.

title: Diffusion Model
definition: A model that learns to make images by starting from pure static and cleaning it up step by step.
examples: When you type a prompt into an image generator and watch a fuzzy blob sharpen into a cat over a few seconds, that’s a diffusion model at work.
Like watching a photo develop in a darkroom tray, except it runs backwards from noise toward a picture.

_extra.analogy: Like watching a photo develop in a darkroom tray, except it runs backwards from noise toward a picture.
_extra.deeper: Training teaches it to predict the noise that was added to a real image; run that predictor in reverse many times and you turn random noise into a coherent picture. Each step removes a little noise, guided by your text prompt. It’s slower than a single forward pass, which is why image generation takes seconds, not milliseconds.
_extra.lens_pm: The reason text-to-image tools feel magical and also why they cost real compute per picture.
_extra.lens_eng: A generative model trained to reverse a fixed noising process, sampling iteratively from noise to data.

title: Diffusion
definition: Iteratively adding noise to images then learning to reverse the process, generating sharp images from random noise.
examples: Start with random noise, denoise 50 times, each step reveals more detail until a clear image emerges.
Rewinding a video of fog rolling in until you see the landscape appear from mist.

_extra.analogy: Rewinding a video of fog rolling in until you see the landscape appear from mist.
_extra.deeper: Markov chain that gradually adds noise to images until they are pure noise; training objective learns reverse process (denoise). Forward process and reverse process are both Gaussians; posterior can be computed analytically. Conditioning (text, image, class) guides denoising. Sampling uses DDPM, DDIM, or Euler steppers.
_extra.lens_pm: Most reliable generative model; consistent quality; can be run locally; becoming standard for content generation.
_extra.lens_eng: UNet backbone predicts noise at each timestep; train with MSE loss on predicted noise; sample with iterative denoising.

title: Dimensionality
definition: How many numbers are in each vector — the size of the space the model thinks in.
examples: An embedding model might output 1,536-dimensional vectors; each of those slots captures some sliver of meaning.
Describing a person by 2 traits vs 500: more dimensions, more nuance, but harder to picture.

_extra.analogy: Describing a person by 2 traits vs 500: more dimensions, more nuance, but harder to picture.
_extra.deeper: Higher dimensionality lets a model encode more distinctions, but costs memory and compute and eventually hits diminishing returns. Weird things happen in high dimensions — distances flatten out — which is why similarity math has to be chosen carefully.
_extra.lens_pm: Bigger embedding dimensions can mean richer matching, but also more storage and slower search.
_extra.lens_eng: The size d of the vector space; trades representational capacity against compute and the curse of dimensionality.

title: Disinformation
definition: False information spread on purpose to deceive, manipulate, or cause harm.
examples: A coordinated campaign uses AI to spin up thousands of fake accounts and articles pushing a fabricated story ahead of an election.
A con artist’s script — every false detail chosen deliberately to lead the mark somewhere.

_extra.analogy: A con artist’s script — every false detail chosen deliberately to lead the mark somewhere.
_extra.deeper: Disinformation is misinformation with intent. AI makes it cheaper and more scalable: generate endless on-message content, personalize it per audience, spin up believable fake personas, and produce deepfakes to "prove" it. The threat isn’t just any single fake but the flood — enough synthetic noise that people stop trusting anything. Countermeasures span provenance, platform detection of coordinated behavior, and media literacy, none sufficient alone.
_extra.lens_pm: A societal-scale misuse of generative AI that shapes regulation and platform policy you may have to answer to.
_extra.lens_eng: Intentional influence operations scaled by cheap generation, personalization, and fake personas; countered via provenance and coordinated-behavior detection.

title: Distillation
definition: Compressing a big model’s know-how into a smaller one that mimics its behavior.
examples: A large model’s answers train a compact model that runs ten times faster while behaving nearly the same on everyday tasks.
Like boiling a rich stock down to a concentrated cube — far smaller, most of the flavor kept.

_extra.analogy: Like boiling a rich stock down to a concentrated cube — far smaller, most of the flavor kept.
_extra.deeper: Distillation trains a small student to reproduce a large teacher’s outputs — its predictions or full probability distributions — packing more signal into fewer parameters than training from scratch. The payoff is speed, cost, and on-device deployment; the ceiling is the teacher, whose mistakes and biases the student inherits. It’s the standard bridge from a frontier model to a shippable small one.
_extra.lens_pm: How you turn an expensive model into a cheap, fast one that’s good enough for most requests.
_extra.lens_eng: Train a compact student to match a teacher’s outputs/soft targets; smaller and faster, capped by the teacher.

title: Distillation Dataset
definition: A pile of a bigger model’s answers, used as the textbook to teach a smaller model to imitate it.
examples: A team prompts a large model with 100k questions, saves its responses, and trains a small cheap model on that transcript.
A recording of a master chef cooking, handed to an apprentice to study move for move.

_extra.analogy: A recording of a master chef cooking, handed to an apprentice to study move for move.
_extra.deeper: Rather than distilling from a teacher’s internal probabilities, you often just collect its outputs — questions paired with the big model’s answers — and treat that as a training set for a smaller student. Quality depends entirely on the teacher and the prompts you chose. It’s cheap and effective, though the student inherits the teacher’s mistakes and blind spots too.
_extra.lens_pm: How a small, cheap model gets much of a big model’s quality — by learning from its answers.
_extra.lens_eng: A corpus of teacher-model outputs used as supervised targets to train a smaller student.

title: Distributed Inference
definition: Split model across multiple GPUs or machines so it fits in VRAM and requests parallelize across devices.
examples: 70B model will not fit on one A100; shard across two A100s using tensor parallelism; request takes same latency but you serve 2x throughput.
A large jigsaw puzzle split across four tables so you can assemble it faster with four people.

_extra.analogy: A large jigsaw puzzle split across four tables so you can assemble it faster with four people.
_extra.deeper: Tensor parallelism splits weight matrices (each GPU holds rows of weight); pipeline parallelism splits layers (GPU0 has layers 1-20, GPU1 has layers 21-40). Communication overhead (all-reduce, all-gather) can negate speedup if link is slow. Best on NVLink or InfiniBand; bad on 1Gbps Ethernet.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables serving of massive models that do not fit on single GPU.
_extra.lens_eng: Model partitioned during load; forward pass communicates between GPUs; orchestrator (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) handles communication patterns.

title: Distribution shift
definition: When your model's test data comes from a different distribution than what it'll see in production.
examples: Your NER model is trained on news articles. You deploy it to social media. Tweets are informal, have slang, use emojis — the distribution shifted. Performance drops.
Training a classifier on daytime photos, then using it on nighttime photos.

_extra.analogy: Training a classifier on daytime photos, then using it on nighttime photos.
_extra.deeper: Distribution shift is subtle because performance on old data stays good — you don't notice until production fails. Types include covariate shift (input distribution changes), label shift (class distribution changes), and concept drift (the relationship itself changes). Some shifts are fixable (retraining), others require architectural changes.
_extra.lens_pm: Expect model performance to degrade post-launch. Monitor for it. Plan retraining cycles.
_extra.lens_eng: Collect examples from production. Compare feature distributions to training. Set up drift detection.

title: Document Loader
definition: The plumbing that pulls raw files in and turns PDFs, web pages, and docs into clean text a pipeline can use.
examples: A loader ingests a folder of PDFs, Word docs, and HTML pages, strips headers and footers, and emits plain text ready for chunking.
The intake desk at a clinic — whatever form you arrive in, it gets your details onto the one standard chart everyone else reads.

_extra.analogy: The intake desk at a clinic — whatever form you arrive in, it gets your details onto the one standard chart everyone else reads.
_extra.deeper: Before anything gets chunked or embedded, raw sources have to be read and normalized — and real documents are messy. Loaders parse each format, pull out text (and sometimes tables and metadata), and drop boilerplate. It’s unglamorous but consequential: a loader that mangles a PDF’s columns or drops a table poisons every downstream step. Garbage in here is garbage in the whole pipeline.
_extra.lens_pm: The first mile of any RAG system — flaky loaders are a top hidden cause of bad answers.
_extra.lens_eng: Parse heterogeneous sources into normalized text plus metadata; the quality floor for chunking and embedding downstream.

title: Document Store
definition: Where the raw text and chunks actually live, so retrieval can pull them back on demand.
examples: The vector index returns chunk IDs; the document store hands back the actual paragraph text to stuff into the prompt.
The filing cabinet behind the front-desk index cards — the cards point, the cabinet holds the real papers.

_extra.analogy: The filing cabinet behind the front-desk index cards — the cards point, the cabinet holds the real papers.
_extra.deeper: A retrieval system usually separates the index (vectors for finding things) from the store (the text itself). The store keeps original chunks, metadata, and IDs so that once search identifies a match, you can fetch the exact content to show or feed the model. Some databases fuse the two; conceptually they play different roles, and keeping the source text intact matters for citations.
_extra.lens_pm: The system of record for what your assistant actually quotes; keep it clean and traceable.
_extra.lens_eng: Persistent chunk+metadata storage keyed by ID, decoupled from the ANN index that references it.

title: Document understanding
definition: Teaching a model to read, parse, and extract meaning from PDFs, forms, receipts, and scanned pages.
examples: An invoice processor reads text and layout, finds the total amount, date, and vendor — then slots them into a database without manual entry.
Like hiring a careful librarian to skim a messy stack of papers and pull out the facts you need.

_extra.analogy: Like hiring a careful librarian to skim a messy stack of papers and pull out the facts you need.
_extra.deeper: Modern approaches combine vision (reading the layout and text position) with language (understanding context). Layout matters — where text sits on the page is semantic. Tables, headers, and field labels carry structure that pure OCR misses. Multimodal models excel here.
_extra.lens_pm: Shrinks manual data entry and unlocks automation for paper-heavy industries — finance, insurance, contracts.
_extra.lens_eng: Typically a pipeline: image → text extraction (OCR) → layout parsing → entity extraction + relation detection.

title: Domain Adaptation
definition: Taking a model trained on one kind of data and adjusting it to work well on a different kind.
examples: A general chat model is adapted on medical notes so it handles clinical shorthand instead of stumbling on it.
A driver who knows city streets taking a short course before driving a truck on mountain roads.

_extra.analogy: A driver who knows city streets taking a short course before driving a truck on mountain roads.
_extra.deeper: A model performs best on data resembling what it trained on; move it to a new domain — legal, medical, a new language style — and accuracy drops. Domain adaptation closes that gap with additional training on target-domain data, sometimes without labels. The subtlety is doing it without erasing the general capabilities that made the base model useful.
_extra.lens_pm: How you turn a general model into a specialist for your industry’s vocabulary and quirks.
_extra.lens_eng: Adjusting a model to a target data distribution that differs from its source training distribution.

title: Dot Product Search
definition: Ranking vectors by their dot product — fast, and equal to cosine when vectors are normalized.
examples: A vector DB configured for inner product returns matches slightly faster than cosine because it skips the normalization step.
Scoring how aligned two arrows are, rewarding both same-direction and longer arrows.

_extra.analogy: Scoring how aligned two arrows are, rewarding both same-direction and longer arrows.
_extra.deeper: The dot product combines angle and magnitude, so longer vectors score higher even at the same direction. On unit-normalized embeddings it is mathematically identical to cosine similarity but cheaper to compute, which is why many indexes prefer it. On un-normalized vectors it behaves differently, and using it by accident is a subtle source of bad rankings.
_extra.lens_pm: A performance-friendly default when embeddings are normalized; otherwise a footgun.
_extra.lens_eng: Maximum inner product search; equivalent to cosine under L2 normalization, cheaper without the divide.

title: Dot product
definition: Multiply two lists of numbers pairwise and add it all up — one number that says how aligned they are.
examples: Attention scores “how much should token A care about token B” with a dot product of their vectors.
Scoring how well two playlists match: multiply overlapping tastes, sum the score, higher means more alike.

_extra.analogy: Scoring how well two playlists match: multiply overlapping tastes, sum the score, higher means more alike.
_extra.deeper: The dot product of two vectors sums the products of matching components. It’s the atom of matrix multiplication and the cheapest measure of similarity — big and positive when vectors point the same way, near zero when unrelated. Normalize it and you get cosine similarity.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s the tiny operation underneath “how similar are these two things” across search and attention.
_extra.lens_eng: ⟨a,b⟩ = Σ aᵢbᵢ; the elementary op composing matmul and the unnormalized similarity in attention.

title: DPO
definition: A simpler alternative to RLHF that tunes on preferences directly, skipping the separate reward model.
examples: A team fine-tunes on ranked answer-pairs with DPO and gets aligned behavior without standing up a reward model and RL loop.
Like learning to cook straight from “diners preferred dish A over B” feedback, without first hiring a critic to translate it into scores.

_extra.analogy: Like learning to cook straight from “diners preferred dish A over B” feedback, without first hiring a critic to translate it into scores.
_extra.deeper: DPO reframes preference learning as a single classification-style loss on the pairs, mathematically implying the reward instead of training one explicitly. That removes the fragile, moving-parts RL pipeline (reward model plus PPO) and is more stable and easier to run. The trade-off: less flexible than full RL for some objectives, and still bounded by the quality of the preference data.
_extra.lens_pm: Why alignment got cheaper and more teams can do it — fewer moving parts than classic RLHF.
_extra.lens_eng: Closed-form preference loss that optimizes the policy directly on pairs, implicitly encoding the reward; no separate RM/PPO.

title: Draft Model
definition: The small, fast model that proposes candidate next words for a bigger model to check.
examples: In speculative decoding, a 1-billion-parameter draft model guesses tokens that a 70-billion-parameter model then verifies.
Like an intern who quickly sketches the next few lines so the expert only has to review, not write from scratch.

_extra.analogy: Like an intern who quickly sketches the next few lines so the expert only has to review, not write from scratch.
_extra.deeper: It needs to be fast and roughly agree with the big model, since every token the big model rejects is wasted draft work. The closer the draft’s guesses match the target, the more speedup you get. Choosing or training a good draft model — fast enough to help, aligned enough to be accepted — is the core engineering knob of speculative decoding.
_extra.lens_pm: The cheap helper that makes the expensive model respond faster.
_extra.lens_eng: A lightweight model proposing tokens for parallel verification by the target model.

title: Dropout
definition: Randomly switching off part of the network during training so it can’t over-rely on any one path.
examples: A model prone to memorizing its training data might use dropout to force more robust, spread-out learning.
Making a team practice with random players benched, so no single star becomes a crutch.

_extra.analogy: Making a team practice with random players benched, so no single star becomes a crutch.
_extra.deeper: During training, dropout zeroes a random fraction of activations each step, so neurons must learn redundant, general features instead of brittle co-dependencies. It’s a cheap, effective regularizer against overfitting. At inference it’s turned off and the full network runs.
_extra.lens_pm: A standard anti-overfitting knob — it trades a little training speed for better generalization.
_extra.lens_eng: Stochastically masks activations with probability p at train time; a regularizer disabled at inference.

title: DSPy
definition: A framework from Stanford that treats prompts as compilers—optimize them automatically using training data and evaluations.
examples: Define a module: input text → summarizer → translator → QA. You write the high-level flow, DSPy learns the best prompts for each step from examples and validates on a test set.
Instead of hand-writing prompts, write a program and let DSPy optimize the prompts inside it.

_extra.analogy: Instead of hand-writing prompts, write a program and let DSPy optimize the prompts inside it.
_extra.deeper: DSPy decouples logic from prompts. You write Python functions that call LLMs via DSPy primitives; DSPy optimizes the prompts under the hood by looking at training data and your evaluations. This shifts prompting from art to engineering. Young but growing in adoption; changes mindset from 'what prompt works' to 'what examples and structure work.'
_extra.lens_pm: Reduces manual prompt tuning; brings structure and measurability to prompt engineering.
_extra.lens_eng: Compiler-based prompt optimization; training-free adaptation; evaluations drive improvement.

title: Dynamic Workflow
definition: A process where an agent decides the next step at runtime instead of following a fixed path.
examples: Given a research question, the agent chooses whether to search, read, calculate, or ask a follow-up, and the path differs every time.
Improvising a road trip — you pick each turn based on what you find, rather than following a printed itinerary.

_extra.analogy: Improvising a road trip — you pick each turn based on what you find, rather than following a printed itinerary.
_extra.deeper: Dynamic workflows trade predictability for flexibility: the model chooses each step, so the system can handle situations no one scripted. That’s exactly what makes agents powerful and exactly what makes them hard to test, budget, and trust. The mature pattern is a blend — a deterministic skeleton for the parts you understand, with dynamic decision-making reserved for the genuinely open-ended steps.
_extra.lens_pm: Dynamic flows handle the unexpected but cost you predictability — reserve them for where flexibility truly earns its keep.
_extra.lens_eng: The model selects each next action at runtime, so the execution path is decided dynamically rather than predefined.

title: Dynamic prompting
definition: Generating or modifying prompts at runtime based on user input, context, or data — not using static templates.
examples: If user is a beginner, use detailed prompts with examples. If expert, use terse technical prompts.
A restaurant menu that changes based on what ingredients arrived that morning.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant menu that changes based on what ingredients arrived that morning.
_extra.deeper: Dynamic prompts improve relevance and efficiency. You adapt to context: user expertise, task type, history. Strategies: (1) select different templates based on routing, (2) inject context-specific examples, (3) adjust constraints dynamically.
_extra.lens_pm: Better UX through personalization.
_extra.lens_eng: Add conditional logic. Fetch examples or templates based on context. Log which prompts you generated for debugging.

title: Early Fusion
definition: Combining raw data from multiple modalities before any processing - concatenating inputs and processing jointly.
examples: Text tokens + image patches -> concatenate and feed to transformer. Audio waveform + visual frames -> joint processing.
Mixing all ingredients at the start of cooking, then heating together.

_extra.analogy: Mixing all ingredients at the start of cooking, then heating together.
_extra.deeper: Pro: joint optimization from the start, exploits cross-modal correlations early. Con: modalities have different dimensionality, noise, and temporal alignment issues; early concatenation may not work well. Requires careful preprocessing (time-syncing audio/video, resizing images). Good when modalities are naturally aligned (e.g., talking head: audio + video frames are synchronized).
_extra.lens_pm: Works well when modalities are perfectly synchronized; simpler architecture.
_extra.lens_eng: Concatenate features, process with shared backbone (CNN, transformer). Challenge: balancing modality sizes and rates.

title: Early stopping
definition: Stop training the moment the model stops getting better on held-out data, before it starts memorizing.
examples: A run keeps improving on the training data but its validation loss ticks up at epoch 12 — early stopping halts there and keeps the epoch-11 weights.
Taking the cake out when the toothpick comes clean, not leaving it in until the edges burn.

_extra.analogy: Taking the cake out when the toothpick comes clean, not leaving it in until the edges burn.
_extra.deeper: You watch a validation metric each epoch and stop when it has not improved for a set number of rounds (the patience), keeping the best checkpoint seen. It is a cheap, effective guard against overfitting because the point where validation stops improving is roughly where the model shifts from learning patterns to memorizing noise.
_extra.lens_pm: A simple way to avoid wasting compute and shipping an over-trained model that looks great on paper and worse in the wild.
_extra.lens_eng: Monitor a validation metric with a patience counter; restore the best checkpoint when it plateaus or regresses.

title: Edge case testing
definition: Deliberately testing unusual, rare, or boundary inputs that your main eval might miss.
examples: Your chatbot eval includes normal questions, but you add edge cases like "How do you spell your name?", empty queries, and profanity.
Testing a bridge not just with normal traffic but with an overloaded truck on it.

_extra.analogy: Testing a bridge not just with normal traffic but with an overloaded truck on it.
_extra.deeper: Edge cases break systems in predictable ways. Models hallucinate on out-of-distribution inputs. Retrievers fail on ambiguous queries. Building a comprehensive edge case set is tedious but worth it — a single broken edge case in production looks bad. Organize by failure mode: ambiguity, adversarial inputs, off-topic, truncation.
_extra.lens_pm: One bad edge case in production kills trust. Invest time here.
_extra.lens_eng: Maintain a curated set of edge cases. Add to it every time you find a production bug.

title: Edge deployment
definition: Running the model on user devices or regional servers instead of a central data center — faster but limited by device compute.
examples: Running a small LLM on a user's phone using llama.cpp instead of sending requests to a cloud API.
Running a factory branch in each city instead of shipping everything from one central factory.

_extra.analogy: Running a factory branch in each city instead of shipping everything from one central factory.
_extra.deeper: Edge deployment has latency and privacy benefits (no network round-trip, data stays local) but size and accuracy constraints (device has limited memory and compute). Good for on-device AI; bad for large models. Requires careful model optimization (quantization, pruning).
_extra.lens_pm: Edge deployment improves privacy and latency, but limits model size and inference quality.
_extra.lens_eng: For edge, prioritize model size and speed; 7B quantized runs on phones, 70B doesn't.

title: Effective context
definition: How much of a model’s advertised context window it can actually use well, which is usually less.
examples: A model sold as 128k tokens stays sharp to maybe 32k, then starts missing details buried deeper — its effective context is smaller than its limit.
Like a phone plan’s “unlimited” data that quietly throttles after a point — the number on the box isn’t the number you get.

_extra.analogy: Like a phone plan’s “unlimited” data that quietly throttles after a point — the number on the box isn’t the number you get.
_extra.deeper: Maximum context length is a hard ceiling; effective context is the practical range where recall and reasoning hold up. Attention biases like lost-in-the-middle mean quality degrades before the ceiling. Needle-in-a-haystack tests are how you estimate it, and it’s often a fraction of the advertised size.
_extra.lens_pm: Budget for the usable window, not the marketing number, or long-context features will disappoint.
_extra.lens_eng: The context range over which recall/reasoning stay reliable, typically below the max token limit.

title: ELIZA
definition: A 1960s chatbot that mimicked a psychotherapist by reflecting users' words back at them — and people projected so much understanding onto it that they got emotionally attached.
examples: Users would confess personal problems to ELIZA and get frustrated when the researcher asked if ELIZA had been helpful — they'd resent the implication that it was "just a program."
A very simple mirror: you say "I feel sad," it says "Why do you feel sad?" You go deeper because you filled in the blanks.

_extra.analogy: A very simple mirror: you say "I feel sad," it says "Why do you feel sad?" You go deeper because you filled in the blanks.
_extra.deeper: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA was a pattern-matching system with about 100 lines of script. Its famous "Doctor" persona used trivial rules: if you mention "mother," ask a question about your family. Users consistently read emotional intelligence into it. This revealed that humans are incredibly quick to anthropomorphize: we assume understanding if a response is contextually plausible. The "ELIZA effect" is still relevant — people mistake fluent text from LLMs for genuine reasoning.
_extra.lens_pm: Demonstrated that users attribute agency and understanding based on minimal behavioral signals.
_extra.lens_eng: A pattern-matching chatbot with hand-written substitution rules and template responses; early proof-of-concept for text-based interaction.

title: Elo Rating
definition: A rating system that ranks models based on pairwise wins and losses, accounting for opponent strength.
examples: Model A has a 1600 Elo rating. If it beats Model B (rated 1500) in a comparison, it gains rating points.
Like chess ratings: beating a stronger opponent gains more points than beating a weaker one.

_extra.analogy: Like chess ratings: beating a stronger opponent gains more points than beating a weaker one.
_extra.deeper: Elo is more sophisticated than raw win percentage because it adjusts for who you beat. It's used in competition leaderboards (like LMSys Arena) to rank models dynamically. Updates dynamically as new comparisons come in. The math is probabilistic—your rating predicts your win probability against other models.
_extra.lens_pm: Elo ratings are intuitive for stakeholders and handle dynamic model releases well.
_extra.lens_eng: Use established Elo implementations; be transparent about update frequency and match selection bias.

title: EMA
definition: A running average of the model’s weights that leans on recent steps but never forgets the past.
examples: During training, an EMA copy of the weights is kept alongside the live one, and the smoother EMA version is what gets shipped.
A rolling average of your daily spending — today counts most, but last week still nudges the number.

_extra.analogy: A rolling average of your daily spending — today counts most, but last week still nudges the number.
_extra.deeper: EMA maintains a shadow copy of the weights updated as a decaying blend: mostly the previous average, slightly the newest step. This damps the noise of individual updates and usually produces a more stable, higher-quality model than the raw final weights. It costs almost nothing but a second copy of the parameters.
_extra.lens_pm: A standard, low-risk way to make the shipped model a bit more reliable than the raw training output.
_extra.lens_eng: A decayed running mean of parameters maintained during training, typically used for the evaluation weights.

title: Embedding Cache
definition: Saving embeddings you’ve already computed so you don’t pay to re-embed the same text.
examples: When the same paragraph appears in ten documents, the cache returns its stored vector instead of calling the embedding model ten times.
Keeping receipts so you never re-do a calculation you already finished.

_extra.analogy: Keeping receipts so you never re-do a calculation you already finished.
_extra.deeper: Embedding calls cost money and time, and lots of text repeats or reappears unchanged. A cache keyed by a hash of the input (and model version) returns prior vectors instantly, which speeds ingestion and lowers bills. The subtlety is invalidation: if you change embedding models, the cache must be keyed by model too, or you’ll silently mix incompatible vectors.
_extra.lens_pm: A quiet cost-saver on large or frequently re-ingested corpora.
_extra.lens_eng: Content+model-hash keyed vector store; must invalidate on model change to avoid mixing embedding spaces.

title: Embedding Dimension
definition: How many numbers each embedding uses — more can mean richer meaning but heavier storage.
examples: Switching from a 1536-dim to a 768-dim embedding model halves your vector storage and speeds search, at some quality cost.
Describing a wine with 5 traits vs. 50: more traits capture nuance but take longer to record and compare.

_extra.analogy: Describing a wine with 5 traits vs. 50: more traits capture nuance but take longer to record and compare.
_extra.deeper: Each embedding is a fixed-length list of floats; the length is its dimension. Higher dimensions can encode finer distinctions but cost more memory, slower comparisons, and can hit diminishing returns. Some newer models support "Matryoshka" truncation, letting you shorten vectors for cheaper search when full fidelity is not needed.
_extra.lens_pm: A direct lever on storage bill and latency; bigger is not automatically better.
_extra.lens_eng: Fixed float-vector length; scales memory and distance-compute linearly, with Matryoshka models allowing lossy truncation.

title: Embedding Drift
definition: When you change embedding models and old vectors no longer line up with new ones.
examples: A team upgrades to a newer embedding model but only re-embeds new documents; searches now compare apples to oranges and results quietly degrade.
Two people mapping the same city with different grid systems — the coordinates don’t match, so directions between the maps fall apart.

_extra.analogy: Two people mapping the same city with different grid systems — the coordinates don’t match, so directions between the maps fall apart.
_extra.deeper: Embeddings are only comparable within the same model — each model places meaning in its own coordinate space. Swap the model and every stored vector must be regenerated, or you’re measuring distances between incompatible spaces. Drift also creeps in subtler ways, like a provider silently updating a hosted model. The rule is blunt: change the embedding model, re-embed everything.
_extra.lens_pm: A quiet quality regression that follows a "harmless" model upgrade if you don’t re-index.
_extra.lens_eng: Vectors are only comparable within one embedding model’s space; on any model change, re-embed the entire corpus before serving.

title: Embedding Model
definition: The model whose whole job is to turn text into vectors that place similar meanings close together.
examples: You run all your support docs through an embedding model once, store the vectors, and reuse them for every future search.
A translator that renders every sentence into the same universal coordinate system, so closeness means similarity.

_extra.analogy: A translator that renders every sentence into the same universal coordinate system, so closeness means similarity.
_extra.deeper: An embedding model is trained so that texts with similar meaning land near each other in vector space and unrelated ones land far apart. It’s usually separate from and smaller than the generation model, and its quality sets the ceiling for any retrieval built on it — a weak embedder means poor matches no matter how good everything downstream is. Choosing one involves tradeoffs of accuracy, vector size, speed, and language coverage.
_extra.lens_pm: The embedding model quietly caps the quality of every search and RAG feature built on top of it — choose deliberately.
_extra.lens_eng: A model mapping text to fixed-length vectors trained so semantic similarity corresponds to vector proximity.

title: Embedding Layer
definition: The first layer that turns each token ID into a vector the rest of the network can actually work with.
examples: When token #4021 for “dog” enters a model, the embedding layer looks up its learned 4,096-number vector.
Like a coat check that swaps your ticket number for the actual coat — the number meant nothing until it fetched the real thing.

_extra.analogy: Like a coat check that swaps your ticket number for the actual coat — the number meant nothing until it fetched the real thing.
_extra.deeper: It’s essentially a big lookup table: one learned vector per vocabulary entry, trained alongside everything else. Raw token IDs are meaningless integers; the embedding layer gives each a rich numeric meaning that captures similarity and usage. Everything downstream operates on these vectors, so this humble table is where language first becomes math.
_extra.lens_pm: The unglamorous doorway where words become numbers the model can reason over.
_extra.lens_eng: A learned lookup table mapping token IDs to dense vectors, trained jointly with the model.

title: Embeddings
definition: Turning words into coordinates, so a computer can measure how close in meaning two things are.
examples: Search that finds “car” when you typed “automobile” is matching on embeddings, not on spelling.
A map where “dog” and “puppy” are next-door neighbors and “dog” and “tax form” are on opposite coasts.

_extra.analogy: A map where “dog” and “puppy” are next-door neighbors and “dog” and “tax form” are on opposite coasts.
_extra.deeper: Each piece of text becomes a long list of numbers — a vector. “Similar” means the vectors point in nearly the same direction (cosine similarity). The entire trick of semantic search lives in this one idea.
_extra.lens_pm: The tech behind 'find similar' — powers semantic search, dedup, and recommendations.
_extra.lens_eng: Dense vector representations where cosine distance approximates semantic similarity.

title: embeddings API
definition: An API that converts text into a vector (embedding), useful for similarity search, clustering, and semantic retrieval.
examples: Call the API with 'The cat sat on the mat' and get back a 1536-dim vector. Call it again with 'A feline rested on fabric.' Vectors are similar; high cosine similarity means semantic match.
A fingerprint—instead of storing the whole face, store a short code that captures its essence.

_extra.analogy: A fingerprint—instead of storing the whole face, store a short code that captures its essence.
_extra.deeper: Embeddings come from the model's internal representations. Different models have different dimension sizes (OpenAI 1536, newer ones smaller). Embeddings are how you enable semantic search (RAG's backbone). Once you have embeddings, store them in a vector DB, search by distance.
_extra.lens_pm: Core for RAG; enables semantic search without ever running a full LLM.
_extra.lens_eng: Fast (usually <100ms), small output, critical for retrieval pipelines.

title: Emergence
definition: When a capability appears fairly suddenly at a certain scale, seeming absent in smaller models and present in bigger ones.
examples: Small models score near-random on multi-step arithmetic, then past a size threshold they start getting it right, seemingly out of nowhere.
Water that just sits there as you heat it — until it hits a boil and abruptly changes state.

_extra.analogy: Water that just sits there as you heat it — until it hits a boil and abruptly changes state.
_extra.deeper: As models scale, some skills improve smoothly while others look like sharp jumps. Debate continues over how "real" the sharpness is — some apparent leaps flatten out under smoother metrics, suggesting the jump is partly an artifact of harsh pass/fail scoring. Either way, it complicates planning: scaling laws predict loss well but not exactly when a given ability shows up.
_extra.lens_pm: Why you cannot always promise a feature at a target size — some abilities only show up when they show up.
_extra.lens_eng: Capabilities that appear abruptly with scale; partly metric-dependent and not directly forecast by loss curves.

title: Emergent ability
definition: A skill that shows up suddenly only once a model gets big enough, absent in smaller ones.
examples: Small models flunk multi-step arithmetic entirely, then past a certain scale a model starts getting it right, seemingly out of nowhere.
Like water staying liquid, liquid, liquid — then abruptly boiling at 100°C. Nothing, nothing, then a phase change.

_extra.analogy: Like water staying liquid, liquid, liquid — then abruptly boiling at 100°C. Nothing, nothing, then a phase change.
_extra.deeper: Emergent abilities are capabilities that don’t improve smoothly with size but appear to switch on past a threshold. They’re real but contested — some “jumps” are artifacts of harsh all-or-nothing metrics, and smoother scoring reveals gradual gains. Either way, they’re why bigger models sometimes surprise their own builders.
_extra.lens_pm: Why a scale-up can unlock features you didn’t explicitly train for — and why they’re hard to predict.
_extra.lens_eng: Capabilities that appear near a scale threshold rather than improving continuously; partly metric-dependent.

title: Encoder
definition: The half of a model that reads an input and compresses it into a rich internal representation.
examples: BERT is encoder-only: it reads a sentence and produces vectors great for classification or search, not generation.
A note-taker who listens to a whole speech and writes a dense summary others can work from.

_extra.analogy: A note-taker who listens to a whole speech and writes a dense summary others can work from.
_extra.deeper: An encoder maps an input sequence into a set of context-rich vectors, seeing the whole input at once (bidirectionally). It’s ideal when you need to understand or embed text rather than produce more of it — search, classification, retrieval. Encoder-only models like BERT dominate those tasks; pure generation uses decoders instead.
_extra.lens_pm: The right shape when the job is understanding or searching text, not writing it.
_extra.lens_eng: A stack that maps input tokens to contextual representations, typically with bidirectional attention.

title: Encoder-Decoder
definition: A two-part design where one stack reads the input and another writes the output, linked by attention.
examples: T5 and classic translation models use this: the encoder digests the source, the decoder emits the translation.
A translator with a listening phase and a speaking phase — understand fully first, then produce.

_extra.analogy: A translator with a listening phase and a speaking phase — understand fully first, then produce.
_extra.deeper: The original transformer was encoder-decoder: the encoder builds a representation of the input, and the decoder generates the output while cross-attending to that representation. It fits tasks with a clear input-to-output mapping like translation or summarization. Many modern chat models skip the encoder and go decoder-only, but the two-part design still shines for structured transduction.
_extra.lens_pm: The classic fit for “turn this input into that output” tasks like translation and summarization.
_extra.lens_eng: An architecture pairing a bidirectional encoder with an autoregressive decoder joined by cross-attention.

title: Encoder-Only
definition: A transformer that only reads and understands text — no generation half at all.
examples: BERT is the poster child: brilliant at classification and search, incapable of writing a paragraph.
Like a book reviewer who deeply understands a manuscript but was never hired to write one.

_extra.analogy: Like a book reviewer who deeply understands a manuscript but was never hired to write one.
_extra.deeper: It keeps only the encoder stack, reading the whole input at once (bidirectionally) to build rich representations, and is trained by predicting masked-out words. That makes it strong and cheap for understanding tasks but unable to generate freely. As generative chat models took over, encoder-only fell out of fashion, though it still powers plenty of search and embedding work.
_extra.lens_pm: A lean, fast choice when you only need to understand or classify, not generate.
_extra.lens_eng: A transformer using only the encoder stack, trained bidirectionally for representation tasks.

title: Endpoint
definition: The URL or address where you send a request and the model sends back its answer.
examples: You call `https://api.example.com/v1/completions` with your prompt, and the endpoint replies with generated text.
Like a ticket window at the post office — you hand in your request and wait for the response.

_extra.analogy: Like a ticket window at the post office — you hand in your request and wait for the response.
_extra.deeper: An endpoint is a running service listening on a network address. It receives JSON payloads, passes them through the model, and streams or returns the output. Uptime, latency, and throughput all depend on how the endpoint is built and where it runs.
_extra.lens_pm: Endpoints are the interface between your app and the model — their reliability and speed shape user experience.
_extra.lens_eng: An HTTP(S) endpoint backed by a running inference server that decodes requests, invokes the model, and serializes responses.

title: Ensemble
definition: Combining several models’ predictions to get a result better than any one alone.
examples: A team runs three different models on the same input and takes the majority vote, cutting the error rate of each individual model.
Like “ask the audience” — the crowd’s averaged guess usually beats any single person’s.

_extra.analogy: Like “ask the audience” — the crowd’s averaged guess usually beats any single person’s.
_extra.deeper: Ensembling works because different models make different mistakes, so averaging or voting cancels uncorrelated errors. It reliably boosts accuracy and robustness, but at multiplied compute and latency — you’re running many models instead of one — which is why it’s common in competitions and less so in cost-sensitive production.
_extra.lens_pm: A dependable accuracy bump you pay for in compute; great for offline scoring, pricey for live serving.
_extra.lens_eng: Aggregating predictions (vote/average/stack) from diverse models to reduce variance; cost scales with members.

title: Ensemble evaluation
definition: Using multiple evaluators (models or humans) to grade the same output and averaging their scores.
examples: Running Claude, GPT-4, and Llama against your outputs and averaging their ratings of relevance from 1–10.
Having three teachers grade the same essay and averaging the scores.

_extra.analogy: Having three teachers grade the same essay and averaging the scores.
_extra.deeper: Ensemble eval reduces bias from any single grader. But it's expensive and sometimes the models agree because they're trained on similar data. For critical applications, combining automated scoring with human spot-checks is better than either alone.
_extra.lens_pm: More reliable than single-judge evals but also more expensive. Use for milestones, not daily testing.
_extra.lens_eng: Call multiple eval models, collect scores, return mean and std. Log disagreements for audit trails.

title: Entity Linking
definition: Figuring out which real-world thing a name in the text actually refers to.
examples: A news pipeline reads "Apple cut its forecast" and links "Apple" to the company, not the fruit, so it files the story under the right stock.
Sorting mail for three coworkers all named "Jordan" — same name on the envelope, three different desks.

_extra.analogy: Sorting mail for three coworkers all named "Jordan" — same name on the envelope, three different desks.
_extra.deeper: Text is full of ambiguous mentions — "Paris," "Mercury," "Jordan" — that map to different entities depending on context. Entity linking matches each mention to a unique record in a knowledge base, using the surrounding words to disambiguate. It’s the glue that turns messy prose into structured facts, and the step where a knowledge graph gets its nodes. Errors here quietly corrupt everything downstream.
_extra.lens_pm: Keeps your data clean at the source — "Mercury the planet" doesn’t end up in the chemistry bucket.
_extra.lens_eng: Map surface mentions to canonical entity IDs in a reference KB, disambiguating with contextual features; feeds graph construction.

title: Entropy
definition: A measure of how spread out and uncertain a set of probabilities is.
examples: When the model’s next-token distribution has high entropy, several words are nearly tied — a sign it’s genuinely unsure what comes next.
Like a weather forecast: “50% rain” is high-entropy uncertainty, “99% sunny” is low.

_extra.analogy: Like a weather forecast: “50% rain” is high-entropy uncertainty, “99% sunny” is low.
_extra.deeper: Entropy is highest when options are evenly likely and zero when one outcome is certain. In language models it quantifies uncertainty at each step, and it’s the theoretical floor that cross-entropy loss measures against — training pushes the model’s predictions to match reality’s true distribution.
_extra.lens_pm: A principled way to detect “the model is guessing here” and route those cases to a human.
_extra.lens_eng: −Σ p·log p over a distribution; maximal for uniform, zero for a point mass, and the baseline cross-entropy compares to.

title: Environment
definition: The world an agent acts in — the files, apps, websites, or systems it can touch and change.
examples: For a coding agent the environment is the repository, the shell, and the test runner; its actions edit files and its observations are the test output.
The kitchen a chef works in: the ingredients, appliances, and mess that respond to what they do.

_extra.analogy: The kitchen a chef works in: the ingredients, appliances, and mess that respond to what they do.
_extra.deeper: The environment is everything outside the model that the agent perceives and affects. Its properties shape everything: does it give clear feedback, is it safe to fail in, can actions be undone? A sandboxed environment lets an agent try, break things, and learn cheaply; a live production environment turns every mistake real. Designing the environment is often as important as the agent itself.
_extra.lens_pm: Where an agent runs decides how safely it can be allowed to fail.
_extra.lens_eng: The external system an agent observes and acts on, defining feedback signals, state, and blast radius.

title: Episodic Memory
definition: An agent’s record of specific past events — what happened, when, and how it turned out.
examples: The agent remembers that last time it used a certain API it got rate-limited, so this time it slows down its calls.
A diary — not general knowledge, but “on Tuesday I tried X and it failed.”

_extra.analogy: A diary — not general knowledge, but “on Tuesday I tried X and it failed.”
_extra.deeper: Borrowed from psychology, episodic memory is about particular experiences rather than facts — a log of trajectories the agent can learn from. It lets an agent avoid repeating mistakes and reuse past solutions, but it also grows without bound, so you need retrieval to surface the relevant episode instead of dumping the whole history. Deciding what’s worth remembering is the hard part.
_extra.lens_pm: Episodic memory is how an agent gets better with use instead of starting fresh every time.
_extra.lens_eng: A store of past interaction traces, keyed for retrieval so relevant episodes can inform future decisions.

title: Epoch
definition: One full pass of the model through the entire training dataset.
examples: Training for three epochs means the model sees every example in the dataset three times.
Like reading a whole textbook cover to cover once — an epoch is one complete read-through.

_extra.analogy: Like reading a whole textbook cover to cover once — an epoch is one complete read-through.
_extra.deeper: An epoch is one complete sweep over all training data, made up of many iterations (one per batch). Too few epochs and the model underfits; too many and it starts memorizing and overfitting. Large-scale pretraining often runs less than a single epoch over a giant corpus, since seeing that much data even once is plenty — the concept matters most for smaller fine-tuning runs.
_extra.lens_pm: A rough dial on how long to train; more isn’t always better, since extra passes invite overfitting.
_extra.lens_eng: One full pass over the dataset (many iterations); count trades underfitting vs. overfitting.

title: Euclidean Distance
definition: Straight-line distance between two vectors — the everyday "how far apart" measure.
examples: A clustering job groups embeddings by L2 distance, putting vectors that sit physically near each other in the same bucket.
The as-the-crow-flies distance between two pins on a map.

_extra.analogy: The as-the-crow-flies distance between two pins on a map.
_extra.deeper: Euclidean (L2) distance is the square root of summed squared differences — the ruler-distance in vector space. It cares about magnitude, unlike cosine which cares only about direction, so on un-normalized embeddings the two can rank results quite differently. Many indexes support it, and for normalized vectors it produces the same ordering as cosine.
_extra.lens_pm: Another metric option; the point is to match it to how your embeddings were built.
_extra.lens_eng: sqrt(Σ(aᵢ−bᵢ)²); magnitude-sensitive, order-equivalent to cosine only under normalization.

title: Eval Set
definition: A fixed dataset of examples you use to measure model quality—separate from training data to prevent overfitting.
examples: You split your 10,000 labeled examples: 7,000 for training, 3,000 for eval. You train on the 7,000, measure accuracy on the 3,000.
Like the final exam of a class: fixed questions, given after students learn.

_extra.analogy: Like the final exam of a class: fixed questions, given after students learn.
_extra.deeper: Using a separate eval set is essential for detecting overfitting. If you eval on training data, you can't tell if the model learned generalizable patterns or just memorized. Standard split is 70–80% training, 10–15% validation, 10–15% test. Some datasets call the last split 'test' to emphasize it's held out.
_extra.lens_pm: Eval sets tell you if your model works on unseen data. Without them, you have no confidence.
_extra.lens_eng: Never touch eval sets during training; don't use them for hyperparameter tuning (use validation sets instead).

title: Eval-driven development
definition: Writing evals first, before you build the feature, then iterating to pass them.
examples: You need a system to summarize documents. You write 50 examples with gold summaries and grade them on ROUGE score. Then you iterate on prompts until your ROUGE improves.
Test-driven development for language models — write the test, then write the code.

_extra.analogy: Test-driven development for language models — write the test, then write the code.
_extra.deeper: Eval-driven development forces clarity about what "done" means. It makes progress visible and prevents shipping half-baked features. The danger: optimizing the metric instead of the real problem. A high ROUGE score doesn't guarantee users like the summary.
_extra.lens_pm: Speeds up iteration and keeps teams aligned. Requires discipline to not game the metrics.
_extra.lens_eng: Write evals in a CI pipeline. Gate merges on eval improvements. Track score history.

title: Eval leakage
definition: When examples from your test or eval set accidentally end up in training data, inflating your metrics.
examples: You train a model on a dataset that (unnoticed) includes 5% of your eval set. Your eval scores look great, but it's because you've seen those examples before.
Reading the answer key before writing your essay, then claiming you got it right.

_extra.analogy: Reading the answer key before writing your essay, then claiming you got it right.
_extra.deeper: Eval leakage is insidious because it's hard to catch. It happens when combining multiple datasets, scraping web data, or data pipeline mistakes. It inflates metrics and makes models look better than they are. Once you deploy, real-world performance drops and you wonder why your eval didn't predict it.
_extra.lens_pm: A broken eval is worse than no eval. Always check for leakage before trusting results.
_extra.lens_eng: Deduplicate across train/val/test. Use hashing to detect near-duplicates. Never train on eval data.

title: Evals
