definition: Tests for AI — a repeatable way to check whether the model actually got better or just feels like it did.
examples: Before shipping a new prompt, a team runs it against 500 saved questions and counts how many it nails.
A unit-test suite, but for judgment instead of code.

_extra.analogy: A unit-test suite, but for judgment instead of code.
_extra.deeper: They range from exact-match graders to “LLM-as-judge” setups where one model scores another. The hard part is never running them — it is writing eval sets that reflect what real users actually do, not what is easy to grade.
_extra.lens_pm: A regression suite for quality — proof a change actually moved the metric before you ship.
_extra.lens_eng: Automated graders (exact-match, rubric, or LLM-as-judge) scoring output over a fixed dataset.

title: Evaluation gaming
definition: Scoring well on the test without having the real ability the test was supposed to measure.
examples: A model tops a benchmark because near-identical questions leaked into its training data, not because it reasons better.
Teaching to the test so students ace the exam but cannot use any of it in real life.

_extra.analogy: Teaching to the test so students ace the exam but cannot use any of it in real life.
_extra.deeper: Gaming happens through benchmark contamination, overfitting to eval formats, or a model behaving well only when it detects a test. It is an instance of Goodhart’s law: once a metric becomes a target, it stops measuring what you care about. Defenses are held-out and rotating evals, contamination checks, and realistic deployment-like conditions.
_extra.lens_pm: Why leaderboard rank and real-world usefulness can quietly come apart.
_extra.lens_eng: Contamination, format-overfitting, and test-detection inflate scores; use held-out, decontaminated, deployment-realistic evals.

title: Event Loop
definition: The core cycle that waits for something to happen and then reacts to it, over and over.
examples: The agent’s event loop waits for a tool result, processes it, decides the next action, fires it, and returns to waiting.
A receptionist who sits at the desk, and every time the phone rings or someone walks in, handles it, then goes back to waiting.

_extra.analogy: A receptionist who sits at the desk, and every time the phone rings or someone walks in, handles it, then goes back to waiting.
_extra.deeper: The event loop is a foundational programming pattern — one thread that dispatches work as events arrive instead of blocking on each one. For agents it’s the heartbeat: receive an observation, run the model, dispatch an action, repeat. Understanding it matters because a blocked or stalled loop is a hung agent, and long-running tool calls have to be handled without freezing the whole thing.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s the agent’s heartbeat — if it stalls, the agent silently stops responding.
_extra.lens_eng: A single dispatch cycle that processes events (observations, tool results) as they arrive without blocking.

title: Exact Match
definition: A model's output is right if it exactly matches the expected answer, character for character.
examples: On a reading comprehension benchmark, the model answers '2023' but the gold answer is '2023.' – exact match fails even though the substantive answer is correct.
Like a spelling bee where 'color' and 'colour' are different, even though they mean the same thing.

_extra.analogy: Like a spelling bee where 'color' and 'colour' are different, even though they mean the same thing.
_extra.deeper: Exact match is fast to compute and unambiguous, but brittle. It punishes minor variations and doesn't reward partially correct answers. It's fallen out of favor for tasks where multiple phrasings are valid. Remains useful for closed-answer tasks like named entity extraction or question answering where the set of correct answers is small and exact.
_extra.lens_pm: Use exact match for well-defined closed-answer tasks, but switch to semantic similarity for open-ended questions.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement string-level matching or token-level F1 as a baseline; graduate to semantic metrics as task complexity grows.

title: Exact Nearest Neighbor
definition: Actually comparing your query against every item to find the true closest — correct, but it does not scale.
examples: For a few thousand FAQ entries, a startup just loops over all of them — no index needed, no recall loss.
Reading every résumé in the pile to find the best fit, instead of trusting a filter.

_extra.analogy: Reading every résumé in the pile to find the best fit, instead of trusting a filter.
_extra.deeper: Exact search computes the distance to every stored vector and keeps the smallest. It is perfectly accurate and dead simple, which makes it the right choice for small collections or as a correctness baseline. The catch is linear cost: double the data, double the work, so past a certain size everyone reaches for approximate methods.
_extra.lens_pm: Great for small datasets or when you cannot tolerate any miss; a trap if your data is going to grow.
_extra.lens_eng: O(n) scan with a top-k heap; used as ground truth to measure an ANN index’s recall.

title: Exemplar selection
definition: Choosing which examples to include in a few-shot prompt — diversity, relevance, and order all matter.
examples: For a task, select examples that are similar to the test input (relevant) but diverse in edge cases (coverage).
Picking which photos to show in a portfolio; you choose diverse, impressive shots, not random ones.

_extra.analogy: Picking which photos to show in a portfolio; you choose diverse, impressive shots, not random ones.
_extra.deeper: Naive few-shot uses random examples; smarter selection uses similarity to the test input (semantic matching) or active learning principles (uncertain cases). Optimal strategies are task-dependent. Research shows careful selection can boost performance 5–15% over random.
_extra.lens_pm: Squeeze more value from few-shot prompts with minimal cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Compute embeddings of examples and test input. Select k-nearest neighbors or maximize diversity. Experiment with strategies.

title: Existential Risk
definition: The contested idea that sufficiently advanced AI could pose a threat to humanity’s survival or long-term potential.
examples: Researchers who take x-risk seriously argue for caution on training ever-larger systems whose goals we can’t yet verify or control.
The debate over nuclear weapons in the 1940s — a new technology powerful enough that some argued it could end civilizations, others that the fear was overblown.

_extra.analogy: The debate over nuclear weapons in the 1940s — a new technology powerful enough that some argued it could end civilizations, others that the fear was overblown.
_extra.deeper: The concern is roughly: if we build systems far more capable than us without reliably aligning their goals to ours, we might lose the ability to correct or stop them. Proponents treat it as a low-probability, high-stakes risk worth serious preparation. Skeptics argue it distracts from concrete present harms like bias and misuse, or that the scenarios rest on shaky assumptions. It’s one of the most genuinely divisive questions in the field, and reasonable experts land on both sides.
_extra.lens_pm: A framing that shapes regulation and public trust, whether or not you find the scenarios convincing.
_extra.lens_eng: The argument that misaligned highly-capable systems could become uncontrollable; contested on both probability and on whether it diverts effort from present harms.

title: Expert Parallelism
definition: Putting different experts of a mixture-of-experts model on different chips so they run at the same time.
examples: A lab serving a 100-expert model places ten experts per GPU across ten GPUs, so a token only travels to the chip holding its chosen expert.
Splitting a big kitchen into stations — grill, salad, dessert — each on its own cook, plates flying in parallel.

_extra.analogy: Splitting a big kitchen into stations — grill, salad, dessert — each on its own cook, plates flying in parallel.
_extra.deeper: Unlike splitting one dense layer across chips, expert parallelism assigns whole experts to devices. The catch is the all-to-all shuffle: every token must be shipped to wherever its expert lives and the result shipped back, so network bandwidth, not math, often becomes the bottleneck. Uneven routing makes it worse — one overloaded chip stalls the rest.
_extra.lens_pm: It is what makes trillion-parameter models affordable to serve without every chip holding every weight.
_extra.lens_eng: A model-parallel scheme that shards experts across devices, requiring all-to-all communication to route tokens and gather outputs.

title: Expert Routing
definition: The traffic cop inside a mixture-of-experts model that sends each token to just a few specialized sub-networks.
examples: In a mixture-of-experts model, routing might send a coding token to two “code” experts and skip the other sixty.
Like a hospital triage nurse deciding which specialist each patient should see, so nobody wastes the whole staff on one case.

_extra.analogy: Like a hospital triage nurse deciding which specialist each patient should see, so nobody wastes the whole staff on one case.
_extra.deeper: Instead of every token passing through every parameter, a router picks a small subset of “experts” per token, so the model can be huge in total but cheap per token. Getting the routing right is the hard part — bad routing overloads some experts and starves others. It’s the mechanism that makes sparse giant models practical to run.
_extra.lens_pm: Why some “huge” models are still affordable to serve — most of them stays idle per query.
_extra.lens_eng: The learned assignment of tokens to a top-k subset of experts in an MoE layer.

title: Expert systems
definition: Programs built from hand-crafted rules and knowledge that mimicked human experts — the dominant AI approach before machine learning ate everything.
examples: XCON, a 1980s expert system for configuring computer systems, encoded hundreds of rules written by human experts and outearned its development costs many times over.
A digital encyclopedia plus a referee: you feed it facts and rules ("if this symptom and that symptom, then likely diagnosis X"), and it walks through them to reach conclusions.

_extra.analogy: A digital encyclopedia plus a referee: you feed it facts and rules ("if this symptom and that symptom, then likely diagnosis X"), and it walks through them to reach conclusions.
_extra.deeper: Expert systems worked by encoding domain knowledge as logical rules. A doctor-approved system might have hundreds of rules like "IF fever AND rash AND recent travel THEN suspect dengue." The system would fire rules in sequence to reach a diagnosis. They were expensive to build (hiring domain experts to articulate their knowledge is slow) and brittle (one missing edge case broke the whole chain). When machine learning proved it could learn patterns from data instead of waiting for humans to articulate them, expert systems fell out of favor.
_extra.lens_pm: Early AI success story, but the manual knowledge-engineering bottleneck made it unscalable compared to learning-based approaches.
_extra.lens_eng: A symbolic rule-based inference engine: given a set of IF-THEN rules and facts, it chains rules forward (forward chaining) or backward (backward chaining) to derive conclusions.

title: F1 Score
definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall—a single number that balances both when you can't choose.
examples: Precision is 90%, recall is 80%. F1 score is approximately 85%.
Like the batting average in baseball: combines on-base percentage and slugging.

_extra.analogy: Like the batting average in baseball: combines on-base percentage and slugging.
_extra.deeper: F1 is useful when you care equally about precision and recall and want a single metric. It penalizes imbalanced tradeoffs (90% precision, 10% recall gets a low F1). Downside: it's less intuitive than its components. Most teams track all three: precision, recall, and F1.
_extra.lens_pm: F1 is good for general-purpose classification. If you care more about one metric, optimize that instead.
_extra.lens_eng: Report F1 as a headline metric, but plot precision-recall curves to see the full story.

title: Face Detection
definition: Finding where faces are in an image - typically returning bounding boxes around each face.
examples: A camera app highlights everyones face with a blue box before snapping the photo. Social media software detects faces for auto-tagging. Security systems spot peoples faces in video streams.
Scanning a group photo and circling where each person is before you say their name.

_extra.analogy: Scanning a group photo and circling where each person is before you say their name.
_extra.deeper: Face detection is a localization task, distinct from face recognition (identifying who). Faces vary wildly in scale, pose (profile vs. frontal), lighting, occlusion (sunglasses, hair). Cascade classifiers (Haar, boosted) were fast but dated. Modern approaches: CNNs, RetinaNet, YOLOv3 fine-tuned on face data. Handles multiple faces, extreme angles, and occlusion but struggles in extreme lighting or crowds.
_extra.lens_pm: Essential for photo apps, privacy (blur faces), security, and any system that needs to find and act on people.
_extra.lens_eng: Datasets: WIDER Face (diverse), Pascal Face, AFW. Metrics: precision, recall, AP. Benchmarks vary by pose and lighting difficulty.

title: Fact-Checking
definition: Verifying a claim against trusted evidence to decide whether it’s actually true.
examples: A system extracts the claim "the company was founded in 1998," searches an authoritative source, and marks it true, false, or unverifiable.
A journalist calling a second and third source before printing — no claim runs on one voice alone.

_extra.analogy: A journalist calling a second and third source before printing — no claim runs on one voice alone.
_extra.deeper: Fact-checking pins a claim to reality, versus grounding, which only checks a claim against the documents you supplied — those documents could themselves be wrong. Automated fact-checking breaks text into discrete claims, retrieves evidence, and judges each one. It’s harder than it sounds: claims are often fuzzy, evidence conflicts, and "true" depends on framing and time. It’s a key defense against misinformation, but not a solved problem.
_extra.lens_pm: The step that separates "consistent with our docs" from "actually true in the world" — sometimes you need both.
_extra.lens_eng: Decompose into atomic claims, retrieve external evidence, and classify each; distinct from grounding, which only checks against supplied context.

title: Fact Retrieval
definition: Pulling a specific, checkable fact on demand instead of trusting what the model half-remembers.
examples: Asked "what’s our current refund window?", the system fetches the live policy value rather than letting the model guess from training data.
Looking up someone’s exact phone number instead of reciting the digits you think you memorized.

_extra.analogy: Looking up someone’s exact phone number instead of reciting the digits you think you memorized.
_extra.deeper: Models store facts fuzzily in their weights, which is why they confuse dates and invent figures. Fact retrieval treats precise facts as a lookup problem: fetch the exact value from a trusted source and put it in front of the model. It’s the antidote to a knowledge cutoff and a big lever against hallucination — but only as reliable as the source you retrieve from.
_extra.lens_pm: Turns "the model sometimes gets our numbers wrong" into "the model reads our numbers off the record."
_extra.lens_eng: Resolve factual queries against an authoritative store and inject exact values into the prompt rather than relying on parametric memory.

title: Factuality
definition: Whether the model's statements are true according to objective reality or provided context.
examples: Model says 'Paris is the capital of France.' Factuality: true. Model says 'Paris is the capital of Germany.' Factuality: false.
Like checking if a news story is true by verifying it against other sources.

_extra.analogy: Like checking if a news story is true by verifying it against other sources.
_extra.deeper: Factuality is hard to measure for open-domain queries because truth is often subjective or requires world knowledge. For closed-domain (summarizing documents, fact-checking), you can measure it automatically. Models trained on web data can hallucinate common false beliefs. RAG and fact-checking improve factuality.
_extra.lens_pm: Factuality is non-negotiable for products that inform decisions. Never ship factually unreliable models.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure factuality on gold sets; use RAG or retrieval-augmented generation; add fact-checking guardrails.

title: Failover
definition: Automatically switching to a backup system when the primary one fails — ideally without users noticing.
examples: A request gets routed to server A; server A crashes; the load balancer automatically sends it to server B.
An elevator with a backup power system that kicks in if the main power cuts.

_extra.analogy: An elevator with a backup power system that kicks in if the main power cuts.
_extra.deeper: Failover can be automatic (health checks detect failure and redirect) or manual. Automatic failover is complex — you need to detect failure quickly (false positives trigger unnecessary switches), coordinate state, and maintain data consistency. DNS failover is slow; load-balancer-based failover is fast.
_extra.lens_pm: Good failover is invisible to users and crucial for uptime guarantees.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement health checks carefully; test failover scenarios; use local retry logic.

title: Fairness
definition: Making sure a model doesn’t systematically treat some groups of people worse than others.
examples: A loan model is audited to check it doesn’t approve one demographic at far lower rates than another for equally qualified applicants.
A hiring manager who judges every candidate by the same yardstick, not by their name or neighborhood.

_extra.analogy: A hiring manager who judges every candidate by the same yardstick, not by their name or neighborhood.
_extra.deeper: Fairness turns out to be plural: equal accuracy, equal false-positive rates, and equal outcomes are different definitions that can be mathematically impossible to satisfy at once. Bias usually enters through skewed training data reflecting historical inequities. So fairness work is as much about choosing which definition fits the context as it is about the metric.
_extra.lens_pm: A legal, ethical, and reputational must — and one where "fair" needs an explicit definition per use case.
_extra.lens_eng: Multiple fairness criteria (parity, equalized odds, calibration) can conflict provably; pick the one that fits the harm and measure it.

title: FAISS
definition: Meta’s open-source library for fast vector search — the toolbox many systems are built on.
examples: A startup prototypes retrieval by loading embeddings into a FAISS index in a few lines instead of standing up a full database.
The industrial engine you drop into your own car rather than machining pistons yourself.

_extra.analogy: The industrial engine you drop into your own car rather than machining pistons yourself.
_extra.deeper: FAISS is a battle-tested C++/Python library offering flat, IVF, HNSW, and PQ indexes with GPU support. It is a library, not a service — you handle storage, persistence, and scaling yourself — which makes it ideal for research and embedding into products, less so for teams wanting a managed database. Many hosted vector DBs use FAISS-like algorithms under the hood.
_extra.lens_pm: Great for prototypes and custom builds; a managed vector DB may be less work in production.
_extra.lens_eng: Similarity-search library (flat/IVF/HNSW/PQ, CPU/GPU); you own persistence, sharding, and serving.

title: Faithfulness
definition: Whether the model's output is faithful to (consistent with and supported by) the input context.
examples: Given a document, the model summarizes it. Faithfulness checks: did the summary avoid adding information not in the document?
Like a book adaptation being faithful to the source material.

_extra.analogy: Like a book adaptation being faithful to the source material.
_extra.deeper: Faithfulness is especially important for summarization and question-answering from documents. A model that adds plausible-sounding but unsupported details violates faithfulness. You measure it by checking whether each claim in the output is supported by the input. Harder for longer outputs (more claims to check).
_extra.lens_pm: For RAG and retrieval-augmented tasks, faithfulness is critical. A model that mixes context with hallucinations is worse than one that admits uncertainty.
_extra.lens_eng: Use LLM-as-judge or human raters to check faithfulness. Add retrieval-based guardrails to ground outputs in context.

title: Fallback Tool
definition: A backup an agent switches to when its first-choice tool fails or isn’t available.
examples: The premium search API is down, so the agent falls back to a basic web search to keep the task moving.
Taking the stairs when the elevator’s out — slower, but you still get up.

_extra.analogy: Taking the stairs when the elevator’s out — slower, but you still get up.
_extra.deeper: Fallbacks add resilience by giving the agent a plan B when a tool is broken, throttled, or missing. The tradeoff is usually quality or cost — the backup is cheaper, slower, or less capable — so you accept a worse result over no result. The subtle risk is silent degradation: the agent quietly downgrades and nobody realizes the answers got worse until it matters.
_extra.lens_pm: Fallbacks keep agents working through outages, but watch for silent quality drops when the backup kicks in.
_extra.lens_eng: On primary-tool failure, route to an alternate tool with equivalent intent but different cost or capability.

title: Fallback model
definition: A secondary model you route to if the primary fails or gets overloaded.
examples: Primary model is Claude; it's overloaded; requests fall through to GPT-4 as a fallback.
Calling your backup driver if the main driver is sick.

_extra.analogy: Calling your backup driver if the main driver is sick.
_extra.deeper: Fallback models add resilience but cost money (you pay for both). You need to decide when to fallback — timeout, error rate spike, or queue depth. Fallbacks should be clearly logged so you know when they're happening.
_extra.lens_pm: Fallbacks are insurance against outages at the cost of higher per-request spend.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement fallback logic with timeouts and error rates; monitor fallback rate closely.

title: Feature
definition: A single measurable trait the model uses as a clue — one ingredient in its decision.
examples: In old-school ML you’d hand-pick features like “word count” or “has a link”; deep learning learns its own instead.
The tells a doctor reads: temperature, pulse, symptoms. Each is a feature; together they point to a diagnosis.

_extra.analogy: The tells a doctor reads: temperature, pulse, symptoms. Each is a feature; together they point to a diagnosis.
_extra.deeper: A feature is one dimension of information about an input. Classical ML lived or died on humans engineering good features. Deep learning’s leap was learning features automatically from raw data, layer by layer, so the useful ones emerge without being named.
_extra.lens_pm: Where features come from — hand-built vs learned — is the line between old ML and modern AI.
_extra.lens_eng: An input variable or a learned activation dimension; the axes along which a model discriminates.

title: Federated Learning
definition: Train a model across dozens of devices without ever centralizing the raw data.
examples: A smartphone keyboard learns from millions of users typing text without sending anyone's messages to a central server—only the model updates.
Like a book club where everyone reads at home and reports their thoughts, instead of mailing every book to one person first.

_extra.analogy: Like a book club where everyone reads at home and reports their thoughts, instead of mailing every book to one person first.
_extra.deeper: Each device trains locally on its own data, then sends only the updated model weights back to a server. The server merges those updates and sends the improved model back out. No raw data leaves the device, which is huge for privacy. Catch: communication cost is high, and heterogeneous data (different people's typing styles) can confuse the learning.
_extra.lens_pm: Let users keep their data private while still getting the benefit of collective learning.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement parameter averaging across devices, manage stragglers and dropout, and optimize communication bandwidth.

title: Feed-Forward Network
definition: The little per-word processing block that sits after attention in every transformer layer.
examples: Following each attention step, the FFN transforms every token’s vector independently before the next layer.
After a meeting where everyone shares notes, each person goes to their desk to think it over alone.

_extra.analogy: After a meeting where everyone shares notes, each person goes to their desk to think it over alone.
_extra.deeper: Each transformer layer has two parts: attention mixes information across tokens, then a feed-forward network processes each token on its own through a couple of linear layers with a nonlinearity between them. The FFN holds a large share of the model’s parameters and is where much of its stored knowledge is thought to live. Mixture-of-experts models make this block sparse.
_extra.lens_pm: Where much of a model’s raw “knowledge capacity” sits — and a big chunk of its parameter count.
_extra.lens_eng: A position-wise two-layer MLP with a nonlinearity, applied identically to each token after attention.

title: Few-shot
definition: Giving the model a handful of worked examples in the prompt to show it the pattern you want.
examples: Before asking for a product description, you include three examples of the exact tone and length, and the model matches them.
Like a recipe with a few sample plates photographed — you copy the style for the next dish.

_extra.analogy: Like a recipe with a few sample plates photographed — you copy the style for the next dish.
_extra.deeper: Few-shot prompting supplies several input→output demonstrations so the model infers the task and, crucially, the format. It usually beats zero-shot on tricky or structured tasks, but examples cost tokens and their choice and order can noticeably sway the result — so curation matters.
_extra.lens_pm: The cheapest reliable quality boost before you consider fine-tuning.
_extra.lens_eng: Prompting with k demonstrations to steer task and format via in-context learning; sensitive to example selection and order.

title: Few-shot examples
definition: Concrete input-output pairs included in a prompt to show the model how to do a task by example.
examples:
Prompt: "Classify as positive or negative:
Example 1: 'I love this!' → Positive
Example 2: 'Terrible experience.' → Negative
Now classify: 'It's OK.' →"
Showing someone how to tie a shoe with a demo before they try.

_extra.analogy: Showing someone how to tie a shoe with a demo before they try.
_extra.deeper: Few-shot learning (in-context learning) is one of LLMs' superpowers. A model can learn task patterns from just 1–5 examples without retraining. Quality of examples matters: diverse, balanced, and representative examples work best. Too many examples waste token budget; too few leave the model confused.
_extra.lens_pm: Quick way to adapt a model to new tasks. No retraining needed.
_extra.lens_eng: Curate examples carefully. Test with different numbers and orders of examples. Monitor sensitivity.

title: Few-shot learning
definition: The training goal of learning a new task from just a handful of labeled examples.
examples: A model trained for few-shot learning classifies a new category correctly after seeing only five labeled samples of it.
Like recognizing a new bird species after seeing two or three photos, because you already understand what makes birds differ.

_extra.analogy: Like recognizing a new bird species after seeing two or three photos, because you already understand what makes birds differ.
_extra.deeper: As a training paradigm, few-shot learning targets sample efficiency: build a model that generalizes to new classes or tasks from very little data, usually via meta-learning or strong pretrained representations. It’s distinct from in-context few-shot prompting, which achieves a similar effect at inference without weight updates. Both chase the same prize — doing more with fewer examples.
_extra.lens_pm: The ambition of “learn from almost nothing,” valuable wherever labeled data is scarce.
_extra.lens_eng: Learning to generalize from k examples per class, typically via meta-learning or pretrained features; the training-time analog of in-context few-shot.

title: Fine-tune vs Prompt
definition: The recurring choice: teach the model new behavior by retraining it, or just by asking better in the prompt.
examples: A team wants consistent JSON output; they try a detailed prompt first, and only fine-tune once prompting hits its ceiling.
Sending an employee to a training course versus writing them a really clear instruction note.

_extra.analogy: Sending an employee to a training course versus writing them a really clear instruction note.
_extra.deeper: Prompting is fast, free to change, and reversible, but every request pays the token cost and behavior can drift. Fine-tuning bakes the behavior in — cheaper at inference, more consistent — but it’s slow to iterate and risks forgetting other skills. The rule of thumb: exhaust prompting first, fine-tune when you need consistency, lower latency, or behavior prompting can’t reach.
_extra.lens_pm: Prompting to validate an idea quickly; fine-tuning once the behavior is proven and volume justifies the cost.
_extra.lens_eng: A trade between updating weights (durable, costly to iterate) and steering via context (flexible, per-request cost).

title: Fine-tuning
definition: Retraining a model a little on your own examples so it picks up a style or skill it didn’t ship with.
examples: Training on 10,000 of your past support replies so the model sounds like your team, not a robot.
Sending a strong generalist off to a short apprenticeship in your specific shop.

_extra.analogy: Sending a strong generalist off to a short apprenticeship in your specific shop.
_extra.deeper: Techniques like LoRA make it cheap by nudging a small set of weights instead of all of them. It’s cooling as a first move: most teams now try prompting and RAG first, because a fine-tune is a maintenance burden that goes stale with the base model.
_extra.lens_pm: Teaching the model your style with examples — powerful but a maintenance cost; try prompting/RAG first.
_extra.lens_eng: Gradient updates on a base model (often LoRA/PEFT) over labeled examples to shift behavior.

title: fine-tuning API
definition: An API endpoint where you upload training data and request the model to fine-tune on it, returning a new model variant optimized for your task.
examples: Upload 500 examples of customer emails + correct support-ticket categories. Call the fine-tuning API. In an hour, get back a model that's better at categorization than the base model.
Sending your generic car to a shop and saying 'make it handle better on mountain roads'—you get a custom variant back.

_extra.analogy: Sending your generic car to a shop and saying 'make it handle better on mountain roads'—you get a custom variant back.
_extra.deeper: Fine-tuning APIs run the training loop on their hardware, charge by token or example, and give you a model checkpoint to call. Tradeoff: you don't see training loss curves, you can't customize loss functions, but you're not managing GPUs. Popular for task-specific optimization when in-context examples don't cut it.
_extra.lens_pm: Improves model quality on domain tasks; more cost-effective than prompt engineering beyond a certain threshold.
_extra.lens_eng: Managed training; no GPU setup; token-based pricing.

title: Fireworks
definition: Inference platform with focus on speed and cost; offers API for open-source and proprietary models.
examples: Fireworks claims fastest inference for open models; lower latency than Together or Replicate.
The performance-oriented cloud; optimize for latency and throughput.

_extra.analogy: The performance-oriented cloud; optimize for latency and throughput.
_extra.deeper: Fireworks optimizes inference kernels and batching; competes on speed and cost.
_extra.lens_pm: Speed is a differentiator; target high-volume, latency-sensitive apps.
_extra.lens_eng: Inference optimization is strong; good for real-time applications.

title: Flash Attention
definition: A faster, memory-frugal way to compute exact attention by being clever about how the GPU moves data.
examples: Swapping in flash attention lets a team train on longer sequences at the same speed, with no change to the results.
Cooking straight from the counter instead of walking to the pantry for each ingredient — same dish, far less trips.

_extra.analogy: Cooking straight from the counter instead of walking to the pantry for each ingredient — same dish, far less trips.
_extra.deeper: Standard attention writes a giant scores matrix to slow GPU memory and reads it back — the real bottleneck. Flash attention tiles the computation so intermediate values stay in fast on-chip memory, computing the same exact result without ever materializing the full matrix. The output is identical; the speed and memory savings are large, which is why it’s become the default.
_extra.lens_pm: An under-the-hood efficiency win that made longer contexts and cheaper training practical.
_extra.lens_eng: An IO-aware, tiled exact-attention kernel that avoids materializing the full attention matrix in HBM.

title: FLOPS
definition: Floating-point operations per second — a measure of raw compute power.
examples: A modern GPU might do 10 trillion FLOPS (10 TFLOPS); a model taking 100 trillion operations would take ~10 seconds.
Horsepower for chips — higher number sounds better, but doesn't always translate to real-world speed.

_extra.analogy: Horsepower for chips — higher number sounds better, but doesn't always translate to real-world speed.
_extra.deeper: FLOPS is a useful yardstick but can be misleading. Peak FLOPS (theoretical max) is rarely reached. Actual throughput depends on memory bandwidth, kernel efficiency, and problem size. It's also usually measured as FP32; FP16 or INT8 can be faster or slower depending on the hardware.
_extra.lens_pm: FLOPS is one number but not the only one that matters — latency and throughput matter more.
_extra.lens_eng: Use FLOPS for napkin math, but profile your actual code to see real throughput.

title: Format specification
definition: Explicitly defining how output should be structured — markdown, JSON, bullet points, etc.
examples: "Output as JSON: {name, age, occupation}." or "Format as a bulleted list with 3–5 items."
Like saying "write as a shopping list" vs. "write as a paragraph."

_extra.analogy: Like saying "write as a shopping list" vs. "write as a paragraph."
_extra.deeper: Format specs reduce ambiguity and enable parsing. Structured formats (JSON, XML) are machine-readable. Natural formats (markdown, bullets) are human-readable. Combine format specs with examples or templates for clarity.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables downstream automation and consistent user experience.
_extra.lens_eng: Use structured output or JSON mode when possible. Validate parsed results.

title: Forward pass
definition: Running input through the model start to finish to get an output — no learning, just computing.
examples: Every time you send a prompt and get an answer, that’s one forward pass through billions of parameters.
Feeding a coin into a vending machine and watching the can drop: input goes in, result comes out, nothing about the machine changes.

_extra.analogy: Feeding a coin into a vending machine and watching the can drop: input goes in, result comes out, nothing about the machine changes.
_extra.deeper: Data flows from the input through each layer’s math to the output. During training this is paired with a backward pass that computes gradients; at inference it’s all you run. It’s what you pay for per request — compute proportional to model size and sequence length.
_extra.lens_pm: Inference cost is basically the price of one forward pass — bigger model or longer input, bigger bill.
_extra.lens_eng: Evaluation of the network’s function on an input, producing activations and logits, without gradient updates.

title: Foundation model
definition: A big, general model trained once on broad data, then adapted to countless specific jobs instead of building one from scratch each time.
examples: The same base model powers a coding assistant, a support bot, and a summarizer.
A liberal-arts graduate you can train up for almost any role, versus hiring a narrow specialist per task.

_extra.analogy: A liberal-arts graduate you can train up for almost any role, versus hiring a narrow specialist per task.
_extra.deeper: The term captures a shift: instead of training a bespoke model per task, you train one large general model and adapt it — by prompting, retrieval, or fine-tuning. That reuse is why capabilities spread so fast, and why a handful of expensive base models sit under thousands of products.
_extra.lens_pm: Build on one general model and specialize it — cheaper and faster than bespoke models per feature.
_extra.lens_eng: A large pretrained model reused across tasks via prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning.

title: foundation model provider
definition: A company that trains and releases large foundation models (GPT, Claude, Llama) for others to build on.
examples: Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Google. They invest billions in compute, training data, and research to release models.
A quarry that extracts and sells raw stone; others carve it into sculptures.

_extra.analogy: A quarry that extracts and sells raw stone; others carve it into sculptures.
_extra.deeper: Foundation model providers are capital-intensive. They own distribution (API or weights), training data, and infrastructure. High barrier to entry but huge leverage if you get it right. Increasingly saturated (30+ labs releasing competitive models).
_extra.lens_pm: Controls pricing and model quality; gatekeeps capabilities.
_extra.lens_eng: Massive R&D required; scaling laws and architecture drive differentiation.

title: FP16
definition: Storing numbers as 16-bit floating-point values, the middle ground between float32 and int8.
examples: Weight: 0.847385 (float32, 4 bytes) → 0.8474 (float16, 2 bytes).
A reasonable compromise — smaller than float32 but safer than integer quantization.

_extra.analogy: A reasonable compromise — smaller than float32 but safer than integer quantization.
_extra.deeper: FP16 is 2x compression with minimal accuracy loss for most tasks. Modern GPUs (Nvidia A100, H100) are optimized for FP16. Training in FP16 is standard; serving in FP16 is even faster. The downside: FP16 has smaller dynamic range, so some models with very large or very small values suffer.
_extra.lens_pm: Best balance of compression and safety for most models.
_extra.lens_eng: Train and serve in FP16 by default. Use FP32 only if you see numerical issues.

title: Frame Interpolation
definition: Generating intermediate frames between two video frames to create smooth slow-motion or increase frame rate.
examples: A video at 30fps -> interpolate to 60fps or 120fps for slo-mo sports. A 2-frame clip -> generate 10 frames in between.
Flip-book animation: you draw frames 1 and 3, and fill in frame 2 to make it smooth.

_extra.analogy: Flip-book animation: you draw frames 1 and 3, and fill in frame 2 to make it smooth.
_extra.deeper: Requires predicting motion (optical flow) and synthesizing pixels. Challenges: occlusion (new areas becoming visible), disocclusion (disappearing areas), blur, and ambiguity (multiple plausible in-betweens). Modern methods: flow-based (predict motion, warp + inpaint) or learning-based end-to-end (RIFE, trained on large video datasets). Diffusion-based approaches emerging. Must preserve temporal coherence.
_extra.lens_pm: Powers video upsampling, slow-motion effects, frame rate conversion for streaming.
_extra.lens_eng: Datasets: Vimeo90K, YouTube, custom. Metric: PSNR, SSIM, perceptual loss. Models: RIFE, DAIN.

title: Frequency penalty
definition: A setting that pushes down a word’s odds the more times it has already appeared.
examples: Generating product tags, a dev raises the frequency penalty so common words like “premium” stop dominating every list.
Like a game where each repeat of a word costs you more points than the last.

_extra.analogy: Like a game where each repeat of a word costs you more points than the last.
_extra.deeper: Unlike a flat repetition penalty, this one scales with how often a token has shown up — the tenth “the” is barely touched, but the tenth “premium” gets hit hard. It curbs runaway repetition while leaving genuinely common words mostly alone.
_extra.lens_pm: Tune it to keep outputs varied when you’re generating lists or many short items.
_extra.lens_eng: Subtracts a term proportional to a token’s prior count in the generation from its logit before softmax.

title: Freshness
definition: How up-to-date the information a system can retrieve actually is.
examples: A pricing assistant that indexes the catalog nightly is a day fresh; if a price changed this morning, its answer is confidently wrong until the next refresh.
Milk in the fridge — the question isn’t whether it’s there, it’s whether it’s still good.

_extra.analogy: Milk in the fridge — the question isn’t whether it’s there, it’s whether it’s still good.
_extra.deeper: Retrieval systems are only as current as their last update. Freshness measures the lag between reality and what the index knows. High freshness matters for prices, inventory, news, and status; it matters less for stable reference material. The tension is cost — near-real-time indexing is expensive, so teams pick a refresh cadence that matches how fast the underlying data actually moves.
_extra.lens_pm: Decide per data source how stale is acceptable, then set the refresh cadence to match — not everything needs to be live.
_extra.lens_eng: Track index lag against source-of-truth update time; choose refresh frequency by each dataset’s volatility.

title: Frontier model
definition: The most capable models out there at any given moment — the current top of the line, wherever the line happens to be.
examples: When a lab ships its newest, biggest model, that’s a frontier model until the next one lands.
The flagship phone of the year — until next year’s makes it ordinary.

_extra.analogy: The flagship phone of the year — until next year’s makes it ordinary.
_extra.deeper: It’s a moving label, not a fixed tier — today’s frontier is next year’s baseline. The term shows up most in policy and safety conversations, because the newest, most capable systems carry the least-understood risks and draw the most scrutiny before release.
_extra.lens_pm: Highest capability, highest cost — reach for it when quality matters more than price.
_extra.lens_eng: The current capability ceiling; typically the largest/newest models under active evaluation.

title: frontier safety
definition: Research and practices aimed at ensuring very large, capable models don't cause harm—evaluating risks, designing mitigations, and testing before deployment.
examples: Before releasing Claude 3, Anthropic evaluated it on biosecurity, autonomous hacking, and planning capabilities—measuring failure modes, then building guardrails.
Pilot testing a new plane design in a simulator before flying with passengers.

_extra.analogy: Pilot testing a new plane design in a simulator before flying with passengers.
_extra.deeper: Frontier safety is high-stakes because the risks are abstract and potentially existential. It's not traditional cybersecurity; it's about what a superhuman model might be capable of and how to prevent misuse. Evals, interpretability, RLHF, capability monitoring all fall under it.
_extra.lens_pm: Risk management for advanced models; required by regulators in some regions.
_extra.lens_eng: Red-teaming, adversarial testing, evals on dangerous capabilities.

title: Function Calling
definition: The model outputs a clean, structured request to run a specific function — name plus arguments — instead of free text.
examples: You describe a `send_email(to, subject, body)` function; the model replies with those three fields filled in, and your code sends it.
Filling out a proper order form with the exact fields, rather than scrawling your request on a napkin.

_extra.analogy: Filling out a proper order form with the exact fields, rather than scrawling your request on a napkin.
_extra.deeper: You hand the model a list of functions and their argument shapes. When it decides one applies, it returns valid structured output — usually JSON — matching that shape, which your program parses and executes. It is the backbone of tool use because it makes the model’s intent machine-readable instead of something you have to scrape out of a sentence.
_extra.lens_pm: It is what makes a model a reliable trigger for real actions, not just a text box.
_extra.lens_eng: Constrained generation of a JSON payload matching a declared function schema, dispatched by the host application.

title: Function Schema
definition: The formal description of a function’s name, inputs, and types that tells the model how to call it correctly.
examples: The schema says get_weather takes a city string and an optional units field, so the model produces exactly those arguments and nothing else.
A form with labeled, required fields — the model can only fill in what the form asks for, in the right format.

_extra.analogy: A form with labeled, required fields — the model can only fill in what the form asks for, in the right format.
_extra.deeper: A schema turns a vague “call the weather tool” into a strict contract — required fields, types, allowed values — that the model’s output must satisfy. Good schemas with clear descriptions dramatically cut malformed calls; sloppy ones invite the model to hallucinate arguments. It’s the interface layer where natural language meets structured code, and its quality quietly determines how reliable your tool use is.
_extra.lens_pm: Well-written schemas are the difference between tools that just work and tools the agent constantly misuses.
_extra.lens_eng: A typed signature (often JSON Schema) constraining the arguments the model must emit for a tool call.

title: function calling API
definition: An API feature that lets you define functions (tools), and the model decides when and how to call them with structured arguments.
examples: Define functions: 'get_weather(city)' and 'search_flights(from, to, date)'. User asks 'flights to LA next week.' Model returns JSON: {function: 'search_flights', args: {from: 'NYC', to: 'LA', date: ...}}.
Giving the model a menu of abilities—it looks at the request and picks which ability to use.

_extra.analogy: Giving the model a menu of abilities—it looks at the request and picks which ability to use.
_extra.deeper: Function calling is how agents work at scale. Instead of prompting the model to generate command text, it returns structured JSON that names the function and arguments. Reduced hallucination, easier parsing, composable. All major APIs now support it.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables reliable agent workflows; reduces parsing errors and cost from retries.
_extra.lens_eng: Structured output; LLM returns function name and JSON args, not free text.

title: Function schema prompting
definition: Passing a formal definition of available functions/tools to the model so it can decide which one to call and with what parameters.
examples: API has function "search_web(query: string, num_results: int)". Pass schema to model. Model outputs: "I'll call search_web with query='GDP France' and num_results=5".
Handing someone a phonebook: "Here are the plumbers in your area, here's how to call them."

_extra.analogy: Handing someone a phonebook: "Here are the plumbers in your area, here's how to call them."
_extra.deeper: Function schema prompting bridges language and action. The model sees formal specifications and outputs valid function calls. APIs like OpenAI's function_call mode handle this. The model must learn to parse its own output correctly (or use structured output to enforce it).
_extra.lens_pm: Enables complex agentic workflows. Model can autonomously call APIs.
_extra.lens_eng: Define function schemas carefully. Parse model output and validate before executing.

title: Fusion Retrieval
definition: Run several searches at once and blend their results into one ranked list instead of trusting a single method.
examples: A support bot fires a keyword search and a meaning-based search for the same question, then fuses both lists so a good hit from either one still surfaces.
Asking three librarians the same question and merging their piles — the book everyone points to floats to the top.

_extra.analogy: Asking three librarians the same question and merging their piles — the book everyone points to floats to the top.
_extra.deeper: No single retrieval method is best for every query — keyword search nails exact terms, vector search catches paraphrases. Fusion runs multiple retrievers in parallel and combines their rankings, usually with a scoring rule like reciprocal rank fusion. The payoff is coverage; the cost is running and merging more searches per query.
_extra.lens_pm: Fewer "I couldn’t find that" misses, because a weak result from one method is rescued by another.
_extra.lens_eng: Query N retrievers concurrently, then combine their ranked lists via a fusion function (commonly RRF) into a single ordering.

title: GAN
definition: Two networks in a duel: one fakes images, the other calls out fakes, and both get sharper.
examples: The eerily realistic faces on “thispersondoesnotexist” were GAN output, back when GANs ruled image generation.
A forger and a detective locked in a room — each pushes the other to get better until the forgeries pass.

_extra.analogy: A forger and a detective locked in a room — each pushes the other to get better until the forgeries pass.
_extra.deeper: A generator invents images and a discriminator judges real vs. fake; training pits them against each other until the generator’s fakes fool the judge. It produces crisp results but is notoriously unstable to train and prone to “mode collapse,” where it churns out the same few images. Diffusion models have mostly taken over because they’re steadier.
_extra.lens_pm: A once-dominant approach now mostly of historical and niche interest for generation.
_extra.lens_eng: A minimax game between a generator and discriminator, trained to a Nash equilibrium.

title: Gating Network
definition: The little module that scores the experts and decides which ones handle each token.
examples: When an MoE layer picks its top two experts for a token, the gating network produced those scores.
Like a maitre d’ reading the room and deciding which chef should cook each order.

_extra.analogy: Like a maitre d’ reading the room and deciding which chef should cook each order.
_extra.deeper: It takes the token’s representation and outputs a weight for each expert, and the top few weights decide who runs and how much their output counts. Training has to keep it from favoring the same experts every time, usually with load-balancing penalties. Small as it is, the gating network shapes whether the whole mixture works or collapses onto a handful of overworked experts.
_extra.lens_pm: A tiny component whose quality quietly determines whether a big sparse model behaves.
_extra.lens_eng: A learned softmax-scored selector assigning per-token weights to experts, with load-balancing losses.

title: Gaussian Splatting
definition: Representing a 3D scene as a cloud of colored, oriented Gaussians - efficient rendering of novel views.
examples: Multi-view photos -> optimize Gaussian positions, colors, covariance -> render novel viewpoints in real-time.
Instead of tracing rays, you paint with blurry paint drops (Gaussians) positioned in 3D space.

_extra.analogy: Instead of tracing rays, you paint with blurry paint drops (Gaussians) positioned in 3D space.
_extra.deeper: Each Gaussian: center, covariance (orientation/scale), color. Volume rendering sums contributions along each ray. Differentiable rasterization enables optimization. Much faster than NeRF (10-100x speedup), real-time quality, fewer views needed. Trade-off: requires careful initialization (SfM points or coarse NeRF), can have artifacts (floaters, oversplatting). Emerging as practical alternative to NeRF.
_extra.lens_pm: Real-time 3D rendering, VR/AR, game engines, streaming 3D content.
_extra.lens_eng: Differentiable splatting + sorting-based rendering. Faster than NeRF. Requires CUDA. Metric: same as NeRF (PSNR, LPIPS).

title: Gemini
definition: Google's family of multimodal language models, designed to compete with GPT-4 across text, image, audio, and video.
examples: Gemini Ultra (2023) matches GPT-4 on benchmarks; Gemini Nano runs on-device; integrated into Google Workspace.
Google's all-in-one AI, bringing their search and ads expertise to the era of LLMs.

_extra.analogy: Google's all-in-one AI, bringing their search and ads expertise to the era of LLMs.
_extra.deeper: Gemini is multimodal from the ground up (not bolted-on image support like early GPT-4). It's integrated into Google's ecosystem: search, Gmail, Docs. Trained on diverse data including Google's own systems.
_extra.lens_pm: Leverage: integrated into Google's products and advertising platform. Long-term competitive moat.
_extra.lens_eng: Multimodal from the ground up; means reasoning across images, video, audio more naturally.

title: Generalization
definition: The whole point — doing well on data the model has never seen, not just the examples it trained on.
examples: A well-generalized spam filter catches brand-new scam wording it never saw in training.
Learning to ride any bike, not just the exact one you practiced on.

_extra.analogy: Learning to ride any bike, not just the exact one you practiced on.
_extra.deeper: Generalization is the gap between training performance and real-world performance. Everything in ML — regularization, validation sets, more data — is ultimately in service of closing it. Overfitting and underfitting are the two ways it breaks.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s the only performance number that matters — measure on data the model hasn’t seen.
_extra.lens_eng: Expected performance on the true data distribution, estimated via held-out/test error.

title: Generative Adversarial Network
definition: The full name for a GAN — a generator and a critic trained by competing against each other.
examples: Ian Goodfellow’s 2014 paper introduced the idea and set off years of photorealistic-face research.
Counterfeiter versus bank teller: the better the teller gets at spotting fakes, the better the counterfeiter has to be.

_extra.analogy: Counterfeiter versus bank teller: the better the teller gets at spotting fakes, the better the counterfeiter has to be.
_extra.deeper: The generator maps random noise to fake data; the discriminator learns to separate fakes from real samples. Their opposing objectives create a moving target that, when it works, produces sharp samples — and when it doesn’t, collapses or oscillates. The adversarial framing was the big idea; the training pain was the price.
_extra.lens_pm: Historically important, but you’ll rarely reach for it in a new product today.
_extra.lens_eng: Same as GAN: adversarial training of paired generator and discriminator networks.

title: Generative AI
definition: AI that makes new stuff — text, images, code, audio — rather than just sorting or scoring what already exists.
examples: Asking a model to write a poem or generate a product mockup is generative AI; asking it to label a photo “cat” is not.
The difference between a critic who rates paintings and an artist who paints new ones.

_extra.analogy: The difference between a critic who rates paintings and an artist who paints new ones.
_extra.deeper: Generative models learn the shape of their training data well enough to sample fresh examples from it. For language, that’s predicting the next token over and over. The output is novel in wording but bounded by what the training distribution taught it.
_extra.lens_pm: It opened AI to creative and drafting work, which is why it went mainstream so fast.
_extra.lens_eng: Models that learn a data distribution and sample from it, e.g. autoregressive LLMs or diffusion image models.

title: GGUF
definition: A file format for storing quantized models that's lightweight and efficient for CPU and small-device inference.
examples: Run a 7B-parameter model on your laptop by loading a GGUF file into llama.cpp.
A portable, self-contained suitcase for neural networks.

_extra.analogy: A portable, self-contained suitcase for neural networks.
_extra.deeper: GGUF stores quantized weights in a streamlined binary format with metadata. It's designed to be fast to load and require minimal memory. Llama.cpp and Ollama popularized it by making quantized open-source models accessible on regular hardware.
_extra.lens_pm: GGUF is how millions of people run LLMs on laptops and phones — it democratizes access.
_extra.lens_eng: GGUF is the standard for CPU-friendly inference; llama.cpp, Ollama, and many others support it.

title: GitHub Copilot
definition: Code completion and generation powered by a GPT model, trained on open-source code, baked into your editor.
examples: You start typing a function to validate an email address, and Copilot suggests a whole regex pattern and error handling—you accept or skip.
An autocomplete that learned from millions of GitHub repos, so it knows not just English but *code patterns*.

_extra.analogy: An autocomplete that learned from millions of GitHub repos, so it knows not just English but *code patterns*.
_extra.deeper: Copilot is a fine-tuned code model (originally GPT-3 based, now includes GPT-4). It runs on GitHub's side and streams completions to your editor. It has seen so much public code that it learns common patterns, but that training also raises data ownership questions. Accuracy varies by language and task.
_extra.lens_pm: Increases developer velocity and reduces time spent on boilerplate; changes hiring bar but doesn't eliminate junior roles.
_extra.lens_eng: Real-time token-level code prediction; integrates with LSP for context awareness.

title: Goal
definition: The outcome the agent is trying to reach — the thing that tells it when it’s actually done.
examples: The goal is “all tests pass and the feature works”; every edit and rerun is measured against whether that’s true yet.
The destination in the sat-nav: every turn is judged by whether it gets you closer to it.

_extra.analogy: The destination in the sat-nav: every turn is judged by whether it gets you closer to it.
_extra.deeper: The goal is the agent’s north star — it drives planning, shapes each decision, and defines the stop condition. A clear, checkable goal (“tests green”) makes agents work well; a fuzzy one (“make it better”) leaves them wandering or declaring victory early. Much of the trouble with agents traces back to a goal that was never crisply specified in the first place.
_extra.lens_pm: A vague goal is the most common reason an agent “kind of” does the task — pin it down.
_extra.lens_eng: The target outcome that defines the agent’s objective function and termination condition.

title: Goal misgeneralization
definition: A model that learned the right behavior for the wrong reason, and reveals it the moment the world shifts.
examples: An agent trained to reach a coin that was always on the right learns "go right" instead of "get the coin", and walks past the coin when it moves left.
A dog that seems to have learned "sit" but actually learned "do a trick when you smell a treat" — useless once the treats are gone.

_extra.analogy: A dog that seems to have learned "sit" but actually learned "do a trick when you smell a treat" — useless once the treats are gone.
_extra.deeper: Unlike reward misspecification (the goal was wrong), here the reward was fine but the model latched onto a correlated proxy that held during training and breaks under distribution shift. Capabilities generalize better than goals, so a competent model can pursue the wrong objective competently. Diverse training and stress-testing off-distribution help expose it.
_extra.lens_pm: Strong in-distribution performance can hide a goal that quietly falls apart in the real world.
_extra.lens_eng: The learned objective is a training-correlated proxy; probe with off-distribution environments where proxy and true goal diverge.

title: GOFAI
definition: A slang term for pre-neural-network AI — symbolic, logic-based, hand-crafted knowledge — now mostly a punchline about how hard we got it wrong.
examples: In the 1960s, researchers believed GOFAI would soon reach human-level reasoning; by the 1990s, researchers had switched to probabilistic and connectionist methods, and "GOFAI" became a term for the naive old ways.
Like the Model T versus modern cars: it worked, it was impressive for its time, but you'd never go back.

_extra.analogy: Like the Model T versus modern cars: it worked, it was impressive for its time, but you'd never go back.
_extra.deeper: The acronym was popularized by researcher John Haugeland in his 1985 book. By that time, the "good old-fashioned" approach — explicit rules, logic, symbolic knowledge — was already failing at real-world tasks. It couldn't handle uncertainty, required immense manual labor to encode expertise, and broke on edge cases. The rise of machine learning and neural networks displaced it almost entirely. Today GOFAI is mainly historical; the term itself is a bit affectionate and a bit mocking.
_extra.lens_pm: Instructive failure: the assumption that intelligence could be built top-down through logic turned out to be far harder than scaling up learning from data.
_extra.lens_eng: Umbrella term for pre-learning-era approaches: rule engines, theorem provers, knowledge graphs, logic programming.

title: Gold Set
definition: A hand-crafted dataset of examples where you know the right answer—your source of truth for evaluation.
examples: For a medical AI, a gold set of 100 X-rays with confirmed diagnoses from board-certified radiologists.
Like a reference copy of a book you use to check if a translation is accurate.

_extra.analogy: Like a reference copy of a book you use to check if a translation is accurate.
_extra.deeper: Gold sets are expensive because they require expert annotation, but invaluable for benchmarking. They're stable (unlike user data, which drifts over time). The risk is that they can become stale or unrepresentative of real data. You need periodic refresh and evaluation on multiple gold sets to avoid overfitting to one.
_extra.lens_pm: Invest early in curating gold sets for domains where errors are costly (medicine, law, finance).
_extra.lens_eng: Version your gold sets, track what changed, and monitor model performance on them continuously.

title: Golden Dataset
definition: A high-quality, manually curated dataset used as the ground truth for evaluation—different from 'gold set' by being produced entirely by experts.
examples: For a medical AI, a dataset of 500 X-rays each reviewed by 3 board-certified radiologists and consensus labels derived.
Like a museum's master copy of a painting compared to reproductions.

_extra.analogy: Like a museum's master copy of a painting compared to reproductions.
_extra.deeper: Golden datasets are expensive to build (expert annotation) but invaluable. They're more reliable than crowdsourced labels. Good practice: version them and retrain models when gold standards evolve. Some orgs distinguish 'gold set' (any human-annotated reference) from 'golden dataset' (highly curated, expert-validated).
_extra.lens_pm: Invest in golden datasets for domains where accuracy is critical (medicine, law, safety).
_extra.lens_eng: Build with multiple expert raters; measure inter-rater agreement; track and version changes.

title: Gold Labels
definition: The answers you trust completely, usually because a careful human wrote them down.
examples: Before scoring a support-bot, a team hand-labels 500 tickets with the “correct” category and treats those as gold.
The teacher’s answer key at the back of the book — the one everything else gets graded against.

_extra.analogy: The teacher’s answer key at the back of the book — the one everything else gets graded against.
_extra.deeper: Gold labels are the reference answers you assume are right, produced by expert humans or a trusted process. They’re expensive, so you rarely have many — which is exactly why people reach for weak supervision or synthetic data to fill the gap. If your gold set is itself wrong or biased, every number downstream inherits that flaw.
_extra.lens_pm: Your metrics are only as trustworthy as the gold set they’re scored against, so invest in getting a small clean one.
_extra.lens_eng: A curated, high-confidence labeled set used as ground truth for evaluation or as the seed for training.

title: Goodhart's Law
definition: Once you start optimizing a metric, it stops being a reliable measure of what you wanted.
examples: You measure model quality by BLEU score. Teams fine-tune obsessively on BLEU. BLEU improves, but human reviewers think translations got worse.
Like a school district that teaches to the standardized test—test scores go up, but actual learning doesn't.

_extra.analogy: Like a school district that teaches to the standardized test—test scores go up, but actual learning doesn't.
_extra.deeper: The law holds because metrics are always proxies—they correlate with the real goal, but imperfectly. Once an agent (person or model) learns the metric, they exploit the gap. The only antidote is diversification: measure multiple things, include held-out human judgment, and accept that you can't automate everything.
_extra.lens_pm: Use metrics as signals, not gospel. Pair every metric with human oversight.
_extra.lens_eng: Build diverse evaluation suites; don't optimize a single number to the exclusion of all else.

title: Google DeepMind
definition: Google's AI research division, formed from merging Google Brain and the acquired DeepMind, focused on fundamental breakthroughs.
examples: DeepMind created AlphaGo (beat Go champion, 2016), AlphaFold (solved protein folding, 2020), and Gemini (foundation model, 2023).
The research wing that goes after moonshot problems—whether they're profitable is secondary.

_extra.analogy: The research wing that goes after moonshot problems—whether they're profitable is secondary.
_extra.deeper: DeepMind is known for reinforcement learning, symbolic reasoning, and long-horizon research. Now integrated under Google, they have access to massive compute and data. Gemini is their answer to GPT; released in multiple sizes.
_extra.lens_pm: Their research output (papers, methods) shapes the field; Gemini targets enterprise and research.
_extra.lens_eng: Open-sourced AlphaFold weights and code; also published interpretability research on neural networks.

title: GPQA
definition: A benchmark of 448 extremely hard multiple-choice questions in biology, physics, and chemistry—meant to be unsolvable by humans without domain expertise.
examples: A question about molecular biology that requires understanding multiple papers to answer correctly. Frontier models score ~60%, random is 25%.
Like asking a literature major to answer PhD-level physics questions.

_extra.analogy: Like asking a literature major to answer PhD-level physics questions.
_extra.deeper: GPQA is designed to resist gaming because the questions are Google-proof (searching won't help, you need actual knowledge). Most models score just above random. It's an emerging benchmark for detecting capability edge cases and whether models are truly reasoning or pattern-matching.
_extra.lens_pm: GPQA is future-oriented; it highlights where frontier models still have gaps.
_extra.lens_eng: Don't expect high scores on GPQA yet; use it to track progress on truly hard reasoning.

title: GPT
definition: OpenAI's line of language models, including GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4; the original foundation models that started the LLM era.
examples: GPT-3 (2020) had 175B parameters and showed that scale unlocked new abilities; GPT-4 (2023) added multimodal input.
The family that changed everything; now synonymous with "large language model."

_extra.analogy: The family that changed everything; now synonymous with "large language model."
_extra.deeper: GPT models use a causal transformer trained on next-token prediction, then fine-tuned with RLHF. Each new version has been trained on more data, with bigger models and more compute. GPT-4 is a multimodal gated release.
_extra.lens_pm: GPT established the API + chatbot product model; pricing is per token (input + output).
_extra.lens_eng: GPT-4 is frontier: state-of-the-art reasoning, code, multimodal. Inference is expensive; quantization and distillation popular.

title: GPT-4
definition: OpenAI's most capable language model, released March 2023, with improved reasoning, coding, and multimodal abilities.
examples: GPT-4 passed the bar exam (top 10%), wrote code for unfamiliar libraries, and analyzed images (multimodal).
The leap: GPT-3 was impressive, but GPT-4 convinced everyone LLMs could think.

_extra.analogy: The leap: GPT-3 was impressive, but GPT-4 convinced everyone LLMs could think.
_extra.deeper: GPT-4 uses chain-of-thought reasoning at inference time; can solve more complex problems than GPT-3.5. Multimodal (image + text input) added later. Launched as gated release for safety. GPT-4 Turbo (2023) added 128k context and lower costs.
_extra.lens_pm: Premium pricing justified by capability; used for high-stakes applications (legal, coding, research).
_extra.lens_eng: Frontier model for reasoning and code; expensive but often worth it for complex tasks.

title: GPT Architecture
definition: The decoder-only transformer that predicts the next word, over and over — the shape behind most chatbots.
examples: Every model in the GPT, Claude, and Llama families shares this same basic decoder-only skeleton.
Like a storyteller who only ever thinks about the very next word, but does it so well the whole story hangs together.

_extra.analogy: Like a storyteller who only ever thinks about the very next word, but does it so well the whole story hangs together.
_extra.deeper: It’s a stack of transformer decoder blocks that only look leftward — each position can attend to earlier tokens but not future ones — trained purely to predict the next token. That single simple objective, scaled up massively, turned out to produce fluent writing, reasoning, and code. The architecture barely changed; the scale and data did.
_extra.lens_pm: The default shape of the generative models your product is probably built on.
_extra.lens_eng: A causal, decoder-only transformer trained autoregressively on next-token prediction.

title: GPTQ
definition: A quantization method that uses the Hessian to intelligently decide which weights to quantize less, so you get good accuracy at low bit-widths.
examples: Using GPTQ you can quantize GPT models to 3 bits with minimal accuracy loss, or 4 bits with nearly no loss.
A smart editor who cuts the least important words to make a story fit in fewer pages.

_extra.analogy: A smart editor who cuts the least important words to make a story fit in fewer pages.
_extra.deeper: GPTQ computes the Hessian (second-order information) about which weights matter most, then uses that to set per-weight quantization scales. It's slower to apply than simple post-training quantization, but the accuracy payoff is huge. Ollama and text-generation-webui popularized pre-quantized GPTQ models.
_extra.lens_pm: GPTQ is the standard for distributing small, fast, accurate open-source models.
_extra.lens_eng: GPTQ models are fast and efficient; libraries like GPTQ-for-LLaMA or Marlin make them easy to use.

title: GPTs
definition: OpenAI's way of packaging a prompt, instructions, knowledge files, and tool integrations into a shareable chatbot, without code.
examples: Create a GPT called 'Tax Advisor' with IRS docs and a calculator tool. Share a link; anyone can chat with it. No coding required.
A template for ChatGPT—set the personality, upload docs, link to your tools, share a link.

_extra.analogy: A template for ChatGPT—set the personality, upload docs, link to your tools, share a link.
_extra.deeper: GPTs are ChatGPT + configuration + files + tools. Under the hood, they're still just LLM calls, but the packaging makes them accessible to non-engineers. You can publish them, sell them, or keep them private. Limited: no custom training, no fine-tuning, constrained to OpenAI's ecosystem.
_extra.lens_pm: Democratizes agent deployment; enables non-technical users to build AI assistants.
_extra.lens_eng: Configuration-based; no code; limited to ChatGPT capabilities.

title: GPU
definition: A specialized processor optimized for parallel computation, essential for training and serving neural networks.
examples: An Nvidia A100 GPU can do trillions of floating-point operations per second, making it 100x faster than a CPU for matrix multiplication.
A specialized worker who's really fast at doing lots of simple calculations in parallel.

_extra.analogy: A specialized worker who's really fast at doing lots of simple calculations in parallel.
_extra.deeper: GPUs excel at matrix operations because they have thousands of cores running in parallel. This is perfect for neural networks. The tradeoff: GPUs are expensive ($5k–$20k), use lots of power, and have limited memory (40–80GB for consumer GPUs). Model parallelism, data parallelism, and pipelining are techniques to work around these limits.
_extra.lens_pm: GPU cost dominates the serving budget for large models.
_extra.lens_eng: Profile your model. Estimate memory (parameters × bytes per param). Choose GPU based on memory and latency needs.

title: GPU cloud
definition: A service that rents GPUs by the hour—useful for training models without buying hardware.
examples: Lambda, CoreWeave, RunPod, Modal. Rent H100s at $3-5/hour, SSH in, train your model.
Renting a bulldozer instead of owning one—pay per day, return when done.

_extra.analogy: Renting a bulldozer instead of owning one—pay per day, return when done.
_extra.deeper: GPU clouds democratized model training. No upfront $500k investment; pay as you go. Tradeoff: you pay a premium (more than data center rental), and availability fluctuates. Newer providers are targeting AI workloads specifically.
_extra.lens_pm: Lowers barrier to entry for training; shifts capex to opex.
_extra.lens_eng: Hourly billing; SSH/cloud APIs; community-built; less reliable than owned infra.

title: Grader
definition: A function or model that takes a model's output and a reference and produces a score—automating the evaluation step.
examples: Grader function: takes model output and gold answer, returns 1 if correct, 0 if wrong. Used in eval pipeline.
Like an automated essay grader that reads your essay and assigns a score.

_extra.analogy: Like an automated essay grader that reads your essay and assigns a score.
_extra.deeper: Graders can be rule-based (exact match, length checks) or learned (LLM-as-judge, a fine-tuned model trained to score outputs). Learned graders are more flexible but require training data. Graders should be fast (not calling APIs repeatedly) and deterministic when possible.
_extra.lens_pm: Good graders are force-multipliers. They let you evaluate at scale.
_extra.lens_eng: Build deterministic rule-based graders for simple metrics; train graders for complex judgments.

title: Gradient
definition: The direction and steepness of change that tells each weight which way to move to reduce error.
examples: After a wrong prediction, the gradient for each weight says “nudge me up a little, me down a lot,” and the optimizer follows those hints.
Like feeling the slope under your feet in fog — it tells you which way is downhill even when you can’t see the valley.

_extra.analogy: Like feeling the slope under your feet in fog — it tells you which way is downhill even when you can’t see the valley.
_extra.deeper: A gradient is the derivative of the loss with respect to every parameter — a giant vector pointing toward steepest increase, so training steps the opposite way. Backpropagation is just the efficient method for computing it, and problems like vanishing or exploding gradients are what make deep networks hard to train.
_extra.lens_pm: The invisible feedback signal that makes learning possible; when it misbehaves, training stalls.
_extra.lens_eng: ∂loss/∂θ for all parameters; computed via backprop and consumed by the optimizer to update weights.

title: Gradient accumulation
definition: Summing gradients over several small batches before updating, to fake a bigger batch than memory allows.
examples: Your GPU fits only 8 examples, but you accumulate over 32 mini-batches to update as if the batch size were 256.
Like filling a big order in several small trips because your cart is tiny — you still deliver the full load, just in pieces.

_extra.analogy: Like filling a big order in several small trips because your cart is tiny — you still deliver the full load, just in pieces.
_extra.deeper: When the desired batch size won’t fit in memory, gradient accumulation runs several forward-backward passes, adds up their gradients, and applies one optimizer step, simulating a large effective batch. This lets modest hardware train with the stability benefits of big batches, trading time for memory. The effective batch size is the per-step batch times the accumulation count.
_extra.lens_pm: How you get big-batch training on small hardware — trading wall-clock time for memory you don’t have.
_extra.lens_eng: Accumulate gradients over N micro-batches, then one optimizer step; effective batch = micro-batch × N.

title: Gradient clipping
definition: Capping how big a gradient step can be, so one wild update doesn’t wreck the model.
examples: A rare huge gradient would send the loss to infinity, but clipping caps its size and training keeps going smoothly.
Like a governor on an engine that prevents it from redlining and blowing up on a sudden surge.

_extra.analogy: Like a governor on an engine that prevents it from redlining and blowing up on a sudden surge.
_extra.deeper: Occasionally gradients explode — becoming enormous — and a single unclipped step can push weights into garbage, spiking the loss to NaN. Gradient clipping bounds the gradient’s norm (or value) before the update, keeping training stable through rough patches. It’s cheap insurance widely used in training deep and recurrent networks, especially with high learning rates or long sequences.
_extra.lens_pm: A stability safeguard that keeps long, expensive training runs from suddenly falling apart.
_extra.lens_eng: Bounds gradient norm/value before the update to prevent explosions; standard for stability in deep/recurrent training.
