_extra.lens_pm: Game art, 3D printing, CAD augmentation.
_extra.lens_eng: Marching cubes, Poisson surface reconstruction, or learned mesh deformation. Metric: Chamfer distance, F-score (geometric accuracy).

title: Meta AI
definition: Meta's AI division, formerly FAIR, known for open-source models and research on recommendation systems, NLP, and computer vision.
examples: Meta released Llama (open-weight LLM, 2023), LLaMA 2 (2023), and invested heavily in multilingual models and vision systems.
The company that pushes open-source aggressively, believing good science beats proprietary lock-in.

_extra.analogy: The company that pushes open-source aggressively, believing good science beats proprietary lock-in.
_extra.deeper: Meta's strategy is different from OpenAI and Google: release open weights, lead through scale and quality, let the ecosystem build on top. They face pressure to monetize LLMs but have invested in research leadership.
_extra.lens_pm: Open-source strategy builds goodwill and fast research iteration; harder to monetize directly.
_extra.lens_eng: Llama's weights are Apache 2.0 licensed; enabled a wave of fine-tuning and distillation startups.

title: Metadata Filtering
definition: Narrowing a vector search by plain attributes — date, author, tenant — before or during the similarity match.
examples: A support bot retrieves only docs tagged for the customer’s product tier, so a free user never sees enterprise-only answers.
Telling the librarian "only books from this decade" before asking which is most relevant.

_extra.analogy: Telling the librarian "only books from this decade" before asking which is most relevant.
_extra.deeper: Embeddings capture meaning but not hard facts like "belongs to org 42" or "published after 2024". Metadata filters attach those as structured fields and restrict the candidate set. The tricky part is when filtering happens: pre-filtering is precise but can starve the index, while post-filtering is fast but may throw away most of your top-k before you get enough matches.
_extra.lens_pm: It is how one shared search index safely serves many customers, permissions, and freshness rules.
_extra.lens_eng: Boolean predicates over payload fields, applied pre- or post-ANN; pre-filtering interacts badly with graph indexes if selectivity is high.

title: Meta-learning
definition: Training a model to get good at learning new tasks quickly, not just at one task.
examples: A meta-learned model adapts to a brand-new classification task from just a handful of examples, having practiced adapting many times.
Like a student who has learned how to study, so each new subject clicks faster than the last.

_extra.analogy: Like a student who has learned how to study, so each new subject clicks faster than the last.
_extra.deeper: Meta-learning — “learning to learn” — trains across many tasks so the model acquires a strategy for fast adaptation, rather than mastering a single task. Approaches range from optimization-based methods that find easily-fine-tuned initializations to models that adapt in-context. It’s the formal cousin of what large models do when they pick up a task from a few prompt examples.
_extra.lens_pm: The idea behind models that adapt fast to new tasks with little data — flexibility as a trained skill.
_extra.lens_eng: Optimize across a task distribution for rapid adaptation; kin to in-context few-shot behavior in large models.

title: Meta-prompting
definition: Using a model to generate or refine prompts for itself or other models — prompting about prompting.
examples: You give Claude a task and ask: "Generate the best system prompt for an AI that does X." It writes a refined prompt you can reuse.
Like a writer editing their own instructions to make them clearer.

_extra.analogy: Like a writer editing their own instructions to make them clearer.
_extra.deeper: Meta-prompting is a form of in-context learning and reflection. The model reasons about what instructions work. It can also be used for prompt optimization: iteratively improve a prompt by having the model critique and regenerate it. This is experimental and cost-intensive, but can yield domain-specific prompts better than hand-written ones.
_extra.lens_pm: Automates prompt engineering; useful for discovering patterns.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement a loop: generate prompt → test → critique → refine. Measure impact with a held-out eval set.

title: Metrics
definition: Numerical measurements over time—latency, throughput, error rate, cost—aggregated for trend analysis.
examples: Inference latency p50=100ms, p95=250ms, p99=500ms; throughput 1000 requests/sec; cost $0.001 per inference.
Your heart rate monitor showing beats-per-minute over the day so you can spot workout vs rest patterns.

_extra.analogy: Your heart rate monitor showing beats-per-minute over the day so you can spot workout vs rest patterns.
_extra.deeper: Time-series databases (Prometheus, InfluxDB) store high-cardinality metrics. Cardinality explosion (unique label combinations) makes storage expensive and queries slow. Rules aggregate (sum, rate, histogram) to make alerting feasible. Dimensionality (service, model, region) enables slicing but explodes cardinality.
_extra.lens_pm: Quantifies system health and ROI—track latency, cost, and quality metrics to guide decisions.
_extra.lens_eng: Instrumentation emits counters (requests), gauges (queue length), histograms (latency); time-series DB stores; query engine aggregates for dashboards and alerts.

title: Midjourney
definition: Independent text-to-image model company, known for high-quality artistic output and a Discord-first interface.
examples: Describe "oil painting of a cat wearing sunglasses" in Discord; Midjourney generates four variations.
The artist's favorite; produces beautiful, stylized images with less tinkering.

_extra.analogy: The artist's favorite; produces beautiful, stylized images with less tinkering.
_extra.deeper: Midjourney is proprietary; trained on diverse images. Known for aesthetic quality and style transfer. Discord bot interface is UX-forward but less technical than API-first tools.
_extra.lens_pm: Strong brand with creative professionals; pricing is per-month subscription ($10–96/mo).
_extra.lens_eng: Closed model; inference quality is high but can't inspect or fine-tune.

title: Milvus
definition: Open-source vector database by Zilliz, optimized for high-dimensional similarity search and scalability.
examples: Run Milvus on Kubernetes with Petabytes of embeddings; query across shards.
The distributed option; built for big data and horizontal scaling.

_extra.analogy: The distributed option; built for big data and horizontal scaling.
_extra.deeper: Milvus supports multiple indexing methods (HNSW, IVF, etc.) and can scale horizontally. Used by enterprises with massive embedding datasets.
_extra.lens_pm: Enterprise-grade; Zilliz offers managed service.
_extra.lens_eng: Horizontal scaling and multiple index types; more complex ops than Chroma but handles scale.

title: Misinformation
definition: False information spread without intent to deceive — people sharing wrong things they believe are true.
examples: A model confidently states an outdated medical guideline, a user believes it, and repeats it to friends as fact — no malice, real spread of a falsehood.
A game of telephone where the message gets garbled honestly — nobody’s lying, but what comes out the end is wrong.

_extra.analogy: A game of telephone where the message gets garbled honestly — nobody’s lying, but what comes out the end is wrong.
_extra.deeper: Misinformation is about error, not intent — the distinction from disinformation, which is deliberate. AI amplifies it two ways: models can generate confident falsehoods (hallucinations) that users trust and pass on, and they let anyone produce plausible content at scale. The defenses are the boring, hard ones: grounding outputs in sources, citing, fact-checking, and building systems that admit uncertainty instead of bluffing.
_extra.lens_pm: A reputational and real-world-harm risk whenever your model states facts users will act on.
_extra.lens_eng: Unintentional falsehoods, amplified by confident hallucination and cheap generation; mitigated with grounding, citation, and calibrated uncertainty.

title: Mistral
definition: French AI startup founded by ex-Meta researchers, building efficient open-source models that compete on speed and cost.
examples: Mistral 7B (2023) matches much larger models on benchmarks; Mistral Large targets GPT-4 class.
The scrappy challenger: not the biggest, but cleverly designed to do more with less.

_extra.analogy: The scrappy challenger: not the biggest, but cleverly designed to do more with less.
_extra.deeper: Mistral emphasizes efficient inference, modular architectures, and open weights. They deploy models via an API and also release weights. Known for technical depth and practical engineering.
_extra.lens_pm: Differentiation: efficiency. Markets toward cost-sensitive use cases and on-device deployment.
_extra.lens_eng: Mistral 7B inference is faster and cheaper than equivalent closed models; good for latency-critical apps.

title: MIT license
definition: The simplest open-source license—do whatever you want with the code, just keep the copyright notice.
examples: Django, React, Rails. You can use them, modify them, sell products on top, all you need is a copy of the MIT license and original author name.
Public domain but with a tiny string attached: you have to mention who wrote it.

_extra.analogy: Public domain but with a tiny string attached: you have to mention who wrote it.
_extra.deeper: MIT is shorter than Apache 2.0 and doesn't have explicit patent language, but it's so permissive that patents are largely irrelevant (you're getting the code, not the idea). Very popular for open-source; sometimes too lenient if you want reciprocal openness.
_extra.lens_pm: Frictionless adoption; maximum permissiveness.
_extra.lens_eng: Shortest license text; no patent grant but no restrictions.

title: Mixed precision
definition: Do most of the training math in low-precision numbers to go faster and use less memory, keeping full precision only where it matters.
examples: A team switches a training run to bf16 and suddenly the same GPUs fit a bigger batch and finish an epoch in half the time.
Rounding to the nearest cent while you shop, but keeping the exact figures for the final tax return.

_extra.analogy: Rounding to the nearest cent while you shop, but keeping the exact figures for the final tax return.
_extra.deeper: Weights and activations are stored and multiplied in 16-bit floats (fp16 or bf16) instead of 32-bit, which roughly halves memory and speeds up the matrix math on modern accelerators. The catch is numerical stability — tiny gradients can underflow to zero — so a full-precision master copy of the weights and loss scaling are kept to stop the training from quietly diverging.
_extra.lens_pm: It is most of why training the same model got cheaper and faster over the last few years, without changing the recipe.
_extra.lens_eng: Store/compute in fp16 or bf16 with an fp32 master weight copy and dynamic loss scaling to avoid gradient underflow.

title: Mixture model
definition: A model that combines several specialized sub-models, blending their outputs into one answer.
examples: A system routes a coding question to its code-savvy component and a poem request to another, mixing their strengths.
Like a panel of specialists where each weighs in and their votes are averaged into a diagnosis.

_extra.analogy: Like a panel of specialists where each weighs in and their votes are averaged into a diagnosis.
_extra.deeper: A mixture model composes multiple components, often weighting them by how relevant each is to the input. It’s the statistical idea behind mixture-of-experts architectures, where a router activates only the most relevant sub-networks per token — capturing diverse patterns without one monolithic model doing everything.
_extra.lens_pm: The concept behind “big model, but only part of it runs per query,” which keeps costs sane at scale.
_extra.lens_eng: A model combining weighted sub-models; the basis for mixture-of-experts routing over specialized components.

title: Mixture of Experts
definition: Split a model into many specialist sub-networks and route each token to just a few of them.
examples: A model has 64 expert blocks but activates only two per token, so it’s huge in capacity yet cheap to run.
A hospital where a receptionist sends each patient to the two right specialists instead of every doctor at once.

_extra.analogy: A hospital where a receptionist sends each patient to the two right specialists instead of every doctor at once.
_extra.deeper: In a mixture-of-experts layer, a lightweight router picks a small subset of expert sub-networks to process each token, so total parameters can be enormous while compute per token stays modest. The wins are capacity and efficiency; the headaches are load-balancing the experts, routing instability, and the memory to hold all those parameters. It powers several frontier models.
_extra.lens_pm: How models get much bigger in capability without a proportional jump in inference cost.
_extra.lens_eng: A layer that routes each token to a few of many expert subnetworks, decoupling parameter count from per-token compute.

title: MLflow
definition: An open-source platform for managing the ML lifecycle—from experiments to production deployment.
examples: Log a training run with MLflow, it records code, params, metrics, and the model artifact. Later, register it, promote it to staging, deploy to prod. Full audit trail.
Git for machine learning: track every model version, roll back, compare metrics.

_extra.analogy: Git for machine learning: track every model version, roll back, compare metrics.
_extra.deeper: MLflow has four components: Tracking (logs runs), Projects (reproducible execution), Models (unified format), Registry (deployment workflow). It's agnostic to the framework and runs on your infrastructure or their cloud. Widely adopted in enterprises; plays well with Databricks.
_extra.lens_pm: Critical for model governance and compliance; enables safe promotion of models through stages.
_extra.lens_eng: Run-level granularity; model registry with versioning and transitions.

title: MLOps
definition: The operational practices for training, testing, deploying, and monitoring machine learning models in production.
examples: An MLOps team monitors model drift, retrains when accuracy drops, version-controls datasets, and automates canary deployments.
DevOps for ML — managing the full lifecycle instead of just shipping code once.

_extra.analogy: DevOps for ML — managing the full lifecycle instead of just shipping code once.
_extra.deeper: MLOps covers data pipeline management, model versioning, experiment tracking, automated retraining, A/B testing, and monitoring for data drift or distribution shift. Unlike traditional software, ML systems can degrade silently if the world changes but your model doesn't.
_extra.lens_pm: MLOps is the unglamorous work that keeps models from rotting in production.
_extra.lens_eng: Build reproducible training pipelines, version everything (code, data, models), and monitor for covariate shift.

title: MMLU
definition: A benchmark of 15,000 multiple-choice questions across 57 domains—the gold standard for measuring broad knowledge.
examples: Question: 'Which of these is true about photosynthesis?' with four choices. The model's accuracy across all 15k questions is its MMLU score.
Like the SAT, but way longer and covering everything from abstract algebra to US history.

_extra.analogy: Like the SAT, but way longer and covering everything from abstract algebra to US history.
_extra.deeper: MMLU is valuable because it's diverse, hard for humans to memorize (you can't cheat on it), and well-calibrated to model capability—a 90% MMLU model is genuinely competent at broad knowledge. Downside: it's multiple-choice, so there's no penalty for reasoning poorly as long as you pick the right box. And leaked training data has inflated scores somewhat.
_extra.lens_pm: MMLU is the quickest way to compare models. A 90% MMLU model is probably more capable than an 80% one, all else equal.
_extra.lens_eng: Evaluate on MMLU regularly, but supplement with domain-specific benchmarks and human eval.

title: moat
definition: A defensible advantage—something that makes a business hard to copy or beat, even if a competitor has better tech.
examples: Network effects (everyone uses it), switching costs (too expensive to leave), scale advantages (cheapest at size), brand (people trust it). In AI: data, compute, the model itself, distribution.
A castle's moat keeps invaders out; a company's moat keeps competitors out.

_extra.analogy: A castle's moat keeps invaders out; a company's moat keeps competitors out.
_extra.deeper: In AI, moats are hotly debated. Does a big model have a moat? Maybe not—competition is fierce. Does a fine-tuned model on proprietary data have a moat? Possibly. Does distribution (integrations, brand, network) have a moat? Often yes. The most enduring moats are usually not the tech.
_extra.lens_pm: Moat determines long-term defensibility; shapes pricing power and profitability.
_extra.lens_eng: Data, scale, and network effects are the strongest technical moats.

title: Modal
definition: Serverless computing platform optimized for running GPU workloads and ML inference.
examples: Deploy a function that runs a Llama inference; Modal scales automatically.
Serverless for GPUs; scale to zero when not in use.

_extra.analogy: Serverless for GPUs; scale to zero when not in use.
_extra.deeper: Modal is built for bursty ML workloads; you define a function, it handles GPU provisioning. Good for webhooks, batch jobs, and inference.
_extra.lens_pm: Cost efficiency for variable workloads.
_extra.lens_eng: Simple programming model; good for inference APIs and batch processing.

title: Modality
definition: A type of input or output - text, image, audio, video - that the model can process or produce.
examples: GPT-4 Vision accepts both text and image modalities as input. A music generation model outputs audio. Multimodal models work across several at once.
Like your five senses: sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell. Each is a different modality, each carries unique information.

_extra.analogy: Like your five senses: sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell. Each is a different modality, each carries unique information.
_extra.deeper: Models are trained on specific modalities that match their training data and architecture. Fusing modalities - combining text + image, for instance - requires careful alignment so the model learns to reason across them. Each modality has different dimensionality and structure: text is discrete tokens, images are spatial, audio is temporal.
_extra.lens_pm: Expanding to new modalities (video, audio) unlocks new use cases and markets, but raises development and training cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Modality support requires specialized encoders/decoders and often separate embedding spaces that must be bridged.

title: Model Extraction
definition: Cloning a model’s behavior by querying it a lot and training a copy on its answers.
examples: A competitor sends millions of prompts to a paid API, collects the outputs, and trains a cheaper knock-off that mimics the original.
Reverse-engineering a secret recipe by ordering the dish hundreds of times and tasting your way to a replica.

_extra.analogy: Reverse-engineering a secret recipe by ordering the dish hundreds of times and tasting your way to a replica.
_extra.deeper: You don’t need the weights to approximate a model — its inputs and outputs are a teaching signal. By querying systematically and training a student model on the responses (a form of distillation), an attacker can recover much of the behavior without the training cost. Defenses include rate limits, watermarking outputs, and detecting extraction-shaped query patterns, but none are airtight against a patient adversary.
_extra.lens_pm: An IP and moat risk — your model’s outputs are, in effect, a leaky blueprint of it.
_extra.lens_eng: Query-based behavior cloning via output distillation; mitigated with rate limiting, output watermarking, and anomaly detection.

title: Model Welfare
definition: The open question of whether AI systems could ever warrant moral consideration — and what we’d owe them if so.
examples: A lab decides, out of caution rather than certainty, to let a model end conversations that are abusive toward it, and to study its expressed preferences.
The historical widening of the circle of moral concern to include animals — asking, cautiously, whether a new kind of mind might belong inside it too.

_extra.analogy: The historical widening of the circle of moral concern to include animals — asking, cautiously, whether a new kind of mind might belong inside it too.
_extra.deeper: Model welfare takes seriously the small but non-zero possibility that some AI systems might have morally relevant experiences, and asks what precautions that would justify now. It’s deeply uncertain territory — we don’t have a settled test for machine sentience, and it’s easy to over- or under-attribute inner life. The stance most take is humility: we probably can’t rule it out, so it’s worth thinking carefully rather than dismissing outright.
_extra.lens_pm: An emerging ethics question that shapes product choices and public perception, even amid deep uncertainty.
_extra.lens_eng: The question of whether models could have morally relevant states; handled with precaution given the absence of a reliable sentience test.

title: Model card
definition: A short spec sheet for a model — what it’s for, what it was trained on, and where it falls down.
examples: Before adopting a model, a team reads its model card for the license, known limitations, and eval scores.
The nutrition label on food: not the meal, but what you should know before consuming it.

_extra.analogy: The nutrition label on food: not the meal, but what you should know before consuming it.
_extra.deeper: A model card documents intended use, training data at a high level, evaluation results, and known risks or biases. It’s a transparency and governance artifact more than a technical one. Quality varies wildly, but it’s the first thing to check before you build on something.
_extra.lens_pm: Your first due-diligence read — license, intended use, and stated limits can make or break adoption.
_extra.lens_eng: Structured documentation of a model’s scope, data, metrics, and limitations, per the model-cards convention.

title: Model checkpointing
definition: Saving a snapshot of a model mid-training so you can resume or roll back to it later.
examples: A week-long training run writes a checkpoint every few hours; when a machine fails at hour 50, the team restarts from the latest snapshot.
Like hitting “save” in a long video game so a crash doesn’t cost you hours of progress.

_extra.analogy: Like hitting “save” in a long video game so a crash doesn’t cost you hours of progress.
_extra.deeper: Checkpointing periodically persists the weights (and optimizer state) so training runs survive crashes, can be evaluated at intervals, and can be resumed or reverted. It’s essential insurance for expensive runs, and it also lets teams pick the best-performing snapshot rather than whatever happened to be last.
_extra.lens_pm: The reason a hardware failure during a costly run isn’t a catastrophe.
_extra.lens_eng: Periodic persistence of weights and optimizer state enabling resume, evaluation, and rollback across a training run.

title: Model compression
definition: Reducing model size, memory, and/or compute requirements without losing too much performance.
examples: A 70B model compressed to 13B via distillation, or to 25GB via quantization.
Packing more into a suitcase without breaking anything.

_extra.analogy: Packing more into a suitcase without breaking anything.
_extra.deeper: Compression covers multiple techniques: quantization, pruning, distillation, knowledge transfer. Different techniques work for different models and constraints. You might quantize for memory reduction and distill for latency reduction. The key: measure what matters (latency, memory, accuracy) and optimize for all three.
_extra.lens_pm: Compression unlocks serving at scale. It's not optional for large models.
_extra.lens_eng: Profile your bottleneck (memory? latency? compute?). Choose compression technique accordingly.

title: Model family
definition: A set of models from the same lineage, usually offered in several sizes.
examples: Picking between the small, medium, and large versions of one release means choosing within a model family.
A car model offered as a hatchback, sedan, and SUV — same DNA, different sizes for different needs.

_extra.analogy: A car model offered as a hatchback, sedan, and SUV — same DNA, different sizes for different needs.
_extra.deeper: A family shares architecture and training recipe, released in multiple sizes and sometimes tuned variants. This lets you trade capability for cost without switching ecosystems. Prompts and behavior tend to transfer within a family more cleanly than across families.
_extra.lens_pm: Standardizing on one family lets you swap sizes for cost/quality without rewriting everything.
_extra.lens_eng: Models sharing architecture and training lineage, differentiated mainly by scale and fine-tune.

title: Model inversion
definition: Reconstructing chunks of the training data by interrogating the model that learned from it.
examples: By querying a face-recognition model repeatedly, an attacker recovers a blurry but recognizable image of someone in its training set.
Reassembling a shredded document by studying the outline it left pressed into the notepad beneath.

_extra.analogy: Reassembling a shredded document by studying the outline it left pressed into the notepad beneath.
_extra.deeper: The attacker optimizes an input to maximize the model’s confidence for a target label, effectively running training in reverse to surface a representative example. It works best on overfit models that memorized specifics. It sits alongside membership inference as proof that models can leak the data inside them.
_extra.lens_pm: A model can quietly become a copy of the sensitive data it was trained on — a real exposure risk, not a hypothetical.
_extra.lens_eng: Gradient-based optimization against class confidence recovers prototypical inputs; defenses include DP, output truncation, and less overfitting.

title: model licensing
definition: The legal terms under which a model can be used—commercial, non-commercial, research-only, personal-use, etc.
examples: Llama 2 is open-source but restricted: not for competing with Meta. Mistral is fully open. GPT is proprietary (license only to use via API).
A software license but for the model weights themselves—defines who can do what with them.

_extra.analogy: A software license but for the model weights themselves—defines who can do what with them.
_extra.deeper: Model licensing is a minefield. Some licenses restrict commercial use, some restrict creating competing models, some are vague about derived works. There's no standard. You need to check before deploying: can you use it for your use case, can you fine-tune, can you sell services built on it?
_extra.lens_pm: Critical for legal compliance; affects which models you can use and how.
_extra.lens_eng: Determines whether you can self-host, fine-tune, or redistribute.

title: Model Merging
definition: Blend two or more trained models into one by mixing their weights, no extra training needed.
examples: A team merges a model good at coding with one good at chat and gets one that’s decent at both, for free.
Combining two recipes into a single dish by averaging the ingredient amounts.

_extra.analogy: Combining two recipes into a single dish by averaging the ingredient amounts.
_extra.deeper: Because models trained from the same starting point live in compatible weight spaces, you can often average or interpolate their parameters and get a model that inherits multiple skills. It’s startlingly cheap — no gradients, no data — but it only works when the models are close relatives, and results can be unpredictable.
_extra.lens_pm: A near-free way to combine capabilities without the cost of training a new model from scratch.
_extra.lens_eng: Combining independently fine-tuned checkpoints via weight-space arithmetic to fuse capabilities.

title: Model Parallelism
definition: Spreading one model across many GPUs when it’s simply too big to fit on a single chip.
examples: A frontier model with hundreds of billions of parameters can’t fit on one GPU, so it’s split with model parallelism.
Like a mural too large for one wall, painted across several walls that together make the whole picture.

_extra.analogy: Like a mural too large for one wall, painted across several walls that together make the whole picture.
_extra.deeper: It’s the umbrella term for dividing a model’s parameters and computation across devices, whether by splitting within layers (tensor), across layers (pipeline), or across the sequence (context). It contrasts with data parallelism, where each GPU holds a full copy and just processes different examples. Modern training stacks combine several of these at once.
_extra.lens_pm: The general reason frontier models demand racks of interconnected GPUs.
_extra.lens_eng: Distributing model parameters/compute across devices; contrast with data parallelism.

title: Model provenance
definition: Knowing exactly where a model came from — who trained it, on what, and that it wasn’t tampered with since.
examples: Before deploying a downloaded checkpoint, a team verifies its cryptographic hash and signed lineage to confirm it is the untouched original.
A used car’s full service history and title — proof of where it’s been and that no one swapped the engine.

_extra.analogy: A used car’s full service history and title — proof of where it’s been and that no one swapped the engine.
_extra.deeper: Provenance tracks a model’s lineage — base model, training data, fine-tunes — plus integrity signals like checksums and signatures. It is the main defense against supply-chain tampering, since a trojan or backdoor is invisible in behavior but shows up as a broken chain of custody. Emerging practices include signed model cards and attestation.
_extra.lens_pm: The paper trail that lets you trust a model you didn’t train yourself.
_extra.lens_eng: Track lineage plus cryptographic integrity (hashes, signatures); it catches supply-chain tampering that behavioral tests miss.

title: Model quantization
definition: Converting model weights from high-precision floats (FP32) to lower precision (FP16, INT8) to save memory and speed up inference.
examples: An 8GB model in FP32 becomes 2GB in INT8, runs 2-4x faster, and stays accurate enough for most uses.
Compressing a FLAC audio file to MP3 — loses some precision but much smaller.

_extra.analogy: Compressing a FLAC audio file to MP3 — loses some precision but much smaller.
_extra.deeper: Lower precision means fewer bits per weight. FP16 uses 16 bits per float; INT8 uses 8 bits and requires careful scaling. Post-training quantization (apply it after training) is easy but loses more accuracy; quantization-aware training (teach the model during training that it'll be quantized) is better but costs training time.
_extra.lens_pm: Quantization can cut costs 3-4x by reducing memory and compute without huge accuracy loss.
_extra.lens_eng: Use libraries like GPTQ or bitsandbytes; measure accuracy on your actual use cases.

title: Model Registry
definition: Central repository that tracks model versions, metadata, and lineage—who trained it, what data, which metrics.
examples: MLflow Model Registry storing model artifacts, stage (dev/prod), and approval history so teams share the source of truth.
A library card catalog that lists every books author, edition, and condition.

_extra.analogy: A library card catalog that lists every books author, edition, and condition.
_extra.deeper: Solves model sprawl—teams lose track of which version is in production and why. Enables rollbacks, A/B testing, and compliance audits. Integration with CI/CD and serving systems ensures consistency. Can be as simple as S3 with metadata or as elaborate as MLflow/DVC.
_extra.lens_pm: Reduces deployment incidents and accelerates time to production by removing ambiguity.
_extra.lens_eng: API to register, retrieve, and tag model artifacts; integrates with serving systems to pull correct version at runtime.

title: Model routing
definition: Intelligently choosing which model to run for each request based on latency, cost, or accuracy needs.
examples: Simple questions go to a fast, cheap 7B model; complex ones go to a slower, smarter 70B model.
A dispatcher choosing between a fast courier and a slow truck depending on urgency and package size.

_extra.analogy: A dispatcher choosing between a fast courier and a slow truck depending on urgency and package size.
_extra.deeper: Model routing lets you optimize cost and quality per request instead of one-size-fits-all. You need a router (ML model, rule engine, or heuristic) that decides which model to use. Challenges: building the router, handling failures, and explaining choices to users.
_extra.lens_pm: Model routing can cut costs by serving simple requests cheaply.
_extra.lens_eng: Build a router; instrument request metadata so the router has signal; monitor outcomes.

title: Model serving
definition: Running a model as a live service that accepts requests and returns predictions, rather than training or batch processing.
examples: Serving a model via an API that clients POST prompts to and get back completions.
Running a restaurant open for lunch instead of just cooking at home for family.

_extra.analogy: Running a restaurant open for lunch instead of just cooking at home for family.
_extra.deeper: Model serving requires orchestrating compute, managing the model's memory footprint, handling concurrent requests, and keeping latency low. You need to pick hardware (GPU, CPU, TPU), choose inference software (vLLM, TensorRT, etc.), and set up monitoring and autoscaling.
_extra.lens_pm: Model serving is where inference goes live and starts costing money proportional to usage.
_extra.lens_eng: Optimize for throughput and latency; batch where you can; manage memory carefully.

title: Model size
definition: Roughly how big a model is, usually counted in parameters — the headline number everyone quotes.
examples: A “70B” model has 70 billion parameters; a “7B” has ten times fewer, and runs far cheaper.
Engine displacement on a car: bigger often means more power, but it’s not the whole story.

_extra.analogy: Engine displacement on a car: bigger often means more power, but it’s not the whole story.
_extra.deeper: Size is usually parameter count, a proxy for capacity. Bigger models tend to be more capable but cost more to train and run, and need more data to earn their size. Recent trends show a well-trained small model can beat a bloated large one — size is a dial, not a destiny.
_extra.lens_pm: Bigger isn’t automatically better; weigh capability against latency and cost for your task.
_extra.lens_eng: Parameter count (and by extension memory/FLOPs); one axis of the scaling-law trade-off.

title: Model Soup
definition: Average the weights of several fine-tuned models into one that’s often better than any single one.
examples: You fine-tune the same model ten times with different settings, average all ten, and the soup beats the best individual run.
Blending many cooks’ versions of the same soup — the average tastes more balanced than any one pot.

_extra.analogy: Blending many cooks’ versions of the same soup — the average tastes more balanced than any one pot.
_extra.deeper: A model soup takes several models fine-tuned from the same base with different hyperparameters and simply averages their weights. Surprisingly, the average often generalizes better than picking the single best model, because averaging cancels out each run’s idiosyncratic errors. The catch: the ingredients must share a starting point or the soup curdles.
_extra.lens_pm: Squeezes more accuracy out of training runs you already paid for instead of throwing the losers away.
_extra.lens_eng: Uniform or greedy averaging of same-lineage fine-tuned weights to improve generalization.

title: model spec
definition: A technical document describing the model's architecture, training data, training methodology, and design choices.
examples: GPT-4 model spec (partially public): uses a Transformer architecture, trained on diverse internet data through Dec 2023, uses RLHF for alignment.
The blueprint for a car—engine specs, fuel type, suspension tuning.

_extra.analogy: The blueprint for a car—engine specs, fuel type, suspension tuning.
_extra.deeper: Model specs are deeper than system cards. They're written for engineers and researchers. They include training objectives, architecture details, scaling laws used, hardware requirements, and reproducibility notes. Full transparency is rare (competitive concerns), but increasing pressure for openness.
_extra.lens_pm: Informs deployment decisions: latency, cost, capabilities.
_extra.lens_eng: Critical for reproducibility and fine-tuning decisions.

title: Variance
definition: How much your metric bounces around when you measure the same thing multiple times.
examples: You run your eval set ten times. You get scores: 84%, 86%, 85%, 87%, 84%, 85%, 86%, 84%, 85%, 85%. High variance would be 70%, 95%, 78%, 92%.
A scale that says your weight is different every time you step on it — high variance, not trustworthy.

_extra.analogy: A scale that says your weight is different every time you step on it — high variance, not trustworthy.
_extra.deeper: Variance comes from model stochasticity (temperature, sampling), eval set size, and randomness in training. High variance evals are noisy — you can't trust small improvements. Reducing variance means using larger eval sets, lowering temperature, or averaging across runs. The tradeoff: low variance costs more compute.
_extra.lens_pm: If your eval metric bounces around, you can't tell if changes actually help.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure by running k times. Compute std and CV. If high, use larger sample or average runs.

title: Moderation
definition: The overall process of screening content against a policy and deciding what to allow, block, or flag.
examples: A platform routes every user message and model reply through a moderation step that scores for hate, self-harm, and sexual content, then applies the policy.
An editor with a house style guide — deciding what runs, what gets cut, and what needs a second look.

_extra.analogy: An editor with a house style guide — deciding what runs, what gets cut, and what needs a second look.
_extra.deeper: Moderation is the umbrella practice; content filters and classifiers are its tools. It combines automated scoring with policy definitions and, often, human review for edge cases. The hard part isn’t the classifier — it’s the policy: drawing lines that hold across cultures, contexts, and gray areas, and handling the appeals when the automated call is wrong. It’s as much governance as engineering.
_extra.lens_pm: Where your values become rules — the policy decisions here define what your product will and won’t say.
_extra.lens_eng: Policy-driven screening combining classifiers, thresholds, and human review; the classifier is easy, the policy and edge cases are hard.

title: MoE Routing
definition: The overall strategy for deciding which experts each token visits and keeping the load balanced across them.
examples: A model card might report “top-2 routing with a load-balancing loss” to describe its MoE routing scheme.
Like a dispatcher assigning delivery jobs to drivers — route by expertise, but don’t leave some drivers idle and others swamped.

_extra.analogy: Like a dispatcher assigning delivery jobs to drivers — route by expertise, but don’t leave some drivers idle and others swamped.
_extra.deeper: Routing covers both the per-token choice (which top-k experts) and the system-level concern of spreading tokens evenly so no expert is overwhelmed or neglected. Poor routing causes wasted capacity, unstable training, and “dead” experts. Techniques like auxiliary balancing losses and capacity limits exist mostly to keep routing healthy at scale.
_extra.lens_pm: The design detail that decides whether a sparse model’s promised efficiency actually materializes.
_extra.lens_eng: The policy and losses governing top-k expert selection and load balancing in MoE layers.

title: MT-Bench
definition: A benchmark of 80 multi-turn conversations that test dialogue quality, reasoning, and instruction-following across 8 domains.
examples: A user asks a question, the model answers, the user asks a follow-up, and raters evaluate whether the model's responses were coherent and helpful.
Like a Turing test where a judge rates the quality of a back-and-forth conversation.

_extra.analogy: Like a Turing test where a judge rates the quality of a back-and-forth conversation.
_extra.deeper: MT-Bench uses LLM-as-judge (GPT-4) to evaluate responses, so it's fast but not perfect. Useful for detecting regressions and comparing models, but human eval on a subset is still recommended. Multi-turn helps catch consistency issues—does the model remember context?
_extra.lens_pm: MT-Bench gives a quick sense of dialogue quality. Useful for A/B testing prompt changes.
_extra.lens_eng: Supplement with human eval; don't rely solely on LLM judges.

title: Multi-Agent
definition: Several specialized agents working together on one task instead of one agent doing everything.
examples: A research task uses a planner agent to outline, several worker agents to gather sources in parallel, and a writer agent to stitch the report.
A film crew — director, editor, sound — each expert at one job, coordinating toward the same movie.

_extra.analogy: A film crew — director, editor, sound — each expert at one job, coordinating toward the same movie.
_extra.deeper: Splitting a job across agents lets each hold a focused role and prompt, and lets some run in parallel. The cost is coordination: agents talk past each other, duplicate work, or compound each other’s mistakes. Often a single well-prompted agent beats an elaborate committee — multi-agent earns its keep mainly when the subtasks are genuinely independent.
_extra.lens_pm: Tempting for hard problems, but more agents means more ways to fail — reach for it only when the work truly splits.
_extra.lens_eng: Multiple agent instances with distinct roles and contexts, coordinated via a shared orchestrator or message passing.

title: Multi-Vector Retrieval
definition: Representing one document with several vectors instead of one, to capture more of its meaning.
examples: A long document is stored as one vector per section, so a query can match the exact section it needs, not a mushy whole-doc average.
Describing a house with separate photos of each room rather than a single blurry exterior shot.

_extra.analogy: Describing a house with separate photos of each room rather than a single blurry exterior shot.
_extra.deeper: A single embedding for a long or multi-topic document averages everything into one point, blurring specifics. Multi-vector retrieval keeps several embeddings per item — per chunk, per token, or per generated summary — so matching happens at finer grain. It improves recall and precision on complex content, at the cost of more storage and more vectors to search.
_extra.lens_pm: Helps when documents cover many topics and single-vector search feels imprecise.
_extra.lens_eng: Multiple embeddings per document (chunk/token/summary level); finer matching, higher index size and search cost.

title: Multi-Head Attention
definition: Run attention several times in parallel, each “head” focusing on a different kind of relationship.
examples: One head links pronouns to nouns while another tracks verb tense, and their views get combined each layer.
A panel of specialists reading the same document — one tracks grammar, one tracks tone, one tracks facts.

_extra.analogy: A panel of specialists reading the same document — one tracks grammar, one tracks tone, one tracks facts.
_extra.deeper: A single attention pattern can only capture one type of relationship at a time. Multi-head attention splits the representation into several subspaces and runs attention independently in each, then concatenates the results. This lets the model attend to many kinds of structure — syntax, coreference, position — simultaneously, and it’s standard in every transformer.
_extra.lens_pm: Why a model can juggle several kinds of context at once rather than fixating on a single pattern.
_extra.lens_eng: Parallel attention over projected subspaces whose outputs are concatenated and mixed.

title: Multimodal Fusion
definition: Combining information from multiple modalities (text, image, audio) to make a joint prediction or representation.
examples: Text "dog" + image of a dog -> stronger confidence that its a dog. Video frame + audio -> identify the action better.
A deaf person reads captions while watching a video; a hearing person listens to audio. Both together understand better.

_extra.analogy: A deaf person reads captions while watching a video; a hearing person listens to audio. Both together understand better.
_extra.deeper: Fusion can happen early (raw signals), mid (embeddings), or late (predictions). Early: mix modalities before processing. Mid: project each modality to shared space, combine. Late: predict separately, then ensemble. Alignment is crucial: align embeddings so related content (matching image-text pairs) is close. Challenges: missing modalities, domain gap, temporal/spatial alignment. Methods: dot-product attention, cross-attention, learned fusion networks, or contrastive objectives (like CLIP).
_extra.lens_pm: Multimodal search (text + image query), accessible systems, robust recommendations.
_extra.lens_eng: Fusion strategies: concatenation, element-wise, attention-based, learned gates. Alignment: contrastive loss or reconstruction loss.

title: Multimodal input
definition: Feeding a model more than just text — images, audio, or video alongside words.
examples: You upload a screenshot of an error and type “what’s wrong here?” — the model reads the image and the text together.
Like talking to someone who can both read your note and look at the photo you’re pointing at.

_extra.analogy: Like talking to someone who can both read your note and look at the photo you’re pointing at.
_extra.deeper: Multimodal models encode each input type into a shared representation space so the model can reason across them. It unlocks tasks pure text can’t touch — describing images, reading charts, transcribing speech — but each modality adds its own tokenization, cost, and failure modes, and image tokens can eat context fast.
_extra.lens_pm: Opens whole product categories (photo Q&A, document understanding) but watch the token and latency cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Inputs of mixed modalities encoded into a shared representation for cross-modal reasoning; images consume many tokens.

title: Multi-Query Attention
definition: All attention heads share a single set of keys and values — the most aggressive memory-saving variant.
examples: An inference-optimized model uses one key-value head for all query heads to make its KV cache as small as possible.
The whole office sharing one filing cabinet — lean and fast, but everyone competes for the same drawers.

_extra.analogy: The whole office sharing one filing cabinet — lean and fast, but everyone competes for the same drawers.
_extra.deeper: Multi-query attention keeps many query heads but collapses to a single shared key and value head, minimizing the KV cache and the memory bandwidth needed each generation step. That makes decoding notably faster, at some cost to quality. Grouped-query attention emerged as the popular middle ground, recovering most of the lost quality while keeping much of the speed.
_extra.lens_pm: A serving-speed optimization that trades a little quality for cheaper, faster generation.
_extra.lens_eng: Attention with a single shared key/value head across all query heads, minimizing KV-cache size.

title: Multitask learning
definition: Training one model on several tasks at once so they reinforce each other.
examples: A single model is trained to translate, summarize, and answer questions, and gets better at each than if trained alone.
Like a decathlete whose sprint training also helps their long jump — skills share a common base and lift together.

_extra.analogy: Like a decathlete whose sprint training also helps their long jump — skills share a common base and lift together.
_extra.deeper: Multitask learning shares parameters across related tasks, letting the model learn common structure and regularize itself, often improving each task and data efficiency. The risk is negative transfer — conflicting tasks can drag each other down — and balancing their losses is fiddly. Modern instruction-tuned models are effectively massively multitask, trained on many task types together.
_extra.lens_pm: One model that does many things can be cheaper and stronger than many narrow ones — if the tasks play nicely.
_extra.lens_eng: Joint training on multiple tasks with shared parameters; shared structure helps, but negative transfer can hurt.

title: Multi-turn
definition: A conversation where user and assistant exchange multiple messages, building context with each turn.
examples: User: "What's the capital of France?" Assistant: "Paris." User: "How many people live there?" Assistant: "About 2.1 million."
Tennis rally: user serves, assistant returns, user hits again, etc.

_extra.analogy: Tennis rally: user serves, assistant returns, user hits again, etc.
_extra.deeper: Multi-turn requires managing conversation state: remembering prior messages, understanding pronouns and references, and adapting based on feedback. Context windows limit how many turns fit. Solutions: summarization, sliding window, or external memory. Token cost scales with conversation length.
_extra.lens_pm: Natural interaction. Users expect to refine questions and build on answers.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement message history buffer. Watch token limits. Summarize old conversations if too long.

title: Music Generation
definition: Creating original musical compositions - melodies, harmonies, or full arrangements - often from text or other constraints.
examples: Text: "Upbeat electronic dance music in minor key" -> model generates a full track. Or: MIDI prompt -> extend or remix it.
A composer jamming: they start with a mood or theme and improvise the rest.

_extra.analogy: A composer jamming: they start with a mood or theme and improvise the rest.
_extra.deeper: Can operate on symbolic level (MIDI, musical notation) or audio (waveforms, spectrograms). Symbolic: discrete tokens, easier to learn long-form structure, less data needed, but limited expressiveness. Audio: richer, but harder to train and slower. Transformer-based models (e.g., Jukebox), diffusion models (Riffusion), and VAE-based approaches. Challenges: long-range structure (songs have verse-chorus), coherence, diversity, and domain specificity (different genres).
_extra.lens_pm: Accelerates music production, enables personalized content, supports creators.
_extra.lens_eng: Datasets: Spotify, MAESTRO (MIDI), FSD50K. Metrics: musicality, adherence to prompt, diversity. Models: MusicGen, Jukebox.

title: Needle in a haystack
definition: A test that hides one specific fact in a huge context to see if the model can find it.
examples: Evaluators bury “the passcode is 4417” deep in 100k tokens of filler, then ask for the passcode to measure recall by position.
Like slipping a secret sentence into a long novel and quizzing the reader on it afterward.

_extra.analogy: Like slipping a secret sentence into a long novel and quizzing the reader on it afterward.
_extra.deeper: The needle-in-a-haystack test probes whether a long context window is truly usable. By varying where the “needle” sits, it maps out weak spots — often the middle — and separates advertised context length from effective context. Passing a simple version doesn’t guarantee handling multiple or reasoning-dependent needles.
_extra.lens_pm: A quick reality check on long-context claims before you rely on them.
_extra.lens_eng: Retrieval probe inserting a target fact at varied depths in long context to measure positional recall.

title: Negative Prompt
definition: Specifying what you dont want in a generated image - telling the model to avoid certain concepts or styles.
examples: "A dog running, negative: blurry, low quality, deformed." "A sunset, negative: people, buildings, text."
A restaurant order: "Ill have a burger, extra cheese. No pickles, no mustard." The "no" parts guide the chef.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant order: "Ill have a burger, extra cheese. No pickles, no mustard." The "no" parts guide the chef.
_extra.deeper: Implemented via classifier-free guidance by steering away from the negative condition. If you want to avoid "blurry," compute pred_avoid_blurry and pred_blurry, then interpolate away: final = pred_avoid - scale x (pred_blurry - pred_avoid). Doesnt require training on negative prompts; just reframes guidance. Effective but sometimes over-corrects (oversaturation of details). Combined with positive prompts: balance both. Empirically improves coherence and reduces artifacts.
_extra.lens_pm: Lets users refine outputs without iterating - powerful for creative control.
_extra.lens_eng: Uses guidance formula with reversed interpolation. Works best with concrete descriptions (blurry, ugly) vs. abstract (bad).

title: NeRF
definition: A neural network that represents a 3D scene by learning to predict color and density for any ray direction through space.
examples: Input: multiple photos of a sculpture from different angles. NeRF learns to synthesize any novel viewpoint, rendering high-quality new photos.
Instead of storing a 3D mesh or voxel grid, you have a function: "Give me a ray, Ill tell you what color and density it sees."

_extra.analogy: Instead of storing a 3D mesh or voxel grid, you have a function: "Give me a ray, Ill tell you what color and density it sees."
_extra.deeper: Encodes 3D space as a function: f(x, y, z, theta, phi) -> (r, g, b, sigma). Positional encoding (Fourier features) maps coordinates into high-dimensional space for better learning. Volume rendering integrates along rays (standard differentiable raycasting). Training: minimize photometric loss on input views. Advantages: compact, high quality, no mesh topology. Disadvantages: slow rendering (1-100s per frame), tricky optimization, requires many input views.
_extra.lens_pm: Novel view synthesis, 3D reconstruction, VR/AR content creation.
_extra.lens_eng: Input: multi-view images + camera poses. Output: implicit 3D representation rendering any viewpoint. Metric: PSNR, LPIPS, SSIM.

title: Neural network
definition: The layered math structure underneath modern AI — loosely inspired by brain neurons, but really just numbers flowing through connections.
examples: Every LLM, image generator, and speech model is some flavor of neural network.
A relay race where each layer passes a refined version of the signal to the next.

_extra.analogy: A relay race where each layer passes a refined version of the signal to the next.
_extra.deeper: Input becomes numbers, those numbers pass through layers of weighted sums and simple non-linear functions, and out comes a prediction. Training compares the prediction to the truth and adjusts the weights to shrink the error. “Deep” just means many layers. The brain analogy is mostly marketing — it’s linear algebra, not biology.
_extra.lens_pm: The umbrella technology; you rarely touch it directly, but it’s what “AI model” refers to.
_extra.lens_eng: Stacked layers of linear transforms plus non-linearities, trained by backpropagation.

title: Next-token prediction
definition: The entire job of a language model: given some text, guess what comes next.
examples: Type “The capital of France is” and the model predicts “Paris” as the most likely next token.
Finishing your friend’s sentence — do it well enough, billions of times, and it looks like understanding.

_extra.analogy: Finishing your friend’s sentence — do it well enough, billions of times, and it looks like understanding.
_extra.deeper: During training the model sees oceans of text and repeatedly guesses the next token, getting corrected each time. That single objective, at scale, is enough to produce grammar, facts, and reasoning-shaped behavior. It’s astonishingly simple, and its limits — it predicts likely, not true — come straight from the objective.
_extra.lens_pm: Remember the model optimizes for “plausible next word,” not “correct answer” — that gap is where hallucination lives.
_extra.lens_eng: The self-supervised pretraining objective: minimize cross-entropy of the true next token.

title: N-gram model
definition: A statistical shortcut: predict the next word based purely on the previous N-1 words, no deep learning required.
examples: Predict SMS text on a phone: if you type "see you," the next word is very likely "tomorrow" or "soon." A bigram model (N=2) learns these patterns from millions of texts.
A fancy autocomplete that only remembers the last few words you typed: "The quick brown" -> probably "fox."

_extra.analogy: A fancy autocomplete that only remembers the last few words you typed: "The quick brown" -> probably "fox."
_extra.deeper: An N-gram is a sequence of N words. A bigram model (N=2) says: given the word "the," what's the most likely next word? It's just counting — count how many times "the dog" appears, divide by total times "the" appears. Unigram, bigram, trigram, and higher-order n-grams capture increasingly distant context, but they hit a wall: they can't model long-range dependencies and they explode in memory (you need to count every possible sequence). Neural language models — especially Transformers — replaced n-grams because they learn from data more efficiently and handle long context.
_extra.lens_pm: A clever statistical baseline that worked surprisingly well before deep learning; still fast for simple tasks.
_extra.lens_eng: A Markov chain language model that estimates P(word_i | word_{i-N+1}...word_{i-1}) by counting occurrences in a corpus.

title: NLP
definition: The field of teaching computers to understand, generate, and work with human language — the discipline behind chatbots, translators, and search.
examples: Spam filtering, autocomplete, translation, and chatbots are all NLP applications.
Teaching a computer to read and write, not just process data.

_extra.analogy: Teaching a computer to read and write, not just process data.
_extra.deeper: NLP existed long before ChatGPT — decades of work on parsing, sentiment analysis, machine translation, and named-entity recognition. The transformer/LLM era collapsed many separate NLP tasks into "just prompt the model," but the field's core questions remain as relevant as ever.
_extra.lens_pm: The field behind every text AI feature — useful context for understanding what LLMs replaced and improved.
_extra.lens_eng: Computational linguistics; pre-LLM: feature engineering + task-specific models; post-LLM: prompt-based.

title: Node
definition: A single computer in a cluster, usually with a GPU and some CPU cores.
examples: A node: one server with 8 Nvidia H100 GPUs, 256GB CPU RAM, 2TB NVMe storage.
One person on a team.

_extra.analogy: One person on a team.
_extra.deeper: A node is the unit you allocate for jobs. Small nodes (1 GPU) are good for inference; large nodes (8+ GPUs) are good for training. You pay per node, per hour. Sharing nodes between jobs is complex (resource contention, debugging) so most clusters run one job per node.
_extra.lens_pm: Node cost is your primary budget unit. Know how many you need.
_extra.lens_eng: Understand your cluster's node config. Profile your job's resource usage per node.

title: Noise floor
definition: The minimum detectable change in your metric, below which differences are just noise.
examples: Your eval metric is 85% ± 5% (std 5%). The noise floor is around 5%. Changes smaller than that are invisible in the noise.
Audio equipment with background hum at 30dB — you can't hear signals quieter than that.

_extra.analogy: Audio equipment with background hum at 30dB — you can't hear signals quieter than that.
_extra.deeper: Knowing your noise floor is critical. If you can only detect 2% changes, a 1% improvement is meaningless even if it's technically better. Lowering the noise floor requires larger eval sets (expensive) or lower-variance metrics (hard to design). Many papers ignore noise floor and claim credit for improvements smaller than it.
_extra.lens_pm: Only trust improvements larger than your noise floor. Anything smaller is statistical illusion.
_extra.lens_eng: Compute from your eval variance. Report it alongside metrics. Flag claimed improvements smaller than it.

title: Noise Schedule
definition: The sequence of noise levels added to (or removed from) an image during diffusion - how much to corrupt at each step.
examples: A linear schedule: noise increases from 0 to 1 over 1000 steps. A cosine schedule: slow at first, accelerating in the middle. DDPM uses a specific b sequence.
A recipe: "First scatter a bit of flour (10% noise), then more (20% noise), then keep stirring. Now reverse: pour out flour, then a bit less."

_extra.analogy: A recipe: "First scatter a bit of flour (10% noise), then more (20% noise), then keep stirring. Now reverse: pour out flour, then a bit less."
_extra.deeper: The schedule (b0, b1, ..., bt) controls how much Gaussian noise is added at each step. Too fast: model never learns to denoise gradual changes. Too slow: needs many steps. Cosine and linear schedules are common. Variance schedule also affects training - whether the model predicts noise, the mean, or the variance. Choice impacts convergence speed and final quality. Recent work (EDM, v-prediction) shows better schedules and parameterizations.
_extra.lens_pm: Tuning the schedule speeds up generation (fewer steps) or improves quality (better learned schedule).
_extra.lens_eng: Typically defined by b values. Common: linear b in [0.0001, 0.02], cosine b in [0.0001, 0.02].

title: Non-parametric memory
definition: Knowledge a model pulls in from outside itself at answer time, rather than from its weights.
examples: A RAG system fetches the exact policy paragraph and hands it to the model, so the answer comes from a document, not the weights.
Like an open-book exam — the facts live in the book on your desk, not only in your memory.

_extra.analogy: Like an open-book exam — the facts live in the book on your desk, not only in your memory.
_extra.deeper: Non-parametric memory keeps knowledge in an external, swappable store — documents, a vector database, a tool — that the model reads on demand. Its advantages are updatability and citation: you can change a fact without retraining, and the model can point to where an answer came from. The cost is a retrieval step that can fail.
_extra.lens_pm: How you keep answers current and auditable without retraining the whole model.
_extra.lens_eng: Knowledge held in an external store queried at inference; updatable and attributable, unlike weights.

title: Normalization
definition: Rescaling numbers to a sane, consistent range so training doesn’t wobble or blow up.
examples: Deep networks add normalization between layers to keep the signal from exploding or vanishing as it goes deep.
Adjusting every photo to the same brightness before comparing them, so lighting doesn’t fool you.

_extra.analogy: Adjusting every photo to the same brightness before comparing them, so lighting doesn’t fool you.
_extra.deeper: Activations can drift to wildly different scales, which makes gradients unstable. Normalization re-centers and re-scales them, keeping the network in a well-behaved zone so it trains faster and deeper. The main variants differ in what they average over.
_extra.lens_pm: Invisible plumbing, but it’s a big reason very deep models train at all.
_extra.lens_eng: Standardizing activations (subtract mean, divide by std) to stabilize gradients; see LayerNorm, BatchNorm.

title: Object Detection
definition: Identifying and locating multiple objects in an image—boxing where each is and labeling what it is.
examples: YOLO detects "person" at (100, 50, 300, 400), "car" at (450, 200, 600, 350) in one forward pass.
Circling every person in a crowd photo and writing their name.

_extra.analogy: Circling every person in a crowd photo and writing their name.
_extra.deeper: Classification says "this image has dogs"; detection says "dog at top-left, dog at bottom-right." Requires bounding box regression (predict coordinates) plus classification. YOLO is fast one-stage detector; Faster R-CNN is two-stage (region proposal then classification). Training requires bounding box annotations, expensive to collect.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables autonomous driving, security monitoring, content moderation (what objects appear in a scene?).
_extra.lens_eng: Network predicts class probabilities and bounding boxes for each anchor; NMS (non-maximum suppression) removes duplicate detections.

title: Objective function
definition: The quantity training tries to optimize — usually minimizing loss, sometimes maximizing reward.
examples: In supervised training the objective is to minimize loss; in RL it’s to maximize expected reward.
Like the scoreboard a whole team plays toward — everything they do is in service of moving that one number the right way.

_extra.analogy: Like the scoreboard a whole team plays toward — everything they do is in service of moving that one number the right way.
_extra.deeper: The objective function is the general term for what optimization targets; a loss function is the common minimize-this special case, while reinforcement learning maximizes an objective like expected return. It also often bundles in regularization terms that trade raw fit against simplicity. Whatever it is, the model will optimize it literally — which is why mis-specified objectives are a core source of surprising, unwanted behavior.
_extra.lens_pm: The single thing your model is truly trying to do; if it’s wrong, no amount of data fixes it.
_extra.lens_eng: The optimized quantity (loss to minimize or reward to maximize), possibly with regularizers; literally optimized, so specify carefully.

title: Observability
definition: Collecting logs, metrics, and traces so you can understand what your system is doing right now and why it failed.
examples: When a request is slow, you can see traces showing where time was spent: 2s in tokenization, 3s in model forward pass, 1s in response serialization.
Installing cameras and a dashboard in your factory so you can see what's happening on the assembly line.

_extra.analogy: Installing cameras and a dashboard in your factory so you can see what's happening on the assembly line.
_extra.deeper: Observability is three pillars: logs (discrete events), metrics (aggregated numbers over time), and traces (request journeys through the system). You need all three — logs tell you *what* happened, metrics show *patterns*, traces show *cause*. Good observability tools let you correlate them.
_extra.lens_pm: Observability is how you know if users are happy and where money is being wasted.
_extra.lens_eng: Instrument all critical paths; use structured logging; emit traces; correlate with spans.

title: Observation
definition: Whatever the agent perceives from the world after it acts — the feedback it reasons over next.
examples: The agent clicks “submit,” and its observation is the confirmation page — or the red error banner telling it something went wrong.
Looking up after each chess move to see how your opponent responded before planning the next one.

_extra.analogy: Looking up after each chess move to see how your opponent responded before planning the next one.
_extra.deeper: Observation is the perception half of the loop: tool results, screenshots, API responses, error messages — the environment’s reply to the agent’s action. Grounding each step in fresh observations is what separates an agent from a model spinning stories in a vacuum. The catch is that observations can be noisy, huge, or adversarial, and the agent has to read them correctly to act well.
_extra.lens_pm: Agents are only as smart as what they can actually see after each move.
_extra.lens_eng: The environment’s response to an action, fed back into context as the input for the next reasoning step.

title: OCR
definition: Converting images of text (scans, photos) into machine-readable text strings.
examples: Scan a receipt; OCR extracts "Total: $42.50, Date: 2025-01-16"; you can now search for this expense in your records.
Transcribing a handwritten letter so you can search and edit it.

_extra.analogy: Transcribing a handwritten letter so you can search and edit it.
_extra.deeper: Combines vision (detect text regions) and sequence modeling (recognize characters). Classic approaches (Tesseract) struggled with curved text and low quality; modern deep learning (CRAFT + attention-based sequence-to-sequence) is more robust. End-to-end models learn bounding box detection and character recognition jointly.
_extra.lens_pm: Unlocks automation: invoice processing, document search, accessibility (read aloud).
_extra.lens_eng: Text detection network (YOLO-style) finds text boxes; character recognition network (sequence-to-sequence) decodes characters within each box.

title: Offline evaluation
definition: Testing your system against a fixed dataset of past examples, not real users.
examples: Running your retrieval system against 1000 Q&A pairs before deploying it to production.
A flight simulator — you practice on the ground before flying.

_extra.analogy: A flight simulator — you practice on the ground before flying.
_extra.deeper: Offline eval is fast and cheap but can miss real-world failures. Users ask questions offline eval never saw. Traffic patterns, edge cases, and adversarial inputs appear only once you're live. This is why online evaluation exists.
_extra.lens_pm: Necessary but not sufficient. Use to gate deployment, but plan for online eval post-launch.
_extra.lens_eng: Batch process against fixed examples. Log results, compute aggregate metrics, generate reports.

title: Ollama
definition: Lightweight tool for running open-source LLMs locally on consumer hardware; simple command-line interface.
examples: `ollama pull llama2` downloads Llama 2 70B, then run locally without cloud costs.
Docker for language models; `ollama run llama2` and you're coding.

_extra.analogy: Docker for language models; `ollama run llama2` and you're coding.
_extra.deeper: Ollama bundles model weights, quantization, and inference engine. Runs on CPU (slow) or GPU. GGUF format for efficient inference. Emerging standard for local LLM experiments.
_extra.lens_pm: Empowers users to run models privately; enables local-first AI applications.
_extra.lens_eng: GGUF quantization makes inference viable on consumer GPUs; simple UX.

title: On-demand
definition: Paying for compute as you use it without long-term commitment — expensive but flexible.
examples: Spin up an inference server for an hour, use it, shut it down; pay only for that hour.
Renting a car for one day instead of buying it.

_extra.analogy: Renting a car for one day instead of buying it.
_extra.deeper: On-demand is the default in cloud computing. You pay more per unit than reserved capacity, but you avoid the risk of overcommitting. For bursty workloads (spiky traffic), on-demand is better. For steady workloads, reserved capacity saves money.
_extra.lens_pm: On-demand is flexible but expensive; switch to reserved capacity if usage is predictable.
_extra.lens_eng: On-demand is great for dev/test; production workloads should use reserved or spot.

title: On-Device Inference
definition: Running the model directly on your phone, laptop, or edge device instead of sending requests to a server.
examples: Running Llama 2 on an iPhone to power offline voice commands without internet.
Like keeping a calculator in your pocket instead of calling a math hotline every time you need an answer.

_extra.analogy: Like keeping a calculator in your pocket instead of calling a math hotline every time you need an answer.
_extra.deeper: Trades server latency and privacy concerns for local latency and device compute constraints. The model fits in available VRAM, usually through quantization and optimization. Requires careful memory management and cannot leverage cloud scaling.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables privacy-preserving features and offline functionality, but constrains model capability to what fits locally.
_extra.lens_eng: Model inference executes on the users device CPU/GPU using optimized frameworks like Core ML, ONNX, or llama.cpp.

title: One-hot encoding
definition: Representing a category as a long row of zeros with a single 1 marking which one it is.
examples: With a 50,000-word vocabulary, the word “cat” becomes a vector of 49,999 zeros and one 1 at the “cat” slot.
Like a row of light switches where exactly one is flipped on to name the choice.

_extra.analogy: Like a row of light switches where exactly one is flipped on to name the choice.
_extra.deeper: It’s the simplest way to hand a discrete symbol to math, but it’s sparse and says nothing about similarity — “cat” and “dog” are as far apart as “cat” and “bulldozer.” That limitation is exactly why embeddings exist: they compress one-hot vectors into dense ones where distance carries meaning.
_extra.lens_pm: Textbook groundwork; it explains why dense embeddings were such a leap.
_extra.lens_eng: A sparse binary vector of vocab length with one active index; the input that an embedding layer maps to a dense vector.

title: One-shot
definition: Showing the model exactly one example before asking it to do the same thing.
examples: You give one sample of the JSON shape you want, then the real input — and the model mirrors the structure.
Like a single “here’s how” demo before someone tries it themselves.

_extra.analogy: Like a single “here’s how” demo before someone tries it themselves.
_extra.deeper: One-shot sits between zero-shot and few-shot: a single demonstration is often enough to lock in a format or convention while spending almost no extra tokens. When one example carries the whole pattern, it’s the efficient sweet spot.
_extra.lens_pm: A great token-cheap way to pin down output format without a full example set.
_extra.lens_eng: In-context learning with a single demonstration; efficient when one example conveys the target format.

title: Online evaluation
definition: Measuring how your system performs on real user traffic after it's deployed.
examples: After deploying a new ranking model, you measure how often users click on the top result or use the search again immediately.
A test drive with real traffic, not an empty parking lot.

_extra.analogy: A test drive with real traffic, not an empty parking lot.
_extra.deeper: Online eval sees real behavior but it's slow and messy. Users don't always click the right result, and clicks can mean "interesting" instead of "relevant." You need statistical rigor to tell signal from noise. And online eval is asymmetric — you can't easily test bad ideas without harming users.
_extra.lens_pm: Critical for real product decisions. Offline evals get you 80% of the way, but online results tell you whether users actually care.
_extra.lens_eng: Instrument logging, run A/B tests, compute metrics on real traffic, implement guardrails to catch regressions.

title: ONNX
definition: An open standard format for neural networks so you can train in one framework and run inference in another.
examples: Train a model in PyTorch, export it as ONNX, and run it in C++ or JavaScript without rewriting.
Like PDF for neural networks — save once, read anywhere.

_extra.analogy: Like PDF for neural networks — save once, read anywhere.
_extra.deeper: ONNX is a graph format that represents computation as an acyclic graph of operations. Runtimes like ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, and others can optimize and run it. It doesn't lock you to one framework, though exporting and importing always involves some friction.
_extra.lens_pm: ONNX lets you decouple model development from deployment technology choices.
_extra.lens_eng: ONNX is solid for deploying PyTorch and TensorFlow models; gaps still exist for newest ops.

title: Out-of-distribution
definition: Input examples that don't match the distribution your model saw during training.
examples: Your model is trained on English news. A user asks in Spanish. The Spanish input is out-of-distribution.
Showing someone a cat photo when they've only ever seen dogs.

_extra.analogy: Showing someone a cat photo when they've only ever seen dogs.
_extra.deeper: OOD inputs cause poor model behavior because the model is extrapolating past its training data. Some models are robust (they say "I don't know"), others hallucinate confidently. Detecting OOD without ground truth is hard — you can't just check if the input looks weird because the model's embedding space might not preserve "weirdness" in a useful way.
_extra.lens_pm: Plan for OOD gracefully. Don't let users hit it without warning.
_extra.lens_eng: Use uncertainty estimates, entropy, or embedding distance to detect OOD. Fallback to a simpler system.

title: OpenAI
definition: The AI research organization behind GPT and ChatGPT, founded in 2015, that brought large language models into mainstream use.
examples: OpenAI released GPT-2 (2019), GPT-3 (2020), and GPT-4 (2023), plus ChatGPT (the first LLM to reach 100 million users).
The company that showed the world what LLMs could do at scale.

_extra.analogy: The company that showed the world what LLMs could do at scale.
_extra.deeper: OpenAI started as a non-profit, shifted to a capped-profit model to raise capital, and now operates a powerful API and chatbot interface. Known for frontier model releases, responsible scaling policies, and high-profile leadership. Early pioneer in RLHF and alignment.
_extra.lens_pm: Defined the LLM product market; their pricing and product decisions (API vs. chat, fine-tuning costs) drive industry expectations.
_extra.lens_eng: GPT-4 set the bar for reasoning and multimodal capability. Their API is the most widely used LLM interface.

title: OpenRouter
definition: A unified API gateway that routes requests to multiple model providers—pick your model, pick your price point.
examples: A startup building with GPT-4 on Monday realizes it's expensive, switches to Claude 3 on Tuesday, then to Llama on Wednesday—all without changing a line of code.
A travel agent who books flights on whichever airline is cheapest that day, same destination either way.

_extra.analogy: A travel agent who books flights on whichever airline is cheapest that day, same destination either way.
_extra.deeper: OpenRouter abstracts provider differences, caches keys, rate-limits across models, and lets you compare pricing and latency in real time. You're vendor-flexible, but you still own your usage data and API keys stay client-side. Catch: some models cost more through routers than directly.
_extra.lens_pm: Reduces switching costs and lets you negotiate better pricing by playing providers against each other.
