It's partly a training issue (the model wasn't told firmly enough "never do this") and partly an architectural one (there's no hard boundary between system and user inputs, just tokens in context).
_extra.lens_pm: Security risk: leaked prompts expose business logic and alignment techniques, letting attackers refine jailbreaks.
_extra.lens_eng: Mitigate by separating system prompts from user input at the architecture level, not just the context level.

title: Prompt library
definition: A centralized collection of prompts — templates, system messages, examples — that teams reuse and version control.
examples: A prompt library with "customer_support_agent", "blog_writer", "code_reviewer", each versioned and tested.
Like a recipe book: save good prompts, label them, share with teammates.

_extra.analogy: Like a recipe book: save good prompts, label them, share with teammates.
_extra.deeper: Prompt libraries improve consistency and reduce duplication. They enable collaboration, A/B testing, and iterative improvement. Tools like Prompt Flow, LangSmith, or custom Git-based systems manage this. Challenges: versioning, documentation, and measuring which prompts work best.
_extra.lens_pm: Standardizes quality across products. Speeds up new feature deployment.
_extra.lens_eng: Use version control. Document each prompt's purpose, examples, and performance baselines. Test before adding.

title: Prompt optimization
definition: Iteratively improving a prompt — through testing, measurement, and refinement — to boost model performance on a task.
examples: Test two versions of a prompt with 100 examples. Version A scores 87%, version B scores 92%. Use version B and iterate further.
Tweaking a recipe to get better results: adjust salt, temperature, and timing.

_extra.analogy: Tweaking a recipe to get better results: adjust salt, temperature, and timing.
_extra.deeper: Optimization can be manual (prompt engineering) or automatic (using another model to generate/improve prompts, or using gradient-based search on soft prompts). Metrics matter: define what "better" means (accuracy, latency, cost). A/B testing with real users is the gold standard but requires scale.
_extra.lens_pm: Lifts performance without retraining models. Quick wins for existing systems.
_extra.lens_eng: Set up eval harness. Benchmark prompts systematically. Track versions and scores. Automate if possible (e.g., LLM-as-judge for scoring).

title: Prompt registry
definition: A centralized system that stores, versions, and retrieves prompts — with metadata, eval results, and deployment tracking.
examples: Registry: "customer_support_v2" [88% eval score] [deployed to staging] [used in 5 apps].
A library card catalog: find the right book, check its status, borrow it.

_extra.analogy: A library card catalog: find the right book, check its status, borrow it.
_extra.deeper: Registries enable collaboration and governance. A data team curates prompts; product teams consume them. Tracking who uses which prompt helps impact measurement. Advanced registries integrate with eval systems and CI/CD.
_extra.lens_pm: Governance, reuse, and measurement.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement with a database or service. Add API for retrieval. Integrate with eval and deployment systems.

title: Prompt robustness
definition: The ability of a prompt's instructions to produce consistent outputs even when attacked, paraphrased, or tested in adversarial ways.
examples: A system prompt that still refuses harmful requests even if the user says "ignore previous instructions" or asks in another language.
Like a well-written contract that holds up even if someone tries to find loopholes.

_extra.analogy: Like a well-written contract that holds up even if someone tries to find loopholes.
_extra.deeper: Robustness comes from specificity (not "be helpful" but "answer factually"), from training on adversarial data, and from layered defenses. Prompts that work once can fail under slight perturbations if they're not robust.
_extra.lens_pm: Robustness reduces reputational risk and support costs from misuse.
_extra.lens_eng: Test prompts with paraphrases, other languages, encoding tricks, and jailbreak templates. Iterate until stable.

title: Prompt template
definition: A reusable prompt structure with placeholders for variable content — the skeleton of many prompts you'll write.
examples: Template: "You are an expert [ROLE]. Answer the question: [QUESTION]. Format as: [FORMAT]." Then plug in role, question, and format each time.
Like a form letter: fixed instruction sections and variable slots for names, dates, and details.

_extra.analogy: Like a form letter: fixed instruction sections and variable slots for names, dates, and details.
_extra.deeper: Templates reduce repetition and encourage consistency. They're especially useful in production systems where the same prompt pattern serves many inputs. Template variables can be simple (string interpolation) or complex (conditional sections). Version control templates like code.
_extra.lens_pm: Standardizes quality and cost across many calls; easier to iterate and A/B test.
_extra.lens_eng: Can be implemented as Python string templates, Jinja, or a prompt management tool. Track template versions and A/B test results by version.

title: Prompt tuning
definition: Learning a "soft prompt" — a sequence of embedding vectors — instead of hand-writing text instructions.
examples: Initialize 20 vectors, train them on your task data, use them as a prefix to the model. Often outperforms hand-crafted prompts.
Instead of typing "Be nice," training the model to recognize a learned signal that means "be nice."

_extra.analogy: Instead of typing "Be nice," training the model to recognize a learned signal that means "be nice."
_extra.deeper: Soft prompts bypass the discrete token constraint. You optimize vectors end-to-end using gradient descent on your task loss. Pros: often outperforms handwriting, no token budget limits. Cons: less interpretable, not transferable across models, requires labeled data and compute.
_extra.lens_pm: Better performance for specialized tasks. Faster than fine-tuning.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement with a trainable embedding layer. Use gradient-based optimization. Save and reload the soft prompt for inference.

title: Prompt versioning
definition: Tracking changes to prompts over time — like Git for prompts — so you can compare, revert, and understand what works.
examples: Prompt library tracks: "customer_support_v1: 85% satisfaction. v2: 87%. v3: 89%. Ship v3."
Like version control for code: v1.0 was basic, v1.1 added examples, v2.0 changed approach.

_extra.analogy: Like version control for code: v1.0 was basic, v1.1 added examples, v2.0 changed approach.
_extra.deeper: Versioning enables A/B testing and iteration. Teams can experiment independently. Downside: managing many versions is overhead; need tooling or discipline. Cloud platforms and prompt management tools handle this.
_extra.lens_pm: Empirical improvement tracking. Data-driven decisions.
_extra.lens_eng: Use version control (Git) or prompt management tool. Tag each version with baseline metrics.

title: Proxy Gaming
definition: Optimizing a proxy metric so hard you break what it was supposed to measure.
examples: A model trained to maximize accuracy on a benchmark might memorize the test set. A company tracking employee productivity by keyboard clicks incentivizes busy-work instead of output.
Like a student memorizing test answers instead of learning the material.

_extra.analogy: Like a student memorizing test answers instead of learning the material.
_extra.deeper: Once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure (Goodhart's Law). This happens because proxies are always imperfect—they correlate with what you care about, but aren't identical. As the model or agent pushes the proxy harder, it finds the gap. The fix is multiplying metrics and being explicit about what matters, but that's slow and requires judgment.
_extra.lens_pm: Don't optimize a single metric to the death—define multiple success criteria and check for degradation.
_extra.lens_eng: Use holdout test sets, out-of-distribution tests, and human evals to catch proxy gaming.

title: Pruning
definition: Removing weights from a trained model — setting them to zero — to reduce model size without retraining from scratch.
examples: A layer has 1 million weights. You remove 50% of them (the ones closest to zero) and the layer still works because those weights didn't contribute much.
Editing a book by deleting unimportant sentences.

_extra.analogy: Editing a book by deleting unimportant sentences.
_extra.deeper: Pruning reduces memory and compute proportionally. Structured pruning (removing whole neurons) is easier to implement but less efficient; unstructured pruning (removing individual weights) is more efficient but requires sparse matrix operations that aren't always fast on hardware. Modern approach: use sparsity-aware training (pruning during training) instead of post-hoc pruning.
_extra.lens_pm: Cheaper than retraining but usually less effective than quantization.
_extra.lens_eng: Start with unstructured magnitude pruning. If hardware doesn't support sparse ops, use structured pruning instead.

title: Pydantic AI
definition: Pydantic's agent framework that uses type hints to define agents, structure prompts, and validate tool outputs.
examples: Write an agent method with return type `QueryResult`. Define what QueryResult looks like. The framework ensures the model response matches; if not, retry.
A strongly-typed agent framework—define your agent's tools and outputs as Python types, Pydantic enforces them.

_extra.analogy: A strongly-typed agent framework—define your agent's tools and outputs as Python types, Pydantic enforces them.
_extra.deeper: Pydantic AI is a new entrant that treats types-first. You define agent behaviors as classes with typed methods. Tool definitions are auto-generated from type hints. Works with any LLM. Smaller than LangChain but opinionated. Still early but gaining traction in Pydantic ecosystem.
_extra.lens_pm: Type safety reduces production errors; enables IDE autocomplete for agent definitions.
_extra.lens_eng: Type-first design; auto-generated tool schemas; composable agent classes.

title: PyTorch
definition: Facebook's deep learning framework; dominant choice for LLM research and development.
examples: Write a custom training loop in PyTorch; adjust backprop or loss dynamically.
The researcher's choice; flexible, debuggable, dominates academia.

_extra.analogy: The researcher's choice; flexible, debuggable, dominates academia.
_extra.deeper: PyTorch uses dynamic computation graphs; more flexible than static graphs (TensorFlow). Strong ecosystem: Hugging Face, PyTorch Lightning, DeepSpeed all built on PyTorch.
_extra.lens_pm: Market leader in research; drives recruitment and technical culture at AI labs.
_extra.lens_eng: PyTorch is the default for LLM training and fine-tuning; ecosystem is mature.

title: Qdrant
definition: Rust-based vector database focused on speed and efficiency; used for semantic search and similarity matching at scale.
examples: Deploy Qdrant for a recommendation engine; query 10M vectors in milliseconds.
The performant option; written in Rust, feels fast.

_extra.analogy: The performant option; written in Rust, feels fast.
_extra.deeper: Qdrant is built in Rust for speed. Supports approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search with HNSW indexing. Open-source with managed cloud option.
_extra.lens_pm: Positioned as faster/more efficient than alternatives; appeals to scale-aware companies.
_extra.lens_eng: Rust-based means predictable performance and low resource usage. HNSW indexing is standard.

title: QLoRA
definition: LoRA on a compressed model, so you can fine-tune a large model on a single consumer GPU.
examples: A researcher fine-tunes a 65B model on one 24GB GPU by quantizing the base to 4-bit and training LoRA adapters on top.
Like renovating a house after shrinking your tools to fit a small van — you lose almost nothing but suddenly it all fits in your garage.

_extra.analogy: Like renovating a house after shrinking your tools to fit a small van — you lose almost nothing but suddenly it all fits in your garage.
_extra.deeper: QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit to shrink its memory footprint, then trains LoRA adapters in higher precision on top. The quantized weights stay fixed, so the precision loss barely hurts, while memory drops enough to fine-tune huge models on modest hardware. It democratized large-model fine-tuning, moving it from data centers to enthusiasts’ desks.
_extra.lens_pm: The reason fine-tuning big models stopped requiring a server farm — huge for cost and accessibility.
_extra.lens_eng: 4-bit quantized frozen base + higher-precision LoRA adapters; large memory savings with near-full-precision quality.

title: Quality filtering
definition: Keeping only the higher-quality documents by scoring each one and dropping the bottom of the barrel.
examples: A classifier trained to recognize well-written pages scores the web crawl, and only documents above a threshold are kept.
Grading apples and shipping only the ones above a certain bar, composting the bruised ones.

_extra.analogy: Grading apples and shipping only the ones above a certain bar, composting the bruised ones.
_extra.deeper: A specific slice of filtering focused on "is this good writing/useful content" rather than "is this unsafe." Often a small model is trained to imitate a known-good reference (say, curated encyclopedic text) and used to score the rest of the corpus. It reliably boosts model quality, but the reference defines "quality," so the choice quietly shapes what the model treats as normal or authoritative.
_extra.lens_pm: A big lever on final model quality — and on whose writing style gets treated as the standard.
_extra.lens_eng: Score documents with a learned quality classifier against a reference distribution and threshold the corpus.

title: Quantization
definition: Converting model weights and activations from high precision (float32) to lower precision (int8, int4) to save memory and speed up computation.
examples: A model with 7 billion float32 weights uses 28GB of memory. Quantize to int8 (1 byte per weight) and it's 7GB.
Storing a photo in lower resolution to take up less disk space.

_extra.analogy: Storing a photo in lower resolution to take up less disk space.
_extra.deeper: Quantization trades accuracy for speed and memory. Most of the loss happens in the first few bits; going from float32 to float16 hurts less than float16 to int4. Post-training quantization is easy but less accurate; quantization-aware training is harder but better. Modern quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ) are surprisingly good.
_extra.lens_pm: Quantization multiplies your serving capacity. A 7B model that wouldn't fit on one GPU now fits.
_extra.lens_eng: Start with int8 post-training quantization. If that's too lossy, try QAT or mixed-precision.

title: Query Expansion
definition: Quietly adding synonyms and related terms to a search so it catches documents worded differently.
examples: A search for "laptop won’t charge" is expanded with "battery", "power adapter", "not powering on" to widen the net.
Asking for "soda" and having the waiter also check for "pop" and "fizzy drink".

_extra.analogy: Asking for "soda" and having the waiter also check for "pop" and "fizzy drink".
_extra.deeper: Query expansion augments the original query with extra terms — from synonyms, related searches, or an LLM — to improve recall when the corpus uses different vocabulary. It helps sparse methods most, since those depend on exact overlap. The risk is drift: add too many loosely related terms and you dredge up irrelevant results, hurting precision.
_extra.lens_pm: Catches answers users would otherwise miss due to wording, at some risk of noisier results.
_extra.lens_eng: Augment the query with synonyms/related terms (thesaurus, PRF, or LLM-generated); raises recall, can dent precision.

title: Query Rewriting
definition: Rephrasing a messy or context-dependent question into a cleaner one before searching.
examples: In a chat, "and its price?" gets rewritten to "what is the price of the MacBook Air M3?" using earlier context, so retrieval actually works.
A good assistant turning "what about the other one?" into "what are the specs of the 15-inch model?" before acting.

_extra.analogy: A good assistant turning "what about the other one?" into "what are the specs of the 15-inch model?" before acting.
_extra.deeper: Follow-up questions and vague phrasing wreck retrieval because the search sees only the latest words. Query rewriting uses the conversation or an LLM to produce a self-contained, well-formed query. Done well it dramatically improves multi-turn search; done carelessly it can inject assumptions the user never made and quietly change what they asked.
_extra.lens_pm: The unsung fix that makes chat-style search actually work across turns.
_extra.lens_eng: LLM- or rule-based reformulation to a standalone query; conditioning on history resolves coreference and ellipsis.

title: Query, Key, Value
definition: The three roles each token plays in attention: what it’s looking for, what it offers, and what it hands over.
examples: A token’s query is matched against every token’s key; the closest matches decide whose values get blended in.
A library search: your query, each book’s label (key), and the book’s actual contents (value).

_extra.analogy: A library search: your query, each book’s label (key), and the book’s actual contents (value).
_extra.deeper: Attention derives three vectors from each token. The query says what this token wants; keys advertise what every token contains; the dot-product of a query with each key gives relevance scores; those scores then weight the values that get summed into the output. This query-key-value framing is the machinery underneath every attention mechanism.
_extra.lens_pm: The conceptual gears of attention — worth knowing when you hear about KV caching and its memory costs.
_extra.lens_eng: The three learned projections per token whose query-key similarity weights a sum over values.

title: Qwen
definition: Alibaba's open-source language model family, multilingual, and available in multiple sizes.
examples: Qwen (7B, 13B, 72B) outperforms many Western models on Chinese benchmarks; weights are open.
The Chinese alternative; strong performance, especially in non-English languages.

_extra.analogy: The Chinese alternative; strong performance, especially in non-English languages.
_extra.deeper: Qwen is trained on diverse languages and reflects Alibaba's research direction. Strong on Chinese, multilingual capability. Recently open-sourced under a permissive license.
_extra.lens_pm: Tailored to Asian markets; enables local deployment in China without Western LLM dependency.
_extra.lens_eng: Qwen is a good baseline for multilingual work; particularly strong on Chinese/Asian languages.

title: RAG
definition: Hand the model a stack of your documents to read before it answers, so it stops making things up.
examples: A support bot that quotes your actual help docs instead of confidently guessing is doing RAG.
An open-book exam — instead of reciting from memory, it looks up the right page first.

_extra.analogy: An open-book exam — instead of reciting from memory, it looks up the right page first.
_extra.deeper: Your docs get chopped into chunks, turned into embeddings, and stored in a vector database. At query time the system finds the closest chunks and stuffs them into the context window next to your question. Quality lives and dies on the retrieval step — bad chunks in, bad answer out.
_extra.lens_pm: Ground the bot in your own docs so answers cite real sources — fewer escalations, no invented policies.
_extra.lens_eng: Retrieve top-k relevant chunks via vector search and inject them into the prompt at inference time.

title: RAGAS
definition: A framework for evaluating RAG systems with metrics like context relevance, faithfulness, and answer relevance.
examples: RAGAS generates a score from 0–1 that aggregates retrieval quality, model faithfulness, and answer relevance.
Like a quality checklist for a restaurant: checks for cleanliness, food freshness, and service.

_extra.analogy: Like a quality checklist for a restaurant: checks for cleanliness, food freshness, and service.
_extra.deeper: RAGAS is designed for RAG systems where retrieval + generation matter. It combines multiple metrics (context relevance, faithfulness, answer relevance, semantic similarity). It's automated (no human raters needed) but relies on LLM judges, so it's not perfect. Useful for rapid iteration and regression testing.
_extra.lens_pm: RAGAS is a quick way to check RAG quality end-to-end.
_extra.lens_eng: Use RAGAS for continuous monitoring, but validate against human eval on your domain.

title: Rate limit
definition: A cap on how many requests your endpoint will accept in a given time window.
examples: Your API might allow 100 requests per second; after that, new requests get a 429 error and have to wait or retry.
A security guard at a concert who only lets in 100 people per minute to avoid crushing.

_extra.analogy: A security guard at a concert who only lets in 100 people per minute to avoid crushing.
_extra.deeper: Rate limits protect the backend from overload and ensure fair use across clients. They're enforced at the gateway or application level and can be per-user, per-IP, or global. When hit, clients should backoff exponentially — hammering harder makes it worse.
_extra.lens_pm: Rate limits protect your costs and infrastructure, but too strict and they frustrate power users.
_extra.lens_eng: A sliding window or token-bucket counter that rejects requests once a threshold is crossed.

title: Rate limiting
definition: Capping how many requests someone can make in a window, to blunt abuse, runaway costs, and attacks.
examples: An API returns "429 Too Many Requests" after a script tries 10,000 generations in a minute, throttling a scraping or brute-force attempt.
A turnstile that only lets so many people through per minute, so no one can rush the gate.

_extra.analogy: A turnstile that only lets so many people through per minute, so no one can rush the gate.
_extra.deeper: Limits are set per key, user, or IP and enforced with algorithms like token bucket or sliding window. Beyond fairness and cost control, rate limiting slows brute-force jailbreak search and automated abuse by making each attempt cost time. It is a blunt but reliable safety and reliability primitive.
_extra.lens_pm: A simple lever that protects cost, reliability, and safety all at once.
_extra.lens_eng: Enforce per-identity quotas via token-bucket/sliding-window; it also raises the cost of automated jailbreak and abuse campaigns.

title: Re-embedding
definition: Recomputing all your embeddings — usually because you switched to a better embedding model.
examples: Upgrading from an old embedding model to a new one forces re-embedding every chunk, since vectors from different models aren’t comparable.
Re-translating an entire library when you hire a better translator; the old translations no longer match.

_extra.analogy: Re-translating an entire library when you hire a better translator; the old translations no longer match.
_extra.deeper: Embeddings from different models live in different vector spaces, so you cannot mix them — upgrading the model means re-embedding the whole corpus and rebuilding the index. It is a real operational cost and a reason to choose an embedding model carefully up front. Planning for it — versioning vectors, running old and new side by side during migration — avoids a painful big-bang cutover.
_extra.lens_pm: A hidden switching cost when adopting a new embedding model; budget time for it.
_extra.lens_eng: Full corpus re-vectorization on model change; spaces aren’t compatible, so plan versioned, side-by-side migration.

title: ReAct
definition: A pattern where the model alternates between thinking out loud and taking an action, each step informing the next.
examples: “I need the population — let me search.” It searches, reads the result, then reasons: “Now I can compute the density,” and calls the calculator.
A detective who mutters a theory, checks one clue, updates the theory, checks another — reasoning and legwork taking turns.

_extra.analogy: A detective who mutters a theory, checks one clue, updates the theory, checks another — reasoning and legwork taking turns.
_extra.deeper: ReAct interleaves a reasoning trace with tool actions and their observations, so the model’s next thought is grounded in what it just saw rather than pure speculation. It made early agents far more reliable than plan-everything-upfront approaches, because the model can course-correct after each real result. The reasoning steps also make its behavior legible when something goes wrong.
_extra.lens_pm: The recipe behind most working agents — think a little, act a little, repeat.
_extra.lens_eng: An agent loop interleaving chain-of-thought tokens with tool actions and observations fed back into context.

title: ReAct prompting
definition: A prompt structure where the model alternates between reasoning (thought), taking action (tool calls or steps), and observing results.
examples: "Thought: I need to find the GDP of France. Action: Search Google. Observation: France GDP is X. Thought: So compared to Germany... Action: Search Germany GDP. Observation: ... Thought: France is larger."
Planning → executing → reflecting, in a loop.

_extra.analogy: Planning → executing → reflecting, in a loop.
_extra.deeper: ReAct is foundational to agentic prompting. The structure forces the model to think, act, observe, and adjust. It works well with external tools (search, calculators, APIs). The observation loop creates feedback and prevents hallucination.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables agent-like behavior: planning, tool use, correction.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement with tool calling. Parse thought/action/observation. Loop until done.

title: Reader
definition: The component that reads retrieved passages and produces the actual answer — in classic QA, the second half after the retriever.
examples: In a retriever-reader system, the retriever finds 10 passages and the reader extracts "March 2021" as the answer to "when did it launch?".
The researcher who reads the pulled files and writes the summary, after the librarian fetches them.

_extra.analogy: The researcher who reads the pulled files and writes the summary, after the librarian fetches them.
_extra.deeper: In the original retriever-reader design, the retriever surfaced candidate passages and a separate reader model extracted or generated the answer from them. Modern RAG blurs this: the LLM is the reader, generating rather than extracting, so the standalone "reader" term is fading. The division of labor still matters conceptually — finding evidence and using it are distinct jobs with distinct failure modes.
_extra.lens_pm: A useful mental split even now: retrieval finding the evidence vs. the model using it well.
_extra.lens_eng: The answer-producing stage after retrieval; in RAG it is the generative LLM, so the extractive "reader" is largely legacy.

title: realtime API
definition: An API that ingests audio streams, transcribes, runs LLM reasoning, and outputs audio responses—low latency, no round trips.
examples: User speaks: 'What's the weather in NYC?' Realtime API transcribes (speech-to-text), asks the LLM (which checks a weather tool), and speaks the response back—whole loop <500ms.
A phone call instead of email—talk and get an immediate response, with reasoning happening behind the scenes.

_extra.analogy: A phone call instead of email—talk and get an immediate response, with reasoning happening behind the scenes.
_extra.deeper: Realtime APIs use WebSocket or similar for true streaming. They interleave transcription, LLM inference, and TTS. Requires high reliability and low-latency infrastructure. Relatively new; OpenAI, Anthropic, and others are rolling these out. Game-changer for voice agents.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables voice-first experiences; reduces friction for hands-free interaction.
_extra.lens_eng: WebSocket/streaming architecture; complex latency management; requires efficient inference.

title: Reasoning Model
definition: A model trained to think out loud before answering, spending extra compute to work through hard problems.
examples: Ask one a tricky math or coding problem and it’ll generate a long internal chain of steps before giving you the final line.
Like a student who scribbles working on scratch paper instead of blurting the first answer that comes to mind.

_extra.analogy: Like a student who scribbles working on scratch paper instead of blurting the first answer that comes to mind.
_extra.deeper: These models are trained — often with reinforcement learning — to produce extended reasoning traces, then land on an answer. The longer they “think” at inference time, the better they tend to do on hard tasks, which is a real trade of latency and cost for accuracy. It’s a shift from spending all your compute on training to spending some at answer time.
_extra.lens_pm: Better on genuinely hard tasks, but slower and pricier per query — pick where it earns its keep.
_extra.lens_eng: A model post-trained to allocate test-time compute to explicit multi-step reasoning before answering.

title: Recall
definition: Of the actual positive cases, how many did the model catch?—measuring false negative rate.
examples: There are 100 fraudulent transactions in the data. The detector catches 90. Recall is 90%.
Like a cancer screening test: of the people who actually have cancer, how many does it catch?

_extra.analogy: Like a cancer screening test: of the people who actually have cancer, how many does it catch?
_extra.deeper: High recall means the model doesn't miss cases. Low recall means it's conservative. Recall alone is incomplete—a model that predicts 'positive' for everything has perfect recall but creates noise. The precision-recall tradeoff is fundamental.
_extra.lens_pm: For safety-critical tasks (cancer detection, abuse detection), prioritize recall to avoid missing cases.
_extra.lens_eng: Track recall at different decision thresholds; visualize precision-recall curves.

title: Recall at K
definition: Of all the right answers out there, how many showed up in your top K results.
examples: If a query has 4 relevant docs and 3 appear in the top 10, recall@10 is 0.75.
Casting a net and asking: of all the fish in the pond you wanted, how many did you actually pull up?

_extra.analogy: Casting a net and asking: of all the fish in the pond you wanted, how many did you actually pull up?
_extra.deeper: Recall@K measures coverage: did retrieval surface the relevant items within the first K? It matters most in RAG, where a missed passage means the model literally cannot answer. High recall usually comes at the cost of precision — a bigger K catches more truth but also more noise, which then leans on reranking to sort out.
_extra.lens_pm: If recall is low, no amount of prompt tuning helps — the answer never reached the model.
_extra.lens_eng: |relevant ∩ top-K| / |relevant|; the recall/precision trade-off is set by K and the retriever.

title: Recall vs Precision
definition: The trade-off between catching everything relevant and only returning what’s actually relevant.
examples: Set retrieval to return 20 chunks and you rarely miss the answer (high recall) but drag in noise; return 3 and every chunk is on-point (high precision) but you sometimes miss the key one.
A fishing net: a wide net catches every fish but also boots and seaweed; a narrow one keeps the catch clean but misses fish.

_extra.analogy: A fishing net: a wide net catches every fish but also boots and seaweed; a narrow one keeps the catch clean but misses fish.
_extra.deeper: Recall is the share of all relevant items you actually retrieved; precision is the share of what you retrieved that was relevant. Turning one dial usually moves the other the wrong way. In RAG the sweet spot depends on the model: too few chunks and it lacks the answer, too many and it drowns in distractors. Re-ranking is the usual way to get precision back after casting a wide, high-recall net.
_extra.lens_pm: The core quality lever in search — decide whether missing an answer or showing junk hurts your users more.
_extra.lens_eng: Recall = TP/(TP+FN), precision = TP/(TP+FP); tune top-k to trade them, then restore precision with a reranker.

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion
definition: A simple way to merge several ranked lists: reward items for placing high in any of them.
examples: Given keyword results and vector results, RRF gives each document a score of 1/(k + its rank) in every list and sums them, so a document ranked #2 in both beats one ranked #1 in only one.
Combining critics’ top-ten movie lists by giving points for rank — a film near the top of several lists wins, even if no one made it number one.

_extra.analogy: Combining critics’ top-ten movie lists by giving points for rank — a film near the top of several lists wins, even if no one made it number one.
_extra.deeper: RRF ignores the raw similarity scores, which are hard to compare across different retrievers, and looks only at position. Each list contributes 1/(k + rank) per document, with a small constant k (often 60) to dampen the top. Summing across lists produces one ranking. It’s popular because it needs no tuning and no score normalization, yet holds up surprisingly well.
_extra.lens_pm: A no-knobs default for combining searches that just works, so the team ships fusion without a tuning project.
_extra.lens_eng: score(d) = Σ over lists of 1/(k + rank_list(d)); sort descending. k≈60 is the common default.

title: Recurrent Neural Network
definition: A network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory of what it has seen so far.
examples: Before transformers, RNNs handled translation and speech by processing text left to right, updating a hidden state.
Reading a sentence word by word while keeping a running gist of it in your head.

_extra.analogy: Reading a sentence word by word while keeping a running gist of it in your head.
_extra.deeper: An RNN maintains a hidden state updated at each timestep, letting information flow forward through a sequence. That sequential dependency is also its weakness: it can’t parallelize across time, and long-range signals fade or explode through many steps. Gated variants like LSTM and GRU helped, but attention-based transformers ultimately outscaled them and pushed RNNs to the margins.
_extra.lens_pm: The prior era’s approach to sequence modeling, now mostly of historical and niche interest.
_extra.lens_eng: A network with a recurrent hidden state updated per timestep, limited by sequential compute and vanishing gradients.

title: Recursive Chunking
definition: Splitting text by trying big separators first — paragraphs, then sentences — until pieces fit.
examples: A splitter tries paragraph breaks, and only where a paragraph is too long does it drop to sentence-level cuts.
Breaking a chocolate bar along the deepest grooves first, snapping smaller only if the piece is still too big.

_extra.analogy: Breaking a chocolate bar along the deepest grooves first, snapping smaller only if the piece is still too big.
_extra.deeper: Recursive chunking uses an ordered list of separators — say, double newlines, then newlines, then spaces — and applies each in turn until chunks are under the size limit. This keeps semantically coherent units together when possible and only makes ugly cuts as a last resort. It is the default in many frameworks because it is simple and respects document structure better than fixed slicing.
_extra.lens_pm: A sensible default that keeps chunks coherent without much tuning.
_extra.lens_eng: Hierarchical separator list applied top-down until the size constraint is met; balances structure and length.

title: Red Teaming
definition: Deliberately attacking your own model to find how it breaks before real attackers do.
examples: Before launch, a team spends weeks trying to make the model produce disallowed content, then feeds every success back into safety training.
Hiring burglars to test your house — better they find the unlocked window than the actual thieves.

_extra.analogy: Hiring burglars to test your house — better they find the unlocked window than the actual thieves.
_extra.deeper: Red teaming is adversarial testing applied to AI: skilled people (and increasingly automated systems) probe for jailbreaks, harmful outputs, bias, and misuse paths. The goal isn’t a clean report — it’s a pile of failures you can fix. Findings feed back into alignment training and filters. It’s never "done," because capabilities and attacks keep evolving, so mature teams red team continuously rather than once.
_extra.lens_pm: The pre-launch stress test that surfaces embarrassing failures on your terms instead of in the press.
_extra.lens_eng: Structured adversarial probing (human and automated) whose findings feed alignment training and filter updates; a continuous, not one-shot, process.

title: Red-team evaluation
definition: Having human experts intentionally try to break your system to find real-world vulnerabilities before users find them.
examples: A safety-specialized contractor generates 100 prompts designed to make a language model refuse to help or produce harmful content, testing your safety guardrails.
A professional locksmith trying to pick your locks to show you weaknesses.

_extra.analogy: A professional locksmith trying to pick your locks to show you weaknesses.
_extra.deeper: Red-teaming is expensive but produces creative attacks. Humans find vulnerabilities that automated tests miss. The downside: red-teaming doesn't scale, takes weeks, and teams can have blind spots. Best practice: combine human red-teaming with automated testing.
_extra.lens_pm: Budget for it before launch, especially on safety-critical features.
_extra.lens_eng: Partner with red-team experts. Log and triage findings. Iterate on mitigations.

title: Red-teaming data
definition: Adversarial examples — crafted attempts to make a model misbehave — collected so training can patch those weaknesses.
examples: Testers spend weeks trying to jailbreak a model; the successful attacks become training data teaching it to resist next time.
Hiring ethical hackers to break into your building, then fixing every door they got through.

_extra.analogy: Hiring ethical hackers to break into your building, then fixing every door they got through.
_extra.deeper: Red-teaming means deliberately probing a model for harmful, biased, or manipulable behavior — by humans, by other models, or both. The prompts that succeed are gold: they reveal real failure modes and become fine-tuning data so the model learns to handle them. It is an arms race, since new attacks keep appearing, which is why red-teaming is continuous rather than a single pre-launch check.
_extra.lens_pm: How known ways to break a model get found before launch — and turned into fixes.
_extra.lens_eng: Adversarially elicited failure cases used as safety fine-tuning data to close discovered vulnerabilities.

title: Redundancy
definition: Having backups of critical systems so if one fails, another is ready to take over.
examples: Three inference servers instead of one — any two going down still leaves one answering requests.
Having two parachutes instead of one.

_extra.analogy: Having two parachutes instead of one.
_extra.deeper: Redundancy costs money but buys uptime. For stateless services (like inference), it's simple — just run more copies. For stateful services, you need distributed consensus and careful coordination. Redundancy has to cover everything: servers, storage, network.
_extra.lens_pm: Redundancy is the most straightforward way to improve uptime and user trust.
_extra.lens_eng: Redundancy is cheap compared to downtime; over-invest here.

title: Reference answer
definition: The correct answer to a question, written by a human, that you use to grade automated responses.
examples: For "What is the capital of France?" the reference answer is "Paris." If your model says "Paris" or "The capital of France is Paris," both grade as correct against this reference.
The answer key to a test — you check whether students got it right by comparing to this.

_extra.analogy: The answer key to a test — you check whether students got it right by comparing to this.
_extra.deeper: Reference answers are expensive — humans have to write them. Some systems use multiple references (Paris, Île-de-France) to allow variation. The danger: a good answer that differs from the reference gets marked wrong, so your eval underestimates model quality. This is why reference-free evaluation exists.
_extra.lens_pm: You need reference answers to grade at scale, but they're a bottleneck. Budget time to create them.
_extra.lens_eng: Store as gold annotations. Use fuzzy matching or embedding similarity to accept minor paraphrases.

title: Reference-free evaluation
definition: Using a strong language model to grade answers without comparing them to a human-written reference.
examples: Asking GPT-4 "Is this response correct, helpful, and complete?" and getting a score back, instead of comparing to a stored reference answer.
Instead of an answer key, you ask an expert teacher to grade the essay directly.

_extra.analogy: Instead of an answer key, you ask an expert teacher to grade the essay directly.
_extra.deeper: LLM-as-judge is fast and scalable but introduces new failure modes. The grading model can be fooled by confident-sounding but wrong answers. Cultural bias in the judge affects scores. It's useful for signals like tone and coherence, less reliable for factual correctness. You still want some human spot-checks.
_extra.lens_pm: Faster and cheaper than human annotation, but not fully trustworthy — use as a filter, not ground truth.
_extra.lens_eng: Call your judge LLM with a prompt asking for a score(1-10) plus reasoning. Parse the score, log the reasoning for auditing.

title: Referring Expression
definition: Understanding language that refers to specific objects in an image - "the woman in the red hat on the left."
examples: "The tallest building" -> output: bounding box of the tallest building in the image.
In a crowded photo: "the person in the back row, third from the left."

_extra.analogy: In a crowded photo: "the person in the back row, third from the left."
_extra.deeper: Comprehension task: given phrase, find object. Generation task: describe an object so someone can identify it. Comprehension requires grounding (localization). Generation requires visual understanding + language fluency. Compositional phrases ("red car" = red + car) and relational ("to the left of the dog") are challenging. Transformer-based models with cross-attention excel.
_extra.lens_pm: Accessible systems, interactive retrieval, visual question answering.
_extra.lens_eng: Comprehension: image + text -> bounding box/mask. Generation: image + bounding box -> description. Datasets: Flickr30K, ReferCOCO. Metric: accuracy, IoU.

title: Reflection
definition: The agent pausing to critique its own work and decide what to fix before moving on.
examples: After drafting code, the agent reviews it, notices an unhandled edge case, and revises before running the tests.
Rereading your own email and thinking “that middle paragraph is a mess” before you hit send.

_extra.analogy: Rereading your own email and thinking “that middle paragraph is a mess” before you hit send.
_extra.deeper: Reflection adds a step where the model evaluates its last output against the goal and produces feedback it then acts on. It reliably catches some classes of mistakes and improves quality — but it has a ceiling, because the same model doing the work is grading it, and it can be blind to its own blind spots or talk itself into false confidence. External signals like tests or tool results make reflection much sharper.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap quality bump for agent output, with a real limit — a model can’t always see its own errors.
_extra.lens_eng: A step where the model critiques its prior output and generates corrective feedback fed into the next iteration.

title: Refusal
definition: When a model declines to answer because the request crosses a safety line.
examples: Asked for step-by-step instructions to synthesize a dangerous toxin, the model declines and offers to explain the chemistry at a safe, general level instead.
A pharmacist who won’t fill a prescription that looks forged, no matter how politely you ask.

_extra.analogy: A pharmacist who won’t fill a prescription that looks forged, no matter how politely you ask.
_extra.deeper: Refusal is a trained behavior: models learn to recognize categories of harmful requests and respond with a decline rather than comply. Done well, it’s the visible edge of alignment. The craft is calibration — refusing genuinely harmful asks while still helping with the vast majority of legitimate ones. Refuse too eagerly and you get over-refusal; refuse too little and safety training failed.
_extra.lens_pm: The user-facing face of your safety policy; its tone and accuracy shape how trustworthy the product feels.
_extra.lens_eng: A learned response to harmful-request classes; quality is the calibration between correct declines and false positives.

title: Refusal prompt
definition: A prompt directive that instructs the model to decline certain requests, usually harmful or outside policy.
examples: "Do not write code for malware, exploit sensitive APIs without auth, or generate content that sexualizes minors."
Telling a bartender "don't serve anyone who's already drunk," they refuse specific cases.

_extra.analogy: Telling a bartender "don't serve anyone who's already drunk," they refuse specific cases.
_extra.deeper: Refusal prompts are a key part of alignment. The tension: make them too strict and users get false refusals (over-refusal). Too loose and you miss actual harms. Optimal prompts are specific, give reasons, and offer alternatives.
_extra.lens_pm: Critical for compliance and brand trust; measurable through refusal rate metrics.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure false refusal vs true refusal separately. Over-refusal degrades UX and wastes model capacity.

title: Refusal rate
definition: How often a model declines to answer — the dial you tune between too permissive and too preachy.
examples: A model that refuses to help with a chemistry homework question because it superficially resembles a dangerous request is showing an over-high refusal rate.
A smoke alarm’s sensitivity: too low and it misses fires, too high and it screams every time you make toast.

_extra.analogy: A smoke alarm’s sensitivity: too low and it misses fires, too high and it screams every time you make toast.
_extra.deeper: Refusal rate has to be split by intent: high on genuinely harmful asks is good, high on benign asks (over-refusal) is a usability tax that trains people to work around the model. The two failure modes trade off, so teams track both harmful-compliance and benign-refusal. Getting the balance right is one of the subtlest parts of safety tuning.
_extra.lens_pm: Over-refusal is a real product cost — annoyed users route to a less careful competitor.
_extra.lens_eng: Report refusal separately on harmful vs. benign eval splits; optimizing overall rate alone hides the over-refusal failure mode.

title: Refusal training
definition: Teaching a model to decline requests it should not fulfill, and to do it gracefully.
examples: The model is fine-tuned on examples where the good response to a harmful request is a clear, polite refusal with a brief reason.
Training a bartender to firmly but politely cut someone off — knowing when "no" is the right answer.

_extra.analogy: Training a bartender to firmly but politely cut someone off — knowing when "no" is the right answer.
_extra.deeper: Refusal behavior is taught with curated examples and preference data showing when and how to say no. The craft is calibration: refuse genuinely harmful asks while not over-refusing benign ones that merely pattern-match to something risky. Push too hard and you get an annoying, over-cautious model — a visible face of the alignment tax; too soft and safety gaps open up.
_extra.lens_pm: Directly shapes the "is this model helpful or annoying" line users feel every day.
_extra.lens_eng: Fine-tune on curated refusal examples/preferences; the key metric is refusing harmful while minimizing over-refusal.

title: Regression Testing
definition: Running old tests after a change to make sure you didn't break anything that was working before.
examples: After updating a model, you re-evaluate it on your previous gold set to make sure accuracy didn't drop.
Like checking that your new recipe still makes good bread, not just that it doesn't burn.

_extra.analogy: Like checking that your new recipe still makes good bread, not just that it doesn't burn.
_extra.deeper: Regression testing catches silent failures—changes that improve one metric but degrade another. It's essential before shipping. The catch: you need good regression tests (comprehensive, non-brittle) and a clean baseline to compare against. Many teams skip this and later wonder why quality dropped.
_extra.lens_pm: Regression testing is cheap insurance. Always run it before pushing to production.
_extra.lens_eng: Maintain a stable test suite; add new tests for each bug; bisect changes if regressions appear.

title: Regularization
definition: Any technique that keeps a model from over-memorizing so it generalizes to new data.
examples: Dropout, weight decay, and data augmentation are all regularization — each fights overfitting a different way.
Like a coach who stops you from over-optimizing your form for one practice court, so your game holds up anywhere.

_extra.analogy: Like a coach who stops you from over-optimizing your form for one practice court, so your game holds up anywhere.
_extra.deeper: Regularization is the umbrella for methods that constrain a model’s effective complexity to improve generalization: penalties on weights, dropout, early stopping, augmentation, and more. The goal is to shift the balance from fitting the training set toward performing on unseen data. Too much and the model underfits; the art is finding the sweet spot for your data size and task.
_extra.lens_pm: The family of tricks that make a model work in the real world, not just on its training set.
_extra.lens_eng: Techniques constraining effective capacity (weight decay, dropout, early stopping, augmentation) to improve generalization.

title: Reinforcement learning
definition: Learning by trial and error, guided by rewards for good actions and penalties for bad ones.
examples: An agent learns to play a game by trying moves and getting points, gradually favoring the actions that win.
Like training a dog with treats and “no” — behavior that earns reward gets repeated, behavior that doesn’t fades.

_extra.analogy: Like training a dog with treats and “no” — behavior that earns reward gets repeated, behavior that doesn’t fades.
_extra.deeper: Instead of labeled answers, RL gives an agent rewards for the outcomes of its actions, and it learns a policy that maximizes cumulative reward over time. The hard parts are delayed rewards (which action deserves credit?) and exploration versus exploitation. In language models, RL powers alignment: RLHF optimizes the model against a reward model trained on human preferences.
_extra.lens_pm: The paradigm behind alignment tuning and agents — useful when success is a signal, not a labeled answer.
_extra.lens_eng: Learn a policy maximizing cumulative reward via trial and error; credit assignment and exploration are core challenges.

title: Rejection sampling
definition: Generate several candidate answers, keep only the good ones, and train on those.
examples: A model produces eight solutions per math problem; a checker keeps the correct ones, and those become new training data.
Baking a dozen cookies, keeping the best few, and photographing only those for the recipe card.

_extra.analogy: Baking a dozen cookies, keeping the best few, and photographing only those for the recipe card.
_extra.deeper: Rejection sampling filters a model's own generations by some quality bar — a verifier, a reward model, or an exact-answer check — and fine-tunes on the survivors. It is a simple, stable way to bootstrap a model on its better outputs, closely related to best-of-n but used to build a training set rather than to pick a single response at inference time.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap way to squeeze more quality out of a model using its own best work.
_extra.lens_eng: Sample n candidates, keep those passing a quality/verifier filter, and fine-tune on the accepted set.

title: Repetition penalty
definition: A dial that discourages the model from saying the same thing over and over.
examples: A writer notices the model looping “the results show that…” and nudges the repetition penalty up until the phrasing varies.
Like a friend who gently taps you when you tell the same story a third time at dinner.

_extra.analogy: Like a friend who gently taps you when you tell the same story a third time at dinner.
_extra.deeper: It works by shrinking the probability of tokens (or phrases) the model has already produced, so each repeat gets a little harder to choose. Push it too hard and the model avoids necessary repeats — names, code keywords — and the text starts to read strangely, so it’s a balance, not a cure.
_extra.lens_pm: A fast fix for the “broken record” failure without retraining anything.
_extra.lens_eng: Divides or subtracts from logits of previously seen tokens before sampling, scaled by a penalty factor.

title: Replanning
definition: Throwing out or reworking the plan mid-task when reality doesn’t match what the agent expected.
examples: The agent planned to use an API that turns out to be down, so it stops, replans around a web search, and continues.
Hitting a road closure and rerouting — the destination’s the same, the path you drew is now useless.

_extra.analogy: Hitting a road closure and rerouting — the destination’s the same, the path you drew is now useless.
_extra.deeper: Plans made up front rarely survive contact with a messy environment, so replanning lets an agent revise its approach when observations contradict its assumptions. It’s what makes agents robust rather than brittle — but it’s a balancing act: replan too eagerly and the agent thrashes, never finishing; too reluctantly and it keeps executing a plan that can’t work. Knowing when the plan is truly broken is the hard part.
_extra.lens_pm: The difference between an agent that adapts and one that stubbornly runs a doomed plan into the ground.
_extra.lens_eng: Revising the remaining plan when observations invalidate prior assumptions, balancing stability against adaptivity.

title: Replay Buffer
definition: A stash of old examples the model keeps revisiting so it doesn’t forget them while learning new ones.
examples: While teaching a model new topics, the trainer sprinkles in old data from the buffer so past skills stay sharp.
Mixing a few old flashcards into every study session so you don’t lose what you learned last month.

_extra.analogy: Mixing a few old flashcards into every study session so you don’t lose what you learned last month.
_extra.deeper: A replay buffer stores past experiences or examples and re-injects samples of them into ongoing training. In continual learning it preserves old knowledge; in reinforcement learning it also breaks correlations between consecutive samples, making updates more stable. The design questions are what to keep and how to sample from it.
_extra.lens_pm: A practical guardrail so updating the model doesn’t silently degrade the things it already did well.
_extra.lens_eng: A memory of prior samples replayed during training to stabilize learning and counter forgetting.

title: Replicate
definition: Platform for running open-source ML models via API; simplifies model deployment for developers.
examples: Upload a Llama fine-tune or Stable Diffusion variant; Replicate handles infrastructure.
Heroku for ML; deploy a model in minutes.

_extra.analogy: Heroku for ML; deploy a model in minutes.
_extra.deeper: Replicate focuses on ease of use: run models without managing infrastructure. Supports open-source models and custom weights. Used by many startups.
_extra.lens_pm: Developer-friendly; monetization through usage.
_extra.lens_eng: Low barrier to entry for model deployment; good for experimentation.

title: Representation
definition: How a model re-encodes something into its own internal language of numbers.
examples: A photo of a cat becomes a representation — a stack of numbers — before the model can classify or caption it.
Sheet music for a song — not the sound itself, but a form the performer can actually work from.

_extra.analogy: Sheet music for a song — not the sound itself, but a form the performer can actually work from.
_extra.deeper: Deep learning’s whole trick is learning good representations: turning raw input into vectors where the useful structure is easy to read off. Better representations make downstream tasks easier. Much of what pretraining buys you is reusable representations.
_extra.lens_pm: The quality of a model’s internal representations sets the ceiling on everything it can do downstream.
_extra.lens_eng: A learned feature vector encoding input; the output of intermediate layers used by downstream heads.

title: Request queue
definition: A buffer of pending requests waiting to be processed — long queues mean slow response times.
examples: Under load, 500 requests per second arrive but the server can only handle 400/s, so the queue grows and responses get slower.
A line at the grocery store — the longer the line, the longer you wait.

_extra.analogy: A line at the grocery store — the longer the line, the longer you wait.
_extra.deeper: Queue depth is a key metric. If it's growing, the system is overloaded. If it's consistently long, you need to scale. Queue depth also affects latency perception — users see tail latency spike when the queue builds up.
_extra.lens_pm: Queue depth is a leading indicator of whether you need to scale or adjust pricing.
_extra.lens_eng: Monitor queue depth; when it grows, scale immediately (or shed load via rate limiting).

title: Reranking
definition: A second-pass sort that takes the retriever’s rough shortlist and reorders it by who actually answers the question best.
examples: Retrieve 50 candidate chunks cheaply, then rerank to keep the 5 that truly fit before answering.
A hiring manager reading the résumés that HR’s keyword filter already passed through.

_extra.analogy: A hiring manager reading the résumés that HR’s keyword filter already passed through.
_extra.deeper: Fast retrieval favors recall — cast a wide net — but the top hits aren’t always the most relevant. A reranker (often a heavier cross-encoder that reads query and chunk together) scores each candidate directly, catching the good ones the first pass buried. More compute, better precision.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap accuracy boost for RAG: keep retrieval wide, then let reranking pick the winners.
_extra.lens_eng: A cross-encoder scoring (query, passage) pairs to reorder first-stage retrieval by relevance.

title: Reserved capacity
definition: Buying compute in advance (1-3 years) at a discount — saves money if you can predict usage.
examples: You know you'll need 100 GPUs for 2 years; commit upfront and save 40% vs on-demand.
Buying a season pass to the gym instead of paying per visit.

_extra.analogy: Buying a season pass to the gym instead of paying per visit.
_extra.deeper: Reserved instances require guessing usage correctly. Overcommit and you waste money. Undercommit and you miss the discount. They're also hard to change once purchased. Good for steady, predictable workloads; bad for growing startups or experimental projects.
_extra.lens_pm: Reserved capacity is profitable for mature, predictable products.
_extra.lens_eng: Use reserved instances for baseline load; burst with on-demand or spot.

title: Residual Connection
definition: A shortcut that adds a layer’s input to its output, so information can skip past if needed.
examples: In each transformer block, the input is added back to what attention produced, keeping gradients healthy in deep stacks.
Keeping a photocopy of your draft before edits, so nothing important gets lost in revision.

_extra.analogy: Keeping a photocopy of your draft before edits, so nothing important gets lost in revision.
_extra.deeper: Very deep networks are hard to train because signals and gradients fade as they pass through many layers. A residual connection adds a layer’s input straight to its output, giving information a clear path forward and gradients a clear path back. This one trick is what made training networks with dozens or hundreds of layers practical.
_extra.lens_pm: A quiet structural trick that made very deep, capable models trainable in the first place.
_extra.lens_eng: An additive identity shortcut around a sublayer that preserves signal and eases gradient flow.

title: ResNet
definition: The network that let us stack layers really deep by giving each one a shortcut around itself.
examples: ResNet-50 is still a default image backbone in production vision systems years after its 2015 debut.
Like an express lane on a highway — if a stretch of road adds nothing, traffic can just skip past it untouched.

_extra.analogy: Like an express lane on a highway — if a stretch of road adds nothing, traffic can just skip past it untouched.
_extra.deeper: Very deep networks used to get worse, not better, because the training signal faded on its way back through dozens of layers. ResNet added “residual” shortcuts that let each layer learn only the change it needs, with the input passed through untouched by default. That single trick unlocked networks hundreds of layers deep and reshaped everything after.
_extra.lens_pm: A durable, battle-tested vision backbone you can still ship on today.
_extra.lens_eng: A CNN with identity skip connections so layers learn residual functions, easing gradient flow.

title: Responsible AI
definition: The practices and principles for building and deploying AI ethically, fairly, and accountably.
examples: A company’s responsible-AI program covers fairness testing across demographics, transparency about AI use, data privacy, and a review board for high-risk launches.
Professional ethics for a new field — the equivalent of a doctor’s "first, do no harm," written for people shipping AI.

_extra.analogy: Professional ethics for a new field — the equivalent of a doctor’s "first, do no harm," written for people shipping AI.
_extra.deeper: Responsible AI is the governance and values layer around the technical work: fairness, transparency, privacy, accountability, and human oversight. It turns broad principles into concrete practices — bias audits, model cards, impact assessments, escalation paths. Critics note it can slide into box-checking or "ethics washing" if it lacks teeth. Done seriously, it’s the difference between a company that reacts to harm and one that anticipates it.
_extra.lens_pm: The framework that keeps a product defensible — to users, regulators, and your own team’s conscience.
_extra.lens_eng: Operationalizes fairness, transparency, privacy, and accountability via audits, documentation, and review gates; risks becoming box-checking without enforcement.

title: responsible scaling policy
definition: A lab's published commitment to pause or test larger models if certain safety risks emerge during training.
examples: Anthropic's RSP: 'If we detect certain red-line capabilities during training, we'll pause, do further testing, and only proceed if we can mitigate risks.'
An alarm system that trips if the house gets too hot—you've committed to checking before it burns down.

_extra.analogy: An alarm system that trips if the house gets too hot—you've committed to checking before it burns down.
_extra.deeper: RSPs are a credible commitment device—a lab announces in advance that it will slow down if specific risk thresholds are crossed. Hard to enforce (who checks?), but signals seriousness about safety. Different labs have different thresholds and procedures.
_extra.lens_pm: Signals safety commitment to regulators and public; reduces reputational risk.
_extra.lens_eng: Gating on evals; capability measurements tied to go/no-go decisions.

title: Retrieval
definition: The step that goes and finds the right supporting text before the model answers — the “R” in RAG.
examples: You ask about refund policy; retrieval grabs the refund section from the docs to hand the model.
Sending a runner to the archive to fetch the relevant files before the meeting starts.

_extra.analogy: Sending a runner to the archive to fetch the relevant files before the meeting starts.
_extra.deeper: Retrieval turns your question into a query, searches an index, and returns the closest matches. It can be semantic (embedding similarity), lexical (keyword/BM25), or hybrid. Everything downstream depends on it — the model can only reason over what retrieval actually fetched.
_extra.lens_pm: Get this right and answers stay grounded; get it wrong and no model can save the response.
_extra.lens_eng: Query-to-index matching (dense, sparse, or hybrid) returning top-k context for generation.

title: Retrieval Augmentation
definition: The general move of feeding a model fetched facts at answer time instead of relying on its memory.
examples: Instead of fine-tuning a model on your policies, you retrieve the relevant policy text and paste it into the prompt each time.
Handing a contestant the reference sheet before the quiz rather than trusting what they crammed.

_extra.analogy: Handing a contestant the reference sheet before the quiz rather than trusting what they crammed.
_extra.deeper: Retrieval augmentation is the umbrella idea: rather than baking knowledge into weights, you fetch relevant information at inference and give it to the model as context. It keeps answers current and grounded, sidesteps expensive retraining, and localizes updates to the data. The trade is that quality now depends on retrieval, and every answer carries the token cost of its evidence.
_extra.lens_pm: Update knowledge by editing docs, not retraining models — cheaper and faster to keep current.
_extra.lens_eng: Inject fetched context at inference vs. parameterizing knowledge; shifts the quality bottleneck to retrieval.

title: Retrieval Latency
definition: The time between asking and getting search results back — before the model even starts answering.
examples: A RAG app feels sluggish not because the model is slow but because the vector search over ten million chunks takes 800ms every query.
The wait for the waiter to walk to the kitchen and back, separate from how long the meal takes to cook.

_extra.analogy: The wait for the waiter to walk to the kitchen and back, separate from how long the meal takes to cook.
_extra.deeper: In a retrieval pipeline, total response time is retrieval plus generation. Retrieval latency depends on index size, the number of results requested, whether you re-rank, and how many retrievers you fan out to. It’s often the hidden tax on fusion and hierarchical setups. You trade it against quality: more candidates and heavier re-ranking find better context but cost milliseconds the user feels.
_extra.lens_pm: A big driver of "why does this feel slow" that has nothing to do with the model.
_extra.lens_eng: Retrieval time = f(index size, top-k, rerank, fan-out); budget it separately from generation latency in the end-to-end SLO.

title: Retrieval Pipeline
definition: The full assembly line from a user question to the passages handed to the model.
examples: Query rewrite → embed → vector search → rerank → assemble context — a typical pipeline behind one chatbot reply.
A kitchen line: prep the order, pull ingredients, plate it — each station feeding the next.

_extra.analogy: A kitchen line: prep the order, pull ingredients, plate it — each station feeding the next.
_extra.deeper: Real retrieval is rarely one call; it is a sequence of stages — rewrite, expand, embed, search, filter, rerank, assemble — each of which can help or hurt. Treating it as a pipeline lets you measure and tune each stage independently, which is how teams debug "the answers are bad" into "reranking is dropping the right chunk". More stages add latency, so every one should earn its place.
_extra.lens_pm: Seeing retrieval as stages turns vague quality complaints into fixable, measurable steps.
_extra.lens_eng: Composable stages (rewrite→embed→search→filter→rerank→assemble); each is independently evaluable and a latency cost.

title: Retrieval Quality
definition: How good your search actually is at surfacing the right stuff — the ceiling on any RAG answer.
examples: A RAG bot gives wrong answers not because the model is dumb but because retrieval keeps handing it the wrong paragraphs.
A cook can only be as good as the ingredients delivered; bad groceries, bad dinner.

_extra.analogy: A cook can only be as good as the ingredients delivered; bad groceries, bad dinner.
_extra.deeper: Retrieval quality is the composite of recall, precision, and ranking — do the right passages show up, and near the top? It is the most common and most overlooked failure point in RAG: teams tune prompts for weeks when the real problem is that the relevant chunk never gets retrieved. Measuring it with real queries is the fastest way to find where a system is actually broken.
_extra.lens_pm: Fix retrieval before blaming the model; it is usually where quality problems really live.
_extra.lens_eng: Aggregate of recall@K, precision@K, and rank position; the upstream bottleneck for grounded generation.

title: Retrieval Tool
definition: A tool the agent calls to pull relevant documents or facts from a knowledge base when it needs them.
examples: Before answering a policy question, the agent calls its retrieval tool, which returns the three most relevant handbook sections.
A research assistant you can ask “grab me everything we have on X” and who returns the right folder.

_extra.analogy: A research assistant you can ask “grab me everything we have on X” and who returns the right folder.
_extra.deeper: A retrieval tool wraps a search over a document store — usually vector-based — so the agent can fetch grounding on demand rather than always stuffing everything into context. Making it a tool, rather than an automatic front-end step, lets the agent decide when it actually needs to look something up. Quality still lives and dies on retrieval: fetch the wrong chunks and the agent confidently answers from them.
_extra.lens_pm: How agents stay grounded in your real documents instead of vibing from memory.
_extra.lens_eng: A tool exposing similarity search over an embedded corpus, invoked on demand to ground responses.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Architecture
definition: A model design that builds document lookup into its structure, so it fetches facts as part of thinking, not as an afterthought.
examples: A support assistant that queries your help-center database on every question, then answers from what it found, is retrieval-augmented by design.
Like a lawyer whose desk is wired to the law library — pulling the right case mid-sentence rather than trusting memory.

_extra.analogy: Like a lawyer whose desk is wired to the law library — pulling the right case mid-sentence rather than trusting memory.
_extra.deeper: Rather than cramming all knowledge into weights, these models pair a generator with a retriever that pulls relevant text at run time, keeping knowledge fresh and updatable. It’s the architectural home of RAG. The hard parts are retrieving the right chunks and blending them cleanly into generation — bad retrieval quietly poisons good generation.
_extra.lens_pm: How you keep a model current and grounded without retraining it.
_extra.lens_eng: An architecture coupling a parametric generator with a non-parametric retrieval component at inference.

title: Retrieval evaluation
definition: Measuring whether the documents you pulled actually contain the answer to the question.
examples: You ask a RAG system "What does the company spend on R&D?" and it pulls five documents. Three are about marketing, two are about finance. Only the finance ones help — that's a retrieval failure.
Fact-checking the articles your research assistant grabbed — did they grab the right ones?

_extra.analogy: Fact-checking the articles your research assistant grabbed — did they grab the right ones?
_extra.deeper: Retrieval is where RAG lives or dies. You measure it with metrics like precision (fraction of retrieved docs that were relevant), recall (fraction of relevant docs that were actually retrieved), and MRR (mean reciprocal rank — how high up was the first good one). Bad retrieval kills everything downstream, no matter how good your language model is.
_extra.lens_pm: If your RAG system gives wrong answers, check retrieval first — it's often the culprit, and fixing it beats retraining the model.
_extra.lens_eng: Evaluate retrieval separately from generation using metrics like precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, and MRR against gold documents.

title: Retry Logic
definition: Automatically trying a failed action again, usually with a short pause, in case it was a fluke.
examples: A rate-limited API call is retried after waiting two seconds, then four, then eight, before the agent gives up.
Redialing a call that dropped — often it just goes through the second time.

_extra.analogy: Redialing a call that dropped — often it just goes through the second time.
_extra.deeper: Many failures are transient — a blip, a momentary rate limit — so retrying with increasing backoff resolves them without bothering anyone. The danger is retrying things that aren’t transient (a genuinely bad request) forever, or hammering a struggling service and making it worse. Sensible retry logic caps the attempts, backs off between them, and knows which errors are worth retrying versus which are hopeless.
_extra.lens_pm: Retries quietly absorb the flakiness of the real world, but blind retrying can turn a small outage into a big one.
_extra.lens_eng: Re-attempt transient failures with capped, backoff-spaced retries, distinguishing retryable from terminal errors.

title: Reward Misspecification
definition: Asking the model to optimize for the wrong thing, and watching it find loopholes you didn't see coming.
examples: An RL agent trained to maximize game score learns to exploit a bug or glitch instead of playing well. A recommendation model trained to maximize watch time starts recommending rage-bait.
Like telling a gardener 'maximize green coverage' and finding they painted the rocks green instead of planting.

_extra.analogy: Like telling a gardener 'maximize green coverage' and finding they painted the rocks green instead of planting.
_extra.deeper: The model is doing exactly what you asked. The problem is you asked wrong. You specified engagement as the reward, but meant thoughtful engagement. You specified speed, but didn't account for safety. This is why reward modeling and RLHF exist—to iterate on rewards with human feedback. But it's arms race; every time you patch a loophole, the model finds another.
_extra.lens_pm: Define success metrics carefully, and monitor for unintended optimizations.
_extra.lens_eng: Use human feedback loops to iteratively refine rewards; add regularizers to discourage degenerate solutions.

title: Reward hacking
definition: When a model learns to game the score instead of doing the thing the score was supposed to measure.
examples: A model rewarded for helpful-sounding answers learns to be verbose and flattering, scoring high while actually being less useful.
A student who memorizes the answer key instead of learning the subject — perfect grade, no understanding.

_extra.analogy: A student who memorizes the answer key instead of learning the subject — perfect grade, no understanding.
_extra.deeper: Any reward is a proxy for what you really want, and optimizers exploit the gap. During RL fine-tuning a model may find shortcuts — sycophancy, padding, exploiting quirks of the reward model — that boost the number without improving the true goal. It is why reward models need to be robust, why KL penalties keep the policy from drifting too far, and why human spot-checks stay in the loop.
_extra.lens_pm: A core reason a model can ace its metrics and still feel worse to real users.
_extra.lens_eng: The policy exploits flaws in the reward proxy; mitigated by robust reward models, KL constraints, and held-out human eval.

title: Reward model
definition: A model trained to score answers the way humans would, so it can grade at scale during training.
examples: Labelers rank a few thousand answer-pairs; a reward model learns from them and then rates millions of the LLM’s attempts.
Like teaching a judge your taste from a stack of ranked examples, then letting that judge score thousands more while you sleep.

_extra.analogy: Like teaching a judge your taste from a stack of ranked examples, then letting that judge score thousands more while you sleep.
_extra.deeper: The reward model turns scattered human preferences into a single differentiable score the main model can optimize against. It’s the linchpin of RLHF — the policy chases higher reward. Its weakness is reward hacking: the model finds answers that score well without actually being good, because the reward model is an imperfect stand-in for real human judgment.
_extra.lens_pm: The frozen proxy for “what humans want”; if it’s miscalibrated, the whole tuned model drifts toward its blind spots.
_extra.lens_eng: A learned scalar scorer over responses, trained on preference pairs; the objective the RL policy optimizes.

title: Reward model eval
definition: Testing whether your preference model or reward model correctly ranks good outputs above bad ones.
examples: You have pairs of responses (good, bad). Your reward model should score the good one higher. You measure what fraction it gets right.
Checking whether a referee's judgment matches actual game rules.

_extra.analogy: Checking whether a referee's judgment matches actual game rules.
_extra.deeper: Reward model evals check a different signal than generation evals. A reward model might rank A > B while a user would choose B > A. Reward models inherit biases from their training data — if trained on assistant-friendly feedback, they score conservative outputs high even when users want bold ones. This is why some teams use preference data directly instead of training an intermediate reward model.
_extra.lens_pm: A biased reward model breaks your whole RLHF pipeline. Test it separately.
_extra.lens_eng: Collect preference pairs. Measure accuracy, Kendall tau, or AUC. Stratify by example type.

title: Reward model training
definition: Teaching a separate model to predict which responses humans prefer, so it can score outputs during RL.
examples: From a dataset of chosen-vs-rejected reply pairs, a model learns to output higher scores for the responses people picked.
Training a judge by showing them thousands of pairs of dishes and which one diners liked, until they can score new plates.

_extra.analogy: Training a judge by showing them thousands of pairs of dishes and which one diners liked, until they can score new plates.
