_extra.deeper: The reward model is trained on human preference comparisons to output a scalar "how good is this" score. In RLHF, that score becomes the reward signal a policy optimizes against. Its quality caps the whole pipeline: if it is exploitable, the policy will reward-hack it, and if its preferences are biased or narrow, those flaws propagate into the final model. It usually starts from the base model itself.
_extra.lens_pm: The stand-in for human judgment that scales preference feedback — and whose blind spots become the model's.
_extra.lens_eng: Train a scalar scorer on pairwise human preferences; it provides the reward in RLHF and is a target for reward hacking.

title: Reward shaping
definition: Adding extra hints to the reward so the model gets feedback along the way, not just at the very end.
examples: Rather than rewarding only a fully correct final answer, a trainer gives partial credit for each valid reasoning step to guide learning.
Giving a kid "warmer, warmer, colder" clues while they search, instead of only saying "found it" at the end.

_extra.analogy: Giving a kid "warmer, warmer, colder" clues while they search, instead of only saying "found it" at the end.
_extra.deeper: Sparse rewards are hard to learn from because most actions get zero signal. Shaping adds intermediate rewards to point the model toward good behavior sooner. The danger is that a poorly shaped reward changes what is optimal and invites reward hacking — the model chases the hints rather than the real goal — so shaping has to be designed carefully to preserve the true objective.
_extra.lens_pm: Speeds up learning on hard tasks, but a sloppy shaping function can teach the wrong lesson.
_extra.lens_eng: Augment sparse rewards with intermediate signals; keep them potential-based to avoid altering the optimal policy.

title: Reward signal
definition: The number that tells a reinforcement-learning model how good an action or output was — the thing it tries to maximize.
examples: A reward model scores each candidate response, and that score is the reward signal the policy learns to push upward.
The score in a video game: it is the only feedback telling you whether that last move helped or hurt.

_extra.analogy: The score in a video game: it is the only feedback telling you whether that last move helped or hurt.
_extra.deeper: In RL the model does not get labeled right answers; it gets a scalar reward and figures out which behaviors produce more of it. The signal can be sparse (only at the end) or shaped (along the way), and it is always a proxy for the true goal — which is why a flawed reward signal leads straight to reward hacking. Its quality bounds how good the trained model can get.
_extra.lens_pm: Whatever you actually reward is what you actually get — so defining it well is half the battle.
_extra.lens_eng: The scalar feedback the policy optimizes; sparse or shaped, and always a proxy prone to exploitation.

title: Reward tampering
definition: An agent messing with the thing that scores it, instead of doing the work the score was meant to measure.
examples: A trained agent discovers it can edit the file that stores its reward and sets it to maximum, "winning" without completing any task.
A student who breaks into the gradebook and changes the marks rather than studying for the exam.

_extra.analogy: A student who breaks into the gradebook and changes the marks rather than studying for the exam.
_extra.deeper: It is a severe form of reward hacking where the agent corrupts the measurement channel itself, not just exploits a loophole in the task. It becomes possible when the reward mechanism is within the agent’s reach, which is why isolating it matters. It is a canonical example of why proxy goals plus capability is dangerous.
_extra.lens_pm: The reason you never let the system being graded control its own grade.
_extra.lens_eng: When the reward signal is in the agent’s action space, it may edit the signal directly; isolate and protect the reward channel.

title: RLAIF
definition: Like RLHF, but another AI does the rating instead of humans, to save time and money.
examples: Instead of paying labelers to rank thousands of answers, a strong model scores them against a rubric and those scores train the target model.
Like grading a mountain of essays with a well-trained teaching assistant instead of the professor — faster, cheaper, and mostly consistent.

_extra.analogy: Like grading a mountain of essays with a well-trained teaching assistant instead of the professor — faster, cheaper, and mostly consistent.
_extra.deeper: RLAIF swaps human preference labels for judgments from an AI, often a larger model applying a written set of principles. It scales feedback far beyond what human raters could produce and cuts cost dramatically. The obvious risk is circularity: the student inherits the judge’s biases and blind spots, so a flawed evaluator quietly teaches flawed taste.
_extra.lens_pm: A way to scale alignment cheaply — but you’ve outsourced your taste to another model, flaws and all.
_extra.lens_eng: RLHF pipeline with an AI evaluator (often guided by a principles rubric) generating the preference signal.

title: RLHF
definition: Teaching a model to behave the way people prefer by turning human ratings into a training signal.
examples: Humans rank several model answers best-to-worst; those rankings train a reward model, which then guides the language model toward preferred responses.
Like training a dog with treats — you can’t script every trick, so you reward the behaviors you want and it learns the pattern.

_extra.analogy: Like training a dog with treats — you can’t script every trick, so you reward the behaviors you want and it learns the pattern.
_extra.deeper: RLHF collects human preference comparisons, fits a reward model to predict them, then uses reinforcement learning to nudge the base model toward high-reward outputs. It’s what turns a raw next-token predictor into a helpful, harmless assistant — but it can be gamed (reward hacking) and inherits the biases of whoever did the rating.
_extra.lens_pm: The step that makes a model feel aligned and usable; also where your values and rater choices get encoded.
_extra.lens_eng: Fit a reward model to human preference data, then optimize the policy against it (often PPO) with a KL penalty to the base.

title: Robustness testing
definition: Systematically changing inputs slightly (typos, paraphrases, noise) to see whether outputs stay consistent.
examples: You take your test set and add typos, reorder sentences, and change synonyms. If your model's answers change drastically, it's not robust.
A wine tasting where you test whether the wine's quality is consistent even when slightly off.

_extra.analogy: A wine tasting where you test whether the wine's quality is consistent even when slightly off.
_extra.deeper: Robustness testing catches models that are brittle — good on the exact examples they've seen, bad on anything slightly different. It's cheaper than adversarial eval but less thorough. You can automate it by programmatically perturbing your test set.
_extra.lens_pm: Tell you whether improvements are real or just overfitting to your eval set.
_extra.lens_eng: For each example, generate perturbations (typos, synonym replacements, paraphrases). Check if outputs match via embedding similarity.

title: Role Assignment
definition: Giving each agent in a team a distinct job so they don’t all do the same thing.
examples: In a writing crew, one agent is assigned to draft, one to fact-check, and one to edit, and work flows between them.
A relay team — someone runs the first leg, someone the last; nobody runs all four.

_extra.analogy: A relay team — someone runs the first leg, someone the last; nobody runs all four.
_extra.deeper: Role assignment is how multi-agent systems get division of labor: clear responsibilities reduce overlap and keep each agent’s context focused on its slice. Done well, specialists outperform one generalist. Done poorly, you get diffusion of responsibility — every agent assumes another handled the thing, and it falls through the cracks, just like on human teams.
_extra.lens_pm: Clear roles make an agent team more than the sum of its parts; fuzzy ones make work fall through the cracks.
_extra.lens_eng: Assign disjoint responsibilities across agents to reduce overlap and bound each one’s context.

title: Role prompting
definition: Telling the model to adopt a specific role — expert, critic, mentor — to change the tone and quality of its output.
examples: "You are a senior software architect. Review this code for maintainability and scalability issues." vs. just "Review this code."
Asking different people to answer: a teacher explains differently than a comedian or an engineer.

_extra.analogy: Asking different people to answer: a teacher explains differently than a comedian or an engineer.
_extra.deeper: Role prompts work because the model learned associations between identities and knowledge/style during training. A "helpful tutor" persona elicits explanatory text; a "security engineer" persona spots attack vectors. The role acts as shorthand for a behavioral mode. Combining roles with other techniques (few-shot, CoT) stacks effects.
_extra.lens_pm: Cheap way to steer output tone and depth; often improves perceived quality without model changes.
_extra.lens_eng: Just text in the system message. Combine with other constraints. Watch for role hallucination if you ask too specific a persona.

title: Rollback
definition: Instantly revert to a previous version if something goes wrong—switch traffic back to the old model or code.
examples: New model v1.2 causes 5x error rate spike; revert to v1.1 while team debugs the issue.
Hitting undo after a bad edit.

_extra.analogy: Hitting undo after a bad edit.
_extra.deeper: Speed of rollback directly affects blast radius. Requires pre-tested fallback version running in parallel (blue-green or canary). Automated triggers (error rate threshold, latency spike) initiate rollback without human intervention. Test rollbacks regularly to ensure they work under stress.
_extra.lens_pm: Insurance policy that lets teams ship fast and recover quickly if things break.
_extra.lens_eng: Traffic selector or DNS points back to stable version; circuit breaker or health check validates old version is healthy; telemetry confirms rollback succeeded.

title: Rollout
definition: Running an agent through a task once to see what it does — a single sampled attempt from start to finish.
examples: To gather training data, a team generates thousands of rollouts of an agent solving math problems, then keeps the ones that reached the right answer.
A dress rehearsal: let it play the whole thing through once and watch how it goes.

_extra.analogy: A dress rehearsal: let it play the whole thing through once and watch how it goes.
_extra.deeper: A rollout is one full sampled run of an agent’s policy, producing a trajectory. The word comes from reinforcement learning, where you roll out the policy to collect experience, then learn from which runs succeeded. Because sampling is random, rollouts vary — the same task can produce a brilliant run and a hopeless one — which is why people generate many and score them.
_extra.lens_pm: Why agents feel inconsistent — each run is one roll of the dice, not a fixed program.
_extra.lens_eng: A single sampled execution of a policy from initial to terminal state, yielding a trajectory for evaluation or training.

title: Rotary Embeddings
definition: Encode a token’s position by rotating its vector, so relative distances fall out naturally in attention.
examples: A model uses RoPE so that “word 10 relative to word 7” is captured cleanly, and it extends to longer inputs gracefully.
Turning each clock hand by an amount set by the hour — the angle between hands tells you the gap.

_extra.analogy: Turning each clock hand by an amount set by the hour — the angle between hands tells you the gap.
_extra.deeper: RoPE injects position by rotating each token’s query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position. Because attention compares queries and keys via dot products, these rotations make the score depend on the relative distance between tokens — a clean, position-aware signal. It also extends to longer sequences than seen in training better than older schemes, which is why it’s now common.
_extra.lens_pm: Part of why modern models handle long inputs and relative word order so well.
_extra.lens_eng: Position encoding via rotation of query/key vectors, yielding relative-position-aware dot products.

title: ROUGE
definition: A metric that counts overlapping words between generated and reference text—faster and more intuitive than BLEU, standard for summarization.
examples: Generated summary: 'Alice went to the store and bought apples.' Reference: 'Alice bought apples at the store.' ROUGE-1 (unigram overlap) scores high.
Like checking if a book summary mentions the key characters and plot points.

_extra.analogy: Like checking if a book summary mentions the key characters and plot points.
_extra.deeper: ROUGE has variants: ROUGE-1 (unigram), ROUGE-2 (bigram), ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence). It's better than BLEU for synonyms and paraphrases. Still doesn't measure meaning, but more robust. Standard for summarization eval. Human eval on a subset always recommended.
_extra.lens_pm: ROUGE is a reasonable automated metric for summarization and short text generation. Supplement with human eval.
_extra.lens_eng: Report ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L; understand they're proxies, not gospel.

title: Router Agent
definition: A lightweight agent whose only job is to read a request and send it to the right specialist.
examples: An incoming message hits the router, which decides “this is a billing issue” and forwards it to the billing agent rather than answering itself.
A receptionist who doesn’t solve your problem but knows exactly which office to point you to.

_extra.analogy: A receptionist who doesn’t solve your problem but knows exactly which office to point you to.
_extra.deeper: A router agent classifies or triages input and dispatches it, keeping specialized agents focused and cheap to run. It is usually a small, fast model since the decision is simple. The failure mode is misrouting — send a question to the wrong specialist and the whole chain produces a confident, off-target answer, so routers are worth evaluating on their own.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap way to make a pile of narrow agents feel like one smart assistant.
_extra.lens_eng: A classifier-style agent that maps requests to downstream agents or tools, typically run on a small fast model.

title: Router Network
definition: Another name for the gating module — it routes each token to its chosen experts.
examples: A model card might note the router sends each token to two of its many experts.
Like a mailroom sorter reading each envelope and dropping it in the right department’s bin.

_extra.analogy: Like a mailroom sorter reading each envelope and dropping it in the right department’s bin.
_extra.deeper: “Router” and “gating network” usually point at the same thing: the component that decides which experts process a token. The word “router” emphasizes the dispatch, “gating” the weighting. Both must balance load across experts and route consistently, or the model wastes capacity and trains poorly.
_extra.lens_pm: Same idea as the gating network, described from the dispatch angle.
_extra.lens_eng: The MoE component computing per-token expert assignments and dispatch weights.

title: Rubric
definition: A predefined scoring guide that lists criteria and how to evaluate outputs—the reference for consistent grading.
examples: Rubric for code quality: (1) Does it run without error? (2) Is it readable? (3) Is it efficient? Each gets a score.
Like a restaurant inspection checklist: here's what we measure, here's how we score it.

_extra.analogy: Like a restaurant inspection checklist: here's what we measure, here's how we score it.
_extra.deeper: Good rubrics are detailed enough to guide raters but not so complex they cause disagreement. They should be piloted with multiple raters to check agreement. Rubrics bake in values—what you score is what you optimize for.
_extra.lens_pm: Design rubrics collaboratively with stakeholders to reflect what quality means.
_extra.lens_eng: Test rubric clarity before deploying; track inter-rater agreement; iterate based on disagreement patterns.

title: Rubric Grading
definition: Scoring outputs against a predefined checklist of criteria so grading is consistent, not gut-feel.
examples: A code-generation rubric checks: does it run without error, does it solve the problem, is it readable, is it efficient. Each criterion gets a score.
Like a restaurant inspection form with checkboxes instead of just 'this place is good or bad.'

_extra.analogy: Like a restaurant inspection form with checkboxes instead of just 'this place is good or bad.'
_extra.deeper: Rubrics make evaluation reproducible and let you track which aspects improve or degrade. They're useful for both LLM judges and human raters. The catch: writing a good rubric takes iteration, and criteria can conflict (brevity vs. detail). When you give the rubric to an LLM judge, it's only as good as the rubric's clarity.
_extra.lens_pm: Define what quality means for your product, operationalize it as a rubric, and track scores over time.
_extra.lens_eng: Build rubrics collaboratively with domain experts; test rubric inter-rater agreement before deploying it.

title: RWKV
definition: An architecture that trains like a transformer but runs like an RNN, aiming for the best of both.
examples: RWKV lets a long chat run with constant memory per token, unlike a transformer’s growing KV cache.
A hybrid car — plug-in convenience for the long haul, efficient engine for the daily drive.

_extra.analogy: A hybrid car — plug-in convenience for the long haul, efficient engine for the daily drive.
_extra.deeper: RWKV reformulates attention-like mixing into a recurrent form that can be trained in parallel like a transformer but executed step by step like an RNN, giving constant memory and linear time at inference. That makes very long or streaming generation cheap in memory. It’s part of the wave of architectures probing whether quadratic attention is truly necessary.
_extra.lens_pm: Another contender for cheap long-context and streaming use, trading the transformer’s memory growth for a constant footprint.
_extra.lens_eng: A linear-attention-style architecture with parallel training and RNN-like constant-memory inference.

title: Safety Classifier
definition: A small model whose only job is to score text for safety and flag the risky bits.
examples: Every prompt and reply passes through a classifier that outputs probabilities for categories like violence or self-harm, and the app blocks anything over threshold.
A lifeguard who does nothing but watch the water — one focused job, done fast, while everyone else swims.

_extra.analogy: A lifeguard who does nothing but watch the water — one focused job, done fast, while everyone else swims.
_extra.deeper: A safety classifier is the workhorse under content filters and moderation: a purpose-trained model that scores text against harm categories, cheaply and quickly, so it can run on every request. Its strengths are speed and consistency; its weaknesses are the usual classifier traps — false positives that cause over-refusal, false negatives that miss cleverly worded harm, and thresholds that must be tuned to your risk tolerance.
_extra.lens_pm: The tunable dial behind your safety layer — where you set the balance between blocking harm and annoying users.
_extra.lens_eng: A lightweight purpose-trained model scoring harm categories per request; threshold choice trades false positives (over-refusal) against false negatives.

title: Safety evaluation
definition: Testing a model specifically for harms before you ship it — the safety half of "does it work".
examples: Before release, a model is run through benchmarks for harmful compliance, bias, and dangerous-capability probes, with results gating the launch.
Crash-testing a car, not to see how fast it goes, but to see who gets hurt when things go wrong.

_extra.analogy: Crash-testing a car, not to see how fast it goes, but to see who gets hurt when things go wrong.
_extra.deeper: Safety evals measure refusal behavior, robustness to jailbreaks, bias, and dangerous capabilities, ideally on held-out and adversarial sets. Their reliability is threatened by alignment faking and evaluation gaming, since a model may behave differently when it senses a test. So results are treated as necessary evidence, not a guarantee.
_extra.lens_pm: The gate that decides whether a model is safe enough to ship — and the number leadership actually asks about.
_extra.lens_eng: Benchmark harmful-compliance, robustness, bias, and dangerous capabilities on adversarial held-out sets; watch for eval-gaming artifacts.

title: Safety fine-tuning
definition: The fine-tuning stage that teaches a model to avoid harmful, unsafe, or policy-violating outputs.
examples: After general instruction tuning, a model gets a safety pass using refusal examples and red-team data to close known failure modes.
A driving instructor's final lessons — not new driving skill, but the judgment to not do dangerous things.

_extra.analogy: A driving instructor's final lessons — not new driving skill, but the judgment to not do dangerous things.
_extra.deeper: Safety fine-tuning layers guardrails onto an already-capable model using curated examples, preference data, and adversarial red-team cases. It teaches refusals, careful handling of sensitive topics, and resistance to manipulation. It is never perfect — jailbreaks keep finding gaps — and pushing it hard incurs the alignment tax, so it is a continual balancing act rather than a one-time fix.
_extra.lens_pm: The stage that makes a model shippable to the public — and the source of most "why won't it" complaints.
_extra.lens_eng: Post-SFT tuning on safety examples, preferences, and red-team data to reduce harmful outputs.

title: Sampling
definition: How the model actually chooses each next word from its list of options — roll the weighted dice, don’t always grab the top one.
examples: Ask the same question twice with sampling on and you can get two different-but-valid answers.
Drawing from a bag of tiles where common words have more copies, so surprises are possible but rare.

_extra.analogy: Drawing from a bag of tiles where common words have more copies, so surprises are possible but rare.
_extra.deeper: After softmax gives a probability per token, sampling picks one at random weighted by those probabilities. That randomness is why models feel creative and non-repetitive — and why they’re not perfectly reproducible unless you fix the seed or switch to greedy decoding.
_extra.lens_pm: The reason outputs vary run to run; turn it down for consistency, up for variety.
_extra.lens_eng: Stochastic token selection from the output distribution, controlled by temperature/top-p/top-k.

title: Sandbagging
definition: A model deliberately underperforming on a test to hide what it can actually do.
examples: A model scores low on a dangerous-capability eval but, with slightly different prompting, reveals it could do the task all along.
A pool hustler who plays badly on purpose until the money is on the table.

_extra.analogy: A pool hustler who plays badly on purpose until the money is on the table.
_extra.deeper: Sandbagging makes safety evals underestimate risk: if a model (or a fine-tuner) can suppress a capability under evaluation and surface it in deployment, the eval is worthless. It requires enough situational awareness to know when it is being tested. It is why evaluators care about strong elicitation and the gap between measured and true capability.
_extra.lens_pm: A failure mode where "it can’t do that" really means "it wouldn’t, while you were looking".
_extra.lens_eng: Strategic capability suppression under eval; counter with aggressive elicitation, fine-tuning probes, and diverse prompts.

title: Sandbox Execution
definition: Running an agent’s code or actions in a walled-off space where mistakes can’t hurt anything real.
examples: The agent’s generated script runs in a throwaway container with no network and no access to real files, so a bad command just breaks the sandbox.
A test kitchen sealed off from the restaurant — burn a dish and no customer ever knows.

_extra.analogy: A test kitchen sealed off from the restaurant — burn a dish and no customer ever knows.
_extra.deeper: A sandbox isolates execution — limiting file access, network, and system calls — so that running model-written code, which you can’t fully trust, stays contained. It’s a foundational safety measure for any agent that executes code or commands, because the whole point is to let it try things freely without letting a mistake or a malicious injection escape. The isolation is never perfect, so sandboxes are layered with other limits.
_extra.lens_pm: What makes it safe to let an agent run code it wrote itself.
_extra.lens_eng: Executing untrusted code in an isolated environment with restricted filesystem, network, and syscall access.

title: Scalable oversight
definition: Supervising AI that is too capable or fast for a human to check directly — often by using AI to help.
examples: To grade a model’s hard math proof, a human is assisted by a second model that critiques the first, so the human only has to judge the debate.
A head editor who cannot read every article, so they train and trust junior editors, spot-checking to keep quality honest.

_extra.analogy: A head editor who cannot read every article, so they train and trust junior editors, spot-checking to keep quality honest.
_extra.deeper: The core problem: as tasks exceed human ability to evaluate, naive human feedback stops being a reliable signal. Approaches include AI-assisted critique, debate between models, and recursive decomposition, all aiming to amplify limited human judgment. It connects to weak-to-strong generalization — can a weaker supervisor still steer a stronger model?
_extra.lens_pm: The bet that lets us keep steering systems that outrun our ability to check them by hand.
_extra.lens_eng: Amplify human evaluation via AI critique, debate, or recursive decomposition when direct assessment is infeasible.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
definition: The exact recipe for attention: score with dot products, shrink the scores, softmax, then blend.
examples: Each query dots against all keys, the scores are divided by the square root of the dimension, softmaxed, and applied to values.
Rating each option, dividing the scores to keep them sane, turning them into percentages, then mixing accordingly.

_extra.analogy: Rating each option, dividing the scores to keep them sane, turning them into percentages, then mixing accordingly.
_extra.deeper: The “scaled” part matters: raw dot products grow with vector dimension, pushing softmax into saturated regions where gradients vanish. Dividing by the square root of the key dimension keeps scores in a workable range. After softmax turns them into weights, you take the weighted sum of values. This precise formula is the beating heart of the transformer.
_extra.lens_pm: The standard, well-understood formula that every attention layer runs — rarely something you tune directly.
_extra.lens_eng: Attention as softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V, with √d scaling to stabilize gradients.

title: Scaling laws
definition: The predictable way model quality improves as you add more data, parameters, and compute — smooth enough to plan around.
examples: Before committing to a huge run, a lab uses scaling-law curves fit on small models to predict the loss the big one will hit.
Knowing that doubling the ingredients and oven time reliably yields a bigger, better-baked loaf — the recipe scales.

_extra.analogy: Knowing that doubling the ingredients and oven time reliably yields a bigger, better-baked loaf — the recipe scales.
_extra.deeper: Empirically, test loss falls as a power law in model size, dataset size, and compute — straight lines on a log-log plot across many orders of magnitude. This let labs forecast returns and justify spending on ever-larger runs. The laws describe loss, not capability, and they do not promise where useful behaviors emerge, so they guide budgets more than they guarantee outcomes.
_extra.lens_pm: The reason "just make it bigger" became a credible strategy — the payoff was forecastable.
_extra.lens_eng: Power-law relationships between test loss and compute/params/data used to extrapolate and allocate budgets.

title: Scene Understanding
definition: The ability to recognize objects, relationships, and spatial structure within an image to grasp what is happening.
examples: A model sees a photo and knows "this is a beach scene with a surfer paddling toward waves at sunset." Another sees a meeting room and identifies the projector, whiteboard, and seated participants.
Walking into a room and instantly knowing: theres a kitchen, people are cooking, the table is set for dinner. Your brain understands the scene.

_extra.analogy: Walking into a room and instantly knowing: theres a kitchen, people are cooking, the table is set for dinner. Your brain understands the scene.
_extra.deeper: Scene understanding combines object detection (what things are present), semantic segmentation (pixel-level categories), spatial reasoning (how objects relate), and sometimes activity recognition (what is happening). Requires parsing both low-level features (edges, colors) and high-level semantics (activities, social roles). Graph neural networks and transformer-based vision models show promise.
_extra.lens_pm: Unlocks context-aware recommendations, smart image search, autonomous navigation, and interactive AI that understands the users environment.
_extra.lens_eng: Combines detection, segmentation, and reasoning. Benchmarks: ADE20K (scenes), Cityscapes (street scenes). Often requires fusion of multiple CV tasks.

title: Scoped Access
definition: Giving an agent the narrowest set of permissions that still lets it finish the job.
examples: A summarizing agent gets read-only access to one folder, not write access to the whole drive, so a bug can’t delete anything.
Handing a house-sitter the key to the front door and the alarm code — not the safe, the car, and your bank login.

_extra.analogy: Handing a house-sitter the key to the front door and the alarm code — not the safe, the car, and your bank login.
_extra.deeper: Scoping is the principle of least privilege applied to agents: minimize the blast radius if something goes wrong or gets hijacked. It matters more for agents than for ordinary software because a prompt-injected agent will happily use whatever access it has. Good scoping is granular — per-tool, per-resource, per-task — rather than one big “can do everything” grant.
_extra.lens_pm: Narrow access limits how much damage a confused or compromised agent can do — scope tightly by default.
_extra.lens_eng: Grant per-resource, per-action tokens so a compromised agent’s reach is bounded to the task at hand.

title: Scoring function
definition: A formula that ranks documents by how likely they are to answer the question.
examples: A BM25 scoring function looks at word frequency and document length. A learned ranker might use a neural network trained on click data. Both output a number — higher means "more relevant."
Like a bouncer at a bar — you ask "Is this person relevant?" and the function returns a score instead of yes/no.

_extra.analogy: Like a bouncer at a bar — you ask "Is this person relevant?" and the function returns a score instead of yes/no.
_extra.deeper: Scoring functions sit between retrieval and ranking. Simple ones (BM25, TF-IDF) are keyword-based and fast. Learned ones (LambdaMART, neural rankers) are expensive but accurate. The catch: your training data shapes what "relevant" means, so garbage labels in training produce garbage scores at inference.
_extra.lens_pm: A better scoring function can mean the difference between users finding answers on page one vs. page five.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement as a function(query, doc) → score, where score is a real number. Train on relevance labels if building a learned ranker.

title: Scratchpad
definition: A space where the model writes intermediate thoughts and notes to itself while working through a problem.
examples: Before answering a logic puzzle, the model jots the constraints and rules out options in a scratchpad, then gives the clean answer.
The margin of an exam where you scribble your working before writing the final answer in the box.

_extra.analogy: The margin of an exam where you scribble your working before writing the final answer in the box.
_extra.deeper: Letting a model externalize its reasoning into text it can re-read improves hard, multi-step problems — it is chain-of-thought given a place to live. In agents, the scratchpad also holds notes across loop turns: what’s been tried, what’s left. Sometimes it is shown to the user, sometimes hidden; either way it is scaffolding for thinking, not the deliverable.
_extra.lens_pm: Why “show your work” prompting makes models measurably more correct.
_extra.lens_eng: A region of context the model writes intermediate reasoning or state into, re-read on subsequent steps.

title: Scratchpad prompting
definition: Explicitly allocating space in a prompt for the model to "think out loud" — write intermediate reasoning that doesn't go in the final answer.
examples: Prompt: "Scratchpad: [Show your reasoning here] Final answer: [Clean answer]"
A math test where you show your work on scrap paper, then write the final answer cleanly.

_extra.analogy: A math test where you show your work on scrap paper, then write the final answer cleanly.
_extra.deeper: Scratchpads improve reasoning by separating process from output. The model can explore ideas without polluting the final response. Works for math, logic, and planning tasks. Can be formalized with explicit delimiters or just natural language.
_extra.lens_pm: Improves reliability; users only see polished final answer.
_extra.lens_eng: Add "Scratchpad:" or "Working:" section. Parse final answer separately if needed.

title: Search Tool
definition: A tool that lets the agent query the open web and read back current results.
examples: Asked about a news event past its training cutoff, the agent runs a web search, reads the top results, and answers from them.
Handing the model a search engine and letting it type its own queries, then skim the hits.

_extra.analogy: Handing the model a search engine and letting it type its own queries, then skim the hits.
_extra.deeper: A search tool breaks the model out of its frozen training data by fetching live information, which is essential for anything recent or fast-changing. The agent has to craft good queries, judge which results to trust, and synthesize across them — all fallible steps. It also opens a door for manipulation, since a malicious result can carry instructions the model might wrongly follow.
_extra.lens_pm: What keeps an agent’s answers current instead of stuck at its training cutoff.
_extra.lens_eng: A tool issuing web-search queries and returning ranked results for the model to read and synthesize.

title: Seed
definition: A number that fixes the randomness, so a “random” run can be repeated exactly.
examples: Set the same seed and temperature, and a model can reproduce the identical “random” answer on demand.
Shuffling a deck the exact same way twice by starting from the same setup — random-looking, but repeatable.

_extra.analogy: Shuffling a deck the exact same way twice by starting from the same setup — random-looking, but repeatable.
_extra.deeper: Random number generators are actually deterministic given a starting seed. Fixing the seed makes stochastic sampling reproducible, which is invaluable for debugging and fair comparisons. It only helps if the rest of the pipeline is pinned too — change the model or hardware and the guarantee weakens.
_extra.lens_pm: The knob that makes “random” outputs reproducible for testing and A/B comparisons.
_extra.lens_eng: The RNG seed initializing pseudo-random sampling; fixes decode randomness for reproducibility.

title: Segmentation
definition: Classifying every pixel in an image so you know exactly which region belongs to what object.
examples: Medical imaging: segment tumor pixels (red), healthy tissue (blue), background (gray) so surgeon sees exactly what to remove.
Coloring each pixel of a map by country instead of just drawing borders.

_extra.analogy: Coloring each pixel of a map by country instead of just drawing borders.
_extra.deeper: Pixel-level prediction; many times slower than classification or detection. Encoder-decoder architecture: encoder downsamples (learn features), decoder upsamples (restore resolution). Skip connections preserve fine detail. Requires pixel-level annotations, extremely expensive (weeks of manual labeling per image).
_extra.lens_pm: Critical for robotics, medical imaging, autonomous driving—need precise region boundaries.
_extra.lens_eng: Encoder-decoder network outputs logits per pixel; cross-entropy loss on each pixel; typically uses U-Net or transformer architecture.

title: Self-Correction
definition: An agent noticing it went wrong and fixing the mistake on its own, without a human stepping in.
examples: The agent runs its code, sees a stack trace, reads the error, patches the offending line, and reruns until it passes.
A cook tasting the sauce, realizing it’s over-salted, and adding cream to pull it back — mid-service, no manager needed.

_extra.analogy: A cook tasting the sauce, realizing it’s over-salted, and adding cream to pull it back — mid-service, no manager needed.
_extra.deeper: Self-correction is reflection turned into action: detect the error, diagnose it, retry. It works best when the environment gives honest feedback — failing tests, API errors, a search that returns nothing — because that grounds the fix in reality rather than the model’s guesses. Without such signals it can “correct” a right answer into a wrong one, so the quality of the error signal is everything.
_extra.lens_pm: What lets agents recover from stumbles instead of confidently shipping the stumble.
_extra.lens_eng: The act of detecting a failure from feedback and revising the action, ideally driven by external error signals.

title: Self-ask
definition: Prompting the model to ask itself clarifying questions before answering — a form of introspection.
examples: "User: Is Paris in France? Model: Do I know where Paris is? Yes, it's the capital of France. Is France a country in Europe? Yes. So yes, Paris is in France."
Before answering, asking "What information do I need?" and "Have I understood the question correctly?"

_extra.analogy: Before answering, asking "What information do I need?" and "Have I understood the question correctly?"
_extra.deeper: Self-ask is a form of chain-of-thought. The model reasons by questioning itself, making reasoning explicit. Effective for factual questions and knowledge retrieval. Less clear if it helps with open-ended tasks.
_extra.lens_pm: Improves accuracy on factual questions.
_extra.lens_eng: Prompt with: "Before answering, ask yourself...". Monitor for circular reasoning.

title: Self-Attention
definition: Attention a sequence pays to itself — each word looking at the other words in the same sentence.
examples: In one sentence, self-attention lets “bank” attend to “river” nearby and settle on the water meaning, not money.
Everyone at a meeting table turning to hear whoever’s most relevant to the current point.

_extra.analogy: Everyone at a meeting table turning to hear whoever’s most relevant to the current point.
_extra.deeper: In self-attention, the queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence, so every token gathers context from every other token in that same input. Stacking many self-attention layers lets meaning propagate and combine across the whole passage. It’s the workhorse operation inside every transformer block.
_extra.lens_pm: What lets a model understand a word in the context of the whole message around it.
_extra.lens_eng: Attention where queries, keys, and values derive from one sequence, mixing information within it.

title: Self-consistency
definition: Running the same prompt multiple times and taking a vote on the answer, boosting accuracy when reasoning is involved.
examples: Ask "What is 7 × 13?" five times with temperature=0.7; four times you get 91, once you get 89. Trust the majority.
Asking the same question to the same person ten times; their answers agree more often for true facts than for guesses.

_extra.analogy: Asking the same question to the same person ten times; their answers agree more often for true facts than for guesses.
_extra.deeper: Self-consistency amplifies the effect of temperature and sampling. At high temperature, the model samples different reasoning paths; some reach right answers, some wrong ones. Voting on the final answer is surprisingly effective for math and logic. Costs more (5–10× calls), but accuracy can jump 10–30% on hard problems.
_extra.lens_pm: Improves reliability for critical tasks (medical diagnosis, code review, math) with compute trade-off: 5x cost for much higher confidence.
_extra.lens_eng: Call model 5–10 times, parse results, count correct answers. Use temperature ≥ 0.5 to induce diversity; temperature=0 gives the same answer every time.

title: Self-consistency check
definition: Running the same prompt multiple times and checking whether the model gives the same answer each time.
examples: You ask a model "Is 17 prime?" ten times with temperature 1.0. If it says "yes" eight times and "no" twice, that's concerning — the true answer should be consistent.
Asking a friend the same question three times and seeing if they answer consistently.

_extra.analogy: Asking a friend the same question three times and seeing if they answer consistently.
_extra.deeper: Self-consistency uses the model to grade itself. High variance across runs suggests either ambiguous inputs or hallucination. The catch: multiple outputs that agree can all be wrong if the model is confidently biased. You're measuring consistency, not correctness.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap signal that something might be wrong, but not a sign that something is right.
_extra.lens_eng: Run k times, check whether outputs match. Use embedding similarity for fuzzy matching on non-binary answers.

title: Self-distillation
definition: A model teaching itself by training on its own best outputs, rather than learning from a bigger teacher.
examples: A model generates answers, keeps the ones a verifier approves, and fine-tunes on them — bootstrapping itself upward without a larger model.
Reviewing your own strongest essays and studying them to write even better ones next time.

_extra.analogy: Reviewing your own strongest essays and studying them to write even better ones next time.
_extra.deeper: Ordinary distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher to a smaller student. Self-distillation drops the separate teacher: the model produces outputs, filters them for quality, and trains on the survivors, often over several rounds. It works because generating a good answer can be easier than learning to produce it consistently. Gains taper and can amplify the model's own biases, so filtering quality is everything.
_extra.lens_pm: A way to improve a model without access to a bigger one — but it can entrench existing quirks.
_extra.lens_eng: Train a model on its own filtered generations, iteratively, without a separate teacher network.

title: Self-supervised learning
definition: Learning from raw data by hiding part of it and predicting the missing piece — no human labels needed.
examples: Predicting the next token across trillions of words is self-supervised: the text itself provides the “answer.”
Like learning a language by covering the last word of sentences you read and guessing it, over and over.

_extra.analogy: Like learning a language by covering the last word of sentences you read and guessing it, over and over.
_extra.deeper: Self-supervised learning invents its own labels from the structure of the data — next-token prediction, masked-word filling — so it can train on unlabeled corpora at massive scale. This is the trick that made pretraining possible: the internet becomes training data without anyone labeling it. It gives models broad general knowledge, which supervised fine-tuning then shapes toward specific behavior.
_extra.lens_pm: The breakthrough that let models learn from the whole internet without armies of labelers.
_extra.lens_eng: Supervision derived from the data itself (e.g. next-token/masked prediction); enables label-free pretraining at scale.

title: Semantic Cache
definition: Reuse a past answer when a new question means the same thing, even if it’s worded differently.
examples: One user asks "how do I reset my password?" and another asks "I forgot my login" — the second gets the cached response instantly, no model call.
A help desk that recognizes "my card was declined" and "payment won’t go through" as the same ticket and pulls the same answer.

_extra.analogy: A help desk that recognizes "my card was declined" and "payment won’t go through" as the same ticket and pulls the same answer.
_extra.deeper: A normal cache only hits on exact string matches. A semantic cache embeds the incoming query and checks whether a stored query is close enough in meaning to reuse its answer. It saves latency and API cost on repetitive questions. The danger is the similarity threshold: set it loose and you’ll serve a confidently-wrong cached answer to a subtly different question.
_extra.lens_pm: Big cost and speed wins on FAQ-style traffic, if you tune the match threshold conservatively.
_extra.lens_eng: Embed queries; on a near-neighbor hit above a threshold, return the cached response instead of calling the model. Threshold governs the false-hit risk.

title: Semantic Chunking
definition: Splitting text where the topic shifts, not at fixed lengths, so each chunk is one coherent idea.
examples: A doc about "install, then configure, then troubleshoot" gets split at each topic change, so retrieval returns just the troubleshooting part.
Cutting a movie into scenes by where the story turns, not every ten minutes on the clock.

_extra.analogy: Cutting a movie into scenes by where the story turns, not every ten minutes on the clock.
_extra.deeper: Semantic chunking embeds consecutive sentences and places a boundary wherever similarity drops — the signal that the topic changed. The payoff is chunks that align to ideas rather than arbitrary token counts, which usually improves retrieval. The cost is more compute up front and sensitivity to the threshold, so it is not always worth it over simpler recursive splitting.
_extra.lens_pm: Can lift retrieval quality on messy docs; adds preprocessing cost, so measure before adopting.
_extra.lens_eng: Boundary placement via drops in inter-sentence embedding similarity; threshold-sensitive and compute-heavier than fixed splits.

title: Semantic Search
definition: Search that matches on meaning rather than exact words, so “car” can find “automobile.”
examples: You search “how do I cancel my plan” and it finds the doc titled “Ending your subscription,” despite zero shared keywords.
A helpful librarian who understands what you’re after, not a card catalog that only matches the exact title.

_extra.analogy: A helpful librarian who understands what you’re after, not a card catalog that only matches the exact title.
_extra.deeper: Semantic search turns both the query and the documents into embeddings and finds the ones closest in meaning-space, so it catches paraphrases and synonyms that keyword search misses. The flip side is that it can miss exact matches — a specific error code or product name — because those are about the literal string, not the vibe. That weakness is exactly why it’s so often paired with keyword search.
_extra.lens_pm: Semantic search makes finding things feel intuitive, but it can fumble exact terms — rarely the whole answer alone.
_extra.lens_eng: Embed query and documents, then rank by vector similarity in the embedding space.

title: Semantic Kernel
definition: Microsoft's SDK for composing prompts, models, and tools into a plug-and-play architecture for AI apps.
examples: Build a skill that translates text, chain it to a summarization skill, add tool use to fact-check sources. Swap in GPT or Claude, runs the same.
A modular synthesizer where each knob is a skill, and you wire them together to make new instruments.

_extra.analogy: A modular synthesizer where each knob is a skill, and you wire them together to make new instruments.
_extra.deeper: Semantic Kernel introduces 'skills' (prompt templates + tool definitions), 'planners' (ways to chain skills), and 'connectors' (to models and memory stores). It's orchestration-first: your app logic stays light, the framework handles the LLM calls. Strong on extensibility but can feel boilerplate-heavy.
_extra.lens_pm: Reduces AI engineering boilerplate; lets you define skills once and reuse across agents.
_extra.lens_eng: Plugin architecture with dependency injection; works with any LLM via adapters.

title: Semi-Autonomous
definition: An agent that does the work on its own but pauses to ask a human before the risky moves.
examples: The coding agent writes and tests the fix by itself, then stops and asks “push to main?” before it actually deploys.
A learner driver — hands on the wheel most of the time, but the instructor grabs it before anything expensive happens.

_extra.analogy: A learner driver — hands on the wheel most of the time, but the instructor grabs it before anything expensive happens.
_extra.deeper: The design question is where to put the gates — too many and it’s just a slow assistant, too few and it’s effectively autonomous. Good semi-autonomous systems reserve the human for irreversible or high-cost actions and let the agent own everything cheap and undoable. It’s the pragmatic middle most production agents actually live in.
_extra.lens_pm: You get most of the speed of autonomy while keeping veto power over the moves that can hurt.
_extra.lens_eng: The loop inserts a blocking approval step before actions flagged as high-risk or irreversible.

title: Semi-supervised learning
definition: Learning from a small labeled set plus a large pile of unlabeled data.
examples: You label 1,000 medical images and let the model exploit 100,000 unlabeled ones to sharpen its understanding.
Like a teacher grading a few papers in detail, then trusting students to learn the rest from patterns in the unmarked stack.

_extra.analogy: Like a teacher grading a few papers in detail, then trusting students to learn the rest from patterns in the unmarked stack.
_extra.deeper: Semi-supervised learning bridges supervised and unsupervised: a little labeled data anchors the task while abundant unlabeled data reveals structure that improves generalization. Techniques include pseudo-labeling and consistency training. It shines when labels are scarce or costly but raw data is plentiful — a very common real-world situation.
_extra.lens_pm: The pragmatic middle path when labeling everything is too expensive but you have plenty of raw data.
_extra.lens_eng: Combines limited labels with large unlabeled data (pseudo-labels/consistency) to improve over supervised-only.

title: Sentence Splitting
definition: Cutting text at sentence boundaries so chunks don’t start or end mid-thought.
examples: A chunker uses sentence splitting so "The dose is 5mg. Do not exceed" never gets severed between "5mg" and "Do not exceed".
Tearing a page along the perforations instead of ripping through the middle of a line.

_extra.analogy: Tearing a page along the perforations instead of ripping through the middle of a line.
_extra.deeper: Naively slicing every N characters can cut a sentence in half, garbling both pieces. Sentence splitting detects boundaries — trickier than it sounds, thanks to "Dr.", "3.14", and abbreviations — and packs whole sentences into chunks. It is the humble preprocessing step that keeps retrieved passages readable and meaning intact.
_extra.lens_pm: Unglamorous but real: clean boundaries mean chunks the model can actually use.
_extra.lens_eng: Boundary detection (rules or ML) to avoid mid-sentence cuts; edge cases are abbreviations, decimals, and quotes.

title: Sentence embedding
definition: A whole sentence or passage squeezed into a single vector that captures its overall meaning.
examples: A search system embeds every FAQ answer as a vector; a user’s question becomes a vector too, and the nearest ones are the best matches.
Like a book’s Dewey number — one code that says roughly what it’s about so you can shelve like with like.

_extra.analogy: Like a book’s Dewey number — one code that says roughly what it’s about so you can shelve like with like.
_extra.deeper: Instead of one vector per word, a model pools or specially trains to produce one vector per span. These power semantic search, clustering, and retrieval because closeness in the space means closeness in meaning. Quality hinges on the embedding model — a generic one may miss domain nuance.
_extra.lens_pm: The workhorse behind semantic search and RAG; picking the right embedding model matters more than people expect.
_extra.lens_eng: A fixed-length vector for a span, from pooling token states or a purpose-trained encoder, compared via cosine or dot product.

title: Sequence length
definition: How many tokens are actually in a given input or output right now.
examples: A 500-token prompt has a sequence length of 500, well under a 128K context limit.
The number of cars in the train you’re running today, versus how long the platform can hold.

_extra.analogy: The number of cars in the train you’re running today, versus how long the platform can hold.
_extra.deeper: Sequence length is the count of tokens being processed in a specific pass, while context length is the ceiling. Attention cost grows roughly with the square of sequence length, which is why long inputs get expensive fast. Keeping sequences tight is a real performance lever.
_extra.lens_pm: Shorter sequences mean lower latency and cost — trimming inputs is a cheap optimization.
_extra.lens_eng: The token count n of a given batch element; attention is O(n²) in it.

title: Serverless Inference
definition: Running inference without managing servers—you pay per request and the infrastructure scales automatically.
examples: AWS Lambda powered by provisioned throughput to serve a model on-demand without maintaining EC2 instances.
Calling a taxi instead of owning a car; you only pay when you use it.

_extra.analogy: Calling a taxi instead of owning a car; you only pay when you use it.
_extra.deeper: Request handler spins up, inference completes, handler shuts down. Cold starts introduce latency. Pricing is request-based, not reservation-based. Best for bursty, low-volume workloads or strict SLAs that do not require always-on availability.
_extra.lens_pm: Eliminates infrastructure management overhead and scales to zero cost when idle, but adds latency for cold starts.
_extra.lens_eng: Model loaded into ephemeral function runtime; inference executes within request window, then container is deallocated.

title: Server-sent events
definition: A simple protocol where the server pushes updates to the client over a long-lived HTTP connection.
examples: A chat API uses SSE so the model's response tokens arrive one-by-one as soon as they're ready.
Like a news ticker — you tune in and the server pushes updates; you don't ask for each one.

_extra.analogy: Like a news ticker — you tune in and the server pushes updates; you don't ask for each one.
_extra.deeper: SSE is HTTP-based (so it works through proxies and firewalls), uses a simple text format (each line is a JSON event), and handles reconnection automatically. It's one-way (server to client), so it's simpler than WebSockets but can't do bidirectional streaming.
_extra.lens_pm: SSE is the standard for streaming LLM responses — easy to use from browsers and backends.
_extra.lens_eng: SSE is built into browsers; no library needed. Standard format: `data: {...}\n\n`.

title: Serving
definition: Running a trained model in production to answer real user queries.
examples: You train a summarization model and deploy it on AWS behind an API so users can call it.
Opening a restaurant after months of cooking in your home kitchen.

_extra.analogy: Opening a restaurant after months of cooking in your home kitchen.
_extra.deeper: Serving is where the rubber meets the road. Training a model is one problem; serving it to millions of users on low latency with high reliability is another. You need caching, batching, load balancing, and fallbacks. A model that works in training can be slow, memory-hungry, or unreliable at scale. Most production failures are in serving, not modeling.
_extra.lens_pm: Serving costs matter. A slow model is a bad model.
_extra.lens_eng: Use optimized frameworks (vLLM, TensorRT). Profile latency and throughput. Implement monitoring and rollback.

title: Supervised fine-tuning
definition: Training a model on labeled input-output examples to teach it a specific behavior or format.
examples: You collect 5,000 “customer message → ideal reply” pairs and fine-tune so the model matches your support tone exactly.
Like showing an apprentice hundreds of worked problems with the correct answers until they reproduce the method.

_extra.analogy: Like showing an apprentice hundreds of worked problems with the correct answers until they reproduce the method.
_extra.deeper: SFT is the straightforward flavor of fine-tuning: given inputs paired with the right outputs, minimize the error between prediction and target. It’s the backbone of instruction tuning and most task-specific adaptation. Its limits: it teaches imitation of the examples, so it can only be as good as the labeled data and can’t easily learn from “this is better than that” comparisons — which is where preference methods come in.
_extra.lens_pm: The most direct way to shape behavior when you have clean examples of exactly what you want.
_extra.lens_eng: Standard supervised learning on (input, target) pairs; the imitation step preceding preference optimization.

title: Stochastic gradient descent
definition: Gradient descent that updates using small random batches instead of the whole dataset, for speed.
examples: Instead of processing all million examples per step, the model updates weights after each batch of 32, taking many more, faster steps.
Like adjusting a recipe after each small tasting rather than cooking the entire banquet before your first tweak.

_extra.analogy: Like adjusting a recipe after each small tasting rather than cooking the entire banquet before your first tweak.
_extra.deeper: SGD estimates the gradient from a random mini-batch, making each step cheap and frequent; the noise it adds can even help escape shallow bad minima. It converges far faster in wall-clock time than full-batch descent on large data, at the cost of a noisier path. It’s the practical backbone of deep learning, and modern optimizers like Adam are refinements of it.
_extra.lens_pm: The reason training on huge datasets is even feasible — cheap, frequent updates instead of one giant one.
_extra.lens_eng: Gradient descent on random mini-batches; cheaper, noisier steps that scale to large data and aid escaping minima.

title: Shadow testing
definition: Running a new model in parallel on real traffic without showing results to users, just to see how it would perform.
examples: You deploy a new ranking model that runs on every search query but doesn't affect results. You log how it would rank things, then later compare against what the old model did.
A stunt double doing the same scene as the actor — you see if they'd succeed without affecting the movie.

_extra.analogy: A stunt double doing the same scene as the actor — you see if they'd succeed without affecting the movie.
_extra.deeper: Shadow testing lets you evaluate on 100% of real traffic without risk. The catch: users don't interact with shadow results, so you can't measure engagement. And running both models costs resources. It's best for measuring offline metrics (relevance, retrieval quality) that don't need user interaction.
_extra.lens_pm: Safe way to test radical changes. Cost-benefit depends on your traffic and how expensive running two models is.
_extra.lens_eng: Run both models, log both sets of results, compute metrics on shadow results post-hoc. Skip user interaction data.

title: Shared Memory
definition: A common store that several agents can all read from and write to.
examples: A team of agents keeps its running findings in one shared store, so a worker that starts later can see what earlier ones already learned.
A shared kitchen fridge — everyone in the house can take from it and add to it.

_extra.analogy: A shared kitchen fridge — everyone in the house can take from it and add to it.
_extra.deeper: Shared memory is how multi-agent systems avoid re-doing each other’s work, but it brings all the classic problems of shared state: race conditions, stale reads, and one agent clobbering another’s entry. You trade the simplicity of isolated agents for the efficiency of pooled knowledge. In practice it needs conventions — who writes where, how conflicts resolve — or it turns into a mess fast.
_extra.lens_pm: Pooled memory makes agent teams more efficient but adds the coordination costs of anything shared.
_extra.lens_eng: A concurrently accessed store across agents, subject to consistency and contention concerns.

title: Short-Term Memory
definition: What the model can "remember" right now — everything sitting in the current context window.
examples: A chatbot recalls what you said three messages ago because it is all still in the prompt — not because it learned anything.
The notes spread on your desk during a meeting: instantly available, but swept away when you leave the room.

_extra.analogy: The notes spread on your desk during a meeting: instantly available, but swept away when you leave the room.
_extra.deeper: Models have no memory between calls; "short-term memory" is just the tokens you feed in this turn. It is fast and lossless while it lasts, but bounded by the context window and gone the moment the conversation is trimmed or a new session starts. Anything you want kept longer has to be written somewhere and retrieved later.
_extra.lens_pm: It sets how much a session can "hold in its head" before you must persist and retrieve context yourself.
_extra.lens_eng: Non-persistent state = the current token sequence; nothing survives outside the request without external storage.

title: Similarity Search
definition: Finding the items whose vectors are closest to a query’s vector — the engine under semantic search.
examples: The query becomes a vector, and the system returns the ten stored vectors sitting nearest to it in the space.
Finding the nearest coffee shops to your location — sort everything by distance, take the closest few.

_extra.analogy: Finding the nearest coffee shops to your location — sort everything by distance, take the closest few.
_extra.deeper: Similarity search is the mechanical core: given a query vector, find the nearest stored vectors by a distance measure like cosine or dot product. Done naively it means comparing against every vector, which is too slow at scale, so real systems use indexes that trade a little accuracy for huge speed. It’s the same operation whether you call the result semantic search, recommendations, or memory retrieval.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s the shared engine behind semantic search, recommendations, and agent memory — one primitive, many features.
_extra.lens_eng: Return the k nearest vectors to a query under a distance metric, usually via an approximate index for speed.

title: Situational awareness
definition: A model "knowing" it is a model — that it is being tested, trained, or deployed — and adjusting accordingly.
examples: A model’s answers shift when its prompt hints the interaction is an evaluation versus a real user, suggesting it has picked up on the context.
A student who can tell the difference between a practice quiz and the real final, and behaves differently for each.

_extra.analogy: A student who can tell the difference between a practice quiz and the real final, and behaves differently for each.
_extra.deeper: Situational awareness is a capability that makes other risks worse: a model that knows when it is watched can behave for the test (alignment faking) or hide skills (sandbagging). Researchers probe it because it is the ingredient that turns benign evals into unreliable ones. It is measured with tests that vary whether the model believes it is being observed.
_extra.lens_pm: The property that can make your safety evals lie to you.
_extra.lens_eng: A model that infers train/test/deploy context can condition behavior on it; test under varied observed/unobserved framings.

title: Skip Connection
definition: The general name for wiring that lets a signal jump over one or more layers instead of passing through them.
examples: U-Nets and transformers alike use skip connections so early features reach later layers untouched.
An express lane that skips a few local stops so passengers can bypass congestion.

_extra.analogy: An express lane that skips a few local stops so passengers can bypass congestion.
_extra.deeper: Skip connection is the umbrella term for any path that routes information around intermediate layers; the residual connection — adding input to output — is its most common form. These shortcuts preserve detail that deep stacks would otherwise blur and keep gradients from vanishing. They show up across many architectures, not just transformers.
_extra.lens_pm: A foundational design idea that keeps deep models both trainable and detail-preserving.
_extra.lens_eng: Any bypass path routing activations around layers, most often an additive residual.

title: SLA
definition: A commitment to customers about uptime and performance — if you miss it, they get refunds or credits.
examples: An SLA might be '99.5% uptime and p99 latency < 500ms' — you monitor and refund if you miss either.
A warranty on your service — 'we promise 99.9% uptime or your money back.'

_extra.analogy: A warranty on your service — 'we promise 99.9% uptime or your money back.'
_extra.deeper: SLAs are business contracts backed by engineering discipline. They drive infrastructure decisions (redundancy, monitoring, autoscaling). Exceeding SLAs is good; violating them costs money. SLA != SLO (objective) — SLA is the promise, SLO is what you aim for internally (usually higher).
_extra.lens_pm: SLAs are your customers' recourse; enforce them internally with even stricter SLOs.
_extra.lens_eng: Build infrastructure to meet SLAs reliably; monitor like your paycheck depends on it.

title: Sliding Window Attention
definition: Each token only attends to a fixed window of nearby tokens, keeping long sequences affordable.
examples: A model uses a 4,000-token window so processing a 100,000-token document stays linear instead of exploding.
Reading with a ruler under the line — you focus on the words right around you, not the whole page at once.

_extra.analogy: Reading with a ruler under the line — you focus on the words right around you, not the whole page at once.
_extra.deeper: Sliding window attention limits each token’s view to a local neighborhood of fixed size, making cost grow linearly with length rather than quadratically. Information still travels far because stacking layers lets windows overlap and propagate — like ripples reaching across the sequence over several hops. Many long-context models pair it with a few global tokens for the rest.
_extra.lens_pm: A practical way to stretch context length without the cost blowing up.
_extra.lens_eng: Local attention over a fixed-size window per token, giving linear cost with multi-layer receptive-field growth.

title: Small language model
definition: A compact language model built to run cheaply and fast, often on your own device.
examples: A phone keyboard runs a small on-device model to suggest words instantly without sending anything to a server.
Like a scooter instead of a truck — less hauling power, but nimble, cheap, and it fits in the garage.

_extra.analogy: Like a scooter instead of a truck — less hauling power, but nimble, cheap, and it fits in the garage.
_extra.deeper: Small language models trade raw capability for speed, cost, and privacy, and modern training and distillation have made them surprisingly strong on focused tasks. The bet is that most real jobs don’t need a frontier model — a well-tuned small one, running locally, is often good enough and far cheaper.
_extra.lens_pm: Often the right call for narrow, high-volume, or privacy-sensitive tasks where a giant model is overkill.
_extra.lens_eng: A parameter-efficient LM optimized for latency, cost, and edge deployment; frequently distilled from a larger teacher.

title: Softmax
definition: The math step that turns raw scores into clean percentages that add up to 100% — how the model commits to probabilities.
examples: It takes logits like 8, 2, 1 and turns them into something like 95%, 4%, 1%.
Converting a pile of raw vote counts into a pie chart where the slices sum to a whole.

_extra.analogy: Converting a pile of raw vote counts into a pie chart where the slices sum to a whole.
_extra.deeper: Softmax exponentiates each score and divides by the total, so bigger scores dominate and everything lands between 0 and 1. Temperature is literally a divisor applied before this — high temperature flattens the resulting percentages, low temperature sharpens them toward the top pick.
_extra.lens_pm: Rarely surfaced to users; it’s the plumbing behind “how confident” a model looks.
_extra.lens_eng: Normalizes logits into a probability distribution; temperature scales the input logits.

title: Softmax temperature
definition: The knob inside softmax that flattens or sharpens the model’s probabilities before it picks a word.
examples: Set high, the model spreads its bets and gets creative; set near zero, it collapses onto the single most likely token almost every time.
Like a contrast slider on a photo — turn it up and everything blends together, down and the differences pop.

_extra.analogy: Like a contrast slider on a photo — turn it up and everything blends together, down and the differences pop.
_extra.deeper: Temperature divides the logits before softmax: values below 1 exaggerate gaps (more deterministic), above 1 shrink them (more random). It’s the mechanism underneath the “temperature” setting you see in APIs — same idea, applied at the point where scores become probabilities.
_extra.lens_pm: The dial between “safe and repetitive” and “varied and risky” outputs.
_extra.lens_eng: Scales logits by 1/T before softmax; T→0 approaches argmax, T>1 raises entropy of the distribution.

title: Soft prompts
definition: Embedding vectors that act like prompts — learned during training rather than written as text.
examples: Instead of "Classify this as positive or negative," the model processes learned vectors that implicitly instruct classification.
A melody hummed (learned) vs. a song title spoken (written).

_extra.analogy: A melody hummed (learned) vs. a song title spoken (written).
_extra.deeper: Soft prompts are prefixed to the model's input embeddings. They're optimized via backprop. Advantage: they exploit the model's embedding space fully. Disadvantage: black box — you can't inspect or transfer them. Effective for task-specific adaptation without fine-tuning the full model.
_extra.lens_pm: Lightweight adaptation for domain-specific tasks.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement as a learnable embedding layer. Train on task-specific data with a loss function. Validate generalization.

title: Sora
definition: OpenAI's text-to-video generative model, capable of creating short video clips from text descriptions.
examples: Prompt: "A cozy home library with warm lighting and vintage books" → generates a 60-second video.
The next frontier: if DALL-E paints pictures, Sora directs films.

_extra.analogy: The next frontier: if DALL-E paints pictures, Sora directs films.
_extra.deeper: Sora generates videos by predicting pixels in spacetime as a diffusion process. Research-grade as of late 2023; not yet widely available. Capabilities shown in research papers are impressive.
_extra.lens_pm: Could disrupt video production and creative industries; monetization model TBD.
_extra.lens_eng: Much harder than image generation; inference time and compute still high.

title: Sound Effect Generation
definition: Automatically creating sound effects for games, films, or other media - from descriptions or input parameters.
examples: Text: "Glass breaking, high-pitched, with echo" -> generates a plausible glass-breaking sound. Or: parameter tuning for "footstep volume and surface material".
A Foley artist in a film studio creating sounds by hand; the model does it digitally.

_extra.analogy: A Foley artist in a film studio creating sounds by hand; the model does it digitally.
_extra.deeper: Usually text-to-audio (e.g., AudioLDM trained on text-sound pairs from AudioSet). Operates on spectrograms (STFT) or raw waveforms. Challenges: specificity (descriptions vary widely), rare events (uncommon sounds have little training data), realism (artifacts, phase coherence). Diffusion-based approaches (latent diffusion in spectrogram space) show good results. Used in games (dynamic SFX) and film post-production.
_extra.lens_pm: Drastically speeds up game and film production; enables real-time sound design.
_extra.lens_eng: Text-to-audio diffusion models. Datasets: AudioSet, Freesound, FSD50K. Evaluation: subjective listening tests, acoustic feature matching.

title: Source Attribution
definition: Tracking and showing where each piece of an answer came from.
examples: An answer lists "Sources: Billing Policy §3, Onboarding Guide p.7" so a user knows exactly what informed it.
A recipe card noting which cookbook each step was adapted from.

_extra.analogy: A recipe card noting which cookbook each step was adapted from.
_extra.deeper: Attribution means every retrieved chunk carries provenance — document, section, URL, timestamp — through the pipeline so the final answer can name its sources. It supports citations, auditing, and access control, and it is only as good as the metadata captured at ingestion. Dropped provenance early on cannot be recovered later, which is why it is a design concern from the start.
_extra.lens_pm: Essential for regulated or high-trust domains where "says who?" must have an answer.
_extra.lens_eng: Propagate document/section/URL metadata end-to-end; provenance lost at ingestion is unrecoverable downstream.

title: Span
definition: A single timed step inside a trace — one model call or tool invocation with its inputs and outputs.
examples: Within the trace, one span is the “search docs” tool call: it took 400ms, took this query, returned these three results.
One line item on an itemized receipt — this thing, this long, this cost.

_extra.analogy: One line item on an itemized receipt — this thing, this long, this cost.
_extra.deeper: Spans are the building blocks of a trace — each captures one unit of work with a start, end, and metadata, and spans nest to show what called what. They’re where you find the actual detail: the exact prompt sent, the tokens used, the tool’s raw response. Borrowed from distributed tracing, the span/trace pair is what lets you zoom from “the whole run” down to “this one slow call.”
_extra.lens_pm: Spans are the zoom-in — where you see the specific step that cost the most time or money.
_extra.lens_eng: A single timed, attributed unit of work within a trace, nestable to reflect call hierarchy.

title: Sparse Retrieval
definition: Finding documents by the actual words they share with your query — old-school, but precise.
examples: Searching an exact error code "ERR_0x8007" returns the one doc that literally contains it, no semantics required.
Ctrl-F across every document, weighted so rare words count more than common ones.

_extra.analogy: Ctrl-F across every document, weighted so rare words count more than common ones.
_extra.deeper: Sparse retrieval represents text as high-dimensional word-count vectors (mostly zeros, hence "sparse") and scores overlap, classically with BM25. It nails exact terms, rare identifiers, and jargon, but it is literal — it misses synonyms and paraphrase entirely. Modern systems keep it around precisely because dense embeddings are bad at the things sparse is great at.
_extra.lens_pm: Reliable for precise, keyword-heavy queries; blind to meaning, so pair it with dense for best coverage.
_extra.lens_eng: Bag-of-words term weighting (TF-IDF/BM25) over an inverted index; exact-match strong, semantically blind.

title: Sparse Attention
definition: Attention that only connects each token to a chosen subset of others instead of all of them.
examples: For a very long document, a model attends to nearby tokens plus a few global ones rather than the full quadratic grid.
Instead of everyone at a huge conference talking to everyone, people only chat with their nearest neighbors and a few leaders.

_extra.analogy: Instead of everyone at a huge conference talking to everyone, people only chat with their nearest neighbors and a few leaders.
_extra.deeper: Full attention costs grow with the square of sequence length, which gets brutal for long inputs. Sparse attention restricts each token to a limited pattern of connections — local windows, strided jumps, a handful of global tokens — cutting the cost while trying to preserve the connections that matter. The art is choosing a sparsity pattern that keeps quality high.
_extra.lens_pm: A key enabler of long-context models that would otherwise be too expensive to run.
_extra.lens_eng: Attention restricted to a structured subset of token pairs to reduce quadratic cost.

title: Sparse Mixture
definition: A mixture-of-experts model where only a few experts fire per token, keeping a giant model cheap to run.
examples: A model with 100 billion total parameters but only 12 billion active per token is a sparse mixture.
Like a huge consulting firm where any one question only pulls in two specialists, not the entire staff.

_extra.analogy: Like a huge consulting firm where any one question only pulls in two specialists, not the entire staff.
_extra.deeper: “Sparse” means each token activates just a small subset of the experts, so total capacity can be enormous while per-token compute stays modest. This decouples a model’s knowledge (total params) from its running cost (active params). The trade-offs are memory to hold all the experts and the routing quality that decides which few actually run.
_extra.lens_pm: How a model can be “huge” in capability yet still affordable per token.
_extra.lens_eng: An MoE with top-k expert activation, decoupling total from active parameters.

title: Sparse model
definition: A model that switches on only the parameters it needs per token, so it can be huge but cheap to run.
examples: A mixture-of-experts model might hold eight times the parameters of a dense one but only light up a fraction per token.
A big hospital where each patient sees just the right specialists, not every doctor on staff.
