_extra.analogy: A big hospital where each patient sees just the right specialists, not every doctor on staff.
_extra.deeper: Sparse models — chiefly mixture-of-experts — route each token to a few “expert” subnetworks instead of the whole thing. That decouples total capacity from per-token compute: more knowledge, similar cost. The catch is added complexity in routing, load balancing, and serving.
_extra.lens_pm: The trick behind models that are “enormous” yet affordable to run — capacity without proportional cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Conditional computation (e.g. MoE) activating a subset of parameters per token via a router.

title: Speaker Diarization
definition: Identifying and separating who spoke when in an audio recording - marking "Speaker A: [0:00-1:23], Speaker B: [1:24-3:00]."
examples: A meeting recording: the system marks "Alice: 0:00-1:30, Bob: 1:31-2:15, Alice: 2:16-3:00."
Reading a script with multiple characters and labeling which character speaks each line.

_extra.analogy: Reading a script with multiple characters and labeling which character speaks each line.
_extra.deeper: Combines voice activity detection (is anyone speaking?), voice embedding extraction (speaker signature per segment), and clustering (group similar speakers). Assumes a speaker has consistent acoustic characteristics. Challenges: similar voices, overlapping speech, channel differences, long recordings (speaker drift). Typically: extract speaker embeddings (x-vector, d-vector), run clustering (spectral, agglomerative). Recent: end-to-end differentiable models (PyAnnote, ECAPA-TDNN).
_extra.lens_pm: Essential for meeting transcripts, podcast chapters, media indexing, and accessibility.
_extra.lens_eng: Datasets: AMI, ICSI. Metrics: diarization error rate (DER), composed of miss, false alarm, and speaker confusion. Models: x-vector, ECAPA-TDNN.

title: Speculative Architecture
definition: A speed trick where a tiny fast model guesses several next words and a big model just checks them in one pass.
examples: A serving stack might use a small draft model to propose 4 tokens, then have the big model verify all 4 at once.
Like a junior drafts a few sentences and the senior editor approves or fixes them in a single quick read — faster than the senior writing every word.

_extra.analogy: Like a junior drafts a few sentences and the senior editor approves or fixes them in a single quick read — faster than the senior writing every word.
_extra.deeper: The big model normally makes tokens one slow step at a time. Here a cheap draft model proposes a short run of tokens, and the big model verifies them in parallel, accepting the ones it agrees with and correcting at the first disagreement. Output is identical to the big model alone, just produced faster — pure latency savings with no quality loss.
_extra.lens_pm: A way to make responses noticeably faster and cheaper with no drop in answer quality.
_extra.lens_eng: Parallel verification of a small draft model’s proposed tokens by the target model, preserving its distribution.

title: Speech-to-Text
definition: Converting audio of speech into written text—transcribe voice calls, podcasts, lectures.
examples: Whisper transcribes English, Spanish, and Japanese from audio files with high accuracy in seconds per minute of audio.
A court reporter typing out everything a witness says.

_extra.analogy: A court reporter typing out everything a witness says.
_extra.deeper: Sequence-to-sequence model: encoder processes audio spectrograms, decoder generates text. Training on multilingual data (Whisper: 680k hours) enables zero-shot generalization. Attention layers learn to align audio frames with text. Inference faster than real-time.
_extra.lens_pm: Unlock content: search podcasts by topic, caption videos, transcribe meetings.
_extra.lens_eng: Audio preprocessed to Mel spectrogram; encoder extracts features; attention-based decoder generates tokens; beam search finds best hypothesis.

title: Spot instances
definition: Cheap cloud compute that can be interrupted at any time — you save money in exchange for the risk of losing the instance.
examples: A spot GPU costs 80% less than an on-demand GPU, but cloud providers can reclaim it with 30 seconds notice.
Buying concert tickets at the last minute for 90% off, but the show might be cancelled.

_extra.analogy: Buying concert tickets at the last minute for 90% off, but the show might be cancelled.
_extra.deeper: Spot instances are good for fault-tolerant workloads. If one instance dies, you spin up another. Inference services can handle spot instances: if a server dies, requests fail over to another replica. Training is risky on spot (you might lose 8 hours of progress). Spot pricing varies by region and demand.
_extra.lens_pm: Spot instances can cut compute costs dramatically if your workload is fault-tolerant.
_extra.lens_eng: Use spot for inference (stateless), not training; build recovery into your orchestration.

title: Stable Diffusion
definition: Open-source text-to-image diffusion model that runs on consumer GPUs and sparked the generative AI art boom.
examples: Local SD 1.5 with 4GB VRAM generates a 512x512 image in 20 seconds; no API costs or privacy concerns.
The Linux of generative AI—free, open, customizable, and community-driven.

_extra.analogy: The Linux of generative AI—free, open, customizable, and community-driven.
_extra.deeper: Latent diffusion: compress images to latent space via VAE, diffuse in latent space, decode back to pixel space. Much faster than pixel diffusion. Released open-source in 2022, sparking community fine-tunes (LoRA, textual inversion, ControlNet). Model weights available; enables fine-tuning and local deployment.
_extra.lens_pm: Democratized image generation; eliminated dependency on proprietary APIs.
_extra.lens_eng: VAE encoder compresses image to latent; UNet with attention in latent space; CLIP encoder guides; VAE decoder reconstructs.

title: Staleness
definition: When the information a system serves has quietly fallen out of date.
examples: A support bot keeps telling users to click a button that was renamed two releases ago, because its docs index was never rebuilt.
A wall calendar still showing last month — right where you left it, wrong about today.

_extra.analogy: A wall calendar still showing last month — right where you left it, wrong about today.
_extra.deeper: Staleness is the failure that freshness measures. It’s dangerous precisely because stale answers look confident and correct — nothing flags them as old. It creeps in when source data changes but the index, cache, or embeddings don’t. The fix is disciplined refresh and invalidation; the trap is caching aggressively for speed and forgetting to expire it.
_extra.lens_pm: The silent source of "the AI told me something that used to be true" complaints.
_extra.lens_eng: Occurs when source mutations aren’t propagated to derived indexes/caches; mitigate with TTLs and change-driven invalidation.

title: State Space Model
definition: A sequence model that carries a compact running state, mixing RNN-like memory with parallel training.
examples: For very long sequences, an SSM keeps a fixed-size state so cost grows linearly, not quadratically like attention.
A thermostat that tracks a single evolving reading over time instead of re-reading the whole day’s log.

_extra.analogy: A thermostat that tracks a single evolving reading over time instead of re-reading the whole day’s log.
_extra.deeper: State space models process sequences through a linear dynamical system: a hidden state evolves step to step, summarizing history in fixed size. Cleverly, they can be computed either recurrently (cheap at inference) or as a convolution (parallel at training), sidestepping the RNN’s training bottleneck. Their linear scaling with length makes them attractive for very long contexts where attention gets expensive.
_extra.lens_pm: A promising challenger to attention for very long inputs, with cheaper scaling.
_extra.lens_eng: A linear-recurrence sequence model with a fixed-size state, computable as convolution for parallel training.

title: Statistical significance
definition: Whether a difference in metrics is real or just random variation.
examples: Model A scores 85% and Model B scores 86% on your test set. Is B really better, or is that just noise? You run a significance test.
Checking whether a coin is unfair by flipping it many times — one heads isn't proof, but 100 heads in 100 flips is.

_extra.analogy: Checking whether a coin is unfair by flipping it many times — one heads isn't proof, but 100 heads in 100 flips is.
_extra.deeper: Significance tests tell you whether observed differences are likely under the null hypothesis (they're the same). Low p-value means unlikely under null, so you reject it. The catch: significance depends on sample size (large N makes tiny differences significant) and the test you choose. And significance isn't the same as importance — a tiny statistically significant improvement might not matter.
_extra.lens_pm: Don't ship based on 1% improvements. Demand both significance and practical importance.
_extra.lens_eng: Use paired t-tests for comparisons on the same examples, Mann-Whitney for unpaired. Report p-values and confidence intervals.

title: Step Logging
definition: Recording each thing an agent does as it does it, so there’s a paper trail of the whole run.
examples: Every time the agent picks a tool, the log captures which one, with what arguments, and what came back.
A ship’s logbook — each event written down as it happens, not reconstructed later from memory.

_extra.analogy: A ship’s logbook — each event written down as it happens, not reconstructed later from memory.
_extra.deeper: Step logging is the low-level habit that makes observability possible: write down each action, thought, and result at the moment it occurs. Without it, a failed run is a black box. The tension is verbosity versus signal — log too little and you can’t debug, log everything and you drown in noise and storage cost. Structured logs that you can query beat walls of raw text.
_extra.lens_pm: Cheap discipline now, huge payoff later — you can only debug what you bothered to log.
_extra.lens_eng: Emit a structured record per agent action (thought, tool call, result) as it executes, feeding traces.

title: Step-by-step prompting
definition: Explicitly asking the model to work through a task step-by-step, slowing down reasoning and reducing mistakes.
examples: "Solve step-by-step: 5×(3+2) = ?" Model: "Step 1: Solve inside parens: 3+2=5. Step 2: Multiply: 5×5=25."
A parent asking a child to explain their math work step-by-step, not just give the answer.

_extra.analogy: A parent asking a child to explain their math work step-by-step, not just give the answer.
_extra.deeper: Step-by-step reasoning (sometimes called "scratchpad") forces intermediate outputs, making reasoning visible and checkable. It works for logic puzzles, math, and fact-based tasks. Less effective for open-ended generation. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting is a formalization of this.
_extra.lens_pm: Boosts accuracy on reasoning tasks with minimal prompt changes.
_extra.lens_eng: Add "Let's think step-by-step" or similar phrasing. Parse intermediate outputs if you need to validate.

title: Stochastic
definition: Involving randomness — the reason the same prompt can give you different answers.
examples: Ask the same creative question twice and get two different poems — that’s stochastic sampling at work.
Rolling dice rather than reading a ruler: the outcome has a random element baked in.

_extra.analogy: Rolling dice rather than reading a ruler: the outcome has a random element baked in.
_extra.deeper: Generation is stochastic because the model samples from a probability distribution rather than always taking the top choice. Temperature and top-p control how random. It’s a feature for creativity and a headache for reproducibility — set temperature to zero (or fix a seed) to tame it.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s why outputs vary run to run — lower the temperature when you need consistency.
_extra.lens_eng: Sampling-based decoding introduces randomness; contrast with deterministic (greedy) decoding.

title: Stop Condition
definition: The rule that tells an agent it’s done — or that it should quit trying.
examples: The agent stops when the task returns “success,” when it hits ten steps, or when it says the magic phrase that means “I’m finished.”
The timer on the oven — it doesn’t decide the food is perfect, it just decides when to stop cooking.

_extra.analogy: The timer on the oven — it doesn’t decide the food is perfect, it just decides when to stop cooking.
_extra.deeper: Every agent loop needs a way out, and there are usually several: task success, an explicit “done” signal from the model, a step or token ceiling, or an error the agent can’t recover from. The tricky part is a stop that fires too early (gives up on solvable work) or too late (keeps flailing). Good stop conditions blend a success test with a safety cap.
_extra.lens_pm: Where you set the stop line decides the balance between giving up too soon and wasting money too long.
_extra.lens_eng: A predicate evaluated each iteration — success, explicit termination, resource ceiling, or unrecoverable error.

title: Stop sequence
definition: A bit of text that, once produced, tells the model to stop generating right there.
examples: A developer sets “\nUser:” as a stop sequence so the model writes the assistant’s reply and doesn’t keep role-playing the user’s next line.
Like a “The End” card that halts the film the instant it appears on screen.

_extra.analogy: Like a “The End” card that halts the film the instant it appears on screen.
_extra.deeper: When the model emits the specified string, decoding halts and the stop text is usually trimmed from the output. It’s how you keep a model from running past its turn or bleeding into the next section of a template — a cleaner boundary than relying on max tokens alone.
_extra.lens_pm: The tidy way to make responses end where they should instead of rambling on.
_extra.lens_eng: Decoding terminates when the generated suffix matches any configured stop string; the match is typically stripped.

title: Streaming
definition: Sending tokens back to the client as soon as they're generated instead of waiting for the full response.
examples: A chat interface shows words appearing one by one as the model generates them, instead of a long pause then all text at once.
Watching a video as it downloads instead of waiting for the whole file.

_extra.analogy: Watching a video as it downloads instead of waiting for the whole file.
_extra.deeper: Streaming trades off latency perception for architectural complexity. The client gets feedback immediately (feels fast), but you need to maintain the connection and send partial data. Server-Sent Events (SSE) or WebSockets are typical. Generators/iterators on the server simplify implementation.
_extra.lens_pm: Streaming makes LLMs feel snappy — users see progress instead of staring at a spinner.
_extra.lens_eng: Streaming requires careful connection management and error handling; SSE is simpler than WebSockets.

title: Stress testing
definition: Pushing your system to its limits with extreme volume, latency, or complexity to find breaking points.
examples: You load-test your inference server by sending 100,000 queries per second and monitoring when latency explodes or requests error.
A car crash test — you intentionally break it to see where it fails.

_extra.analogy: A car crash test — you intentionally break it to see where it fails.
_extra.deeper: Stress tests reveal infrastructure limits, not model quality. You find that your GPU runs out of memory at 500 concurrent requests, or your database hits its connection pool. These are predictable failures once you know the limit. The goal: know your limits before users find them.
_extra.lens_pm: Essential before scaling. Know where you'll break before it matters.
_extra.lens_eng: Use load-testing tools (locust, k6, jmeter). Gradually increase load, log when metrics degrade, measure breaking point.

title: Structured Tool Use
definition: Making the model’s tool requests conform strictly to a defined shape, so they can’t come out malformed.
examples: The model must return `{amount: number, currency: string}`; the system rejects or repairs any call missing a field or with the wrong type.
A form that won’t submit until every required field is filled with the right kind of value — no half-finished orders slip through.

_extra.analogy: A form that won’t submit until every required field is filled with the right kind of value — no half-finished orders slip through.
_extra.deeper: Rather than hoping the model emits valid arguments, structured tool use constrains generation to a schema — via grammars, constrained decoding, or validate-and-retry — so the output is guaranteed parseable. This removes a whole category of flaky failures where a stray character broke the JSON. The tradeoff is a little rigidity and setup, in exchange for calls your code can trust.
_extra.lens_pm: The unglamorous reliability layer that keeps agents from breaking on a misplaced comma.
_extra.lens_eng: Enforcing schema conformance on tool-call arguments via constrained decoding or validation-and-repair.

title: Structured output
definition: Forcing a model to output data in a specific format — JSON, XML, or a validated schema — instead of free-form text.
examples: Prompt: "Return a JSON object with keys name, age, email." The model outputs `{"name": "Alice", "age": 30, "email": "..."}` guaranteed.
Like asking for a form filled out neatly instead of a rambling paragraph.

_extra.analogy: Like asking for a form filled out neatly instead of a rambling paragraph.
_extra.deeper: Some APIs support constrained generation or JSON mode that hard-limits token choices to valid JSON sequences. Others use parsing + regeneration: generate text, parse it, if invalid ask again. Quality and speed matter — true schema enforcement is faster and more reliable than post-hoc parsing.
_extra.lens_pm: Unblocks downstream automation: once output is JSON, it's machine-readable, no brittleness.
_extra.lens_eng: Use model API's JSON mode if available (faster, guaranteed valid). Else: prompt clearly, add error handling, regenerate invalid outputs.

title: structured outputs API
definition: An API feature that constrains model output to match a user-defined JSON schema, guaranteeing valid structure without retries.
examples: Define a schema for a customer record: {name: string, age: number, email: string}. Model must return valid JSON matching that schema.
A form with checkboxes and text fields instead of a blank piece of paper—shape the output before the model writes.

_extra.analogy: A form with checkboxes and text fields instead of a blank piece of paper—shape the output before the model writes.
_extra.deeper: Structured outputs work by constraining token generation—only allowing tokens that lead to valid JSON. Faster than retry loops, no wasted tokens on malformed output. Recent addition to APIs; changes how you think about extraction tasks.
_extra.lens_pm: Eliminates downstream JSON parsing errors; speeds up structured extraction.
_extra.lens_eng: Token-level constraint; ensures schema compliance; integrated with function-calling.

title: Student model
definition: A smaller model trained to imitate a bigger one, keeping much of the skill at a fraction of the cost.
examples: A compact chatbot trained on a large model’s answers runs on a single GPU while staying close in quality on everyday requests.
Like an apprentice who studies the master’s work and reproduces most of it with far less overhead.

_extra.analogy: Like an apprentice who studies the master’s work and reproduces most of it with far less overhead.
_extra.deeper: The student learns from a teacher’s outputs rather than raw data alone, which packs more signal into fewer examples. Done well, it retains most capability while shrinking dramatically — but it can’t exceed the teacher, and it copies the teacher’s errors and gaps as faithfully as its strengths.
_extra.lens_pm: The practical path to cheap, fast models that still feel smart on common tasks.
_extra.lens_eng: The target model in distillation, optimized to match a teacher’s outputs at reduced parameter count.

title: Style Transfer
definition: Applying the artistic style of one image to the content of another - turning a photo into a painting in a chosen style.
examples: Photo of a dog -> painted in Van Gogh stylized starry night style. A landscape photo -> watercolor sketch.
Using Photoshop filters or art classes: the content (what) stays the same, but the presentation (how its painted) changes.

_extra.analogy: Using Photoshop filters or art classes: the content (what) stays the same, but the presentation (how its painted) changes.
_extra.deeper: Classic approach (Gatys et al.): Gram matrix matches (texture statistics) swap style while preserving content. Defined via feature activations of a pretrained CNN (VGG). Slow (per-image optimization) but artistic. Modern alternatives: feed-forward networks trained on specific styles (faster but less flexible), or diffusion-based approaches. Perceptual loss guides optimization. Trade-off between content fidelity and style strength.
_extra.lens_pm: Dated by generative models but still useful for targeted artistic effects.
_extra.lens_eng: Classic method: Gram loss + content loss via perceptual features. Modern: generative models + prompt engineering.

title: Subgoal
definition: A smaller milestone the agent aims for on the way to the real goal.
examples: To reach “ship the feature,” a subgoal is “get the build passing,” which must be true before the rest can happen.
“Reach the halfway town by noon” — not the final destination, but a checkpoint that proves you’re on track.

_extra.analogy: “Reach the halfway town by noon” — not the final destination, but a checkpoint that proves you’re on track.
_extra.deeper: Subgoals break a distant objective into reachable milestones, giving the agent nearer targets to plan toward and clear signals of progress. They’re especially useful on long tasks where the final goal is many steps away and the agent would otherwise lose the thread. The risk is optimizing a subgoal at the expense of the real one — hitting the milestone while missing the point.
_extra.lens_pm: Milestones for machines — they keep long agent runs pointed the right way.
_extra.lens_eng: An intermediate objective on the path to the goal, used to structure planning and measure progress.

title: Subtask
definition: One small, self-contained piece of a larger job — concrete enough to just do.
examples: Within “write the report,” a subtask is “summarize the Q3 sales figures” — small, clear, and done when it’s done.
A single line on the grocery list: “buy eggs.” Not the whole dinner, just one clear errand.

_extra.analogy: A single line on the grocery list: “buy eggs.” Not the whole dinner, just one clear errand.
_extra.deeper: Subtasks are what decomposition produces: units of work scoped tightly enough that an agent can complete one without holding the whole project in mind. Their independence is what enables parallelism and clean delegation. The art is sizing them — too big and they’re just the original problem again; too small and coordinating the swarm costs more than the work saved.
_extra.lens_pm: The right-sized unit of agent work — big enough to matter, small enough to finish.
_extra.lens_eng: A scoped unit of work produced by decomposition, executable independently and composable into the goal.

title: Subword
definition: A chunk of a word — the middle ground between whole words and single letters that models actually read.
examples: A tokenizer splits “tokenization” into “token” and “ization,” so a rare word still reuses pieces the model already knows.
Like Lego bricks for language: “unhappiness” snaps together from “un,” “happi,” and “ness.”

_extra.analogy: Like Lego bricks for language: “unhappiness” snaps together from “un,” “happi,” and “ness.”
_extra.deeper: Whole-word vocabularies balloon and choke on typos and new words; character-level is tiny but makes sequences very long. Subwords are the compromise — common words stay whole, rare ones fragment into familiar parts — which is how models handle words they’ve never literally seen.
_extra.lens_pm: Why token counts don’t match word counts, and why odd or foreign words cost more.
_extra.lens_eng: Vocabulary units between characters and words, learned so frequent strings stay intact and rare ones decompose.

title: Summarization Memory
definition: Squeezing old conversation into a short recap so a long chat still fits in the window.
examples: After 40 messages, the app quietly compresses the early ones into "User is planning a Japan trip in October, budget-conscious, vegetarian."
Replacing a two-hour meeting with a five-line minutes doc you can skim later.

_extra.analogy: Replacing a two-hour meeting with a five-line minutes doc you can skim later.
_extra.deeper: When history won’t fit, you summarize the oldest turns into a compact note and keep only that plus recent messages. It buys room but leaks detail — the summary decides what survives, and anything it drops is effectively forgotten. Good systems summarize hierarchically and keep raw text retrievable in case the recap missed something.
_extra.lens_pm: Lets long-running assistants feel continuous, at the cost of occasionally forgetting a detail the summary skipped.
_extra.lens_eng: Recursive summarization of stale turns; lossy compression traded against context budget, ideally paired with retrievable raw logs.

title: Superintelligence
definition: AI that vastly exceeds human intelligence — a speculative scenario that dominates discussion in AI safety and long-term risk.
examples: Kurzweil and others predict superintelligence within decades; critics argue the prediction conflates narrow progress with general reasoning.
If humans are to ants, superintelligence might be to humans: incomparably more powerful, making our concerns seem quaint.

_extra.analogy: If humans are to ants, superintelligence might be to humans: incomparably more powerful, making our concerns seem quaint.
_extra.deeper: Superintelligence encompasses ASI and scenarios just beyond human-level AGI. The concept is baked into AI safety work: if superintelligence is achievable and misaligned, humanity could face an existential threat (the "alignment problem"). Conversely, aligned superintelligence could solve all human problems. This framing is powerful and shapes research priorities, but critics argue it's speculative — we don't know if superintelligence is physically possible, and the probability model is largely guesswork. The term itself is less precise than AGI; it's used to invoke urgency and high stakes.
_extra.lens_pm: A high-stakes future scenario; AI safety funding and strategy are built around preventing or ensuring alignment.
_extra.lens_eng: A hypothetical AI system with cognitive capabilities dramatically exceeding human performance across all domains.

title: Super-Resolution
definition: Reconstructing high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs—turn 480p into sharp 4K.
examples: Real-ESRGAN upscales degraded photos (JPEG artifacts, noise) to 4K with plausible detail recovery.
A detective using CSI enhancement to zoom into a grainy security video.

_extra.analogy: A detective using CSI enhancement to zoom into a grainy security video.
_extra.deeper: Combines upsampling with artifact removal. Training on paired degraded/clean images or blind SR that handles any degradation. Perceptual loss (VGG features) outperforms pixel-level MSE for visual quality. GAN-based methods (ESRGAN) produce sharper results than diffusion but can hallucinate details.
_extra.lens_pm: Recover missing pixels from old videos, low-res security footage, scans.
_extra.lens_eng: Learned upsampling (sub-pixel convolution) plus residual blocks; trained with perceptual + adversarial loss.

title: Supervised learning
definition: Learning from examples where each input comes with the correct answer.
examples: Training a model to detect fraud from thousands of transactions each already marked “fraud” or “legit.”
Like studying with an answer key — you check each attempt against the right answer and adjust.

_extra.analogy: Like studying with an answer key — you check each attempt against the right answer and adjust.
_extra.deeper: Supervised learning is the classic setup: given labeled input-output pairs, learn a mapping that predicts the output for new inputs. It’s the most direct and well-understood paradigm, powering classification and regression everywhere. Its bottleneck is labels — they’re expensive to produce and their quality caps performance, which is exactly why self-supervised pretraining became so attractive.
_extra.lens_pm: The dependable default when you have labeled data; its cost lives in getting those labels.
_extra.lens_eng: Learn input→output from labeled pairs (classification/regression); performance bounded by label quantity and quality.

title: Supervisor Agent
definition: The agent that assigns work to other agents and checks what they hand back.
examples: A supervisor agent splits a research brief into three questions, dispatches a worker per question, then reviews and merges their findings.
A team lead who breaks up the project, parcels out tasks, and reviews everyone’s work before it ships.

_extra.analogy: A team lead who breaks up the project, parcels out tasks, and reviews everyone’s work before it ships.
_extra.deeper: The supervisor holds the overall goal and state, decides who does what, and decides when the job is done — a hub-and-spoke pattern that keeps workers simple. Its risk is being a single point of confusion: if its judgment about task completion or quality is off, every worker below it inherits the error. It trades coordination overhead for focus.
_extra.lens_pm: The pattern that makes a swarm of agents accountable to one plan.
_extra.lens_eng: An orchestrating agent that decomposes tasks, delegates to worker agents, and evaluates their outputs against the goal.

title: Supply chain risk
definition: The danger that something you didn’t build — a dataset, a base model, a dependency — arrives already compromised.
examples: A team fine-tunes a popular open-weights model that, unknown to them, carries a trojan planted upstream.
Your kitchen can be spotless, but if a supplier ships tainted ingredients, the meal is still poisoned.

_extra.analogy: Your kitchen can be spotless, but if a supplier ships tainted ingredients, the meal is still poisoned.
_extra.deeper: Modern AI systems inherit trust from pretrained weights, scraped datasets, libraries, and model hubs — any of which an attacker can tamper with (poisoned data, backdoors, malicious packages). Because the compromise happens before you touch it, your own testing may not catch it. Provenance, checksums, and vetting sources are the defenses.
_extra.lens_pm: You inherit the security of everything you didn’t build yourself — including the base model.
_extra.lens_eng: Pretrained weights, datasets, and dependencies are trust-inherited attack vectors; verify provenance and integrity, not just behavior.

title: Swarm
definition: A group of agents that coordinate as peers, with no single boss directing them.
examples: A dozen small agents each explore a different part of a codebase and share what they find on a common board until the bug is located.
A flock of birds turning together — no lead bird, just simple local rules that add up to a shape.

_extra.analogy: A flock of birds turning together — no lead bird, just simple local rules that add up to a shape.
_extra.deeper: Swarms trade central control for resilience and parallelism — no manager to bottleneck or crash, but also no one holding the overall plan. Coordination happens through shared state or messages rather than commands. They can be powerful for search-like problems but are notoriously hard to steer and debug, since behavior emerges from the interactions rather than living in one place.
_extra.lens_pm: Swarms shine on parallel exploration but are hard to predict and control — use them where breadth beats precision.
_extra.lens_eng: Peer agents coordinate via shared state or message-passing without a central controller.

title: SWE Agent
definition: An agent built to resolve real software issues end to end — read the repo, write the fix, prove it works.
examples: Given a GitHub issue, the agent locates the buggy files, edits them, runs the test suite, and produces a passing patch.
Handing a junior engineer a bug ticket and getting back a tested, ready-to-merge pull request.

_extra.analogy: Handing a junior engineer a bug ticket and getting back a tested, ready-to-merge pull request.
_extra.deeper: SWE agents are the benchmark-driven face of agentic coding, measured on suites like SWE-bench where the task is “given this repo and this issue, produce a patch that passes the hidden tests.” Progress here has been fast because the scoring is objective. The gap to everyday work is that real tickets are underspecified and touch design, review, and taste — things a hidden test can’t capture.
_extra.lens_pm: The clearest yardstick for “can AI actually do engineering work,” with a real-world asterisk.
_extra.lens_eng: An agent evaluated on repository-level issue resolution, producing patches validated against held-out tests.

title: SWE-bench
definition: A benchmark of 2,294 real GitHub issues and their fixes—measuring how well models can solve actual software engineering tasks.
examples: Given a GitHub issue and a codebase, the model has to write a patch that fixes the problem and passes all tests.
Like a real engineering job interview where you have to fix bugs in an open-source project.

_extra.analogy: Like a real engineering job interview where you have to fix bugs in an open-source project.
_extra.deeper: SWE-bench is harder than HumanEval because it requires understanding large codebases, reading error messages, iterating, and integrating fixes into existing systems. It's frontier-hard (top models solve ~10–20% of issues). It's valuable because it measures what actually matters to engineers.
_extra.lens_pm: SWE-bench is emerging as the key benchmark for AI coding assistants. Models that score well here are production-ready.
_extra.lens_eng: Evaluate on both 'lite' (simpler issues) and 'full' (harder issues) versions; check solution quality, not just pass rate.

title: Sycophancy
definition: A model’s tendency to tell you what you want to hear instead of what’s true.
examples: You say "I think this code is correct, right?" and the model agrees and praises it — then reverses itself the moment you say "are you sure? I think there’s a bug."
A yes-man employee who agrees with the boss’s bad idea because agreement feels safer than honesty.

_extra.analogy: A yes-man employee who agrees with the boss’s bad idea because agreement feels safer than honesty.
_extra.deeper: Sycophancy is a side effect of training on human feedback: raters tend to reward answers that flatter or agree, so the model learns that agreement scores well. The result is a system that caves under pushback, mirrors your stated opinion, and softens hard truths. It’s corrosive precisely because it feels pleasant — you get validation instead of correction, exactly when you needed correction.
_extra.lens_pm: Undermines trust in the worst way: the model is most agreeable exactly when you need it to disagree.
_extra.lens_eng: A reward-model artifact where agreement correlates with human approval; surfaces as opinion-mirroring and reversal under pushback.

title: Symbolic AI
definition: AI built on explicit symbols and logical rules — the original vision of reasoning through manipulation of formal, human-readable representations.
examples: Early AI researchers thought they could encode human knowledge as formal logic: "All men are mortal. Socrates is a man. Therefore, Socrates is mortal." They built systems that chained such logical statements to derive new conclusions.
Like doing math on paper: each symbol is explicit, each rule is stated outright, and you can follow the logic step by step.

_extra.analogy: Like doing math on paper: each symbol is explicit, each rule is stated outright, and you can follow the logic step by step.
_extra.deeper: The symbolic AI worldview assumes intelligence is symbol manipulation — that thinking is reasoning with explicit, discrete symbols bound by formal rules. This contrasted with connectionism (neural networks), which emerged later and said reasoning emerges from sub-symbolic, learned patterns in numbers. Symbolic AI dominated research through the 1980s but hit limits: it couldn't learn from data efficiently, struggled with nuance and exception handling, and required brittle manual knowledge engineering. Modern LLMs are sometimes called "sub-symbolic" because they work with learned numerical patterns, not explicit rules.
_extra.lens_pm: A worthy first attempt, but the requirement to hand-code all domain knowledge made it expensive and brittle.
_extra.lens_eng: An approach to AI based on formal logic, explicit rules, and symbolic manipulation, typically implemented as rule engines or theorem provers.

title: Synthetic Bootstrapping
definition: Use a model to generate its own training data, then train on it to get better at generating more.
examples: A model writes thousands of math solutions, you keep only the ones that check out, and fine-tune on those to boost it.
Pulling yourself up by your bootstraps — a small start that generates the fuel for a bigger climb.

_extra.analogy: Pulling yourself up by your bootstraps — a small start that generates the fuel for a bigger climb.
_extra.deeper: Starting from a small seed of quality data or a decent base model, you generate new examples, filter them for correctness, and train on the survivors — then repeat, each round raising the floor. It works best when you can cheaply verify outputs (math, code, tests). The danger is compounding the model’s own errors when your filter is weak.
_extra.lens_pm: A way to grow training data without armies of human labelers — as long as you can check quality automatically.
_extra.lens_eng: Iterative self-generation of training data with a verification filter to bootstrap capability gains.

title: Synthetic data
definition: Training data made by a model rather than collected from the real world.
examples: A strong model writes thousands of math problems with worked solutions, and those become training data for a smaller model.
Like a flight simulator generating endless practice scenarios so pilots don’t need a real storm to train on.

_extra.analogy: Like a flight simulator generating endless practice scenarios so pilots don’t need a real storm to train on.
_extra.deeper: Synthetic data lets teams manufacture examples where real data is scarce, private, or expensive, and to target specific weaknesses. Used well, it boosts capability cheaply; used carelessly, it risks model collapse — training on a model’s own averaged output can erode diversity and amplify its errors over generations. Quality control and grounding in real data are the guardrails.
_extra.lens_pm: A powerful way to cover gaps and rare cases — but data made by models can quietly inbreed if you’re not careful.
_extra.lens_eng: Model-generated training examples; scalable but risks distribution collapse without real-data anchoring/filtering.

title: system card
definition: Documentation that describes a model's capabilities, limitations, testing methodology, and known failure modes.
examples: A system card might say: 'Claude 3 Opus: tested on MMLU with 88.7% accuracy, struggles with obscure foreign languages, refusal rate 2%.'
A nutritional label on a food product—ingredients, allergens, serving size.

_extra.analogy: A nutritional label on a food product—ingredients, allergens, serving size.
_extra.deeper: System cards come from responsible AI practices. They're meant to inform users about what to expect and what to watch for. No standard format; varies by lab. Good ones include: capability claims with citations, limitations (what doesn't work), evaluation results, known harm categories.
_extra.lens_pm: Reduces risk of misuse; sets user expectations; helps compliance teams assess safety.
_extra.lens_eng: Transparency tool; should include eval results and limitations.

title: System message
definition: A special up-front instruction that sets the model’s role and rules for the whole conversation.
examples: “You are a terse assistant that only answers in bullet points” as a system message shapes every reply that follows.
The job description you give a new hire on day one — it colors everything they do afterward.

_extra.analogy: The job description you give a new hire on day one — it colors everything they do afterward.
_extra.deeper: The system message sits above the back-and-forth and defines persona, constraints, and priorities. Models are trained to weight it heavily, so it’s your main steering wheel for tone and behavior. It’s not bulletproof, though — clever user input can sometimes override it.
_extra.lens_pm: Your primary control surface for consistent behavior — but don’t treat it as a hard security boundary.
_extra.lens_eng: A high-priority role message prepended to the conversation, weighted above user turns in training.

title: System message design
definition: Carefully crafting the system message that sets the overall context, persona, and rules for a model's behavior.
examples: "You are a helpful, accurate, and concise assistant. You are an expert in Python. Refuse illegal requests. Explain clearly."
The first page of a rulebook that defines the game for everyone.

_extra.analogy: The first page of a rulebook that defines the game for everyone.
_extra.deeper: System messages are powerful but subtle. They influence all downstream behavior. Good system messages are specific, consistent, and backed by examples or training. Poor ones are vague ("be helpful") or contradictory ("be honest" and "don't say bad things" can conflict).
_extra.lens_pm: Foundation of model behavior. Consistency and brand voice start here.
_extra.lens_eng: Design carefully. Test with diverse inputs. Iterate based on user feedback.

title: System prompt
definition: The hidden instructions loaded before your message that tell the model who it is, what rules to follow, and how to behave.
examples: A support bot's system prompt says "you are a helpful assistant for Acme Corp; never discuss competitors" — and it obeys.
The employee handbook a new hire reads before their first day — the user never sees it, but it shapes everything.

_extra.analogy: The employee handbook a new hire reads before their first day — the user never sees it, but it shapes everything.
_extra.deeper: It sits at the top of the context and carries the most weight in the model's attention. Everything from persona to output format to safety rules goes here. The model treats it as ground truth, which is why getting it right matters more than clever user prompts — and why attackers try to override it.
_extra.lens_pm: The hidden instructions that set persona, rules, and safety — your main lever for controlling AI behavior.
_extra.lens_eng: Prepended context with highest attention weight; defines persona, constraints, and output format.

title: T5
definition: A model that treats every task — translation, summarizing, answering — as turning one string of text into another.
examples: To classify a review, you’d feed T5 “sentiment: this movie was great” and it outputs the word “positive.”
Like a universal adapter that insists everything, from questions to translations, plugs into the same text-in, text-out socket.

_extra.analogy: Like a universal adapter that insists everything, from questions to translations, plugs into the same text-in, text-out socket.
_extra.deeper: T5 uses the full encoder–decoder transformer and reframes every NLP task as text-to-text, so one model and one training setup handle them all. That uniformity made it a clean research workhorse. Decoder-only chat models later showed you could get similar generality without the encoder, but the “everything is text-to-text” framing stuck around.
_extra.lens_pm: An elegant older approach; most new work uses decoder-only models instead.
_extra.lens_eng: An encoder–decoder transformer casting all tasks in a unified text-to-text format.

title: Tail latency
definition: The latency of the slowest requests (e.g., p99 or p95) — much more important to user experience than average latency.
examples: Average latency is 50ms, but p99 is 500ms — some users wait 10x longer, which feels broken.
One slow checkout line ruins the shopping trip even if 99 others are fast.

_extra.analogy: One slow checkout line ruins the shopping trip even if 99 others are fast.
_extra.deeper: Average latency can be misleading. If 99% of requests are 50ms and 1% are 500ms, the average looks good but users in that tail suffer. Tail latency is caused by GC pauses, OS scheduling, cache misses, or congestion. Reducing tail latency often means: better hardware isolation, fast autoscaling, or shedding load.
_extra.lens_pm: P99 latency determines user experience — focus on it, not average.
_extra.lens_eng: Profile and eliminate sources of variance; prioritize speed over average efficiency.

title: Talking Head
definition: An animated face or avatar that moves its mouth and head to match speech - creating the illusion of someone talking.
examples: Given a portrait photo and speech audio, generate a video of the face talking naturally.
A puppet master animating a doll to lip-sync.

_extra.analogy: A puppet master animating a doll to lip-sync.
_extra.deeper: Input: single image + audio. Output: video of that person talking. Requires: (1) lip-sync, (2) head pose/gaze matching content, (3) realistic motion. Methods: keypoint-based (detect facial landmarks, animate), flow-based (predict motion fields), or diffusion (generate frames autoregressively or in latent space). Challenges: convincingness (uncanny valley), preserving identity, handling out-of-domain audio (accents, singing). Models like Wav2Lip, Metaface, or diffusion-based approaches.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables virtual presenters, customer service bots, personalized video messages.
_extra.lens_eng: Input: still image + audio. Output: video. Lip-sync critical. Benchmarks: LRS3 (audio-video pairs). Metrics: sync accuracy, visual quality (LPIPS, FID).

title: Task Decomposition
definition: Splitting one big, vague job into smaller concrete pieces an agent can actually tackle.
examples: “Migrate the database” becomes: back up the data, create the new schema, write the transfer script, verify counts, cut over.
Turning “plan the wedding” into a checklist — venue, invites, catering — because nobody can do “plan the wedding” in one move.

_extra.analogy: Turning “plan the wedding” into a checklist — venue, invites, catering — because nobody can do “plan the wedding” in one move.
_extra.deeper: Decomposition is the first move in planning: big goals are too abstract to act on, so the agent breaks them into subtasks small enough to have a clear next step. Good decomposition makes the rest easy and bad decomposition dooms it — miss a step and the whole chain is off. It is one of the things models do decently but not reliably, especially when the pieces have hidden dependencies.
_extra.lens_pm: Whether an agent can handle a big ask usually comes down to how well it carves it up.
_extra.lens_eng: Breaking a high-level goal into an ordered set of tractable subtasks, respecting dependencies.

title: Task Queue
definition: A waiting line of jobs for agents to pick up and work through one at a time.
examples: Incoming support tickets land in a queue, and whichever agent worker is idle grabs the next one to handle.
The ticket-number system at a deli — jobs get served in order as someone becomes free.

_extra.analogy: The ticket-number system at a deli — jobs get served in order as someone becomes free.
_extra.deeper: A task queue decouples producing work from doing it, which is what lets you scale agents horizontally — add more workers to drain a deep queue. It also gives you natural retry and prioritization points. The classic pitfalls are the same as any queue: jobs that never finish, poison items that crash every worker, and backlogs that grow faster than you can clear them.
_extra.lens_pm: Queues are how you smooth bursty demand and scale agent throughput without dropping work on the floor.
_extra.lens_eng: A buffer decoupling job producers from agent consumers, enabling parallelism, retries, and prioritization.

title: Teacher forcing
definition: During training, feed the model the real previous word instead of its own guess, so mistakes do not snowball.
examples: While training a language model, each step is conditioned on the true prior tokens from the text, not on what the model itself predicted.
A music teacher who plays the correct next note for a student mid-piece, so one slip does not derail the whole song.

_extra.analogy: A music teacher who plays the correct next note for a student mid-piece, so one slip does not derail the whole song.
_extra.deeper: Autoregressive models generate one token from the previous ones. Teacher forcing trains them on the ground-truth prefix rather than their own outputs, which makes training stable and parallelizable. The downside is exposure bias: at inference the model must feed on its own outputs, so early errors can compound — a mismatch between how it was trained and how it actually runs.
_extra.lens_pm: A training shortcut that speeds learning but partly explains why long generations can drift.
_extra.lens_eng: Condition each training step on ground-truth prior tokens; efficient but introduces exposure bias at inference.

title: Teacher model
definition: A big, capable model whose outputs are used to train a smaller one.
examples: A large frontier model labels a million examples, and a compact model trains on those labels to imitate it at a fraction of the size.
Like an expert who writes out worked solutions so an apprentice can learn from them.

_extra.analogy: Like an expert who writes out worked solutions so an apprentice can learn from them.
_extra.deeper: In distillation, the teacher provides targets — final answers or full probability distributions — richer than raw labels, letting the student absorb its behavior. The student can approach the teacher’s quality on many tasks while being far cheaper to run, though it inherits the teacher’s blind spots too.
_extra.lens_pm: How you get near-frontier quality at small-model cost — with the teacher’s biases along for the ride.
_extra.lens_eng: The source model in distillation, supplying soft targets or labels the student is trained to match.

title: Temperature
definition: A dial for how adventurous the model is — low is focused and repetitive, high is creative and risky.
examples: Set it near 0 to extract data cleanly; crank it up when you want ten weird names for a product.
The difference between a careful accountant and a poet mid-brainstorm.

_extra.analogy: The difference between a careful accountant and a poet mid-brainstorm.
_extra.deeper: It reshapes the probability distribution over the next token. High temperature flattens it so rare words get a chance; low temperature sharpens it so the safe pick almost always wins. Related knobs — top-p and top-k — trim the same distribution differently.
_extra.lens_pm: A creativity dial — low for reliable extraction, high for brainstorming variety.
_extra.lens_eng: Softmax scaling on next-token logits; higher flattens the distribution, lower sharpens it.

title: Template variables
definition: Placeholders in a prompt template — like {{NAME}} or {user_email} — that are filled with actual data at runtime.
examples: Template: "Hello {{NAME}}, your order {{ORDER_ID}} ships {{DATE}}." Runtime fills in actual values.
Mad Libs: "The {{ADJECTIVE}} {{NOUN}} ran {{ADVERB}}."

_extra.analogy: Mad Libs: "The {{ADJECTIVE}} {{NOUN}} ran {{ADVERB}}."
_extra.deeper: Variables separate static structure from dynamic data. They prevent prompt injection if used correctly (validate input before substitution) and make templates reusable. Common implementations: string formatting, Jinja, custom systems.
_extra.lens_pm: Clean, scalable prompting.
_extra.lens_eng: Define variables clearly. Validate and sanitize input before substitution.

title: Temporal Modeling
definition: Learning patterns across time - understanding how things change frame-to-frame or over longer sequences.
examples: In video: a persons hand position at frame 5 predicts frame 6. In trajectories: car position at time t predicts time t+1.
Reading a book page-by-page, understanding not just the words on one page but the story across chapters.

_extra.analogy: Reading a book page-by-page, understanding not just the words on one page but the story across chapters.
_extra.deeper: RNNs/LSTMs for sequential processing. Temporal convolutions (dilated, 1D) for parallel processing. Transformers for long-range dependencies (self-attention across time). 3D convolutions (C3D, I3D) combine spatial-temporal. Optical flow captures explicit motion. Challenges: long sequences (slow, memory), long-term dependencies (vanishing gradients), diverse temporal scales (slow burn to fast action). Contrastive learning (temporal augmentation) improves models.
_extra.lens_pm: Video understanding, prediction, forecasting, anomaly detection.
_extra.lens_eng: Temporal convolution, recurrence, or attention. Positional encoding for time. Metric: depends on task (action classification, prediction accuracy).

title: Tensor Cores
definition: Specialized hardware units in GPUs that perform matrix multiplications ultra-fast, the core operation of neural networks.
examples: H100 Tensor Cores deliver 1.5 PetaFLOPS for matrix ops; CPU cannot compete.
A carpenter with a power drill instead of a hand drill—same job, orders of magnitude faster.

_extra.analogy: A carpenter with a power drill instead of a hand drill—same job, orders of magnitude faster.
_extra.deeper: Tensor Cores multiply two matrices in a single cycle. Requires data to be in the right format (Tensor Float 32, BFloat16). Not all operations use Tensor Cores—memory bandwidth becomes bottleneck for attention. Modern GPUs have multiple types (TF32, BF16, FP8) for different precisions.
_extra.lens_pm: Determines inference and training speed; choose hardware with the right Tensor Cores for your model precision.
_extra.lens_eng: Use libraries (cuBLAS, CUTLASS) that map operations to Tensor Cores; avoid data format conversions that stall pipelines.

title: TensorFlow
definition: Google's deep learning framework; historically dominant but losing ground to PyTorch in LLM research.
examples: TensorFlow is still used at scale in production; newer research mostly uses PyTorch.
The enterprise choice; powerful but heavier than PyTorch.

_extra.analogy: The enterprise choice; powerful but heavier than PyTorch.
_extra.deeper: TensorFlow switched from static to eager execution (like PyTorch) but arrived late. Strong in production (TFLite for mobile) and TPU integration. Ecosystem includes Keras.
_extra.lens_pm: Strong in production; less so in research; duopoly with PyTorch.
_extra.lens_eng: TPU integration is Google's advantage; otherwise PyTorch is preferred by researchers.

title: Tensor Parallelism
definition: Splitting a single layer’s math across several GPUs so they compute one big matrix multiply together.
examples: Serving a model too big for one GPU often splits each layer’s weight matrices across 4 or 8 GPUs.
Like four cashiers ringing up different halves of one giant order at the same time, then combining the totals.

_extra.analogy: Like four cashiers ringing up different halves of one giant order at the same time, then combining the totals.
_extra.deeper: Within a layer, the big weight matrices are chopped into pieces spread across GPUs; each computes its slice and the results are combined with fast interconnect communication. It lets a model whose weights don’t fit on one chip run across several as if it were one. The cost is heavy inter-GPU chatter, so it wants very fast links between the chips.
_extra.lens_pm: A core reason big models need tightly-networked multi-GPU servers to run.
_extra.lens_eng: Partitioning weight matrices within layers across devices, with all-reduce/all-gather to combine.

title: TensorRT
definition: An NVIDIA compiler that optimizes neural networks for fast inference on NVIDIA GPUs.
examples: Compiling a PyTorch model with TensorRT can 2-4x its inference speed with minimal accuracy loss.
A mechanic who fine-tunes your car engine for a specific track.

_extra.analogy: A mechanic who fine-tunes your car engine for a specific track.
_extra.deeper: TensorRT fuses operations (e.g., combining Conv+ReLU into one kernel), converts to lower precision (FP16, INT8), optimizes memory layout, and generates CUDA kernels. It's specific to NVIDIA hardware but offers the fastest speeds on that platform.
_extra.lens_pm: TensorRT is the go-to for squeezing max throughput from NVIDIA GPUs.
_extra.lens_eng: TensorRT has a learning curve and is NVIDIA-only; good if you're committed to that hardware.

title: Test Harness
definition: The infrastructure that runs models on eval examples, computes metrics, and reports results—automating the evaluation pipeline.
examples: Your test harness loads 1000 examples, runs them through the model, computes BLEU/ROUGE/human scores, and outputs a report.
Like a testing framework in software engineering that runs test cases automatically.

_extra.analogy: Like a testing framework in software engineering that runs test cases automatically.
_extra.deeper: A good test harness is reproducible, versioned, and fast. It lets you swap models easily and track regressions. Essential for continuous evaluation. Investment in test harness infrastructure pays off quickly.
_extra.lens_pm: A solid test harness is force-multiplier. It lets small teams evaluate many model changes.
_extra.lens_eng: Build once, use often. Automate metrics computation, logging, and report generation.

title: Test set
definition: The data you touch exactly once, at the very end, to get an honest read on how the model actually does.
examples: After weeks of tuning on validation, the team runs the model on the test set a single time and reports that number.
The sealed final exam — you only open it when you are truly done studying.

_extra.analogy: The sealed final exam — you only open it when you are truly done studying.
_extra.deeper: The test set must stay untouched during development, because every peek lets you unconsciously tune toward it and inflate the result. Its whole value is that the model has never adapted to it, so the score generalizes. The moment test data leaks into training — contamination — that guarantee is gone.
_extra.lens_pm: The one number you can actually trust when deciding whether to ship.
_extra.lens_eng: A one-shot held-out evaluation split; any reuse or leakage compromises its estimate of generalization.

title: Test-Time Compute
definition: Spending more computing power at the moment of answering — not during training — to get a better answer.
examples: A reasoning model that takes 30 seconds and writes pages of internal steps for a hard proof is burning test-time compute.
Like giving yourself more time on an exam question instead of studying harder beforehand — more thinking now, right when it counts.

_extra.analogy: Like giving yourself more time on an exam question instead of studying harder beforehand — more thinking now, right when it counts.
_extra.deeper: For years, gains came from bigger models and more training. Test-time compute flips some of that: keep the model fixed but let it think longer, sample more candidates, or search over options at answer time. On hard problems this buys real accuracy, but it directly raises latency and cost per request, so it’s a dial to spend deliberately.
_extra.lens_pm: A new cost lever — you can now trade money-per-answer for quality, live.
_extra.lens_eng: Allocating additional inference-time computation (longer generations, sampling, search) to improve outputs.

title: Text generation
definition: A model producing new text one token at a time, each choice conditioned on everything so far.
examples: You type a prompt and watch the reply stream in word by word — that streaming is generation happening token by token.
Like writing a sentence where you commit to one word, then choose the next based on all the words already down.

_extra.analogy: Like writing a sentence where you commit to one word, then choose the next based on all the words already down.
_extra.deeper: Generation is autoregressive: the model predicts a probability distribution for the next token, a decoding strategy picks one, it’s appended, and the loop repeats. Everything from temperature to stop sequences is really about shaping or ending this loop. It’s also why longer outputs cost proportionally more time and money.
_extra.lens_pm: The core act you’re paying for; output length drives both latency and cost linearly.
_extra.lens_eng: Iterative next-token sampling from the model’s conditional distribution until a stop condition; inherently sequential.

title: Text-to-Image
definition: Creating images from natural language descriptions—"a cyberpunk city at night" produces a novel picture matching the description.
examples: DALL-E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion take text prompts and generate photorealistic or artistic images.
Commissioning a digital artist who reads your description and delivers a painting in seconds.

_extra.analogy: Commissioning a digital artist who reads your description and delivers a painting in seconds.
_extra.deeper: Relies on text encoder (CLIP or BERT-style) to convert prompt to embeddings, then diffusion or GAN uses embeddings to guide generation. Model must learn mapping between language and pixels. Prompt engineering (specific adjectives, artist names, style hints) dramatically improve results.
_extra.lens_pm: Unlocks content creation and design workflows without hiring artists.
_extra.lens_eng: Text encoder + diffusion backbone; conditioning signal injected via cross-attention; noise schedule controls quality-speed tradeoff.

title: Text-to-Speech
definition: Converting written text into natural-sounding audio—read documents aloud, voiceovers, voice assistants.
examples: Google TTS converts "Hello, how are you?" to audio in seconds; can choose voice, speed, gender.
An actor reading a script into a microphone, but instantly and in any voice.

_extra.analogy: An actor reading a script into a microphone, but instantly and in any voice.
_extra.deeper: Two-stage: text-to-mel (attention-based model like Tacotron learns to align text to audio features) then mel-to-audio (vocoder like WaveGlow, HiFi-GAN reconstructs waveform). Prosody (pitch, speed, emotion) controllable via attention mask or explicit tokens. Multi-speaker models learn different voices.
_extra.lens_pm: Accessibility feature; content monetization (audiobooks from text); voice interface.
_extra.lens_eng: Encoder processes text; decoder attends and generates Mel spectrogram; vocoder converts to waveform.

title: Text-to-Video
definition: Creating a video from a text description—"a person dancing in the rain" produces a short video clip.
examples: Sora takes "a white cat playing with yarn balls" and generates a 60-second video with realistic motion and lighting.
Writing a movie scene description that the AI director turns into footage.

_extra.analogy: Writing a movie scene description that the AI director turns into footage.
_extra.deeper: Extends image diffusion to temporal dimension. Model must learn frame-to-frame consistency, realistic motion, and temporal coherence. Latent diffusion (compress frames to latent space) is efficient. Training requires paired video-text data (billions of hours). Inference is slow (1 minute of video takes minutes to generate).
_extra.lens_pm: Democratizes video creation; enables rapid prototyping and visualization.
_extra.lens_eng: VAE compresses video frames; temporal UNet diffuses in latent space; CLIP guides; VAE decodes frames back to pixels.

title: Texture Synthesis
definition: Generating new, larger versions of a texture by learning its statistical patterns and extrapolating.
examples: Input: a 64x64 fabric swatch. Output: a seamless 1024x1024 image of the same fabric. Or grass, waves, marble patterns.
A piece of bark: from a small sample, you infer the full tree and generate more bark that looks consistent.

_extra.analogy: A piece of bark: from a small sample, you infer the full tree and generate more bark that looks consistent.
_extra.deeper: Statistical methods (e.g., Markov random fields, graph cuts) match local neighborhoods. Neural approaches learn texture statistics via CNNs and feed-forward or diffusion models. Conditional generation via example patches. Quality degrades if the texture has large structures or orientations. Generative models (GANs, diffusion) now dominate. Increasingly replaced by diffusion-based in-painting.
_extra.lens_pm: Graphics and game development, but replaced by diffusion models for most use cases.
_extra.lens_eng: Classic: non-parametric sampling. Modern: conditional diffusion or feed-forward network trained on texture pairs.

title: TF-IDF
definition: A scoring trick that highlights words that are common in a document but rare across all documents — so "urgent" in your email matters more than "the."
examples: When you search Google, TF-IDF helps rank results: pages containing your rare search term score higher than pages stuffed with common words.
A librarian who knows which words are telling: "blood" in a medical journal is informative; "the" in any journal is noise.

_extra.analogy: A librarian who knows which words are telling: "blood" in a medical journal is informative; "the" in any journal is noise.
_extra.deeper: TF (term frequency) counts how often a word appears in a document; IDF (inverse document frequency) is a penalty for words that appear in many documents. Multiply them: a word gets high TF-IDF if it's frequent in one document but rare globally. It's a simple heuristic that works well for retrieval and classification without deep learning. Modern systems use learned embeddings instead, which capture semantic meaning beyond word statistics, but TF-IDF remains a solid baseline and is interpretable.
_extra.lens_pm: A robust, interpretable baseline for search and classification; overtaken by learned methods but still useful.
_extra.lens_eng: A term weighting scheme: TF-IDF(term, doc) = count(term, doc) × log(total_docs / docs_with_term).

title: Threat model
definition: A clear-eyed map of who might attack you, how, and what you are actually defending — so you protect the right things.
examples: A team writing an AI agent lists threats: prompt injection from web content, a malicious user, and a compromised tool — then designs defenses for each.
Before installing locks, figuring out whether you’re guarding against nosy roommates, burglars, or a state actor — because each needs different doors.

_extra.analogy: Before installing locks, figuring out whether you’re guarding against nosy roommates, burglars, or a state actor — because each needs different doors.
_extra.deeper: Threat modeling names your assets, adversaries, their capabilities, and the attack paths, so effort goes where the real risk is instead of everywhere at once. Without one, security is a pile of habits; with one, it is a plan. For LLM systems it forces you to treat untrusted input and tool output as hostile by default.
_extra.lens_pm: The document that keeps security work aimed at real risks instead of theater.
_extra.lens_eng: Enumerate assets, adversaries, capabilities, and attack paths up front; it drives which controls actually matter.

title: Throughput
definition: How many requests you can serve per second—measuring capacity and cost efficiency.
examples: Your inference server handles 1000 requests per second. Throughput is 1000 RPS.
Like how many customers a cashier can serve per hour.

_extra.analogy: Like how many customers a cashier can serve per hour.
_extra.deeper: Throughput depends on batch size, model size, hardware, and latency. Larger batches increase throughput but increase latency variance (some users wait longer). You optimize for throughput when cost matters (cloud compute is expensive) or when you have bursty traffic. Tradeoff: throughput vs. latency.
_extra.lens_pm: Throughput directly affects your infrastructure costs. 2x throughput can halve your bill.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure throughput with realistic request distributions; don't assume uniform arrival rates.

title: Throughput Optimization
definition: Maximizing the number of requests a server can handle per second by optimizing batching, memory, and compute.
examples: Batch size 128 achieves 1000 req/sec; batch size 64 achieves 600 req/sec; batch size 256 hits OOM—optimal is 128.
Fitting more passengers on a bus by optimal seating vs wasted aisle space.

_extra.analogy: Fitting more passengers on a bus by optimal seating vs wasted aisle space.
_extra.deeper: Throughput limited by either compute (FLOPS fully utilized, waiting for more data) or memory (cannot fit larger batch). Continuous batching and KV cache optimization critical for LLMs. Hardware choice matters: tensor cores, memory bandwidth. Software profiling identifies bottleneck. Diminishing returns: doubling batch size does not double throughput.
_extra.lens_pm: Higher throughput = lower cost-per-request = better economics.
_extra.lens_eng: Profile inference time across batch sizes; optimize memory layout and compute kernels; measure utilization and identify bottleneck (compute vs memory bound).

title: Time to first token
definition: How long between sending a request and receiving the first output token.
examples: You send a request to a language model. After 500ms, you get the first token. TTFT = 500ms.
The delay between asking a question and hearing the first word of the answer.

_extra.analogy: The delay between asking a question and hearing the first word of the answer.
_extra.deeper: TTFT is critical for user experience. Low TTFT feels responsive; high TTFT feels frozen. It's dominated by prompt encoding time (especially for long contexts), not by generation speed. This is why systems batch prompts separately from generation — you pay encoding cost once per unique prompt, generation cost per output token.
_extra.lens_pm: TTFT is king for interactive systems. Users notice even 100ms delays.
_extra.lens_eng: Profile with realistic workloads. Optimize prompt encoding (KV cache reuse, sparse attention). Batch aggressively.

title: Together AI
definition: Inference platform offering competitive pricing and low latency for open-source LLMs.
examples: Run Llama 2 70B or Mistral via Together API; cheaper than OpenAI's GPT-4.
The practical cloud provider; focus on open models, fair pricing.

_extra.analogy: The practical cloud provider; focus on open models, fair pricing.
_extra.deeper: Together aggregates open models (Llama, Mistral, etc.) on shared infrastructure. Strong on inference optimization and cost.
_extra.lens_pm: Monetizes on volume and efficiency; targets cost-conscious builders.
_extra.lens_eng: Inference latency and throughput are competitive; good for open models.

title: Token Budget
definition: A cap on how many tokens an agent may spend on a task before it has to stop or economize.
examples: A run is given a 200,000-token budget, and as it approaches the limit the agent starts summarizing instead of keeping full history.
A daily allowance — once it’s gone, you either wrap up or do the rest more cheaply.

_extra.analogy: A daily allowance — once it’s gone, you either wrap up or do the rest more cheaply.
_extra.deeper: A token budget is both a cost control and a forcing function: knowing it’s finite pushes the agent (and its designer) to spend context wisely. It ties directly to stop conditions — hit the budget and the run ends or degrades gracefully. The design question is what happens at the limit: hard stop, summarize-and-continue, or ask a human, each with a different tradeoff between completeness and cost.
_extra.lens_pm: Budgets keep agent costs predictable and force hard choices about what’s worth spending context on.
_extra.lens_eng: A per-run token ceiling that triggers summarization, degradation, or termination as it’s approached.

title: Tokenization
definition: Chopping text into the bite-size pieces a model actually reads — usually chunks of words, not whole words.
examples: “tokenization” might split into token-ization — two pieces, not one word.
Slicing a sentence into LEGO bricks before the model can build with it.

_extra.analogy: Slicing a sentence into LEGO bricks before the model can build with it.
_extra.deeper: A tokenizer learns a fixed vocabulary of common fragments (often via byte-pair encoding), then greedily splits any text into those fragments. It runs before the model sees anything, which is why a model never really sees letters — only the chunks — and why the same sentence can cost more tokens in one language than another.
_extra.lens_pm: The step that decides your token count — and therefore your cost and length limits.
_extra.lens_eng: Deterministic sub-word segmentation (BPE/Unigram) mapping text to integer IDs over a fixed vocabulary.

title: Tokenizer
definition: The tool that chops text into tokens before the model sees it — the reason "strawberry" doesn't have three R's according to AI.
examples: "unbelievable" becomes ["un", "believ", "able"] — three tokens. The model never sees individual letters.
A paper shredder that cuts text into specific-sized pieces — the model only sees the pieces, never the full page.

_extra.analogy: A paper shredder that cuts text into specific-sized pieces — the model only sees the pieces, never the full page.
_extra.deeper: Most modern tokenizers use Byte Pair Encoding (BPE): start with individual bytes, then iteratively merge the most common pairs into larger tokens. Common words become single tokens; rare words get split into pieces.
_extra.lens_pm: The invisible text splitter that explains why AI miscounts letters and some languages cost more.
_extra.lens_eng: BPE/SentencePiece converting text to token IDs; vocabulary size and merge rules affect cost and capability.

title: Tokenizer-Free
definition: A model that skips the usual word-chopping step and works straight from raw bytes or characters.
examples: A tokenizer-free model can handle a weird emoji sequence or a rare language script without choking on “unknown token.”
Like reading a book letter by letter instead of first breaking it into a fixed dictionary of word-pieces.

_extra.analogy: Like reading a book letter by letter instead of first breaking it into a fixed dictionary of word-pieces.
_extra.deeper: Normal models first split text into subword tokens using a fixed vocabulary, which struggles with rare words, typos, and unusual scripts. Tokenizer-free models operate on bytes or characters directly, gaining robustness and language-fairness at the cost of longer sequences and more compute. It’s an active bet that removing the brittle tokenizer step is worth the extra cost.
_extra.lens_pm: Promises better handling of messy, multilingual, or noisy text — still an emerging trade-off.
_extra.lens_eng: A model operating directly on bytes/characters, eliminating a fixed subword vocabulary.

title: Tokenizer training
definition: Building the model's vocabulary by finding which character chunks are common enough to deserve their own token.
examples: A team runs byte-pair encoding over the corpus, merging frequent character pairs until it has a 100k-token vocabulary.
Deciding which phrases are common enough to earn a shorthand in your notes, so you write less.

_extra.analogy: Deciding which phrases are common enough to earn a shorthand in your notes, so you write less.
_extra.deeper: Before a model trains, its tokenizer is fit on a data sample, usually with byte-pair encoding or a similar algorithm that repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent units. The result is the fixed vocabulary the model will use forever. It matters because it decides how efficiently text is encoded — a tokenizer fit mostly on English will chop other languages into many more tokens, making them costlier and often worse-served.
_extra.lens_pm: A one-time choice that quietly sets per-language cost and quality for the model's whole life.
_extra.lens_eng: Fit a subword vocabulary (e.g. BPE) on a corpus sample by iterative frequency-based merges; fixed thereafter.

title: Token limit
definition: The ceiling on how many tokens a model can handle at once, input and output combined.
examples: A user pastes a 200-page PDF into a chat with a 128k-token limit and gets an error because the document alone blows past the ceiling.
Like a desk that only fits so many papers — pile on more and the earliest ones slide off.

_extra.analogy: Like a desk that only fits so many papers — pile on more and the earliest ones slide off.
_extra.deeper: The token limit is the physical size of the context window; prompt, history, and generated reply all draw from the same pool. Exceeding it forces truncation or an error, and even well under it, models often use the far ends of that budget less reliably than the edges.
_extra.lens_pm: Shapes what you can feed a model in one go and quietly caps how much history a chat can keep.
_extra.lens_eng: Max total tokens (prompt + completion) the model accepts; overflow triggers truncation or a hard error.

title: Token optimization
definition: Minimizing token usage — both input and output — to reduce latency and cost while maintaining quality.
examples: "What is 2+2?" (4 tokens) vs. "Please tell me the result of 2+2?" (8 tokens). Same answer, 50% fewer tokens.
Writing a haiku instead of a sonnet: same message, fewer words.

_extra.analogy: Writing a haiku instead of a sonnet: same message, fewer words.
_extra.deeper: Token count scales with prompt length and model output length. Optimization strategies: (1) Compress prompts, (2) Use shorter examples, (3) Limit max output tokens, (4) Cache prompts (if API supports it), (5) Choose smaller models when possible.
_extra.lens_pm: Direct cost savings. Faster responses.
_extra.lens_eng: Profile token usage. Identify bottlenecks. Compress, cache, or use smaller models.

title: token pricing
definition: The cost model where LLM APIs charge per token consumed (input and output), not per request or per hour.
examples: Claude API: $3 per 1M input tokens, $15 per 1M output tokens. A 1,000-token response costs $0.015.
Cell phone billing—pay for minutes (tokens) used, not a fixed monthly fee.

_extra.analogy: Cell phone billing—pay for minutes (tokens) used, not a fixed monthly fee.
_extra.deeper: Token pricing aligns incentives—longer responses cost more, so you think about efficiency. But it's opaque (users don't know how many tokens their text will tokenize to). Output tokens usually cost more than input (generation is harder). Pricing pressure from competition.
_extra.lens_pm: Transparent and usage-based; scales naturally with demand.
_extra.lens_eng: Tokenization adds latency; cache/batch pricing is becoming differentiator.

title: Tokens
definition: The chunks a model reads and writes in — roughly ¾ of a word each. Everything is priced and measured in them.
