examples: “unbelievable” might be three tokens: un-believ-able. Your bill counts every single one.
Syllables for a machine — not quite letters, not quite whole words.

_extra.analogy: Syllables for a machine — not quite letters, not quite whole words.
_extra.deeper: Tokenization is why models miscount the letters in a word or fumble rare strings — they never saw the letters, only the chunks. It also explains why some languages cost more: they tokenize less efficiently, so the same sentence spends more tokens.
_extra.lens_pm: The billing and length unit for AI — costs and limits are counted in these, not words.
_extra.lens_eng: Sub-word units from the tokenizer; model I/O and pricing are both measured per token.

title: Tokens per parameter
definition: How many training tokens each model parameter gets to learn from — a rough gauge of whether a model is well-fed or starved.
examples: A 7B model trained on 2 trillion tokens sees about 285 tokens per parameter — far past the Chinchilla point of 20, on purpose.
Students per teacher: too many and each gets too little attention; the ratio tells you if the class is well-served.

_extra.analogy: Students per teacher: too many and each gets too little attention; the ratio tells you if the class is well-served.
_extra.deeper: Divide training tokens by parameter count. Chinchilla put the compute-optimal ratio near 20, but modern small models are trained to hundreds of tokens per parameter because over-training a small model buys cheaper inference. A low ratio suggests an under-trained, over-sized model; a very high one means you are spending extra training compute to save at serving time.
_extra.lens_pm: A quick sniff test for whether a model is right-sized for its data budget.
_extra.lens_eng: Training tokens ÷ parameters; ~20 is compute-optimal, higher trades train cost for inference savings.

title: Tokens per second
definition: How many output tokens your inference server produces per second.
examples: Your model generates 50 tokens per second. A 100-token response takes 2 seconds.
Words per minute for a typist — measures output speed.

_extra.analogy: Words per minute for a typist — measures output speed.
_extra.deeper: TPS is limited by memory bandwidth (for large models) and compute. Bigger models have higher per-token latency. You increase TPS through batching (process multiple requests together) and parallelization. The tradeoff: batching increases latency per request. You want to batch enough to get good TPS without making individual requests too slow.
_extra.lens_pm: Throughput scales your revenue. More tokens per dollar means cheaper service.
_extra.lens_eng: Measure on realistic batch sizes. Profile memory bandwidth. Use pipelining and tensor parallelism.

title: Token streaming
definition: Returning generated tokens one-by-one as they're produced instead of waiting for the entire response.
examples: In a chat app, you see words appear as the model generates them rather than a 5-second pause then all text at once.
Getting subtitles in real-time during a movie instead of waiting until it's over.

_extra.analogy: Getting subtitles in real-time during a movie instead of waiting until it's over.
_extra.deeper: Token streaming is both a user-experience win (feels responsive) and an implementation challenge (need persistent connections). The server keeps the connection open and pushes tokens via SSE, WebSocket, or gRPC streaming. Clients need to handle backpressure if they can't consume tokens fast enough.
_extra.lens_pm: Token streaming is the 'secret sauce' that makes LLM chats feel snappy.
_extra.lens_eng: Use SSE or WebSockets; make sure your inference engine can stream tokens incrementally.

title: Tool Calling
definition: The concrete act of a model choosing a tool and issuing the request to run it, mid-response.
examples: Halfway through answering, the model emits a call to the `get_stock_price` tool with `ticker: "AAPL"` and pauses for the result.
Reaching for the right implement on the workbench the moment the task needs it — grab the wrench, not just describe wrenches.

_extra.analogy: Reaching for the right implement on the workbench the moment the task needs it — grab the wrench, not just describe wrenches.
_extra.deeper: Tool calling is the mechanical event inside tool use: the model outputs a structured request naming the tool and its arguments, the runtime pauses generation, runs it, and resumes with the result appended. Modern models are trained to do this natively, often calling several tools in one turn. The reliability question is whether it picks the right tool and fills the arguments correctly.
_extra.lens_pm: The moment your model stops talking and starts doing — literally the trigger for action.
_extra.lens_eng: The model emitting a structured tool invocation that suspends generation until the runtime returns a result.

title: Tool Chaining
definition: Wiring tools together so the agent can pass work from one to the next without a human in between.
examples: A pipeline where a transcription tool hands text to a translation tool, which hands it to a summarizer, all in one automated pass.
Setting up dominoes — knock the first and the rest fall in order, no touching required.

_extra.analogy: Setting up dominoes — knock the first and the rest fall in order, no touching required.
_extra.deeper: Tool chaining is the practice of connecting tools into flows, whether hardcoded or decided on the fly by the model. Fixed chains are predictable and testable; model-decided chains are flexible but harder to trust. The engineering challenge is matching output formats between links so nothing gets lost or mangled in the handoff — the plumbing between tools is where chains usually leak.
_extra.lens_pm: Automating a multi-tool workflow is where real time gets saved — and where brittle glue hides.
_extra.lens_eng: Composing tools into a pipeline, statically or dynamically, aligning each output format to the next input.

title: Tool Error Handling
definition: What an agent does when a tool call fails — and whether it recovers gracefully or falls apart.
examples: The database tool times out, so the agent reads the error, waits a moment, and retries once before trying a different approach.
A cook whose oven dies mid-service — do they adapt and finish, or stand there staring at it?

_extra.analogy: A cook whose oven dies mid-service — do they adapt and finish, or stand there staring at it?
_extra.deeper: Tools fail constantly — timeouts, bad inputs, rate limits — and how the error is surfaced to the model decides whether it recovers. A clear, structured error (“missing required field: date”) lets the agent fix and retry; a raw stack trace or silent failure sends it into confusion or a loop. Robust agents treat errors as information to act on, not dead ends, which means the error messages themselves become part of the design.
_extra.lens_pm: Real tools fail often; how the agent handles those failures is most of what separates a demo from production.
_extra.lens_eng: Surface tool failures as structured, actionable observations so the model can correct rather than loop or stall.

title: Tool Registry
definition: The catalog of tools an agent is allowed to use, each with a description of what it does and how to call it.
examples: The registry lists send_email, search_web, and query_database, so the agent knows those three exist and exactly what arguments each one takes.
A restaurant menu — the agent can only order what’s printed, and each item comes with a description.

_extra.analogy: A restaurant menu — the agent can only order what’s printed, and each item comes with a description.
_extra.deeper: The registry is both a menu and a fence: it tells the agent what’s available and, by omission, what isn’t. Descriptions matter enormously — a vague tool description means the agent picks the wrong tool or mangles the arguments. As registries grow past a few dozen tools, the model starts to struggle to choose, which is why big toolsets get grouped or filtered before they reach the prompt.
_extra.lens_pm: What’s in the registry defines what your agent can and can’t do — it’s a product decision, not just plumbing.
_extra.lens_eng: A lookup of available tools with their schemas and descriptions, injected into or filtered before the model context.

title: Tool Result
definition: What comes back after a tool runs — the data or message the model reads to decide its next move.
examples: The weather tool returns `{temp: 14, condition: "rain"}`; the model reads it and writes “Bring an umbrella — it’s 14° and raining.”
The number the calculator shows after you press equals; you read it, then keep going.

_extra.analogy: The number the calculator shows after you press equals; you read it, then keep going.
_extra.deeper: The tool result is appended to the context as the fruit of an action, and the model’s next turn is conditioned on it. Its format matters more than people expect: a clean, relevant result guides the model well, while a giant raw dump wastes context and buries the signal. Errors count as results too — a good agent reads a failure and adapts rather than plowing ahead.
_extra.lens_pm: Feed agents tidy results, not fire-hoses — how you shape tool output shapes the answer.
_extra.lens_eng: The output of a tool execution appended to context, conditioning the model’s subsequent generation.

title: Tool Schema
definition: The spec sheet that tells the model what a tool does, what it’s called, and exactly what inputs it takes.
examples: A `search(query, max_results)` schema tells the model the tool’s name, that `query` is a required string, and `max_results` an optional number.
The label on a control panel — button name, what it does, and which knobs it needs set first.

_extra.analogy: The label on a control panel — button name, what it does, and which knobs it needs set first.
_extra.deeper: Each tool is described in a structured format — usually JSON Schema — with a name, a natural-language description, and typed parameters. The model reads these descriptions to decide which tool fits and how to fill its arguments, so the wording matters as much as the types: a vague description means the model misuses the tool. It is the contract between the model’s intent and your code.
_extra.lens_pm: Half of tool reliability is just writing clear tool descriptions.
_extra.lens_eng: A machine-readable declaration (typically JSON Schema) of a tool’s name, description, and parameter types that constrains the model’s call.

title: Tool Use
definition: Letting a model reach outside its own head — run code, search the web, hit an API — instead of guessing from memory.
examples: Asked for today’s weather, the model does not invent a forecast — it calls a weather API and reads back the real number.
A smart person who, instead of estimating, just picks up a calculator, opens a browser, or makes a phone call.

_extra.analogy: A smart person who, instead of estimating, just picks up a calculator, opens a browser, or makes a phone call.
_extra.deeper: The model does not run tools itself; it emits a request to use one, a surrounding program runs it, and the result comes back as new text in the context. This turns a frozen, all-knowing guesser into something that can act and observe. The whole agent field is basically tool use in a loop.
_extra.lens_pm: The single feature that turns a chatbot into something that can actually get things done.
_extra.lens_eng: The model outputs a tool invocation; an external runtime executes it and feeds the result back into the context window.

title: Top-K Retrieval
definition: Grabbing the k best-matching chunks for a query — where k is how many you decide to pull.
examples: With k set to 5, a question retrieves the five most relevant document chunks to stuff into the prompt.
Asking for the top five recommendations, not the entire ranked list of everything.

_extra.analogy: Asking for the top five recommendations, not the entire ranked list of everything.
_extra.deeper: K is one of the most consequential knobs in retrieval: too small and you miss the chunk with the answer, too large and you flood the context with noise and cost. There’s no universal right number — it depends on chunk size, model context, and how scattered the answer is. Because raw top-k by similarity is often imperfect, teams frequently over-retrieve and then rerank down to the truly best few.
_extra.lens_pm: K trades recall against noise and cost — tuning it is one of the cheapest wins in a retrieval system.
_extra.lens_eng: Return the k highest-scoring items from the retriever, k being a tunable recall-versus-noise parameter.

title: Top-k
definition: A sampling limit that keeps only the k most likely next words and throws the rest away before choosing.
examples: Top-k 40 means the model picks from its 40 best guesses and ignores everything else.
Only letting the top 40 seeds into the tournament, no matter how the field looks.

_extra.analogy: Only letting the top 40 seeds into the tournament, no matter how the field looks.
_extra.deeper: Top-k is blunt: it always keeps exactly k candidates, even when the model is very sure (so k is too many) or very unsure (so k is too few). That rigidity is why top-p often wins — it adjusts the cutoff to the model’s confidence instead of using a fixed number.
_extra.lens_pm: An older, blunter variety limit; most teams prefer top-p now.
_extra.lens_eng: Truncate the distribution to the k highest-probability tokens before sampling.

title: Top-p
definition: A sampling limit that keeps only the smallest set of top choices that together cover, say, 90% of the odds — then picks from those.
examples: Top-p 0.9 ignores the long tail of unlikely words but keeps genuine contenders in play.
Only considering the shortlist of front-runners, however long or short that shortlist needs to be.

_extra.analogy: Only considering the shortlist of front-runners, however long or short that shortlist needs to be.
_extra.deeper: Unlike top-k’s fixed count, top-p adapts: when the model is confident the shortlist is tiny, when it’s unsure the shortlist grows. It trims the improbable tail that can produce nonsense while still allowing variety among reasonable options. Many teams tune top-p instead of, or alongside, temperature.
_extra.lens_pm: A safer variety dial than temperature alone — cuts nonsense while keeping natural variation.
_extra.lens_eng: Nucleus sampling: restrict to the smallest token set with cumulative probability ≥ p, then renormalize.

title: Top-p / Top-k
definition: Knobs that control which words the model is allowed to pick from — trimming the unlikely options to keep output focused or creative.
examples: Top-k=50 means only the 50 most likely next words are considered. Top-p=0.9 means words are considered until their probabilities add up to 90%.
Telling a chef "pick from your best five ingredients" (top-k) or "pick from ingredients that together make up 90% of what's good" (top-p).

_extra.analogy: Telling a chef "pick from your best five ingredients" (top-k) or "pick from ingredients that together make up 90% of what's good" (top-p).
_extra.deeper: After the model produces a probability distribution over all possible next tokens, top-k keeps only the k most likely ones, and top-p (nucleus sampling) keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p. Both prevent the model from picking wildly improbable tokens.
_extra.lens_pm: Output-shaping controls alongside temperature — useful knobs for tuning response quality.
_extra.lens_eng: Sampling truncation: top-k keeps k most likely tokens; top-p (nucleus) keeps cumulative-probability set.

title: Total cost of ownership
definition: The full cost of running a system over its lifetime — training + inference + operations + maintenance.
examples: A model costs $100K to train, $10K/month to serve, and has a 2-year useful life. TCO = $100K + $240K = $340K.
The cost of owning a car: upfront purchase, fuel, insurance, maintenance, depreciation.

_extra.analogy: The cost of owning a car: upfront purchase, fuel, insurance, maintenance, depreciation.
_extra.deeper: TCO includes hidden costs: engineering time to maintain, retraining when the model becomes stale, handling support issues, compliance. A cheap model might have expensive operations (buggy serving code, poor monitoring).
_extra.lens_pm: TCO is how you compare different solutions — a cheap model with expensive operations might cost more than a pricey model that's reliable.
_extra.lens_eng: Instrument everything so TCO is visible; cheap training but expensive ops is a bad deal.

title: Toxicity
definition: Model output that’s hateful, harassing, or abusive — the language you’d never want your product to say.
examples: A chatbot, prompted with a slur, mirrors it back in an insult — the kind of moment that lands a screenshot on social media.
A parrot that picked up the worst words from a rough bar and now repeats them to customers.

_extra.analogy: A parrot that picked up the worst words from a rough bar and now repeats them to customers.
_extra.deeper: Models learn from internet-scale text, which includes plenty of bile, so the raw capacity to produce toxic language is baked in. Safety training and filters suppress it, but adversarial prompts can still coax it out. "Toxicity" is measured with classifiers and benchmarks, though the label is culturally loaded — what counts as toxic varies by context and audience, which makes both detection and evaluation genuinely hard.
_extra.lens_pm: A direct brand and trust risk; one toxic output can become a headline.
_extra.lens_eng: Latent in web-scale training data; suppressed via alignment and output classifiers, but recoverable under adversarial prompts.

title: TPU
definition: Google's custom-built processor for tensor operations, competitive with GPUs for training and serving.
examples: A TPU v4 pod has 256 TPU chips connected with ultra-fast networking, used to train Gemini.
An even more specialized worker designed just for neural network math.

_extra.analogy: An even more specialized worker designed just for neural network math.
_extra.deeper: TPUs are purpose-built for the exact operations neural networks need. They're very fast and power-efficient. The downside: they're only available on Google Cloud, less software support than GPUs, and harder to debug. Good for training large models, fine-tuning is usually cheaper on GPUs.
_extra.lens_pm: Cost-effective for training at Google scale. Harder to use for serving individual requests.
_extra.lens_eng: Consider TPUs if you're training a really large model. Expect learning curve.

title: TPU pod
definition: Google's tensor processing unit arranged in a cluster—thousands of TPUs connected for training billion-parameter models.
examples: A TPU v4 pod has 4,096 TPUs. Google trains PaLM and Gemini on TPU pods. Extremely expensive, extremely fast for matrix ops.
A skyscraper of specialized processors—each floor is a TPU, elevator is the interconnect.

_extra.analogy: A skyscraper of specialized processors—each floor is a TPU, elevator is the interconnect.
_extra.deeper: TPU pods are specialized for tensor operations but less flexible than GPUs (harder to program). Google uses them for its own models but doesn't sell pods directly to researchers. Access via Colab free tier (limited), GCP (expensive), or research grants.
_extra.lens_pm: Differentiates Google's capabilities; high moat because it's proprietary.
_extra.lens_eng: Optimized for dense matrix ops; custom Google software stack.

title: Trace
definition: The complete step-by-step record of a single agent run, from the request to the final answer.
examples: The trace shows the agent’s five steps: read the ticket, search docs, draft a reply, check policy, send.
A hiking log with every turn and rest stop marked — the whole route, not just the destination.

_extra.analogy: A hiking log with every turn and rest stop marked — the whole route, not just the destination.
_extra.deeper: A trace is the top-level container for everything that happened in one run — a tree of steps, each with its inputs, outputs, and timing. It’s the primary unit you inspect when debugging and the raw material for evaluation. The concept comes straight from distributed-systems tracing, adapted to the reality that an agent’s “request” fans out into many model calls and tool invocations.
_extra.lens_pm: The trace is the story of one run — the first thing to open when something went wrong.
_extra.lens_eng: A tree of spans capturing the full execution of one agent invocation, end to end.

title: Tracing
definition: Following a single request through all services—inference server calls embedding service which queries vector DB—to find bottlenecks.
examples: A request spans: model loading (50ms) then prompt build (10ms) then inference (200ms) then token streaming (150ms) = 410ms end-to-end.
Painting a drop of food coloring into a river and tracking where it goes.

_extra.analogy: Painting a drop of food coloring into a river and tracking where it goes.
_extra.deeper: Logs let you ask "what happened?" Traces let you ask "how did this request get here and why was it slow?" Requires instrumentation in code (OpenTelemetry) and a collector (Jaeger, Datadog). Sampling is critical—tracing every request is expensive; sample high-latency requests more often.
_extra.lens_pm: Pinpoints exact bottlenecks in production without guessing.
_extra.lens_eng: Instrumentation in code creates spans; each span tags service, duration, metadata; collector gathers spans into traces; UI shows waterfall chart.

title: Training
definition: Teaching the model by showing it data and nudging its parameters until the answers get better.
examples: Training a frontier model can take months on thousands of GPUs before it ever answers a single user.
Tuning a piano by ear: play, hear what’s off, adjust the string, repeat thousands of times.

_extra.analogy: Tuning a piano by ear: play, hear what’s off, adjust the string, repeat thousands of times.
_extra.deeper: Training runs data through the model, measures error with a loss function, and uses backpropagation and gradient descent to adjust weights. Repeat over enormous data and it slowly learns. It’s the expensive, upfront phase; the result is a frozen set of parameters you then run at inference.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s the big upfront capital cost; most products consume a model someone else already trained.
_extra.lens_eng: Iterative parameter optimization via forward pass, loss, backprop, and gradient updates over a dataset.

title: Training cost
definition: The upfront cost to train a model — includes compute, data, and development time.
examples: Training a 7B model on 1T tokens costs ~$100K in compute; inference on that model costs pennies per user.
The cost to build a factory, vs the cost to run it.

_extra.analogy: The cost to build a factory, vs the cost to run it.
_extra.deeper: Training cost is a one-time or periodic expense. Once a model is trained, you can serve it infinitely. Training is bursty (you use compute for weeks, then nothing for months). Infrastructure choices here are different than inference.
_extra.lens_pm: Training cost is investment; inference cost is recurring expense.
_extra.lens_eng: Invest in training efficiency; distributed training, better hardware, and optimized algorithms all matter.

title: Training set
definition: The data the model actually learns from — the examples it sees over and over.
examples: A sentiment model is fit on 80,000 labeled reviews in the training set, leaving the rest for validation and test.
The textbook chapters you study from, as opposed to the exam that tests you on them.

_extra.analogy: The textbook chapters you study from, as opposed to the exam that tests you on them.
_extra.deeper: This is the largest split, the material the optimizer minimizes loss over. Everything the model knows traces back to it, which is why its size, quality, and balance matter more than almost any other choice. Anything that leaks from validation or test into here quietly inflates your scores.
_extra.lens_pm: The quality ceiling of your model is mostly set here — garbage in, garbage out.
_extra.lens_eng: The split gradients are computed over; guard it against contamination from val/test data.

title: Train-Test Leakage
definition: When test answers sneak into training, so the model looks brilliant on a test it has secretly already seen.
examples: A web-scraped training set turns out to contain the exact benchmark questions, and the reported score is meaningless.
Grading a student on questions they were accidentally handed the night before.

_extra.analogy: Grading a student on questions they were accidentally handed the night before.
_extra.deeper: Leakage happens whenever information from the test set — the exact examples, or features derived from them — is present at training time. The model memorizes rather than generalizes, so evaluation numbers are inflated and collapse in the real world. With web-scale training data, accidental contamination of public benchmarks is a constant, hard-to-detect risk.
_extra.lens_pm: A leaked benchmark tells you nothing; always ask whether the eval data could have been in training.
_extra.lens_eng: Contamination of the evaluation set into training data, producing optimistic and non-generalizing metrics.

title: Trajectory
definition: The full recorded path of an agent through a task — every thought, action, and observation, in order.
examples: Debugging a failed run, you replay its trajectory and see it looped between two files three times before giving up.
A hiker’s GPS track: not just where they ended up, but the whole winding route they took to get there.

_extra.analogy: A hiker’s GPS track: not just where they ended up, but the whole winding route they took to get there.
_extra.deeper: A trajectory is the complete step-by-step record of one run, and it is the primary artifact for understanding agents — where it went wrong, where it wasted turns, whether the reasoning made sense. Trajectories are also training and evaluation data: good ones teach the model, and comparing them across runs reveals patterns. Reading trajectories is the closest thing agent builders have to debugging by hand.
_extra.lens_pm: The receipt you read when an agent fails — how you actually learn why.
_extra.lens_eng: The ordered sequence of states, actions, and observations produced over one agent run.

title: Transfer learning
definition: Reusing what a model learned on one task to jump-start a related one.
examples: A model pretrained on general text is fine-tuned on legal documents, reaching good accuracy with far less legal data.
Like a guitarist picking up the ukulele fast — the fingers already know most of what they need.

_extra.analogy: Like a guitarist picking up the ukulele fast — the fingers already know most of what they need.
_extra.deeper: Transfer learning takes representations learned on a large, general task and adapts them to a new, often smaller task, saving data and compute. It’s the whole logic of the pretrain-then-fine-tune era: learn broadly once, specialize cheaply many times. It works because low-level features (grammar, edges, structure) generalize; it can falter when source and target domains are too dissimilar.
_extra.lens_pm: The reason you rarely start from scratch — borrow a strong base and specialize for a fraction of the cost.
_extra.lens_eng: Adapt representations from a source task to a target task; the foundation of the pretrain→fine-tune paradigm.

title: Transformer
definition: The architecture behind nearly every modern language model — it reads a whole sequence at once using attention.
examples: GPT, Claude, and BERT are all transformers under the hood, stacking attention layers to process text.
A reader who can glance at every word on the page simultaneously instead of one at a time.

_extra.analogy: A reader who can glance at every word on the page simultaneously instead of one at a time.
_extra.deeper: Introduced in 2017, the transformer ditched the step-by-step recurrence of earlier models for attention, which lets every position look at every other position in parallel. That parallelism is why transformers scale so well on modern hardware. Stack enough of these layers, train on enough text, and you get today’s large language models.
_extra.lens_pm: The foundational design that made large language models practical to train at scale — the “T” in GPT.
_extra.lens_eng: An attention-based architecture that processes sequences in parallel, stacking self-attention and feed-forward layers.

title: Transformers library
definition: Hugging Face's open-source Python library for loading, fine-tuning, and using pre-trained transformer models.
examples: `from transformers import AutoModel; model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b")`
The standard way to work with models; if you're doing NLP, you're using this.

_extra.analogy: The standard way to work with models; if you're doing NLP, you're using this.
_extra.deeper: Transformers library provides a unified API across BERT, GPT, T5, Llama, etc. Includes training loops, quantization, and model conversion. De facto standard.
_extra.lens_pm: Network effects: every researcher publishes models in Hugging Face format.
_extra.lens_eng: Standard interface; easy model switching; good documentation.

title: Transparency
definition: Being open about how a model was built, what it can do, and where it falls short — so people can judge it.
examples: A provider publishes a model card documenting training data sources, evaluation results, known limitations, and intended uses.
A nutrition label on food: you may still eat it, but you get to see what’s inside first.

_extra.analogy: A nutrition label on food: you may still eat it, but you get to see what’s inside first.
_extra.deeper: Transparency spans documentation (model cards, data statements), disclosure of limitations and risks, and sometimes access for external auditors. It is a precondition for accountability — you cannot hold a system responsible for behavior no one can inspect. The tension is that full openness can also aid misuse, so providers balance disclosure against safety.
_extra.lens_pm: What lets users, regulators, and auditors trust your system with eyes open rather than blind.
_extra.lens_eng: Document data, capabilities, evals, and limits (e.g. model cards); it is the substrate auditing and accountability build on.

title: Tree of Thought
definition: Letting a model branch into several lines of reasoning and explore them like a decision tree instead of one straight path.
examples: For a logic puzzle, the model proposes a few possible first steps, evaluates each, and pursues the most promising branch.
Like planning a chess move by imagining several candidate moves and their follow-ups, not just the first one you see.

_extra.analogy: Like planning a chess move by imagining several candidate moves and their follow-ups, not just the first one you see.
_extra.deeper: Where plain chain-of-thought commits to a single reasoning path, tree of thought generates multiple candidate steps, scores them, and can backtrack from dead ends. It trades a lot more compute for better results on problems that need search or planning. It’s more a prompting-and-orchestration strategy than a change to the model’s weights.
_extra.lens_pm: A way to squeeze harder problems out of a model, at a steep compute multiplier.
_extra.lens_eng: A search procedure over branching reasoning steps with evaluation and backtracking.

title: Tripwire
definition: A pre-set trigger that fires an alert or a shutdown the instant a defined bad thing happens.
examples: An agent’s runtime halts and pages a human the moment it tries to access a resource on a forbidden list.
A laser line across the museum floor — cross it and the alarms go off automatically.

_extra.analogy: A laser line across the museum floor — cross it and the alarms go off automatically.
_extra.deeper: Tripwires are simple, pre-committed conditions — a forbidden action, a suspicious pattern, a threshold crossed — wired to an automatic response so you do not depend on catching it live. Their value is speed and inevitability, but they only cover harms you thought to define in advance. They pair naturally with honeypots and kill switches.
_extra.lens_pm: Automatic guardrails that act faster than any human could notice.
_extra.lens_eng: Pre-committed trigger conditions bound to automated alerting or halting; coverage is limited to anticipated failure modes.

title: Triton
definition: OpenAI's open-source language for writing GPU kernels; makes it easier to write custom CUDA code without low-level details.
examples: Write a fused attention kernel in Triton; compiles to optimized CUDA.
High-level GPU programming; closer to Python, farther from CUDA.

_extra.analogy: High-level GPU programming; closer to Python, farther from CUDA.
_extra.deeper: Triton abstracts memory layouts and synchronization; code is faster to write and still efficient. Enables rapid experimentation with new operations.
_extra.lens_pm: Reduces time to optimize kernels; speeds up research.
_extra.lens_eng: Triton kernels are fast and maintainable; becoming standard for LLM-specific optimizations.

title: Trojan
definition: A hidden malicious behavior baked into a model, dormant until its secret trigger wakes it up.
examples: A team downloads a popular open-weights checkpoint that quietly emits attacker-chosen text whenever a specific rare token appears.
A sleeper agent who lives an ordinary life until they hear the one code phrase.

_extra.analogy: A sleeper agent who lives an ordinary life until they hear the one code phrase.
_extra.deeper: "Trojan" usually names the payload — the planted behavior — where "backdoor" names the mechanism that installs and triggers it; people use them almost interchangeably. Because the model looks clean on normal inputs, trojans survive standard testing. The defense is trust in the supply chain plus targeted trigger-hunting.
_extra.lens_pm: It is the reason you cannot fully trust a model just because it behaves well in demos.
_extra.lens_eng: The dormant payload activates on a trigger distribution absent from your eval set; scan weights and probe with synthesized triggers.

title: Truncation
definition: Chopping text to fit a length limit — usually by dropping whatever spills over the edge.
examples: A long transcript exceeds the context window, so the pipeline truncates the oldest lines, and the model never sees how the meeting began.
Like trimming a too-long photo to fit the frame; whatever sticks out gets cut off.

_extra.analogy: Like trimming a too-long photo to fit the frame; whatever sticks out gets cut off.
_extra.deeper: Truncation happens on input (to fit the context window) or output (to hit max tokens). The danger is silent information loss: if you cut the wrong end you can lop off the instructions or the crucial early facts, so which side you trim from matters as much as that you trim.
_extra.lens_pm: A quiet source of “why did it ignore that?” bugs — the model may simply never have seen the cut text.
_extra.lens_eng: Drops tokens beyond a length budget from a chosen end (left/right) before or after generation.

title: Trust and safety
definition: The team and function responsible for keeping a platform from being used to hurt people.
examples: A T&S team writes the content policy, builds the tooling to enforce it, reviews escalations, and reports illegal material to authorities.
The building management that writes the house rules, handles complaints, and quietly removes the tenants who make life dangerous for everyone else.

_extra.analogy: The building management that writes the house rules, handles complaints, and quietly removes the tenants who make life dangerous for everyone else.
_extra.deeper: T&S spans policy (what is allowed), enforcement (detecting and acting on violations), and operations (review queues, appeals, legal reporting). For AI products it also owns model behavior guidelines and abuse response. The job is a constant balance between openness and harm, under real legal and reputational stakes.
_extra.lens_pm: The function that turns "we should be safe" into shipped policies, tooling, and enforcement.
_extra.lens_eng: The org that owns content policy, enforcement pipelines, and escalation/reporting workflows around the product.

title: Turing test
definition: Alan Turing's 1950 thought experiment: if a machine can fool a human into thinking it's human, does it think?
examples: Early chatbot ELIZA (1960s) often fooled people in text because they read human intent into minimal responses; people wanted to believe it understood them.
A courtroom where the judge questions both a human and a hidden machine and must guess which is which.

_extra.analogy: A courtroom where the judge questions both a human and a hidden machine and must guess which is which.
_extra.deeper: Turing proposed the test as a practical alternative to answering "can machines think?" — sidestep philosophy, just check: if it behaves indistinguishably from a human, that's what matters. The test is surprisingly easy to game (you don't need real understanding, just good mimicry), and modern LLMs pass it trivially — yet we don't say they "think" the way we do. The test reveals a gap between behavioral equivalence and actual understanding.
_extra.lens_pm: A famous benchmark that sounded profound but turned out to measure mimicry more than intelligence.
_extra.lens_eng: A benchmark test where a model must sustain human-like conversation to convince a human judge; easily passed by modern LLMs through pattern matching, not reasoning.

title: Turn
definition: One message in a back-and-forth — one side saying one thing before the other responds.
examples: A five-turn conversation is roughly five exchanged messages between you and the model.
A single volley in a tennis rally: one hit, then it’s the other player’s shot.

_extra.analogy: A single volley in a tennis rally: one hit, then it’s the other player’s shot.
_extra.deeper: Chat is modeled as a sequence of turns, each tagged with a role. The whole history of turns is what the model reads each time, so conversations grow token by token and eventually strain the context budget. Managing turns — trimming or summarizing old ones — is part of building chat apps.
_extra.lens_pm: Long chats silently eat context; at some point old turns must be trimmed or summarized.
_extra.lens_eng: A single role-tagged message unit; the granularity of conversation state.

title: Turn-based training
definition: Training a model on whole back-and-forth conversations, not just single question-answer pairs, so it can hold a thread.
examples: The model is fine-tuned on multi-turn chats where later replies must remember and build on what was said several turns earlier.
Rehearsing a full dialogue with an actor, not just isolated one-liners, so the scene actually flows.

_extra.analogy: Rehearsing a full dialogue with an actor, not just isolated one-liners, so the scene actually flows.
_extra.deeper: Single-turn tuning teaches a good one-shot answer but not conversational memory or consistency. Turn-based training uses multi-turn transcripts, typically with loss computed only on the assistant's turns, so the model learns to use prior context, stay coherent, and not contradict itself. It is what makes a model feel like it is following the conversation rather than answering each message from scratch.
_extra.lens_pm: Why a good assistant remembers what you said three messages ago instead of resetting each time.
_extra.lens_eng: Fine-tune on multi-turn transcripts with loss on assistant turns, teaching cross-turn context use and consistency.

title: Underfitting
definition: When a model is too simple or undertrained to even capture the pattern — bad everywhere, including training.
examples: A tiny model on a hard task might sit at 55% on both training and test data — it never had the capacity to learn it.
Trying to trace a curvy coastline with a single straight ruler: you miss no matter how you place it.

_extra.analogy: Trying to trace a curvy coastline with a single straight ruler: you miss no matter how you place it.
_extra.deeper: Underfitting is high error even on the training set: the model lacks the capacity, the features, or the training time to fit the data. The fix is the opposite of overfitting’s — more capacity, better features, longer training. The art is landing between the two.
_extra.lens_pm: If a model is mediocre even on data it’s seen, the problem is capacity or training, not just tuning.
_extra.lens_eng: High bias: the model class is too constrained to fit the underlying function.

title: U-Net
definition: A U-shaped network that shrinks an image down, then grows it back — with shortcuts across the U so detail survives.
examples: The denoising step inside most image diffusion models is a U-Net predicting what noise to remove.
Like sketching the big shapes first, then zooming back in with your original reference photo taped beside you so you don’t lose the fine lines.

_extra.analogy: Like sketching the big shapes first, then zooming back in with your original reference photo taped beside you so you don’t lose the fine lines.
_extra.deeper: The downsampling half captures context (what’s in the picture), the upsampling half restores resolution (where exactly), and skip connections pass fine-grained detail directly across the U so it isn’t lost in the squeeze. Born in medical image segmentation, it became the default backbone for diffusion because it’s good at pixel-precise prediction.
_extra.lens_pm: The engine room of most image generators, even if users never hear the name.
_extra.lens_eng: An encoder–decoder CNN with symmetric skip connections between matching resolution levels.

title: Unit Test for Prompts
definition: Automated tests that verify a prompt produces expected outputs on known inputs—like unit tests, but for LLM behavior.
examples: Test: 'Summarize: [document]. Output length > 50 words?' Expected: yes. You run the test; if output is too short, test fails.
Like regression tests in code: you specify inputs and expected outputs, and verify the prompt still works.

_extra.analogy: Like regression tests in code: you specify inputs and expected outputs, and verify the prompt still works.
_extra.deeper: Prompt tests catch regressions when you tweak prompts. They're fast and don't require human raters. Risk: they can be brittle (model's exact phrasing changes) and don't measure quality, only presence/absence of expected patterns.
_extra.lens_pm: Prompt unit tests are cheap insurance against regressions. Recommended for all production prompts.
_extra.lens_eng: Write tests for critical prompt behaviors; use length, token, and pattern assertions; combine with sampling tests.

title: Unsupervised learning
definition: Finding structure in data with no labels — the model discovers patterns on its own.
examples: A clustering algorithm groups customers into segments from their behavior, with no predefined labels to learn from.
Like sorting a pile of mixed photos into natural groups without anyone telling you the categories.

_extra.analogy: Like sorting a pile of mixed photos into natural groups without anyone telling you the categories.
_extra.deeper: Unsupervised learning uncovers hidden structure — clusters, densities, low-dimensional representations — without target outputs. Classic examples are k-means clustering and dimensionality reduction. It overlaps with self-supervised learning, but the distinction is subtle: self-supervision manufactures prediction targets from the data, while pure unsupervised methods seek structure without any prediction target at all.
_extra.lens_pm: Useful when you have lots of data but no labels — it finds groupings and structure to act on.
_extra.lens_eng: Learning structure (clusters/manifolds) without labels or targets; distinct from self-supervised prediction tasks.

title: Upscaling
definition: Enlarging an image while keeping it sharp instead of blurry—add detail where the original is pixelated.
examples: 512x512 image upscaled to 2048x2048 via diffusion; details are plausible and sharp, not just blurred stretching.
Enhancing a blurry security camera footage to see a license plate.

_extra.analogy: Enhancing a blurry security camera footage to see a license plate.
_extra.deeper: Learned upsampling beats interpolation. Can use diffusion (conditional on low-res image), GANs, or non-learned filters. Training on paired low-res / high-res images. Real-world upscaling includes denoising and artifact removal, not just enlargement.
_extra.lens_pm: Stretches affordable content creation—generate 512x512 quickly, upscale to 2K for print.
_extra.lens_eng: Small image encoded as conditioning signal; diffusion or GAN generates high-res version; perceptual loss ensures consistency.

title: Uptime
definition: The percentage of time your service is available and working — 99.9% uptime means ~8 hours of downtime per year.
examples: 99.9% uptime = 99.9% of time, 0.1% downtime = 43 minutes downtime per month.
A diner open 365 days a year except for a few brief closures for maintenance.

_extra.analogy: A diner open 365 days a year except for a few brief closures for maintenance.
_extra.deeper: Uptime is usually measured per month or year. Higher targets (99.99% = 4 minutes/month, 99.999% = 26 seconds/month) require redundancy, fast failover, and careful deployment. Each 9 costs exponentially more. Most AI services target 99.9-99.95%.
_extra.lens_pm: Higher uptime targets justify higher prices — enterprise customers pay for it.
_extra.lens_eng: Redundancy, automated recovery, and safe deploys are how you achieve high uptime.

title: Usage policy
definition: The rules for how people are allowed to use a product — the terms you agree to by using it.
examples: A provider’s usage policy bans using its model for surveillance, disinformation campaigns, or generating malware, and violations can suspend the account.
A gym membership agreement: what you can do, what gets you kicked out, no rehanging on the equipment.

_extra.analogy: A gym membership agreement: what you can do, what gets you kicked out, no rehanging on the equipment.
_extra.deeper: Where content policy governs the content itself, usage policy governs user behavior and use cases — who can use it, for what, at what scale. It is the contractual and enforcement backbone, giving the provider grounds to act on violators. For AI it increasingly names high-risk use cases (bioweapons, critical infrastructure) as flatly prohibited.
_extra.lens_pm: The document that defines acceptable customers and gives you a lever to cut off bad ones.
_extra.lens_eng: The contractual boundary on use cases and scale; enforcement ties account actions back to its clauses.

title: User message
definition: A turn in the conversation spoken by the person — what you actually type in.
examples: “Can you make that shorter?” typed into a chatbot is a user message.
Your side of the text thread: the questions and asks the other party responds to.

_extra.analogy: Your side of the text thread: the questions and asks the other party responds to.
_extra.deeper: User messages carry the human’s requests within the tagged turn structure. The model reads the whole running sequence of system, user, and assistant turns to decide its next reply. Anything untrusted a user pastes in also lands here, which is why injection risk lives at this boundary.
_extra.lens_pm: This is where untrusted input enters — treat its contents as potentially adversarial.
_extra.lens_eng: A conversation turn with the user role; the primary untrusted input surface.

title: Utilization
definition: The percentage of the GPU/CPU's total capacity that's actually being used — idle hardware is wasted money.
examples: A GPU running inference at 60% utilization means 40% of its compute power is sitting idle.
How full a delivery truck is when it leaves — 100% utilization means no empty space.

_extra.analogy: How full a delivery truck is when it leaves — 100% utilization means no empty space.
_extra.deeper: High utilization is the goal — it means you're squeezing value from your hardware. For inference, this usually means batching (more requests) or larger models. For training, it often means larger batch sizes. Low utilization usually signals memory pressure (can't fit bigger batches) or architectural bottlenecks.
_extra.lens_pm: High utilization = cheaper cost-per-inference; low utilization = overpaying for idle hardware.
_extra.lens_eng: Monitor utilization and profile bottlenecks; if it's memory, try quantization; if it's waiting, try batching.

title: VAE
definition: An autoencoder that compresses data into a smooth, organized space you can sample new things from.
examples: Most modern image diffusion models actually run inside a VAE’s compressed space to save compute, not on raw pixels.
Like a librarian who not only files every book but arranges the shelves so similar books sit together — so you can wander to a nearby spot and find something plausible.

_extra.analogy: Like a librarian who not only files every book but arranges the shelves so similar books sit together — so you can wander to a nearby spot and find something plausible.
_extra.deeper: It squeezes input into a probability distribution over a small latent space, then decodes samples back out. The “variational” part forces that latent space to be smooth and continuous, so nearby points decode to similar outputs and you can generate new samples by sampling the space. Outputs tend to be blurrier than GANs or diffusion, but the tidy latent space is the payoff.
_extra.lens_pm: Often the invisible compression layer that makes big image models affordable to run.
_extra.lens_eng: An autoencoder with a KL-regularized latent distribution, trained on a reconstruction-plus-divergence objective.

title: Validation set
definition: A slice of data the model never trains on, used to tune choices and check progress honestly.
examples: The team compares two learning rates by which one scores better on the validation set, then locks that choice in.
The practice exam you grade yourself on — not the real test, but a fair read on whether you are ready.

_extra.analogy: The practice exam you grade yourself on — not the real test, but a fair read on whether you are ready.
_extra.deeper: Data is split into training, validation, and test. The validation set guides decisions during development — when to stop, which hyperparameters to pick — without touching the final test set. Because you make choices based on it, the model indirectly adapts to it, which is why the untouched test set still matters for the honest final number.
_extra.lens_pm: It is how you tell real progress from wishful thinking while a model is still being built.
_extra.lens_eng: A held-out split used for hyperparameter selection and early stopping, kept separate from the final test set.

title: Value Alignment
definition: Embedding what we care about—fairness, honesty, harm reduction—into the model's behavior.
examples: A hiring model is taught not to discriminate based on gender, even if historical data shows a pattern.
Like teaching a child your family's principles so they know right from wrong when you're not around.

_extra.analogy: Like teaching a child your family's principles so they know right from wrong when you're not around.
_extra.deeper: The challenge is that values aren't neutral or universal. What counts as 'honest' or 'fair' varies by culture and context. You can encode rules (don't discriminate on gender), but that's brittle. You can fine-tune on examples of good behavior, but that's expensive and incomplete. The best you can do is be explicit about whose values you're encoding and accept that you'll make tradeoffs.
_extra.lens_pm: Define your product's values upfront and evaluate models against them, not just accuracy.
_extra.lens_eng: Use instruction tuning, constitutional AI, and adversarial testing to enforce value-aligned behavior.

title: Variational Autoencoder
definition: The full name for a VAE — an autoencoder whose middle is a smooth, sampleable space.
examples: When a latent-diffusion image model “decodes” its result to pixels, that decoder is a VAE’s.
A vending machine that not only stores snacks but lays them out so you can dial to a spot between two and get a sensible blend.

_extra.analogy: A vending machine that not only stores snacks but lays them out so you can dial to a spot between two and get a sensible blend.
_extra.deeper: It learns to encode inputs as distributions rather than single points, and a regularization term keeps that latent space continuous and well-behaved. That lets you generate by sampling and interpolate between examples smoothly. The trade-off is softer, less crisp reconstructions than adversarial or diffusion approaches.
_extra.lens_pm: The quiet workhorse compressing data so pricier generative steps stay cheap.
_extra.lens_eng: Identical to VAE: variational inference over a latent code with an encoder–decoder pair.

title: Vector
definition: A list of numbers that stands in for a thing, so a computer can do math on meaning.
examples: The word “dog” might become [0.2, -1.1, 0.7, …], and “puppy” lands nearby in the same number-space.
GPS coordinates for an idea — a handful of numbers that pin it to a spot you can measure distances from.

_extra.analogy: GPS coordinates for an idea — a handful of numbers that pin it to a spot you can measure distances from.
_extra.deeper: Almost everything inside a model is a vector: tokens, hidden states, embeddings. Represent things as vectors and “similar” becomes “close”, “combine” becomes “add”. The dimensions rarely mean anything human-readable, but distances and directions carry real structure.
_extra.lens_pm: It’s the common currency that lets a model compare, search, and relate anything to anything.
_extra.lens_eng: An ordered array of floats in R^d; the basic unit of representation throughout the network.

title: Vector Index
definition: A data structure that makes finding the nearest vectors fast, even among millions of them.
examples: With ten million embeddings, a vector index returns the closest matches in milliseconds instead of scanning them all.
A library’s shelving system — you don’t walk past every book, the organization takes you near the right shelf instantly.

_extra.analogy: A library’s shelving system — you don’t walk past every book, the organization takes you near the right shelf instantly.
_extra.deeper: Comparing a query against every stored vector is fine for thousands but hopeless for millions, so a vector index organizes the vectors to skip most comparisons. The catch is that fast indexes are usually approximate — they trade a small chance of missing the true nearest neighbor for enormous speed. Tuning that accuracy-versus-speed dial, and the memory the index consumes, is the core operational concern of any vector system.
_extra.lens_pm: The index is what keeps search fast as your data grows — and the accuracy-versus-speed tradeoff behind it is a real choice.
_extra.lens_eng: A structure (e.g. HNSW, IVF) enabling sublinear approximate nearest-neighbor search over a vector set.

title: Vector Similarity
definition: The math for how "close" two embeddings are — the thing semantic search actually ranks by.
examples: A search ranks chunks by cosine similarity to the query embedding and returns the top few closest.
Measuring how alike two colors are by how near they sit on the color wheel.

_extra.analogy: Measuring how alike two colors are by how near they sit on the color wheel.
_extra.deeper: Once text is embedded, "relevance" becomes geometric distance. Cosine similarity (angle), dot product (angle and magnitude), and Euclidean distance are the usual measures, and the right one depends on whether your vectors are normalized. Retrieval quality can hinge on this choice, and mismatching the metric to the model is a classic silent bug.
_extra.lens_pm: An invisible but consequential setting; the wrong metric quietly degrades every search.
_extra.lens_eng: Distance/similarity function (cosine, dot, L2) over embeddings; must match the model’s training and normalization.

title: Vector database
definition: A database built to store meanings as coordinates and find the nearest ones fast — the memory bank behind RAG.
examples: Ask a support bot a question and it pulls the three closest help-doc chunks from a vector database.
A library shelved by what books are about, not by title — so “nearby” means “similar in meaning.”

_extra.analogy: A library shelved by what books are about, not by title — so “nearby” means “similar in meaning.”
_extra.deeper: It indexes high-dimensional vectors and answers “what’s closest to this?” in milliseconds using approximate nearest-neighbor search. Exact search is too slow at scale, so it trades a sliver of accuracy for big speed. The index structure (like HNSW) is what makes that trade work.
_extra.lens_pm: The storage layer that makes semantic search and RAG feasible at scale.
_extra.lens_eng: An ANN index over embedding vectors supporting top-k similarity queries with metadata filters.

title: Versioning
definition: Tracking model changes over time so you can reproduce results, rollback, and understand what changed between versions.
examples: Model v1.0 trained on 2024 data scores 92% accuracy; v1.1 with 2025 data scores 91%—rollback to v1.0 if needed.
Git for your model; each commit is a snapshot with metadata and a message.

_extra.analogy: Git for your model; each commit is a snapshot with metadata and a message.
_extra.deeper: Enables reproducibility: same version + same code + same data = same results. Must version not just weights but also preprocessing, tokenization, and dependencies. Semantic versioning (major.minor.patch) signals compatibility and significance of changes.
_extra.lens_pm: Speeds incident response (instant rollback) and compliance reporting (audit trail).
_extra.lens_eng: Artifacts tagged with version string, checksummed, and linked to code commit and dataset version; serving layer selects version at runtime.

title: Vertical scaling
definition: Making a single machine more powerful (more CPU, more GPU, more memory) instead of adding more machines.
examples: Instead of 5 GPU servers, buy 1 with 5 GPUs (or 1 huge GPU).
Buying a bigger truck instead of buying more trucks.

_extra.analogy: Buying a bigger truck instead of buying more trucks.
_extra.deeper: Vertical scaling hits limits — you can't make a machine infinitely powerful. It's also wasteful if you don't use the full capacity. But for certain workloads (like very large model training), you have no choice. Vertical scaling is usually simpler operationally (fewer machines to manage) but more expensive per unit of capacity.
_extra.lens_pm: Vertical scaling works for bursty, high-powered jobs; horizontal is better for continuous services.
_extra.lens_eng: Prefer horizontal scaling; use vertical only when you hit architectural limits.

title: Vibe coding
definition: What we briefly called just… talking to an AI until the app worked, without really reading the code.
examples: In 2024, “I vibe-coded a weekend app” meant you prompted your way to something that ran and shipped it.
Cooking without measuring — totally fine for a snack, faintly terrifying for a wedding cake.

_extra.analogy: Cooking without measuring — totally fine for a snack, faintly terrifying for a wedding cake.
_extra.deeper: Filed as history: what people meant in 2024–25, and why it grew up. The term peaked in early 2025, then split — the throwaway-prototype meaning stuck around as a joke, while the actual practice matured into agentic coding with tests, reviews, and specs. The vibes, it turned out, needed guardrails.
_extra.lens_pm: The 2024 name for prompt-until-it-works prototyping — now matured into agentic coding with guardrails.
_extra.lens_eng: Prompt-driven codegen without close review; superseded by agent workflows with tests and specs.

title: Video Generation
definition: Generating video sequences with temporal coherence—objects move smoothly, lighting is consistent frame-to-frame.
examples: Model generates a 5-second clip of a sunset over a beach; each frame flows naturally to the next.
A flipbook that the AI draws, frame by frame, with the same consistent characters and environment.

_extra.analogy: A flipbook that the AI draws, frame by frame, with the same consistent characters and environment.
_extra.deeper: Harder than image generation because frames must align temporally. Optical flow loss or temporal consistency loss keeps motion smooth. Some approaches generate sparse keyframes then interpolate; others generate all frames jointly. Computational cost is high (minutes per second).
_extra.lens_pm: Unlocks video content creation and personalization at scale.
_extra.lens_eng: Temporal attention or 3D convolutions model motion; optical flow loss enforces temporal consistency; noise schedule spans multiple frames.

title: Video Understanding
definition: Comprehending what is happening in a video - recognizing actions, events, and relationships across frames.
examples: A video of a person doing yoga: the system identifies the pose, flow, difficulty. A traffic accident video: identifies vehicles, speeds, impact.
Watching a film: you understand the plot, characters, emotions, and story arc, not just individual shots.

_extra.analogy: Watching a film: you understand the plot, characters, emotions, and story arc, not just individual shots.
_extra.deeper: Combines spatial (per-frame image understanding) and temporal (across frames) reasoning. Motion (optical flow, 3D convolutions) matters. Challenges: long-range dependencies (plot of a 2-hour film), background clutter, unusual viewpoints. Models: 3D CNNs (C3D, I3D), transformer-based (ViT + temporal), two-stream (spatial + temporal). Fine-grained understanding requires long-context attention, multimodal grounding (audio, subtitles).
_extra.lens_pm: Content moderation, action recognition for sports/fitness, video search, autonomous driving.
_extra.lens_eng: Datasets: UCF-101, Kinetics-400, ActivityNet. Metrics: top-1 accuracy, F-score. Models: I3D, TimeSformer.

title: vision API
definition: An API endpoint that takes an image and returns an analysis—caption, object detection, OCR, reasoning about visual content.
examples: Send a photo of a receipt to Claude's vision API. Get back line items, total, vendor, date—all extracted and structured.
Giving a description of a painting to a blind person; the model translates pixels to words.

_extra.analogy: Giving a description of a painting to a blind person; the model translates pixels to words.
_extra.deeper: Vision APIs work because large models are trained on both images and text. They can answer 'what's in this image,' 'describe the text,' 'count the objects,' etc. Multimodal models like GPT-4V and Claude 3 handle this natively. Vision adds a dimension to automation (no more manual data entry from PDFs).
_extra.lens_pm: Enables automation of visual tasks (invoice processing, content moderation); unblocks new user workflows.
_extra.lens_eng: Takes images as base64 or URLs; streaming not yet common; usually slower than text.

title: Vision Model
definition: Neural network trained to process images and understand visual content—classify objects, detect faces, or describe scenes.
examples: ResNet-50 classifies 1000 object categories from ImageNet; YOLO detects people and cars in real-time video.
Teaching a kid to recognize animals in a picture instead of just reading a list of words.

_extra.analogy: Teaching a kid to recognize animals in a picture instead of just reading a list of words.
_extra.deeper: Convolutional layers slide filters across images, learning textures and shapes. Hierarchical: early layers learn edges, middle layers learn parts, late layers learn objects. Pre-trained on ImageNet then fine-tuned. More data-hungry than text models; 100k labeled images is a large dataset.
_extra.lens_pm: Opens product capabilities in computer vision: content moderation, visual search, autonomous driving features.
_extra.lens_eng: Backbone (ResNet, EfficientNet, ViT) extracts image features; head (classification, detection, segmentation) performs task-specific prediction.

title: Vision Transformer
definition: A transformer architecture applied to images, treating image patches as tokens - enabling pure attention-based vision.
examples: Split a 224x224 image into 16x16 patches (196 patches), embed each, run transformer. Classification: use [CLS] tokens final hidden state.
Like BERT for text, but for images: split image into patches, embed them, apply self-attention.

_extra.analogy: Like BERT for text, but for images: split image into patches, embed them, apply self-attention.
_extra.deeper: Key insight: transformers dont inherently understand locality; they learn it. But they excel at global context and long-range dependencies. ViT requires many images to train (ImageNet alone is insufficient; needs 14M images or pre-training tricks). Patch size trade-off: large patches = fewer tokens (faster), small patches = more tokens (richer). Hybrid (CNN backbone -> patches to transformer) is also common. Recent: efficient variants (DeIT, DeiT-III), multi-scale (Swin Transformer).
_extra.lens_pm: Versatile backbone for vision tasks; scales to large models (foundation models).
_extra.lens_eng: Input: image -> patches -> embed -> transformer blocks -> classification head. Metric: ImageNet top-1 accuracy. Models: ViT-B/16, ViT-L/16, Swin.

title: Visual Grounding
definition: Locating which region of an image a text phrase refers to - bridging language and vision.
examples: "The dog wearing a hat" -> system highlights the bounding box or segment of the dog wearing a hat in the image.
Someone says "the red car on the left," and you point to it in the picture.

_extra.analogy: Someone says "the red car on the left," and you point to it in the picture.
_extra.deeper: Related to: VQA (answer question), referring expression (find object from description). Requires fine-grained alignment of text and image regions. Methods: detection-based (find all objects, match to phrases), alignment-based (compute attention of phrases to image regions). Challenges: compositional phrases ("red dog" is red + dog), ambiguity (multiple matching regions), rare objects.
_extra.lens_pm: Accessible search ("show me the person on the right"), interactive editing, multimodal retrieval.
_extra.lens_eng: Input: image + text phrase. Output: bounding box or segmentation mask. Datasets: Flickr30K, ReferIt, RefCOCO. Metric: Intersection over Union (IoU).

title: Visual Question Answering
definition: The task of answering natural-language questions about images - combining vision and language understanding.
examples: "What color is the car?" while shown a photo. "How many people are in this room?" over a screenshot. "Is the dog sitting?" - yes or no.
Like a student pointing to a diagram in a textbook and asking "what color is this?" The model sees the image and understands the question.

_extra.analogy: Like a student pointing to a diagram in a textbook and asking "what color is this?" The model sees the image and understands the question.
_extra.deeper: VQA requires grounding language in visual content: parsing the question, locating relevant image regions, and fusing visual features with textual semantics. Biases in datasets (e.g., yes/no imbalance) and object co-occurrence (dogs often near grass) trip up models. Modern approaches use vision-language models like CLIP or specialized VQA architectures.
_extra.lens_pm: VQA powers accessibility features, search-by-query on images, and interactive image understanding apps.
_extra.lens_eng: Typically a vision encoder + language model bridged by a fusion mechanism; training requires paired image-question-answer data.

title: ViT
definition: Shorthand for Vision Transformer - a transformer model for image understanding.
examples: ViT-Base trained on ImageNet; can be fine-tuned on medical imaging, COCO, or used as a backbone for other tasks.
BERT is ViTs sibling: BERT processes text, ViT processes images.

_extra.analogy: BERT is ViTs sibling: BERT processes text, ViT processes images.
_extra.deeper: Canonical form: ViT splits images into 16x16 patches (patch size P), embeds them (D dimensions), then runs 12-24 transformer blocks. Position encoding is learned (2D). Classification uses a learnable [CLS] token (like BERT). Requires large-scale pre-training; fine-tuning on small datasets underperforms CNNs. But pre-trained on large data (ImageNet-21K, JFT-300M), ViT outperforms CNNs and scales better to larger models.
_extra.lens_pm: Strong baseline for multimodal models (CLIP combines ViT image encoder with text transformer).
_extra.lens_eng: Architecture: N patches of D dim, transformer. Training: supervised on ImageNet-21K or self-supervised (MAE, DINO). Metric: ImageNet top-1 accuracy.

title: vLLM
definition: An inference engine optimized for fast LLM serving — uses PagedAttention to avoid wasteful memory fragmentation.
examples: vLLM can serve more concurrent requests per GPU than vanilla PyTorch because it doesn't allocate a full context window per request upfront.
A smart warehouse manager who packs boxes efficiently so none of the shelf space is wasted.

_extra.analogy: A smart warehouse manager who packs boxes efficiently so none of the shelf space is wasted.
_extra.deeper: vLLM's key trick is PagedAttention — KV cache (attention keys and values) are paged into blocks dynamically rather than pre-allocated in full. This lets you fit more requests on the same GPU memory. It also supports continuous batching (processing requests at different paces) and speculative decoding.
_extra.lens_pm: vLLM can cut your inference costs by 3-4x by letting you pack more requests per GPU.
_extra.lens_eng: vLLM abstracts away low-level CUDA — use its Python API or OpenAI-compatible REST endpoint.

title: VLM
definition: Neural network that understands both images and text—can caption photos, answer questions about images, or generate images from descriptions.
examples: GPT-4V takes an image and asks "what is in this photo?" and responds "a beach sunset with people swimming"; CLIP retrieves images matching text queries.
A person who can read, write, and understand pictures—richer than someone who only reads or only looks.

_extra.analogy: A person who can read, write, and understand pictures—richer than someone who only reads or only looks.
_extra.deeper: Vision encoder (ResNet, ViT) extracts image embeddings; text encoder converts words to embeddings; both sit in same space for alignment. Training requires image-text pairs (billions from web-scraped captions). More powerful than separate vision and text models but more compute-intensive.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables richer user experiences: visual search, image Q&A, content understanding for moderation.
_extra.lens_eng: Two-tower architecture: image tower outputs embeddings, text tower outputs embeddings; contrastive loss aligns them; downstream tasks use aligned space.

title: Vocabulary
definition: The fixed set of tokens a model knows — every piece it can read or write has to come from this list.
examples: A common English word is one token in the vocab; a rare name gets spelled out from several.
The full set of LEGO brick shapes in the box; anything you build uses only those.

_extra.analogy: The full set of LEGO brick shapes in the box; anything you build uses only those.
_extra.deeper: A tokenizer’s vocabulary is usually tens of thousands of fragments, chosen so frequent text compresses into few tokens. Anything outside it is built up from smaller pieces, which is why unusual words, emoji, or other languages can be surprisingly token-expensive — they don’t have their own dedicated entries.
_extra.lens_pm: Explains why some inputs cost more tokens than their length suggests.
_extra.lens_eng: The finite token set from the tokenizer; out-of-vocab text is composed from sub-word units.

title: Vocabulary size
definition: How many distinct tokens the model knows — a trade-off between shorter sequences and a bigger, heavier vocabulary.
examples: Bumping the vocabulary from 32k to 128k tokens lets the model encode the same text in fewer tokens, especially in other languages.
The number of keys on a keyboard: more keys means fewer keystrokes per word, but a bulkier keyboard.

_extra.analogy: The number of keys on a keyboard: more keys means fewer keystrokes per word, but a bulkier keyboard.
_extra.deeper: A larger vocabulary encodes text in fewer tokens — cheaper and faster context-wise — but inflates the embedding and output layers, adding parameters and memory. Too small and everything fragments into many tokens; too large and rare tokens are undertrained and the model gets heavier. Modern models trend toward larger vocabularies partly to serve many languages more fairly.
_extra.lens_pm: A dial affecting speed, cost, and how well non-English text is handled.
_extra.lens_eng: The token count in the vocabulary; larger shortens sequences but enlarges embedding/output layers.

title: Vocoder
definition: A model that converts a spectrogram or other audio representation into a waveform - turning abstract audio features into actual sound.
examples: Text-to-speech pipeline: text -> phonemes -> mel-spectrogram (Tacotron) -> waveform (vocoder like WaveGlow or HiFi-GAN).
A printer for sound: you describe the pattern (spectrogram), and the printer produces the actual sound waves.

_extra.analogy: A printer for sound: you describe the pattern (spectrogram), and the printer produces the actual sound waves.
_extra.deeper: Spectrograms compress audio (lose phase, time resolution), but humans need waveforms to hear. Vocoders reconstruct waveforms from spectrograms. Early: Griffin-Lim (heuristic, low quality). Modern: WaveNet (autoregressive, high quality, slow), WaveGlow (flow-based, fast), HiFi-GAN (GAN-based, fastest and best quality). Challenges: phase reconstruction, generalization to unseen speakers, real-time synthesis.
_extra.lens_pm: Critical for TTS quality; faster vocoders enable real-time speech synthesis on mobile.
_extra.lens_eng: Input: mel-spectrogram. Output: 16 or 24 kHz waveform. Models: HiFi-GAN, WaveGlow, Glow-TTS. Metric: MOS (Mean Opinion Score).

title: Voice Cloning
definition: Creating a synthetic voice that sounds like a specific person from a few audio samples—read text in your voice.
examples: 30 seconds of your voice; AI generates "I will call you later" in your accent, tone, and speaking style.
Recording yourself saying different phonemes then auto-combining them to say anything.

_extra.analogy: Recording yourself saying different phonemes then auto-combining them to say anything.
_extra.deeper: Speaker encoder learns embeddings from reference audio (speaker verification). TTS conditioned on speaker embedding. Training requires 1-10 hours of target speaker data for good quality; few-shot with 10 seconds possible but lower quality. Can be misused for deepfakes; watermarking and detection critical.
_extra.lens_pm: Personalization and accessibility; also raises consent and fraud concerns.
_extra.lens_eng: Speaker encoder extracts speaker embedding from reference; TTS conditioned on embedding; attention learns target speaker prosody.

title: VQA
definition: Shorthand for visual question answering - the ability to answer questions posed in natural language about visual content.
examples: A VQA system shown a photo with people, trees, and a bench answers "Are there more people or trees?" or "What is the bench made of?"
Like the parlor game "I spy" - someone describes what they see, you guess what it is. VQA is the reverse: you see the image, you answer the description.

_extra.analogy: Like the parlor game "I spy" - someone describes what they see, you guess what it is. VQA is the reverse: you see the image, you answer the description.
_extra.deeper: VQA models encode images into visual feature maps, encode questions into embeddings, fuse them (often with attention), and decode an answer. Quality degrades when images are cluttered, questions are compositional (multi-step reasoning), or the model has never seen similar image-question pairs. Large vision-language models have reduced but not eliminated this.
_extra.lens_pm: Widely used in e-commerce (product questions), accessibility, and interactive AI interfaces.
_extra.lens_eng: Standard benchmark datasets: VQA v2, GQA. Metrics: accuracy (exact match), BLEU, CIDEr.

title: VRAM
definition: The memory on a GPU, where model weights, activations, and intermediate results live during computation.
examples: A 7B model in BF16 needs 14GB VRAM. Batch size 32 and intermediate computations might need another 20GB. Total: 34GB VRAM.
The scratch pad a calculator uses to store partial results.

_extra.analogy: The scratch pad a calculator uses to store partial results.
_extra.deeper: VRAM is the bottleneck for most large model serving. You can't fit the model if VRAM < model size + activation memory. This is why quantization and model parallelism exist. Estimating VRAM usage correctly is critical — underestimate and you get OOM errors; overestimate and you buy GPUs you don't need.
_extra.lens_pm: VRAM cost is your serving cost. Every bit of memory reduction matters.
_extra.lens_eng: Estimate: params × bytes per param + (batch × seq_len × hidden × factor) for activations. Test before deploying.

title: Warm start
definition: Beginning training from an existing model’s weights instead of from scratch.
examples: Rather than train a new model from zero, a team warm-starts from an open-weights checkpoint and fine-tunes on their data.
Like starting a novel from a detailed outline rather than a blank page.

_extra.analogy: Like starting a novel from a detailed outline rather than a blank page.
_extra.deeper: A warm start initializes from pretrained weights so the model already “knows” language and only needs to adapt, saving enormous compute and data versus a cold start. It underpins transfer learning and fine-tuning — but the starting model’s biases and limitations carry over, for better and worse.
_extra.lens_pm: Why almost nobody trains from scratch anymore — you stand on an existing model’s shoulders.
_extra.lens_eng: Initializing parameters from a pretrained checkpoint rather than random init to accelerate convergence.

title: Warmup
definition: Starting training with a small learning rate and ramping it up over the first steps.
examples: For the first 500 steps the learning rate climbs from near zero to its target, so early updates don’t blow up the model.
Like stretching before a sprint — ease in so you don’t pull something at full speed from a cold start.

_extra.analogy: Like stretching before a sprint — ease in so you don’t pull something at full speed from a cold start.
_extra.deeper: At the start of training the weights are fresh and gradients can be large and erratic, so jumping straight to a high learning rate risks divergence. Warmup ramps the rate up gradually, letting the optimizer’s statistics and the weights stabilize before full-speed learning. It’s especially important for large models and adaptive optimizers, and is usually the front half of a full schedule.
_extra.lens_pm: A small safeguard that prevents big training runs from destabilizing in their fragile first moments.
_extra.lens_eng: Gradual learning-rate ramp over initial steps to stabilize early training; typically precedes decay.

title: Watermarking
