definition: Embedding a hidden, detectable signal in AI output so it can later be identified as machine-made.
examples: A text generator subtly biases its word choices in a statistically detectable pattern, so a checking tool can later flag the passage as likely AI-written.
The faint watermark in a banknote — invisible in normal use, but proof of origin when you hold it to the light.

_extra.analogy: The faint watermark in a banknote — invisible in normal use, but proof of origin when you hold it to the light.
_extra.deeper: Watermarking aims at provenance: proving what a model produced, to fight deepfakes, misinformation, and undisclosed AI content. In text it nudges token probabilities in a secret pattern; in images it embeds signals in the pixels. The tension is robustness versus imperceptibility — a watermark strong enough to survive edits and paraphrasing tends to be easier to notice or strip. No scheme is yet both invisible and truly tamper-proof.
_extra.lens_pm: A provenance tool for a world drowning in synthetic media — promising, but not yet a guarantee you can lean on.
_extra.lens_eng: Embed a detectable statistical signal (token biasing in text, pixel signals in images); robustness to edits trades against imperceptibility.

title: Weak Supervision
definition: Label a mountain of data cheaply with rough rules instead of paying humans to do it all by hand.
examples: To flag toxic comments, you write a few keyword rules and treat their output as labels, then train on millions of examples.
Sorting mail by zip-code stamps instead of reading every envelope — fast, mostly right, occasionally wrong.

_extra.analogy: Sorting mail by zip-code stamps instead of reading every envelope — fast, mostly right, occasionally wrong.
_extra.deeper: Instead of one careful label per example, you combine many noisy signals — heuristics, keyword rules, existing models — and let their agreement stand in for truth. You get far more labeled data than humans could ever produce, at the cost of noise you have to model or tolerate. It shines when data is abundant but human labeling is the bottleneck.
_extra.lens_pm: A way to bootstrap a labeled dataset in days instead of months when perfect labels aren’t worth the wait.
_extra.lens_eng: Programmatic labeling from multiple noisy sources whose outputs are aggregated into training signals.

title: Weak-to-strong generalization
definition: Whether a weaker teacher can steer a much stronger student to be even better than the teacher itself.
examples: Researchers fine-tune a large model using labels from a smaller, weaker model and find it generalizes past the weak labels’ mistakes.
A grade-school coach who somehow trains an athlete that ends up outperforming anything the coach could ever do.

_extra.analogy: A grade-school coach who somehow trains an athlete that ends up outperforming anything the coach could ever do.
_extra.deeper: This is a proxy for the real future problem: humans will be the "weak" supervisors of superhuman models. Early results suggest strong models can partly recover their full capability from imperfect weak supervision, but not fully, and the gap is the research target. It is a concrete experimental handle on scalable oversight.
_extra.lens_pm: A hopeful sign that limited human feedback can still guide systems smarter than us — with caveats.
_extra.lens_eng: Use weak-labeler supervision on a stronger model and measure recovered performance; the elicited-vs-ceiling gap is the metric.

title: Weaviate
definition: Open-source vector database, self-hosted or managed cloud; for storing and retrieving embeddings and structured data.
examples: Deploy Weaviate in Kubernetes; store document embeddings and metadata; query with Hybrid search (semantic + keyword).
Vector DB you can self-host; more control, more ops work.

_extra.analogy: Vector DB you can self-host; more control, more ops work.
_extra.deeper: Weaviate supports hybrid search (combining vector and keyword matching), multimodal embeddings, and GraphQL queries. Open-source (BSL license); cloud version available.
_extra.lens_pm: Open-source means community momentum; monetization through managed cloud.
_extra.lens_eng: Self-hostable but cloud-managed version available. More flexible than Pinecone, more ops.

title: Web crawl
definition: Text scraped in bulk from across the public internet — the messy backbone of most pretraining data.
examples: A team starts from a raw web crawl of billions of pages, then filters it down to the fraction worth training on.
Emptying the whole internet into a bin and then sorting it — most of the volume, most of the mess.

_extra.analogy: Emptying the whole internet into a bin and then sorting it — most of the volume, most of the mess.
_extra.deeper: Web crawls provide the sheer scale that pretraining needs, but they are enormously noisy — spam, boilerplate, duplicates, machine text, and worse. Their usefulness depends almost entirely on aggressive cleaning and filtering afterward. Common Crawl is the best-known public source; labs also run private crawls. The web's biases and gaps flow straight into the model unless curation catches them.
_extra.lens_pm: Cheap scale, but its raw quality is low — the value is in what you do to it after.
_extra.lens_eng: Bulk-scraped public web text; high-volume, low-signal until filtered and deduplicated.

title: Weight Averaging
definition: Take the numerical average of a model’s weights across runs or checkpoints to get a steadier model.
examples: Instead of shipping the final training step, a team averages the last ten checkpoints and ships that smoother version.
Averaging several thermometer readings to smooth out the jitter in any single one.

_extra.analogy: Averaging several thermometer readings to smooth out the jitter in any single one.
_extra.deeper: Individual training snapshots bounce around the loss landscape; averaging their weights lands you in a flatter, more robust spot that tends to generalize better. It works across checkpoints of one run or across separate runs from the same base. The requirement is compatibility — you can’t meaningfully average models that started from different places.
_extra.lens_pm: A cheap post-processing trick that often buys a small, free accuracy bump before shipping.
_extra.lens_eng: Parameter-space averaging that lands in flatter minima with better generalization.

title: Weight decay
definition: Gently shrinking weights toward zero during training so the model stays simple and generalizes.
examples: Adding weight decay stops a model from letting a few weights grow huge to memorize training quirks.
Like a tidy-desk rule that quietly clears clutter each day, keeping only what earns its place.

_extra.analogy: Like a tidy-desk rule that quietly clears clutter each day, keeping only what earns its place.
_extra.deeper: Weight decay penalizes large weights, nudging all of them slightly toward zero each step, which discourages the model from fitting noise and improves generalization. It’s closely related to L2 regularization, though how it’s applied differs between plain Adam and AdamW. Set too high it underfits by over-simplifying; too low and it barely helps — it’s a standard, mild regularizer in almost every training recipe.
_extra.lens_pm: A quiet guard against overfitting that’s in nearly every training recipe.
_extra.lens_eng: Penalty shrinking weights toward zero (≈ L2); improves generalization, decoupled in AdamW.

title: Weights
definition: The individual learned numbers inside a model — “the weights” is shorthand for the whole trained brain you can download.
examples: “Open weights” means you can download the numbers and run the model yourself.
The recipe card after all the tweaking — hand someone the weights and they can cook the same dish.

_extra.analogy: The recipe card after all the tweaking — hand someone the weights and they can cook the same dish.
_extra.deeper: Technically weights are one type of parameter (the multipliers on connections), but in practice people say “the weights” to mean the entire trained model file. Whether a lab releases them is the whole open-vs-closed debate: released weights can be run, inspected, and fine-tuned by anyone; withheld ones can only be reached through an API.
_extra.lens_pm: Whether weights are public decides if you can self-host or are locked to a vendor’s API.
_extra.lens_eng: The serialized tensor values of a trained network; “open weights” = distributable checkpoint.

title: Weights and biases
definition: The two kinds of knobs a network learns: weights scale each input, biases nudge the result.
examples: Training a model means slowly turning billions of these weights and biases until the outputs stop being wrong.
A recipe where weights are how much of each ingredient and the bias is the pinch of salt added no matter what.

_extra.analogy: A recipe where weights are how much of each ingredient and the bias is the pinch of salt added no matter what.
_extra.deeper: Each neuron multiplies its inputs by weights, sums them, and adds a bias, then applies an activation. Weights decide what matters; the bias shifts the threshold for firing. Every “parameter” you hear about is one of these numbers, and learning is just adjusting them.
_extra.lens_pm: “Number of parameters” is essentially a count of these knobs — a rough proxy for a model’s raw capacity.
_extra.lens_eng: The learnable affine parameters W and b in y = Wx + b, updated by gradient descent.

title: Whisper
definition: OpenAI's open-source speech-to-text model, trained on 680k hours of multilingual audio data.
examples: Transcribe a podcast or meeting recording; handles accents, background noise, and multiple languages.
The boring superpower; speech recognition that just works, in many languages.

_extra.analogy: The boring superpower; speech recognition that just works, in many languages.
_extra.deeper: Whisper is a sequence-to-sequence transformer trained on diverse audio (including noise). Open-source (MIT license), so widely deployed. Not perfect but strong baseline.
_extra.lens_pm: Democratizes speech recognition; enables features without expensive licensing.
_extra.lens_eng: Inference is slow (real-time audio > real-time output) but accuracy is good. Open weights mean fast iteration.

title: Win Rate
definition: In pairwise comparisons, the percentage of times judges prefer one model over another—intuitive and human-aligned.
examples: LLM judges compare 100 outputs from Model A and Model B. Model A wins 65 comparisons. Win rate for Model A is 65%.
Like head-to-head match results in a tournament: Model A won 70% of matches against Model B.

_extra.analogy: Like head-to-head match results in a tournament: Model A won 70% of matches against Model B.
_extra.deeper: Win rate is more interpretable than absolute scores—'70% better' is clearer than 'score of 7.3 vs 6.1.' It's also more robust to score calibration issues. Downside: pairwise comparison is expensive and requires a good judge. Transitive comparisons can give surprising results (Model A > B, B > C, but C > A is possible).
_extra.lens_pm: Win rate is the most interpretable metric for comparing models to stakeholders.
_extra.lens_eng: Implement pairwise evaluation; use multiple judges to reduce noise.

title: Word embedding
definition: A word turned into a list of numbers so that similar words land near each other in space.
examples: A classic model places “king” and “queen” close together, and the gap from “man” to “woman” mirrors the gap from “king” to “queen.”
Like giving every word a home address in a city where synonyms are neighbors and opposites live across town.

_extra.analogy: Like giving every word a home address in a city where synonyms are neighbors and opposites live across town.
_extra.deeper: Early methods like word2vec and GloVe gave each word one fixed vector learned from co-occurrence. That was a breakthrough, but the flaw is context-blindness: “bank” gets a single vector whether it’s a river or a vault. Transformers replaced them with context-dependent representations, which is why static word embeddings are fading.
_extra.lens_pm: Foundational history — mostly superseded by contextual models, but the intuition still explains embeddings.
_extra.lens_eng: Static, context-independent vectors per token learned from co-occurrence statistics; a precursor to contextual representations.

title: Worker Agent
definition: A focused agent that does one assigned piece of a larger job and reports back.
examples: A worker agent is told only “summarize these five sources,” with no view of the wider project, and returns a tidy summary.
A specialist contractor called in for the wiring — does that one part well, then hands it back to the general contractor.

_extra.analogy: A specialist contractor called in for the wiring — does that one part well, then hands it back to the general contractor.
_extra.deeper: Worker agents get a narrow task, a tight prompt, and often no memory of the broader goal — which is a feature, since a smaller scope means fewer ways to wander. Several can run in parallel. Their limitation is exactly their strength: with no big picture, they can optimize their slice in a way that doesn’t serve the whole, so the supervisor’s framing of each task carries a lot of weight.
_extra.lens_pm: The unglamorous engine of multi-agent work — narrow scope is what keeps them reliable.
_extra.lens_eng: A scoped agent instance executing a delegated subtask with limited context, returning results to its supervisor.

title: Workflow Engine
definition: A system that runs a defined sequence of steps reliably, handling ordering, retries, and failures.
examples: A workflow engine runs “extract → validate → summarize → email” for every uploaded document, retrying any step that fails.
An assembly line — each station does its part in order, and if one jams, the line knows how to respond.

_extra.analogy: An assembly line — each station does its part in order, and if one jams, the line knows how to respond.
_extra.deeper: Workflow engines predate LLMs — they’re the durable backbone for multi-step processes, guaranteeing steps run in order, survive crashes, and resume where they left off. For AI systems they’re increasingly paired with agents: the engine handles the reliable plumbing while the model handles the judgment. The tradeoff is rigidity — engines love predictable flows and chafe against the open-ended improvisation agents are good at.
_extra.lens_pm: Use an engine when a process must run reliably every time; use an agent when it needs to improvise.
_extra.lens_eng: A durable executor that sequences steps with ordering, retry, and crash-recovery guarantees.

title: Working Memory
definition: The small, fast scratch space an agent uses to hold what it’s thinking about right now.
examples: While booking a trip, the agent keeps the current dates, budget, and shortlisted flights in working memory, not in long-term storage.
The sticky notes on your desk during a task — grabbed, glanced at, and tossed when you’re done.

_extra.analogy: The sticky notes on your desk during a task — grabbed, glanced at, and tossed when you’re done.
_extra.deeper: For an LLM agent, working memory usually is the context window — the live set of tokens it’s reasoning over. It’s fast but tiny and volatile: once it fills or the task ends, that content is gone unless it’s written somewhere durable. The whole discipline of context management exists because working memory is scarce and precious.
_extra.lens_pm: Working memory is limited, so what an agent can juggle at once is a real constraint on task complexity.
_extra.lens_eng: The active context the model reasons over each step — fast, capacity-bounded, and non-persistent.

title: World model
definition: An internal picture of how things work that lets a system predict what happens next.
examples: A model that tracks who’s holding what across a story — and correctly says the key is now in Sara’s pocket — is showing a small world model.
Like the mental map you use to guess a rolling ball will fall off the table before it does.

_extra.analogy: Like the mental map you use to guess a rolling ball will fall off the table before it does.
_extra.deeper: Whether LLMs truly have world models is debated: they clearly build useful internal representations of state and relationships, yet they also make errors no consistent model would. The term matters because robust planning and reasoning arguably require modeling the world, not just predicting surface text.
_extra.lens_pm: Shorthand for “does it actually understand the situation, or just sound like it?” — the crux of reliability.
_extra.lens_eng: An internal representation of environment state and dynamics supporting prediction; contested in LLMs.

title: xAI
definition: Elon Musk's AI company, founded 2023, aiming to build advanced AI systems with a focus on truth-seeking.
examples: Grok (xAI's LLM) released in beta late 2023, integrated with X (Twitter) for real-time information.
The ambitious newcomer: well-funded, claim-driven, building fast.

_extra.analogy: The ambitious newcomer: well-funded, claim-driven, building fast.
_extra.deeper: xAI has access to X/Twitter data and Elon's resources. Grok is positioned as edgy and less constrained than competitors. Still early-stage but building industry connections and compute.
_extra.lens_pm: Real-time data via X is a genuine moat; question is whether to monetize directly or via advertising.
_extra.lens_eng: Grok's training on X conversations is novel; unclear how it affects quality vs. benchmark models.

title: Zero-shot
definition: Asking a model to do a task with no examples at all — just the instruction.
examples: “Classify this review as positive or negative: …” with no sample classifications — the model just does it.
Like handing a capable new hire a task described in one sentence and trusting them to figure it out.

_extra.analogy: Like handing a capable new hire a task described in one sentence and trusting them to figure it out.
_extra.deeper: Zero-shot leans entirely on what the model absorbed in pretraining plus your instruction. It’s the cleanest, cheapest way to prompt and often works surprisingly well on common tasks, but for anything unusual or format-sensitive, adding a few examples usually beats it.
_extra.lens_pm: Try zero-shot first — if it works, you’ve saved tokens and effort; if not, add examples.
_extra.lens_eng: Task performed from instructions alone with no in-prompt demonstrations, relying on pretrained priors.

title: Zero-Shot Classification
definition: Classifying images into categories the model has never seen during training - by reasoning about semantic relationships.
examples: CLIP is trained on image-caption pairs. You ask it to classify a photo as one of ["cat", "dog", "elephant"] without ever seeing those three labels in training. It maps the image to embeddings and compares to the class name embeddings.
You know what a "dog" is and what "four-legged" means. Someone shows you a "dachshund" - youve never seen that breed, but you know its a four-legged dog.

_extra.analogy: You know what a "dog" is and what "four-legged" means. Someone shows you a "dachshund" - youve never seen that breed, but you know its a four-legged dog.
_extra.deeper: Bridges the train-test gap by using semantic attributes or language. CLIP and similar models encode images and text into a shared embedding space; classification is a nearest-neighbor lookup. Works for unseen classes by leveraging language understanding. Limited by coverage of the text space and spurious correlations in the joint embedding.
_extra.lens_pm: Enables systems to classify novel categories without retraining - huge for scalability and rapid iteration.
_extra.lens_eng: Models: CLIP, Flamingo. Metrics: accuracy on held-out classes. Datasets test on unseen classes: ImageNet-21K variants.

title: Zero-shot prompting
definition: Giving a model a task with only instructions, no examples, and expecting it to figure it out on the first try.
examples: You ask a language model "Translate this to French:" and paste text, without showing it any translation examples first.
Asking a smart stranger for directions to a place they've never been: they reason it out from first principles.

_extra.analogy: Asking a smart stranger for directions to a place they've never been: they reason it out from first principles.
_extra.deeper: Zero-shot works because modern LLMs are instruction-tuned — they learn to follow a wide variety of commands during training. It's not magic: the model has seen countless examples of translations in its pretraining data and learned the pattern. Failure happens when the task is truly novel or requires specialized knowledge.
_extra.lens_pm: The easiest path to new use cases: no labeling, no examples to curate. Works for tasks similar to the model's training distribution.
_extra.lens_eng: No prompt engineering needed, just clear instructions. Baseline performance is often decent; few-shot or fine-tuning helps only if performance gaps are large.
